text:
The morning after Tuesday's midterms was gloomy and rainy in Minneapolis, but people still gathered at the place where Border Patrol agents shot and killed Alex Pretti, a VA nurse and U.S. citizen, last January. All week, community members have come here to place their "I Voted" stickers at the memorial.

Nicki Adams, who dated Pretti and was his close friend for nearly 17 years, watched quietly as a woman added her sticker to a street lamp completely covered in the red decals.

"I wanted to see all the stickers. I just wanted to be here," she says. "It just means a lot to me. I think it would mean a lot to Alex, too."

A few blocks away, people left their stickers where an ICE officer killed Renee Good, a mom of three and a U.S. citizen, just a few weeks before Pretti's death. In Houston, they left them where an ICE officer killed Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a father of three and a Mexican immigrant, in July.

Adams says these stickers, and the election results this week, send a clear message to Congress: "You work for us, and please carry on these values that we care about … We want to be seen and heard and taken care of and have our neighbors taken care of."

The deaths of Pretti and Good during the ICE surge in Minneapolis marked a pivotal moment for the country, sparking intense public backlash to President Trump's aggressive deportation efforts. But federal law enforcement officials have given little indication they're progressing in investigating their deaths, or the deaths of at least seven other people killed by federal immigration agents since Trump took office again last year. DHS did not respond to an NPR request for the status of those investigations.

Now, after Democrats' sweeping wins this week, their deaths at the hands of immigration agents will likely be the targets of renewed investigations. With a majority in Congress, Democrats can issue subpoenas to the major players in Trump's mass deportation plan, compelling them to testify under oath before the legislature.

That could include White House Border Czar Tom Homan, former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, former Border Patrol Commander Gregory Bovino, and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, among others.

Congress can also demand internal documents like use-of-force reports.

"They can dissect these individual shootings, and really unravel the story of what happened," says Naureen Shah, who leads the ACLU's immigration policy work.

Democrats have already held shadow hearings on the ICE shootings, during which they've called in family members and witnesses to testify.

But Shah says now Congress can ask key questions of top decision makers: What orders were given to immigration officers in the field? What was training like for these officers?

Who made the decision to paint Good and Pretti as threats, including calling Pretti a "would-be assassin" and a domestic terrorist, when video showed otherwise?

"It's like we can turn the faucet on and actually find out so much more," Shah says. "There's an aspect of this that is really about a kind of reckoning with how it's possible that things that seemed unthinkable could happen on American streets. How do you have that reckoning if you don't actually have the ability to force people to explain themselves?"

Democratic leaders have already said that's the plan.

Maryland Democratic Rep. Jamie Raskin, who is expected to lead the House Judiciary Committee, told NPR in a statement that Congress will use "every tool" at its disposal to investigate ICE and that it is time for the agency to "start answering to the American people."

California Democratic Rep. Robert Garcia, expected to lead the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, vowed to take on DHS and ICE abuses in a two-word statement: "Lawyer Up."

Mississippi Democratic Rep. Bennie Thompson, expected to lead the House Committee on Homeland Security, sent a letter on Wednesday to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, demanding the agency "comply with all document preservation requirements."

Illinois Democratic Rep. Delia Ramirez wrote on social media that Noem, Miller, Homan, Bovino and Mullin should "clear" their schedules.

In response to that, DHS general counsel James Percival said Democrats are "more interested in political shenanigans than in governing" but said the agency is prepared to "deal with this nonsense."

There are key limitations to what Democrats in Congress can do with their majority when it comes to ICE accountability, says Rachel Moran, a professor at the University of St. Thomas School of Law.

Major changes, like clawing back funding for the agency, would require a veto-proof majority, something the Democrats don't have.

"You still have a president who has shown a complete lack of interest in accountability for federal agents and in fact, a great deal of knee jerk defensiveness about their conduct," Moran says.

In a statement, a White House spokesperson told NPR "if Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people."

Democrats, the statement added, "should be reminded that we still control the federal government and all of its powers."

But that's not true. Congress has its own powers, one of them being the ability to compel testimony. Moran says a deeper probe into the shootings could still serve important purposes, like making evidence available for states to use in their own criminal investigations.

Minnesota officials, for instance, have been fighting with the federal government to get evidence related to the Pretti and Good killings.

Brent Ganger, Renee Good's brother, says learning more information about his sister's death will be hard to hear, "but I think it's also super important for us to understand what happened that day. I don't want history to keep repeating itself."

It was painful, he says, to watch immigration agents kill more people after his sister. He thought her death would be a turning point. In a way, it might have been the start of one. After the surge in Minneapolis, most Americans said ICE had gone too far.

Ganger, who considers himself a moderate, was happy to see the Blue Wave this week. On election night, he was scrolling Instagram when he saw a photo of his sister's memorial site, with all the "I Voted" stickers.

"I was very grateful to see the repudiation of this administration from the country. It felt very supportive of my entire family," he says.

The next morning, in his home in Colorado, he got up and made biscuits and gravy, his sister's favorite breakfast.

A 21-year-old Wisconsin state trooper was detained by ICE after federal agents detained him at a Madison airport Thursday.

In an update Friday night, Carel Van Der Merwe's lawyer said he was released on supervision after Rep. Derrick Van Orden reportedly "got involved and requested his release."

Trooper's asylum case and career

Van Der Merwe was going to board a flight to visit his parents in New Mexico. He has served in the Wisconsin State Patrol since July 2025, WisDOT said Friday. He has no criminal record.

Timeline:

FOX 9 found video of Van Der Merwe graduating from the academy in 2025. In the video his father pins his uniform.

"Carel very much loves the United States, and he is very much into service," his attorney, Marc Christopher, said.

Christopher said Van Der Merwe fled South Africa with his parents at 14. After first settling in Florida, the family applied for asylum in 2019 and is still waiting for their asylum interview while the case moves through the courts.

Local perspective:

Immigration attorneys have said asylum cases can sometimes take upward of 10 years to complete, and because of that, asylum seekers often get work authorization while they wait.

"Because it takes so long, individuals are allowed to obtain work authorizations. So Carel's parents got work authorizations and then when he wanted to work, he obtained a work authorization," said Christopher.

Christopher said the family followed the legal process. He also said they fear going back to South Africa. "They have indicated that they fear they're going to be jailed or tortured should they be returned back to their home country," said Christopher.

Detention fight now underway

On Thursday, as Van Der Merwe tried to board a flight to visit his parents, ICE agents stopped him and arrested him, according to Christopher. He was being held at the Dodge County Detention Facility waiting a hearing date, when he was released on supervision after Rep. Derrick Van Orden requested it.

What they're saying:

Christopher said Van Der Merwe told agents he was a state trooper and had gone through training and a background process.

"He told him he was an active-duty officer. He told them he's gone through training, that he's going through background. And ICE's response was, 'we don't care,'" said Christopher.

DHS said in a statement, "In defiance of our nation's laws, he overstayed his admission. This illegal alien will receive due process and remain in ICE custody pending removal proceedings. To be clear: work authorization does not confer legal status in the United States."

What's next:

Christopher said he does not see Van Der Merwe as someone who would run or put anyone at risk.

"I don't know how anybody could reasonably look at this case and, in any way, find that this young man is a flight risk or a danger to community," said Christopher. "In fact, he's the exact opposite. He's someone who's sworn to uphold and protect our laws and to protect our citizens."

Immigration attorneys have said that asylum seekers with pending applications and no criminal record can no longer count on the longstanding practice of staying out of custody. DHS also said the Trump administration is working to stop people without green cards from getting on any flight unless they are to self-deport.

Christopher said it could take one to three weeks for Van Der Merwe to get a bond hearing.

text:
Donald Trump just gave the middle finger to millions of American voters.

Any other president who suffered the kind of drubbing at the polls that Trump did this week might have felt at least a sliver of humility – and perhaps even an obligation to work with the new opposition in Congress.

But not for the first time in his political career, Trump veered in the opposite direction. On Friday he made Stephen Miller, condemned by Democrats and civil rights groups as a white nationalist, one of the most powerful unelected officials in Washington by naming him White House chief of staff.

Miller is the architect of Trump’s far-right, nativist immigration agenda. He is, therefore, arguably the architect of the blue wave that engulfed Republicans in Tuesday’s midterm elections as voters – including many Latinos – expressed their disgust. Yet instead of firing Miller, Trump promoted him.

It was a declaration of war. Miller, 41, is a longtime proponent of the presidential authority that Trump has spent the past two years expanding at the expense of Congress. In 2017 he declared: “The powers of the president to protect our country are very substantial and will not be questioned.”

Now Republicans’ catastrophic defeat is likely to leave Trump more reliant on unilateral executive action than ever to advance his domestic agenda.

“In a lot of ways Stephen Miller has been the id to Trump’s authoritarian impulses and machinations,” Kurt Bardella, an adviser to Democrats in Texas, said. “I have to imagine that anointing this person chief of staff – the most powerful non-elected position in all of government – is a signal that they intend to double down on that authoritarianism.

“You’re going to see a lot of executive orders, unilateral action and stress testing of the checks and balances system continue for the final two years of his presidency.”

Trump’s second term has presented a concerted effort to dismantle those checks and balances that have traditionally constrained the occupant of the White House. He has signed 292 executive orders in less than two years, more than in his entire first term and a record pace for a modern presidency.

He has bypassed Congress on military action and tariffs, withheld congressionally approved spending, deployed the National Guard against the will of state authorities, politicised the justice department, punished critics and challenged judicial independence. Congress, dominated by Republicans reluctant to confront him, offered little resistance.

But this week’s landslide, the biggest in a midterm election since Watergate, puts Democrats back in charge of the House of Representatives and Senate. That the elections were free and fair, and that Trump did not dispute the result, was itself a victory for democracy.

Democrats will now seek to rein in the president and block his legislative agenda, bringing them into direct conflict with Miller, who was already a hugely powerful deputy chief of staff at the White House and now takes over from Susie Wiles.

Miller has been a champion of the Iran war and prominent voice on many of the president’s other priorities, including countering diversity initiatives and targeting transgender rights. He is reportedly one of a small group of White House staffers who approve all executive orders.

He is best known for driving the ‌immigration crackdown in Trump’s second term, setting ‌a target of 3,000 arrests per day – far above levels under previous administrations. He has pushed Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to target anybody in ‌the country illegally, not just those with criminal records.

There are limits on what Democrats can do to stop the immigration drive since the One Big Beautiful Bill Act included major increases for Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) that will keep it funded for the rest of Trump’s term.

Even so, they will now chair House committees with the ability to launch investigations, issue subpoenas and hold high profile hearings. Along with ICE, they might scrutinise Jeffrey Epstein files and the department of government efficiency (Doge). They have also vowed to look at how Trump and his family have become wealthier since he returned to office.

The appointment of the pugnacious Miller as Trump’s consigliere suggests that the White House is moving to a war footing. He is likely to marshal a team of lawyers and attack Democrats by accusing them of weaponising the deep state against the president. As a frequent guest on the conservative Fox News network, he will also wage war in the court of public opinion.

“Trump’s decision to elevate Stephen Miller means that he’s spoiling for a fight with Democrats and they’re going to just rely on executive action to try and push their agenda through,” said David Cohen, a political science professor at the University of Akron in Ohio, who studies the American presidency and White House staffing.

Cohen added: “It’s a White House that doesn’t seek out cooperation with Congress. It’s their way or the highway, essentially, and it’s possible Stephen Miller is relishing this because he’s a believer in the unitary presidency and executive presidential action and he views this as a way where he can expand the powers of the presidency.”

Trump is not the first president to seek to consolidate authority. Arthur Schlesinger Jr’s 1973 book The Imperial Presidency warned that an accumulation of presidential power threatened the constitutional separation of powers.

In 1989 the American Enterprise Institute thinktank published The Fettered Presidency, a counterpoint arguing that legal and congressional constraints had unduly weakened the executive. It helped inspire a modern conservative drive to expand presidential authority, which accelerated under George W Bush and was subsequently exploited by Barack Obama as congressional gridlock made legislating increasingly difficult.

The combination of Trump and Miller, however, takes the concept of an American Caesar to a new extreme – and flies in the face of the verdict delivered by the electorate on Tuesday.

“It’s a step that I find hard to fathom except as the president giving the middle finger to the American public,” said Bill Galston, a senior fellow in governance studies at the Brookings Institution thinktank in Washington.

“In the same way that he ransacked the state of Texas for the very worst senatorial nominee imaginable, now he’s done the same thing with the chief of staff position. This is simply outrageous.”

The mayor of Houston, the most populous city in the US state of Texas, has ordered the city’s police force to sharply limit its cooperation with the United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

John Whitmire’s executive order came on Friday, days after Democrats swept statewide offices in the traditionally Republican state.

According to the order, Houston police will contact ICE only when a person is being arrested for a jailable offence, according to the Reuters news agency.

Whitmire said he had consulted Texas’s newly elected governor, lieutenant governor and comptroller before acting, and that the move was meant to reduce fear and anxiety across the city.

“Elections matter,” Whitmire told reporters. “I do this to begin a healing process,” he said, adding he hoped his executive order would become a model for other Texas cities.

Joining Whitmire at the news conference, Houston Police ⁠Chief J Noe Diaz said he supported the change and that his department had already begun to implement the new policy.

Under the new rules, people stopped for minor traffic violations will no longer be referred to ICE simply because they have an administrative immigration warrant.

The decision reverses a policy Whitmire put in place in April under pressure from outgoing Republican Governor Greg Abbott.

Abbott had threatened to withdraw about $110m in state public safety grants, arguing that a city council ordinance limiting police contact with ICE breached Senate Bill 4, a 2017 state law that bars local police from restricting cooperation with federal immigration authorities.

Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton also sued the mayor, the city council and the police chief over the ordinance.

“We’re taking an interpretation of the law today, working with the newly elected members of the state leadership, in implementing this policy,” Whitmire told reporters. “We don’t want people to worry about ⁠their workers, their family members, their students.”

The issue has drawn intense scrutiny in Houston. The Houston Chronicle found that city police contacted ICE at least 107 times in the first eight months of 2025, compared with nine times in the whole of 2024.

In July, an ICE agent shot dead Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a longtime Houston resident.

FIEL Houston, an immigrant rights group, called the order a victory for the city but said it was long overdue. “Today Houston won. Today our community can breathe easier,” FIEL Executive Director Cesar Espinosa said in a statement to KPRC.

Whitmire said he expected Houston’s approach to become a model for other cities. In Austin, Mayor Kirk Watson asked city officials on Friday to revise their own policy on ICE warrants.

text:
The mayor of Houston, Texas, has directed the city's police to limit co-operation with federal immigration officials.

The move by John Whitmire, a Democrat, comes on the heels of stunning victories by the party in Texas during this week's midterm elections. It breaks with policy set by Republican Governor Greg Abbott, who lost his re-election bid.

"I do this to begin a healing process," Whitmire said on Friday, and to "reduce fear and anxiety across our community". He added: "I also do this knowing that elections matter."

There has been months of public outcry in Houston after an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer fatally shot a man who was driving to work.

Houston police chief Noe Diaz said on Friday that officers will now only contact ICE if someone they arrest for a jailable offence also has an administrative ICE warrant, which are issued internally by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), within which ICE operates.

"For example, if our police officers pull someone over for a minor traffic infraction and they write a citation, that person receives a citation and goes about their day," Diaz said.

Under the previous rules, Houston police officers were required to inform ICE if anyone they were dealing with came up as having one of these warrants attached to their name when they were searched on the National Crime Information Center (NCIC) - a digital database that includes records on wanted persons, stolen property, certain missing people and those arrested and fingerprinted for serious offences.

Whitmire said on Friday that he had directed the Houston Police Department to make the changes through an executive order.

He also called on Congress to change federal immigration rules, saying "ICE needs better training. They need body cameras. They need to be trained in de-escalation."

He added, "But this can only be done in Washington. I can only control what I can control."

In response, a spokesperson for the DHS told Houston's NBC affiliate, KPRC 2, in a statement: "We remain disappointed that sanctuary politicians seek to limit cooperation with ICE, as our law enforcement are simply fulfilling their sworn duties to serve and protect our communities."

"Partnerships with law enforcement are critical to having the resources we need to arrest criminal illegal aliens across the country," the spokesperson added.

Another Texas city, Austin, has also begun implementing a similar policy change.

Democrats won both the US Senate and House of Representatives in Tuesday's midterms, taking control of Congress for the rest of Donald Trump's presidency.

Texas, a long-time Republican stronghold, was the site of one of the most stunning upsets in the vote, with the state electing its first Latina governor, Gina Hinojosa, as the first Democrat governor since 1995. It also elected its first Democratic senator since 1988.

text:
A Wisconsin state trooper originally from South Africa is set to be released from custody after he was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials Thursday at an airport while trying to visit his parents.

Carel Aaron Van Der Merwe entered the country in 2019 at 14 years old and attended high school in New Mexico, according to his attorney.

According to Attorney Mark Christopher, Van Der Merwe's parents applied for asylum, and he was granted work authorization because the process can take years. Van Der Merwe attended the New Mexico Military Institute for college and wanted to serve in the U.S. military, but was not permitted because of his immigration status.

Van Der Merwe started working as a Wisconsin state trooper in July 2025. He is authorized to work in the country, according to Christopher.

The Department of Homeland Security said in a statement that Van Der Merwe had legal permission to stay in the country until September 2019 but "in defiance of our nation's laws ... overstayed his admission."

WKBT in La Crosse, Wisconsin, said Friday afternoon that Van Der Merwe had a conversation with Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and will be released.

"It's one of the more egregious and ridiculous cases I've ever come across," said Christopher. "I can't think of any public utility or benefit of detaining him."

text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — After Democrats' overwhelming midterm victories this week, winning candidates spoke of the need, once they are sworn in, to rein in President Donald Trump's mass deportation machine. Some suggested putting forward a new vision for immigration reform while both houses of Congress are in Democratic control.

The lofty goals come after two years in which Democrats, while in the minority, were limited in how much they could counter Trump's supercharged and, at times, chaotic immigration enforcement. But there are clear limits to what they can achieve even after Democrats' epic win, with Trump — who rode into power in part on a promise to curb immigration — in office for another two years and wielding his veto power.

What's more, Republicans have frontloaded billions of dollars for immigration enforcement. And the key architect of the president's hard-line immigration agenda, Stephen Miller, was elevated Friday to become Trump's chief of staff — suggesting immigration enforcement may not slow down any time soon.

Here's a look at what might come next for immigration after Election Day:

Investigating alleged corruption and ICE policies

Democrats appear ready to use the power of congressional oversight to investigate Immigration and Customs Enforcement and the Department of Homeland Security. That strategy will likely resonate with voters angry aboutt how enforcement operations were carried out in places like Minneapolis or ICE arrests of longtime immigrants integrated into American society.

The administration ramped up immigration enforcement during the first two years of Trump's second term, launching major operations in multiple cities and sending arrests soaring. DHS also came under criticism for alleged corruption and misuse of funds it was granted to carry out Trump's immigration agenda.

Nationally, about 6 in 10 voters said the Trump administration's actions on immigration enforcement had "gone too far," according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of more than 100,000 midterm voters. A similar share disapproved of how ICE was doing its job. And about 6 in 10 voters said immigrants to the U.S. today do more to "help the country," while less than half, about 4 in 10, said they do more to "hurt the country."

Rep. Robert Garcia, a Los Angeles-area Democrat who will take over the House Oversight Committee and is a prominent critic of Trump's immigration agenda, warned the administration to "lawyer up," adding that investigating alleged abuses at DHS was one of his priorities.

The next Congress will "address the Trump administration's assault on the rule of law and hold those responsible accountable," said Mississippi Rep. Bennie Thompson, the ranking Democrat on the House Homeland Security committee.

Those investigations could delve into issues like DHS purchases of massive warehouses to hold arrested immigrants; whether ICE cut corners when hiring thousands of new deportation officers; or deaths in ICE detention facilities.

Garcia and Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut held shadow hearings featuring family members of people killed during immigration enforcement operations, a whistleblower exposing problems with ICE training, and American citizens caught up in immigration enforcement operations.

No Republicans attended and Democrats couldn't subpoena witnesses. Now they can, opening up a new level of scrutiny of the administration's actions.

Calls to put forward a Democratic vision for immigration

The last time Congress even came close to passing comprehensive immigration reform was in 2013. That proposal cleared the Senate but died in the House.

Border crossings that surged under the Biden administration further served to dampen any Democratic enthusiasm to talk about legalization for any immigrants.

Sarah Pierce, director of social policy for Third Way, a Washington, D.C., think tank, said Democrats need to show voters their own vision for immigration and border security and not just focus on oversight hearings of what happened during the last two years.

"They should lean into oversight, but I think that they also need to couple that with a proactive vision for what immigration should look like in the United States," said Pierce.

At least one of the party's new senators is ready for the discussion. During an interview with Fox News after the election, Sen.-elect James Talarico of Texas discussed the need to pass comprehensive immigration reform, including a pathway to citizenship for immigrants living and working illegally in the country for years.

In the House, Rep. Gabe Vasquez of New Mexico pointed to the Democratic gains made with Latino voters and the higher numbers of Latino lawmakers who will take office next year as reasons for Democrats to not shy away from talking about immigration issues.

He said Democrats should find ways to address immigration through a lens of affordability, a central issue for voters. For example, they could tackle staffing shortages by creating a new visa class for workers who provide care for children or the elderly.

"This cannot be a third-rail issue for Democrats," said Vasquez. "We can actually reform our immigration system to bring costs down for all Americans and at the same time give people who are either here undocumented or want to come to this country an opportunity to have legal status."

Democrats' power to curb Trump's immigration agenda is limited

Trump, shortly after the election, said he was prepared to work with Democrats on certain issues, highlighting immigration as one of them. But that collaborative tone may not bear out in practice.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin vowed on social media, "Deportations will continue." A few days later, Trump promoted Miller to become his chief of staff.

Immigration and Latino activists lambasted Miller's promotion, calling it an act of defiance after voters spoke clearly at the polls and a sign the president would continue his immigration policies. California's Democratic Sen. Alex Padilla, who's been a key critic of Trump's immigration agenda, said Trump was choosing to double down by picking Miller and vowed, "So will we."

It's unclear if Democrats and the White House will find a middle ground to successfully pass immigration legislation. With Trump in office for another two years, he can veto any Democratic legislation, and Republicans have the money and the personnel to pursue Trump's immigration agenda regardless of Tuesday's results.

Republicans during the summer of 2025 supercharged immigration enforcement with $150 billion intended to expand immigration detention capacity, finish the border wall and hire thousands more deportation officers. Earlier this year they frontloaded routine funding for ICE and Border Patrol for the next three years.

"My fear is that enforcement will get worse. And the country will also see that Congress does not have many tools to stop the executive branch because the executive branch power on immigration has grown so vast," said Andrea Flores, who was a policy adviser in the Obama and Biden administrations.

Conservatives want action from lame duck Congress

Many administration supporters want this current Congress — in the little time it has left — to pass laws solidifying the gains the Trump administration says it has made on border security and immigration. Without codifying changes to asylum law or tightening requirements on employers to verify workers' immigration status, they warn, a different administration could quickly reverse the new immigration landscape Trump has shaped.

NumbersUSA, an advocacy group that seeks to restrict immigration, has a timer on its website counting down the days until this Congress is over with a warning to "make border security permanent."

"If this Congress in the lame duck does not secure the border with lasting legislation," said the organization's co-president, Jeremy Beck, "then this Congress will have failed to meet the moment."

___

Associated Press reporter Linley Sanders contributed to this report.

In at least eight of the cases, medical staff failed to perform CPR correctly, or at all. In only three of the cases, investigators determined that the deficient medical care did not directly contribute to the person’s death.

The agency continues to insist that there has been no spike in detainee deaths, though 2025 saw the most immigrant detainee deaths since 2003. So far in 2026, 31 immigrants have died in ICE detention.

During President Donald Trump’s second term, ICE has subjected tens of thousands of people—including U.S. citizens, lawful immigrants, and immigrants with no criminal convictions—to overcrowded rooms, unsanitary conditions, and insufficient food and water.

In many cases, immigrants report having been denied adequate medical care. Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff released a report in October 2025 documenting at least “85 credible reports of medical neglect” at U.S. detention centers. In January, ICE announced that it had stopped paying for immigrant detainees to receive health care—and wasn’t planning on paying again for months.

For the Trump administration, the cruelty is part of the point. The Department of Homeland Security even rejected plans to construct immigration detention facilities that were more humane.

Stephen Miller will be taking over as White House chief of staff beginning Monday.

Trump made the announcement on Truth Social Friday afternoon, saying that “Susie Wiles, who has done an outstanding job, will be moving over to the Trump Political Operation. I want to thank her for her service as Chief of Staff — She has done a great job! President DONALD J. TRUMP.”

Miller, previously the White House deputy chief of staff for policy and homeland security adviser, is receiving the promotion after serving in both Trump administrations. He is well-known for his hardline, xenophobic, and racist views on immigration, which led to violent and deadly mass deportation policies in Trump’s second term.

Trump’s decision to elevate Miller suggests that he is unrepentant about much of the negative attention brought by ICE’s violence even after Republicans were dealt historic losses in Tuesday’s midterm elections. Earlier this week, Miller was the target of leaks from Republicans and Trump administration officials over how his deportation plans were going too far, with even one anecdote about First Lady Melania Trump complaining to the president about people she knew being deported. Wiles reportedly tried for months to steer Trump away from Miller’s approach, according to The New York Times.

Ultimately, though, Wiles is the one on her way out. She tendered her resignation Thursday night, as Trump has partly blamed her for the GOP’s devastating election losses, Wired journalist Hugo Lowell reported. Rumors that she would be made into a scapegoat for the elections had been floating around for weeks.

In a statement posted on X, Wiles said, “Serving President Trump in the White House has been the honor of a lifetime. I’m so proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First. More than anything, I’m grateful for the extraordinary people I’ve had the privilege of working alongside. While my role may be changing, my commitment to the President and the mission never will.”

Promoting Miller now is a clear message to Democrats after their massive election victory.

The death of nurse Alex Pretti at the hands of ICE agents in January caused a sea change in Americans’ thoughts on immigration, and gave Democrats the edge this November. ICE heavy-handed tactics continued, though. ICE agents have shot at least 25 people in Trump’s second term, according to the Times. On top of that, dozens of immigration detainees have died in ICE custody due to inhumane conditions encouraged by Miller.

But Trump clearly doesn’t care about any of that, and wants to double down on the most brutal part of his second term by elevating his most vile staffer, giving Miller the run of the White House. Any thoughts of Trump moderating or working with Democrats in the final two years of his presidency have been dashed by this move, and Democrats should receive the message loud and clear.

text:
Wisconsin State Trooper Carel Aaron Van Der Merwe

DODGE COUNTY, Wis. (WISN/WKOW) — A Wisconsin state trooper who was detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement at Dane County Regional Airport on Thursday is now set to be released, according to information from U.S. Rep. Derrick Van Orden's office.

Carel Aaron Van Der Merwe, 21, was being held at an immigration detention center in Dodge County. He was detained after a targeted ICE operation, according to the Department of Homeland Security.

WisDOT and its Division of State Patrol became aware of the situation involving Trooper Carel Van Der Merwe. The trooper has been employed with State Patrol since July 13, 2025.

Attorney Marc Christopher had been seeking Van Der Merwe's release on bond, which was likely to take two weeks. He called on DHS to support his immediate release and on Wisconsin's congressional delegation to scrutinize the decision to detain him.

A spokesperson for Van Orden's office said the congressman called DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin about the trooper's status.

Van Orden's office released the following statement to 27 News:

"As soon as Congressman Van Orden became aware of the situation, he contacted Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin to discuss the trooper’s case," a spokesperson from his office said. "The trooper will be released immediately and will be responsible for working with the appropriate authorities to resolve his outstanding immigration paperwork and address his legal status. Congressman Van Orden appreciates Secretary Mullin’s attention to this matter."

Van Der Merwe came to the United States from South Africa legally as a child and has waited seven years for an asylum interview, according to Christopher. Christopher said the family "followed the legal process and have waited seven years for an asylum interview."

"He is included on his father's pending asylum application and holds federal work authorization bearing an expiration date in 2030," Christopher said.

DHS states that Van Der Merwe entered the United States in March 2019 with permission to stay until September 2019. "In defiance of our nation's laws, he overstayed his admission," DHS said in a statement.

"This illegal alien will receive due process and remain in ICE custody pending removal proceedings," DHS said earlier in the day Friday.

Van Der Merwe wanted to serve the U.S., but his pending immigration status prevented him from joining the military, so he chose law enforcement, according to Christopher. Van Der Merwe graduated from New Mexico Military Institute with a degree in criminal justice and became a Wisconsin state trooper a year ago.

He lives in Onalaska and works out of Tomah. His attorney said state patrol allows noncitizens with valid work permits to serve.

According to Van Der Merwe, "the officers said they did not care, placed him in handcuffs and shackles, and transported him to immigration detention in Dodge County."

"ICE says it is going after people who break the law," Christopher said Friday. "Here, it has detained someone whose job is to uphold it."

"To be clear: work authorization does not confer legal status in the United States," DHS said in a statement.

The Wisconsin Law Enforcement Association said it is standing with Trooper Carel Van Der as the situation unfolds.

"We recognize the uncertainty this creates for him, his family and, colleagues," the WLEA said in a statement. "We call for fair treatment and due process as his case is reviewed."

text:
Democratic lawmakers decried Stephen Miller as a “hatemonger”, a “xenophobe” and “vile” after Donald Trump appointed his most trusted adviser as White House chief of staff.

On Friday afternoon, the US president abruptly announced via his Truth Social platform that Miller – the architect of his sweeping immigration crackdown – would replace Susie Wiles, whom he confirmed had been ousted.

The announcement came just days after voters overwhelmingly elected Democrats in the US midterm elections, a sharp rebuke of Trump’s agenda that ended his Republican party’s control of US Congress.

“For Trump to promote this hatemonger shows he has learned nothing,” Dick Durbin, a Democratic senator from Illinois, wrote on X. Chuck Schumer, who is expected to become Senate majority leader, said Trump “learned nothing from his historic defeat” and “couldn’t have made a worse choice” in elevating Miller.

Hakeem Jeffries, the top Democrat in the House of Representatives, who is widely expected to become the chamber’s first Black speaker, called Miller “a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands”, and demanded he be fired.

Chris Van Hollen, a Democratic senator from Maryland, called Trump’s decision to elevate Miller “another kick in the teeth to the American people” and “a sign of Trump’s contempt for the voters”.

Miller, who has been serving as Trump’s deputy chief of staff, has become one of the most controversial figures in the administration. An author of the rightwing Project 2025 manifesto, Miller often makes TV appearances to attack Trump’s opponents or bolster policies such as ending birthright citizenship and suggesting the US could invade Greenland.

As a policy adviser, Miller is credited as the architect of Trump’s mass deportation agenda, which Democrats pointed to in denouncing his promotion.

Gavin Newsom, the outgoing California governor, called Miller “one of the most vile thugs to ever slither into the Oval Office” and said the move was “an insult to every American who voted for change” on Tuesday.

But Trump’s Republican allies and aides celebrated the announcement. Steven Cheung, the White House communications director, called Miller a “Trump OG”, and said: “There is no bigger advocate for the Trump agenda than Stephen.”

Mike Lee, a senator from Utah, said Miller had been “a staunch defender of law and order against illegal invasions and leftist lawlessness”. Eric Schmitt, a senator from Missouri, insisted Miller was exactly what the country needed. “Our country is at a pivotal point and Stephen Miller understands exactly what is at stake,” Schmitt wrote on X.

Cabinet members including JD Vance, defense secretary Pete Hegseth, health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr and secretary of state Marco Rubio also praised Miller’s record.

Not all Republicans were pleased by the appointment, however.

Congressman Marlin Stutzman, an Indiana Republican who held his seat, argued Miller “should be fired” earlier this week amid anger over the administration’s deportation drive. Asked on Friday what he made of Trump’s choice to promote Miller instead, Stutzman told Semafor it was a “horrible decision”.

Miles Taylor, who served as chief of staff at the Department of Homeland Security during Trump’s first term, and later joined the ranks of anti-Trump Republicans, said: “I spent two years working with Stephen Miller. His appointment as White House chief of staff is among the most dangerous personnel decisions in the history of our republic. I say that without reservation.”

text:
ICE took an 8-year-old Haitian boy into custody after calling him in for a check-in Wednesday, sparking outrage among San Diego Unified School District leaders, who said Friday they were unsure where the child was being held.

The boy is a third grader at Fay Elementary School in City Heights and previously had Temporary Protected Status, according to district officials, who said he was staying with his uncle after his father was deported last year.

Video recorded by a volunteer observer at the federal building in downtown San Diego shows three armed federal agents walking the boy away from ICE’s field office and into an elevator.

SDUSD’s superintendent and school board members were among nearly a dozen community leaders who signed a letter Friday to DHS about the case, calling the boy’s detention “particularly troubling,” and expressing concern more broadly on the elimination of TPS and its impact on students.

The district said the child received a letter to meet with an ICE agent and his uncle took him “because he did not want to break the law.” The agent then took the child into custody under a 2008 law protecting trafficking victims, the letter said, “leaving the uncle distraught, and this eight-year-old without the support of their family, community and their school.”

A DHS spokesperson said ICE took the child into custody “out of an abundance of caution and to ensure the child’s safety" after his uncle could not establish legal guardianship.

The agency said a man “claiming to be the child’s uncle took him to an ICE check in” and ICE “confirmed that he was not part of either family unit he had been living with," and “the alleged uncle could not establish legal guardianship.”

The Department of Homeland Security said Customs and Border Protection previously deported the father to Mexico. It’s not clear where the boy’s mother is.

“We are not entirely clear where they are. We believe they may be in Los Angeles. They are certainly not with family or with a designated caregiver,” SDUSD Board Trustee Cody Petterson said. The DHS said the boy was placed in the care of the Office of Refugee Resettlement.

“This could very well be my child, could be your child. It could be any of our child,” Petterson said, noting that this was, to his knowledge, the first time ICE had detained a child who attends an SDUSD school.

A DHS spokesperson said in a statement:

Allegations that ICE took a third grader into custody to be placed in detention are false, and any suggestion otherwise is a depraved attempt to smear our ICE law enforcement officers and undermine the work of President Trump and Secretary Mullin to protect children.

“ICE understands that this is absolutely not where this child should be,” Petterson said. "For us, it's a very clear case in which there's no question that the best place for this child is with their caregiver, their uncle, and one of the worst places they could possibly be is in a cage somewhere with nobody they know, not understanding the process, and not understanding what's about to happen to them."

The board’s letter demands the Trump Administration prioritize keeping children as close as possible to their home schools and communities, as well as coordination with local districts before relocating them.

“Every child deserves stability, dignity, and access to education,” the letter reads. “Regardless of immigration status or family circumstances, children should not bear the educational consequences of policy decisions over which they have no control.”

“Kids are supposed to be sacred,” said San Diego City Councilmember Sean Elo-Rivera, who represents City Heights and signed the letter.

“So when you create a system that you know is going to harm children and don't care, what that tells me is you don't see the humanity of the people who are being impacted. And that scares the hell out of me,” he continued. “Because once that's gone, that opens the door to the worst things that happen in human history, right?”

“We are living under a cloud of terror,” said Guerline Jozef, of the Haitian Bridge Alliance, calling the revocation of TPS and the ensuing arrests of Haitians who have lost their legal status “incredibly painful.”

“Even the ICE locator, what we used to try to find out where a person is - now they have changed that,” Jozef continued. “The moment they kidnap or take a person within the community, we don't know if we will ever hear from them again.”

Rep. Juan Vargas’ office is handling the boy’s casework, they said. In a statement, he said the detention was “despicable” and “inhumane,” calling on the Trump Administration to release the child and restore TPS.

Jozef said her organization is also working to get more information on the child and his family.

“I'm sure he is fearful. He is traumatized,” Jozef said. “So we are praying and we are fighting, and we will continue to fight to get a solution on his behalf.”

“When we put children into that state, the fear, the trauma can stay with them for the rest of their lives.”

text:
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump said Friday that Stephen Miller was replacing Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff, mere days after Republicans lost control of Congress in the midterm elections.

Miller, long a key member of Trump’s inner circle, is a key architect of the administration’s hard-line immigration policies. He is one of Trump’s closest and longest-serving advisers, joining his long-shot 2016 presidential campaign as a speechwriter. He currently serves as White House deputy chief of staff for policy and oversees a broad portfolio, though he is best known for his role in Trump’s immigration policy.

The staff shuffle signals that Trump, now staring down a combative Congress that will soon be controlled by Democrats, is resisting a conciliatory approach after the GOP’s midterm thrashing on Tuesday. Miller is a dogged defender of Trump and his “America First” principles, and has built a deep and sophisticated understanding of a president’s executive power and how the federal government operates, portending a potential burst of executive actions in the final two years of Trump’s presidency.

Wiles gave Trump her resignation on Thursday night, a person familiar with the events said, speaking on condition of anonymity to describe the private conversation. Trump praised Wiles in a Truth Social post and said she’d continue to work for his political organization.

“Serving President Trump in the White House has been the honor of a lifetime. I’m so proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First,” Wiles said in a social media post shortly after Trump’s announcement. She added that her commitment to “the President and the mission” will not change.

Wiles, the steely political operator and longtime adviser to Trump, was the first woman to ever serve in that post and the longest-serving White House chief of staff for Trump, who cycled through four of them during his first four-year term.

The departure also came months after Wiles indicated she no longer showed evidence of breast cancer after she underwent months of treatment for the disease, a diagnosis she went public with in March 2026.

Miller is a longtime Trump aide

During the midterm campaign, Miller took frequent partisan swipes at Democrats, calling them “extremists, freaks and America-hating lunatics” on social media and promoted unfounded theories about election fraud in California and Alaska.

He has been a major part of the Trump administration’s anti-fraud task force targeting benefit programs and a decision to suspend Microsoft and others from a green card program. He also served as homeland security adviser at the White House, giving him a perch from which to coordinate with other agencies across the government.

Miller was a veteran Senate aide who worked for former Sen. Jeff Sessions, R-Ala., before he joined Trump’s nascent presidential campaign in 2016. Sessions was the first senator to endorse Trump in his first run and later served as his attorney general.

But the immigration policies that Miller is so closely allied with were a major liability for Republicans during the just-wrapped election. The midterm AP Voter Poll found that most voters, about 6 in 10, said the administration’s immigration enforcement actions had gone too far and that they “somewhat” or “strongly” disapproved of how Immigration and Customs Enforcement had handled its responsibilities.

“Just days after the American people rejected his corrupt and lawless presidency, Donald Trump is doubling down,” said Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., who is set to become chairman of the powerful House Oversight Committee. “Stephen Miller is the architect of the unconstitutional ICE raids that have terrorized our communities and kidnapped and killed American citizens and immigrant families.”

In a statement, Garcia added: “Stephen Miller should lawyer up.”

Wiles brought order to Trump’s campaign

The veteran Florida operative joined Trump’s team during his 2016 presidential bid to run the campaign in his adopted home state. She performed the same role again in 2020 before overseeing the entire 50-state effort in 2024. She is the second woman to lead Trump’s presidential campaign to victory, although she never embraced the formal title of campaign manager.

Wiles, 69, has been credited with steering the most disciplined of his three presidential bids, and Trump himself has said he was often told that Wiles led his “best-run campaign.” Often called the “ice maiden” by the president, she was seen as the no-brainer choice to serve as White House chief of staff at the start of his second term.

She cut her reputation as someone who brought discipline to the president’s chaotic style and shunned the spotlight, so much so that at Trump’s 2024 election night victory party, she repeatedly shook her head and avoided the microphone as Trump tried to coax her to speak to the crowd.

Wiles showed unusual candor in an interview

But in December 2025, nearing the end of Trump’s first year back as president, Wiles became the headline when Vanity Fair magazine published a series of interviews with her and other top Trump administration officials conducted by the author Chris Whipple, an expert on White House chiefs of staff.

The Wiles interviews stuck out for their candor, which is unusual for a sitting White House chief of staff. She said Trump has an “alcoholic’s personality,” although the president does not drink, and said then-Attorney General Pam Bondi had “whiffed” in her handling of the Jeffrey Epstein files while remarking that Vice President JD Vance has been a “conspiracy theorist for about a decade.”

Trump and other administration aides rushed to defend Wiles, who, in turn, disparaged Vanity Fair for publishing what she called a “disingenuously framed hit piece,” though she did not deny making the comments.

In the interviews, which were conducted over a period of several months, Wiles also revealed a bit of her management style, saying she was “not an enabler.”

“I try to be thoughtful about what I even engage in,” Wiles said. “I guess time will tell whether I’ve been effective.”

Trump went through four chiefs of staff in his first term: Reince Priebus, who Trump fired after just six months; John Kelly, who served the longest at 17 months; Mick Mulvaney, who held the role for a little over a year in an “acting” capacity; and Mark Meadows, who served as gatekeeper for the 10 months before Trump left office.

Wiles overcomes personal health struggle

Six months after her diagnosis, Wiles revealed she was “cancer-free,” indicating she no longer showed evidence of cancer after her pathology results came back clear. She thanked her family, friends, doctors, and gave special thanks to Trump for his “unwavering support” in a statement.

“She’s tough,” Trump said at a White House event in October. “She’s a tremendous fighter.”

In a rare interview, Wiles told Fox News Digital last month that she hadn’t been planning on getting the mammogram that ultimately detected her cancer. Her doctor suggested she do the exam anyway, because a mammogram machine was available that day and her schedule was too busy and unpredictable.

“Had he not encouraged me to do it that day, I would have gone back to work and probably not thought about it again until July,” Wiles told the outlet. “We would be having a very different conversation in that case. Four months may not sound like a long time, but with cancer, early detection matters. I will always be grateful to my doctor for knowing me well enough to insist.”

Wiles is a seasoned political operative

In addition to Trump, Wiles also ran incumbent Sen. Rick Scott’s 2010 campaign for Florida governor and briefly served as manager of former Utah Gov. Jon Huntsman’s 2012 presidential campaign. She spearheaded Ron DeSantis ' successful run for governor in 2018, but DeSantis would eventually urge the Trump campaign in 2020 to cut ties with Wiles, creating a rift that led to a particularly vicious effort by those in Trump’s orbit to mock DeSantis throughout his failed run for the Republican presidential nomination against Trump in 2024.

Wiles, the daughter of the late NFL player-turned-broadcaster Pat Summerall, also worked in the offices of former Jacksonville mayors John Delaney and John Peyton. Her first White House job was as a scheduler for President Ronald Reagan.

In addition to her government and campaign positions, Wiles has worked as a lobbyist. She was a partner at Florida-based Ballard Partners, which rose to prominence in Washington during Trump’s time in the White House. Her clients included General Motors, a trade group for children’s hospitals, homebuilders, and the city of Jacksonville.

She was also registered as a lobbyist for the Venezuelan television network Globovisión, which was owned by businessperson Raúl Gorrín, who was charged in Miami with money laundering. The firm later called its work for Gorrín a mistake and said Wiles had almost no role in managing the relationship with Gorrín.

title: 'What's next for migrants?': The fight for immigration reform after Trump's midterm defeat
description:

“Ronald Reagan did something very smart in supporting immigration reform,” says Raúl Hinojosa, professor of Chicano studies at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA).

In the first year of Trump’s second term alone, nearly 400,000 people were detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).
“One of my core causes has been the fight for immigration reform, because I believe that, just as I was able to legalize my status in this country, many other people should have that opportunity and be able to live peacefully with their families,” says Moreno.
text:
Unprepared for the bluenami — the label for the Democrats’ sweeping midterm victory — U.S. President Donald Trump spent weeks ramping up his anti-immigrant rhetoric at dozens of campaign rallies in support of Republican candidates. “There will be no amnesty for illegals,” he repeated over and over, while blaming undocumented immigrants for crime in U.S. cities and a host of other problems, claims that have been contradicted by numerous studies and reports.

But Trump’s tone began to soften as he watched, like millions of Americans, a new political landscape take shape on television screens: Democrats were storming the polls, heading toward control of Congress and winning governorships in key states such as Texas. One of the president’s first reactions was to strike a more conciliatory note on the issue he had long demonized, saying he was willing to sit down and negotiate with Democrats.

“We can work with them [the Democrats] on Immigration. I’ve always felt like we should be able to work on immigration,” he said in an interview with FOX News the day after those adverse elections.

Activists who have spent decades marching and advocating for immigration reform see the Democrats’ control of Congress as a golden opportunity to reopen that debate. In meetings and discussions since Tuesday’s elections, they have begun talking about returning to the streets to demand an end to immigration raids and the legalization of more than 10 million undocumented immigrants whom the Trump administration has relentlessly targeted since mid-2025. They believe the president, weakened by the election results and facing reduced support in both chambers, may now be willing to compromise.

“The blue wave won — what’s next for migrants? Don’t let the Democrats leave us behind and don’t let what happened with president Barack Obama repeat itself, when he said he would leave immigration reform for his second term and didn’t pass it,” says Francisco Moreno, 66, executive director of the Council of Mexican Federations in North America (COFEM). “I don’t see a Trump determined to do it, but maybe it can be achieved.”

The Democrats’ blue wave has shaken Trump’s administration just as the United States approaches the 40th anniversary of a milestone event for the country’s immigrant community: the amnesty granted by Republican president Ronald Reagan to millions of undocumented immigrants in 1986.

Over the past four decades, much has changed both in the way Republican presidents govern and in the recognition of a population that contributes $1.6 trillion to the country’s gross domestic product. The country has gone from opening the door to the legalization of nearly three million people so they could live and work in peace to a dark era of immigration raids and mass deportations, one marked even by the deaths of migrants and U.S. citizens during violent federal enforcement operations.

The benefits of the 1986 amnesty

On November 6, 1986, when a very different political climate prevailed in the White House, Reagan signed the Immigration Reform and Control Act (IRCA), granting legal status and opening a pathway to permanent residency, and eventually citizenship, for undocumented immigrants who had lived continuously in the United States since before January 1, 1982. Migrants of Mexican origin, who remain the country’s largest immigrant group, were the main beneficiaries.

During a presidential debate in 1984, Reagan had already signaled his position, defending the regularization of people living in the shadows. “I believe in the idea of amnesty for those who have put down roots and lived here, even though sometime back they may have entered illegally,” he said at the time.

“Ronald Reagan did something very smart in supporting immigration reform,” says Raúl Hinojosa, professor of Chicano studies at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA). “Because he was from California and at that time he understood that his political base there was the farmers, who needed migrant labor.”

Various studies have found that immigrants who benefited from Reagan’s amnesty saw improvements in both their earnings and educational attainment. One such analysis found that, by 1992, six years after the immigration reform, the incomes of workers who had obtained legal status had risen by an average of 15%. Women benefited the most, with earnings increasing by 21%. In addition, four out of 10 Mexicans who obtained permanent residency, or a green card, moved into better-paying jobs.

“That initiative helped the U.S. economy more than any other policy decision in the last 40 years. Because it made it possible for millions of people to produce more, earn more, buy homes, start businesses, send their children to college. It was a revolution in those families’ lives,” Hinojosa says. “The problem is that today Donald Trump decided to use the anti-immigrant issue for his own political gain. Not because it benefited the country, nor because it helped the people who voted for him.”

What began as a campaign talking point in 2015, when Trump claimed that Mexico was sending drug traffickers, rapists and criminals to the United States, escalated into a second term defined by relentless efforts to make life so difficult for immigrants that they would effectively deport themselves. In many cases, that strategy has proven effective through a sustained campaign of aggressive immigration enforcement operations. In the first year of Trump’s second term alone, nearly 400,000 people were detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

The crackdown continues despite the damage it has inflicted on sectors that depend heavily on immigrant labor, including agriculture, construction and hospitality.

“They’re coming in from the Congo. They interviewed some people last night. ‘Where are you from?’ ‘Congo.’ ‘Where did you live?’ ‘Prison.’ They’re emptying out their prisons into our country,” Trump said at a rally in Ohio last week, repeating another false claim that was met with applause from his supporters.

In a sign of the Trump administration’s unpredictability, one of its officials made clear, the day after the midterms, that the hard-line approach would continue. “Deportations will continue,” Markwayne Mullin, the secretary of Homeland Security responsible for carrying out the administration’s immigration agenda, warned in a post on X.

Juan José Gutiérrez, head of the Full Rights for Immigrants Coalition, also laments the direction U.S. immigration policy has taken when comparing the approaches of the Reagan and Trump administrations. “The contrast shows us that this country, which was admired and served as an example of how a democracy should work, has regressed and is now closed to migration,” he says.

‘There are grounds for another amnesty’

Moreno believes the case for a new form of immigration relief could build on H.R. 4393, better known as the Dignity Act, introduced in July 2025 by Representative María Elvira Salazar, a Florida Republican, and Representative Veronica Escobar, a Texas Democrat. Escobar was reelected in Tuesday’s elections, while Salazar is still awaiting the outcome of a closely contested race in Miami.

The bill would allow undocumented immigrants who have lived in the United States since before December 31, 2020, to apply for protection from deportation, a work permit and travel authorization. The status would be valid for seven years and renewable indefinitely, but it would cost $7,000 and would not provide a pathway to permanent residency. It would also exclude people convicted of certain crimes, including some misdemeanors.

“There are grounds for another amnesty,” Moreno says. “Regardless of how fickle the president may be, I believe this is the time to start taking action. It’s one thing that the country has turned blue and that, in theory, Democrats are more progressive in their views on migrants and are our allies; but we can ensure that this support has an impact in Congress. The ideal moment is now.”

Moreno is himself a beneficiary of Reagan’s amnesty. Born in the Mexican state of Michoacán, he was 20 in 1980, when he arrived in the United States on a visit and decided to stay. He put his legal studies on hold and began working for a cleaning company in Los Angeles. He had come chasing the dream of becoming a Hollywood actor, but ended up building a different career: one in activism.

In his office, he keeps a collection of mementos from the marches he has taken part in. Among them is a banner from the historic demonstration of March 25, 2006, when an estimated one million people took to the streets of downtown Los Angeles to demand the withdrawal of legislation that would have criminalized undocumented immigrants and those who assisted them. The bill in question was the controversial H.R. 4437, introduced by Republican Congressman James Sensenbrenner, which sparked one of the largest waves of public outrage and protest in recent U.S. history. “Yes to families united! No to criminalization!” reads the banner, now yellowed with age.

“One of my core causes has been the fight for immigration reform, because I believe that, just as I was able to legalize my status in this country, many other people should have that opportunity and be able to live peacefully with their families,” says Moreno. “The worst part of it all is the fear. ‘Let’s see how this president turns out,’ ‘let’s see how this governor turns out,’ ‘let’s see if he starts attacking us.’ Because there have been all kinds of politicians over the last 40 years, but nothing has happened.”

text:
US President Donald Trump announced Friday that White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles will step down, naming his longtime adviser Stephen Miller as her successor, effective Monday, November 9.

The move comes just three days after Republicans suffered a sweeping defeat in the midterm elections, losing control of both chambers of Congress.

The announcement marks a striking reversal for Trump, who categorically denied reports of a possible leadership change on October 16.

“There is zero chance,” Trump told CNN at the time, calling the reports false and insisting that Wiles would remain in her position for a long time.

Wiles, first female White House chief of staff, managed Trump's 2024 campaign

Wiles, 69, one of Trump’s closest and most trusted advisers, managed his successful 2024 presidential campaign and became the first woman in American history to serve as White House chief of staff. In September, she announced that she was cancer-free after undergoing treatment for breast cancer diagnosed earlier this year. She continued working throughout her treatment.

US officials told The Jerusalem Post that Wiles submitted her resignation on Thursday.

The 41-year-old Miller is the grandson of Jewish refugees and has been among Trump’s most influential advisers for nearly a decade. Currently serving as deputy chief of staff for policy and homeland security adviser, he is widely regarded as the chief architect of the administration’s aggressive immigration crackdown, including mass deportations and tighter border enforcement. His influence has also extended into national security and foreign policy.

Miller is a trusted advisor to the US president, and his appointment suggests the White House is "preparing for a confrontation" with the Democrats, who are expected to take control of Congress.

He is also an uncompromising factor in the harsh and negative sense of the word, and it is estimated that this will make Trump's ability to work with the Democrats non-existent.

Far-right Americans celebrated Miller’s appointment, and US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth marked the occasion with a three-word X/Twitter post, saying "Patriots in control."

Trump praises Wiles' 'outstanding job,' says she is to transition to political operation

Trump praised Wiles for having done an “outstanding job” and said she would transition to his political operation, keeping her within his broader political orbit.

In an X post later on Friday, Wiles said she was "proud" of what she and Trump had "accomplished together" during her time as chief of staff.

"More than anything, I’m grateful for the extraordinary people I’ve had the privilege of working alongside," she wrote. "While my role may be changing, my commitment to the president and the mission never will."

Trump addressed the move in remarks to the press on Friday, saying he "wanted to make a change," and that Wiles had done "a great job."

"Stephen has been excellent, and sometimes in life, you have to make moves," Trump told reporters at the White House as he departed for Florida. "Stephen has been with me from the beginning. He understands politics very well and is a very good manager. He will do a great job."

Democrats threaten Miller: 'You’d better get a lawyer'

Democratic Congressman Robert Garcia, poised to become chair of the House Oversight Committee following the Democratic victory in the midterm elections, launched a sharp attack on Miller's appointment later on Friday, warning of impending investigations.

"Just days after the American people rejected his corrupt and lawless presidency, Donald Trump is only doubling down on his policies," Garcia stated. "Stephen Miller is the architect of the unconstitutional ICE raids that terrorized our communities and led to the abduction and death of American citizens and immigrant families."

"Democrats on the Oversight Committee will continue to investigate Miller for his misconduct, and we will fight his policies of hate in Congress and in the courts," he added. "Stephen Miller had better get himself a lawyer."

As early as election night, once it became clear that the Democrats were on track to take control of Congress, Garcia issued a two-word warning to Trump administration officials: "Lawyer up" - alluding to the investigations expected to target senior administration figures once the new Congress takes office in January.

text:
President Donald Trump tapped Stephen Miller to succeed Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff, elevating an adviser who reportedly helped develop plans to advance his agenda without congressional approval as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress in January.

Miller, Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought and White House lawyers have worked since April to identify executive actions Trump could take without new legislation, including measures on immigration, tariffs, housing costs and federal spending, Reuters reported Sunday, citing three people familiar with the planning.

With Democrats set to control Congress in January, Trump will face greater obstacles to passing legislation, while Democratic lawmakers will gain the power to launch investigations into his administration.

"If crazed Democrats want to abuse their power and politicize their process of investigations, subpoenas, and destroying lives, they should be reminded that we still control the federal government and all of its powers," a White House official told Fox News Digital Friday afternoon.

‘LAWYER UP’: DEMS IMMEDIATELY PUT TRUMP ON NOTICE AMID REPUBLICANS' MIDTERM BLOODBATH

Asked by CBS on Tuesday how he would advance his agenda if Democrats took control of Congress, Trump cited the Supreme Court’s June ruling in Trump v. Slaughter, which expanded his authority to remove certain federal officials.

"We won the Slaughter case and the Slaughter case gives the president tremendous powers that it never had before," Trump told CBS in the interview.

TRUMP TOUTS 'ULTIMATE POWER' OF VETO IF DEMOCRATS WIN CONTROL OF HOUSE AND SENATE

In Trump v. The administration will retain authority to implement and enforce immigration policy within existing law while Congress considers any legislative or funding changes.
