Officers were then directed to wait a “reasonable amount of time” for an ICE agent to reach the scene, though that sometimes resulted in officers waiting more than an hour.

READ MORE: Inside the collapse of Houston’s ICE policy

The change comes just two days after Whitmire defended HPD’s existing practice in a written statement as “good policy,” though the mayor on Friday denied saying that.

Several other city leaders, including Controller Chris Hollins and Council Member Alejandra Salinas, had said at Wednesday’s council meeting that they would push to limit ICE cooperation following Abbott’s defeat. The governor, who is leaving office in January, had successfully stopped similar efforts earlier this year in Houston after threatening to revoke state funding.

Whitmire on Friday argued he’d walked a political tightrope with the city’s ICE policies, helping Houston avoid the worst of Trump’s immigration crackdown that some other cities have experienced.

Jennefer Canales-Pelaez, senior policy attorney for the Immigrant Legal Resource Center, argued the mayor was rewriting history, pointing out that ICE agents killed Houstonian Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in July and have injured other residents. None of that was enough to convince Whitmire to limit police involvement with the federal agency, she said.

“Even though this is a win for the community, it’s only because advocates have been continuously showing up, applying pressure and reminding him this community deserves protection,” she said. “He’s only doing this now, when it’s politically feasible.”

INVESTIGATION: HPD quietly ended automatic probes of federal police shootings before ICE shooting of Lorenzo Salgado

Salinas agreed that months of public activism helped spur Friday’s announcement, but also commended Whitmire and Police Chief Noe Diaz for making it.

“This is a critical step toward protecting Houstonians’ constitutional rights and reducing the fear and anxiety too many families have carried that calling for help or being pulled over for a routine traffic stop could lead to them or a loved one being detained by ICE,” she said. “This progress belongs to the families who bravely shared their stories, advocates who tirelessly kept organizing, and hundreds of Houstonians who returned to City Hall again and again, even when change felt out of reach.”

Immigration advocates, who have questioned whether the city’s policy violated the U.S. Constitution by directing officers to detain people based solely upon civil warrants and not criminal charges, celebrated Whitmire’s decision, calling it overdue.

“This is what needed to happen since day 1,” Cesar Espinosa of FIEL Houston said in a statement. “Now it is time to follow (through).”

Whitmire said he hoped the new policy would be a model for other Texas cities under the state’s new Democratic leaders. Travis Fife, an attorney for the Texas Civil Rights Project, said immigration advocates in every city from which Abbott threatened to pull funding were exploring what changes might be possible after Tuesday’s elections.

Hours after Whitmire's announcement, leaders in Austin said they planned to discuss how they might also change their ICE-related policies in light of the election, according to a news report.

Under HPD’s prior policy, which the city negotiated with Abbott’s office, local police handed 17 people to immigration authorities from July through September, according to city data.

Another 13 people were charged with crimes and transferred to county jail, where they are likely to be released to ICE. That group would not be affected by the policy, Whitmire said.

description: ONALASKA, Wis. (WKBT) — A 21-year-old Wisconsin State Trooper who was detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement will be released from ICE custody, according to his attorney.
text:
LANSING, Iowa (WKBT) -- The Mississippi River bridge at Lans…

GREEN BAY — Kevin Zeitler gets it.



ONALASKA, Wis. (WKBT) — A 21-year-old Wisconsin State Trooper who was detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement will be released from ICE custody, according to his attorney.

Carel Aaron Van Der Merwe, who lives in Onalaska and works out of the Tomah post, was detained by ICE agents at Dane County Regional Airport in Madison on Nov. 5 while waiting to board a domestic flight. His attorney Marc Christopher claims when Van Der Merwe showed agents his federal work permit and explained he had a pending asylum application, they told him they "did not care," before detaining and taking him to the Dodge County detention facility.

According to Van Der Merwe's attorney, he will be released shortly and will be placed on an order of supervision which requires Van Der Merwe to meet with ICE regularly and to be monitored by an electronic device. However, his attorney says 'our fight is not over.'

"His release does not erase what he and his family have been through," the office stated. "There is still no explanation why DHS detained him or why exactly he is now being released. Those are the answers we seek and Carel and his family, and work community deserves.  We continue to stress how DHS’s own agency, USCIS, authorized him to work. He used that authorization to serve and protect Wisconsin communities. Yet that same agency, detained him. We hope DHS will provide an explanation."

ICE's detainee locator previously showed a Carel Aaron Van Der Merwe, born in South Africa, was in ICE custody at the Dodge Detention Facility in Wisconsin. Van Der Merwe no longer appears on this site.

In a statement to News 8 Now, ICE said it arrested Van Der Merwe on Nov. 5 during a targeted enforcement operation at Dane County Regional Airport in Madison. ICE says Van Der Merwe entered the country in March 2019 with legal permission to stay until September 2019 but overstayed his admission. ICE added that Van Der Merwe will receive due process and remain in custody pending removal proceedings. ICE also noted that work authorization does not confer legal status in the United States.

The Wisconsin State Patrol confirmed Van Der Merwe's employment in a statement to News 8 Now, saying it is aware of the situation and that Van Der Merwe has been employed with the State Patrol since July 13, 2025.

Van Der Merwe came to the United States legally from South Africa as a child. His family claims they have followed the legal immigration process and waited seven years for an asylum interview. He is listed on his father's pending asylum application and holds a federal work authorization card through 2030, according to Christopher. Wisconsin State Patrol hiring rules allow noncitizens with valid work authorization to serve as troopers.

"Carel came here legally as a child. His family pursued asylum through the legal process. He holds federal work authorization and serves Wisconsin as a State Trooper," Christopher said. "Now the same government that authorized him to work has locked him up."

According to a statement, Van Orden, who represents Wisconsin's 3rd Congressional District, contacted DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin directly after learning of Van Der Merwe's detention.

"As soon as Congressman Van Orden became aware of the situation, he contacted Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin to discuss the trooper's case. The trooper will be released immediately and will be responsible for working with the appropriate authorities to resolve his outstanding immigration paperwork and address his legal status. Congressman Van Orden appreciates Secretary Mullin's attention to this matter."

Congresswoman-elect Rebecca Cooke (D-WI), who will represent Wisconsin's 3rd Congressional District in January, released a statement on the detention prior to Van Orden's announcement.

"I am disturbed at reports that a valued member of our Wisconsin community, Wisconsin State Trooper Carel Aaron Van Der Merwe, was unjustly detained by ICE. If these reports are true, ICE's behavior is unacceptable. This is a public servant who puts his life in danger to keep Wisconsinites safe. And it comes after ICE has repeatedly put our communities in danger by violating fundamental rights. I will investigate this incident and demand an explanation from ICE officials about why a member of Wisconsin law enforcement is being treated this way - and I will stand up for him until he is released."

This is a developing story and will be updated as more information becomes available.

text:
TAMPA, Fla. — U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services played a critical role in an investigation that resulted in the sentencing of five Cuban aliens and one U.S. citizen for their roles in a vast conspiracy involving alien smuggling, asylum fraud, and money laundering. As part of the conspiracy, aliens were charged between $1,500 and $40,000 for their smuggling services, and co-conspirators sometimes chartered private planes to move groups of aliens. The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Middle District of Florida made the announcement.

“Today’s sentencing is a clear warning to anyone seeking to profit by exploiting, abusing, or undermining America’s legal immigration system,” said USCIS Director Joseph B. Edlow. “USCIS will bring to bear all law enforcement resources at its disposal to dismantle criminal operations threatening the American people.”

According to court documents, Liannys Yaiselys Vega-Perez, 27; Miguel Martinez Vasconcelos, 31; Layra Libertad Treto Santos, 30; Luis Emmanuel Escalona-Marrero, 32; Walbis Pozo-Dutel, 32; and Emanuel Martinez Gonzalez, 29, conspired with others to operate an alien smuggling organization that encouraged or induced thousands of Cuban aliens to enter the U.S. The organization smuggled the Cuban aliens illegally across the southern border and used fraudulent Electronic System for Travel Authorization visa waivers to help people enter through ports of entry.

The defendants advertised their smuggling services and bogus immigration services across multiple social media platforms targeted toward Cuban nationals living in Cuba. The organization’s advertised services included assisting Cubans with European citizenship to enter the U.S. on a European tourist visa waiver or ESTA, and it allegedly filed hundreds of fraudulent ESTA applications with U.S. Customs and Border Protection using fake addresses and false information. Cuban residents are not eligible for the ESTA program, and to obtain ESTAs, the alien smuggling organization made false representations that the applicants had not been present in Cuba since 2011. The defendants knew that Cubans are not eligible for the ESTA program and that the applicants were residing in Cuba at the time the ESTA applications were submitted. The defendants also operated a fraudulent immigration benefits business. Once in the United States, the organization assisted many aliens with filing fraudulent asylum paperwork to remain in the country.

Liannys Yaiselys Vega-Perez furthered the conspiracy by assisting in the logistics of moving aliens from their country of origin, including Cuba, into the United States, such as purchasing international and domestic flights for aliens to transport them toward, into, and throughout the United States. Vega-Perez was also the primary manager of the immigration benefits business and personally filed hundreds of fraudulent asylum applications. In addition, she and other defendants prepared, drafted, and submitted fraudulent asylum applications, immigrant visa applications, lawful permanent residence applications, and other applications for immigration benefits, in exchange for a fee.

Miguel Martinez Vasconcelos furthered the conspiracy by purchasing airline tickets to move individuals being smuggled from their country of origin towards the United States. He also provided funding to purchase charter flights to transport aliens to unlawfully enter the United States, with the purpose of growing and advancing the alien smuggling organization’s operations. Vasconcelos personally transmitted at least $150,000 to companies operating outside the United States in furtherance of these unlawful activities.

Layra Libertad Treto Santos furthered the conspiracy by personally filing fraudulent asylum claims on behalf of the immigration fraud benefits business while she was an employee and manager. Treto Santos used the alien smuggling organization’s services for herself and her family members and referred multiple Cuban nationals to the organization for smuggling services.

Luis Emmanuel Escalona-Marrero furthered the conspiracy by working with a co-conspirator in Mexico to ship Cuban passports to the United States. The purpose was to avoid having the passports confiscated by U.S. Border Patrol so that aliens could use the passports to apply for asylum once they entered the United States. He also formed a shell company that, along with other companies, was used to move illegal proceeds of smuggling through to conceal the funds’ source and nature before distributing the funds back to himself and his co-conspirators.

Walbis Pozo-Dutel furthered the conspiracy by assisting with the logistics of transporting foreign nationals from their countries of origin, including Cuba, into the United States. For example, Pozo-Dutel provided foreign hotel and flight information to facilitate the aliens’ travel along the route into the United States. Pozo-Dutel also instructed the individuals on what to say if questioned by CBP officers.

Emmanuel Martinez Gonzalez furthered the conspiracy by helping coordinate the logistics of transporting aliens. Martinez-Gonzalez worked with his paramour and codefendant, Marianny Lucia Lopez-Torres, to arrange the travel of aliens upon their arrival in the United States and accepted payments from those aliens as a part of the smuggling operation.

Vega-Perez, Martinez Vasconcelos, and others conspired to regularly move funds to companies operating outside of the United States and to other places outside the United States, such as by purchasing international flights for aliens to travel into the United States. Between July 2022 and November 2024, the alien smuggling organization spent more than $600,000 with a single airline for commercial flights.

Vega-Perez, Escalona-Marrero, and Treto Santos and others conspired to conduct financial transactions that were designed in whole or in part to conceal and disguise the nature, location, source, ownership, and control of proceeds of alien smuggling. The defendants set up multiple shell companies, through which illegal proceeds were moved before distributing the proceeds to the defendants. Between 2021 and 2025, more than $22 million was laundered by the defendants.

Liannys Yaiselys Vega-Perez was sentenced to four years in prison. Vega-Perez previously pleaded guilty to conspiracy to smuggle aliens for financial gain, conspiracy to commit asylum fraud, conspiracy to commit international money laundering, and conspiracy to commit concealment money laundering. Miguel Martinez Vasconcelos was sentenced to two years in prison. Martinez Vasconcelos previously pleaded guilty to conspiracy to smuggle aliens for financial gain and conspiracy to commit international money laundering. Layra Libertad Treto Santos was sentenced to 30 months in prison. Treto Santos previously pleaded guilty to conspiracy to smuggle aliens for financial gain, conspiracy to commit asylum fraud, and conspiracy to commit concealment money laundering. Luis Emmanuel Escalona-Marrero was sentenced to 30 months in prison. Escalona-Marrero previously pleaded guilty to conspiracy to smuggle aliens for financial gain and conspiracy to commit concealment money laundering. Walbis Pozo-Dutel was sentenced to two years in prison. Pozo-Dutel previously pleaded guilty to conspiracy to smuggle aliens for financial gain. Emanuel Martinez Gonzalez was sentenced to two years in prison. Martinez Gonzalez previously pleaded guilty to conspiracy to smuggle aliens for financial gain. Escalona-Marrero was ordered to forfeit $2.9M, Vasconcelos was ordered to forfeit $150,000, and Treto Santos was ordered to forfeit $95,000.

Twelve individuals were charged in a superseding indictment for their roles in the conspiracy. Yuniel Lima-Santos, 32, and Gisleivy Peralta Consuegra, 41, pleaded guilty and are awaiting sentencing. Erik Ventura-Castro, 25, was sentenced on July 29 to 30 months in prison. Lazaro Alain Cabrera-Rodriguez, 29, was found guilty after trial in September and is awaiting sentencing. Marianny Lucia Lopez-Torres and Frandy Aragon-Diaz are at large.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s Homeland Security Investigations Tampa, U.S. Border Patrol Miami Sector, USCIS’ Fraud Detection and National Security Directorate, and IRS Criminal Investigation led U.S. investigative efforts, with substantial assistance from HSI’s Human Smuggling Unit in Washington, D.C., and CBP’s National Targeting Center International Interdiction Task Force. The Justice Department’s Office of International Affairs and authorities in the Cayman Islands provided valuable assistance.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Courtney Derry for the Middle District of Florida and Trial Attorney Amanda Brown of the Criminal Division’s Human Rights and Special Prosecutions Section are prosecuting the case.

text:
President Donald Trump has named Stephen Miller his new White House chief of staff, elevating the controversial architect of his anti-DEI and immigration policies as civil rights leaders condemn the longtime adviser for what they describe as his white nationalist views.

The appointment comes just days after Republicans suffered major midterm defeats, setting up a political showdown between the Trump administration and the incoming Democratic-controlled Congress.

In a Truth Social post, Trump announced on Friday that Miller, who served as deputy chief of staff for policy for the past two years, would replace Susie Wiles as chief of staff effective Monday, Nov. 9.

“We got to make moves,” Trump told reporters when asked about the decision to elevate Miller, who he described as “great.”

The selection of Miller, a 41-year-old right-wing legal activist, signals that Trump intends to double down on his unpopular MAGA agenda after his Republican Party suffered major defeats in Tuesday’s midterm elections. It also signals Trump is preparing for a political fight as Democrats prepare to launch several investigations into the Trump administration.

“Having a white nationalist running the White House is not a good sign. Stephen Miller’s elevation to a more consequential position of power is a bad signal for what Trump’s endgame will be as a lame-duck president,” says Markus Batchelor, political director at People For the American Way.

He told theGrio, “Miller has been the central figure in Trump’s brazen abuse of executive power, his deadly deportation campaign, and attacks on justice, equity, and inclusion through the courts. As Chief of Staff, he will — unlike Wiles — enable Trump’s worst and most destructive tendencies, and the American people will bear the harm.”

Miller has been in Trump’s inner circle since his first administration, from 2017 to 2021. He infamously masterminded Trump’s Muslim travel ban, which targeted mostly African countries, and the family separation policy. During the second Trump administration, Miller served as lead on the White House’s aggressive immigration policies, including mass deportations.

“Stephen Miller belongs nowhere near the Oval Office,” said NAACP President and CEO Derrick Johnson in a statement provided to theGrio. The civil rights leader added, “He belongs before a judge. He’s a thug who will be remembered as the architect of Trump’s vile and authoritarian regime.”

Miller is known for promoting many of Project 2025’s anti-DEI and anti-immigration policies and has been a vocal advocate for white grievance politics. As a private attorney, Miller founded America First Legal, which filed several lawsuits challenging DEI policies at several U.S. companies and institutions, including against Black farmers. The conservative firm argued that such policies were discriminatory against white men.

U.S. Rep.-elect Chris Rabb (D-Pa.), a Democratic strategist who will be sworn into office in January, slammed Miller as a “white supremacist.” He told CNN that President Trump has “not learned” from the “historic routing” of the midterm elections.

Rabb added, “We haven’t had a win this big since 1974. But [Trump] is reasserting who he is and what the MAGA cult stands for.”

Dreisen Heath, a human rights advocate and policy expert, told theGrio of Miller’s promotion, “Swapping Susie Wiles for Stephen Miller is just white supremacist musical chairs within an authoritarian administration.”

Heath continued, “He is the same person supporting the fast-tracking of white South Afrikaners as refugees while the process remains shut for almost everyone else.” However, she added, “His title doesn’t change what voters rejected. Millions voted in complete rebuke of state-sanctioned violence, unequal conditions, and corruption, across all levels of government.”

Nadine Smith, president and CEO of Color Of Change, told theGrio, “Losing public support does not strip this administration of its power to destroy lives. Giving Miller more authority puts Black communities, immigrants and everyone this administration has targeted in greater danger.”

The social justice leader called on the incoming Democratic-controlled Congress to “investigate abuses, expose who ordered them, and use its power over federal spending to stop them.”

“We must challenge unlawful actions in court and organize to protect our neighbors. Our power did not end when the polls closed,” said Smith. “We built it by bringing people together, and we must keep building until the government fears the consequences of violating our rights more than it fears defying Donald Trump.”

title: Belgium passes law allowing police searches of undocumented migrants' homes
description:
Brussels, Nov. 6 (SANA) The Belgian Parliament approved Friday legislation authorizing police to enter the residences of individuals suspected of residing in the country illegally who have ignored deportation orders.
According to Reuters, the law is part of a broader push by Prime Minister Bart De Wever’s coalition government to curb illegal migration and increase the deportation rate of rejected asylum seekers.
Prior to the vote, Amnesty International urged lawmakers to reject the bill, warning of potential repercussions for individuals assisting undocumented migrants.
Human rights groups and attorneys also argued that police entries for immigration enforcement raise serious constitutional and privacy concerns.
The passage follows protests in Brussels on Wednesday, where approximately 3,000 demonstrators formed a human chain around the Palace of Justice to oppose the legislation.
text:
Brussels, Nov. 6 (SANA) The Belgian Parliament approved Friday legislation authorizing police to enter the residences of individuals suspected of residing in the country illegally who have ignored deportation orders.

According to Reuters, the law is part of a broader push by Prime Minister Bart De Wever’s coalition government to curb illegal migration and increase the deportation rate of rejected asylum seekers.

The government maintained that the searches will be strictly limited to rejected applicants who ignored departure notices and are suspected of posing a threat to public safety or national security.

text:
US President Donald Trump on Friday appointed Stephen Miller, one of the most influential architects of his hardline immigration policy, as his new White House chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles just days after the Republican Party suffered a major defeat in the midterm elections.

Miller, 41, currently deputy chief of staff and homeland security adviser, will assume the position on Monday, November 9, Trump announced on his Truth Social platform.

“I am pleased to announce that Mr. Stephen Miller, the current Deputy Chief of Staff of the Trump Administration, and one of my most trusted advisors, will become the Chief of Staff,” Trump wrote.

Wiles, 69, the first woman to serve as White House chief of staff, will move to Trump's political operation. The president praised her performance, describing her tenure as outstanding.

Wiles confirmed her departure in a statement on X, saying that serving Trump in the White House had been “the honor of a lifetime”. She highlighted the administration's record on border security, tax cuts and its economic policies.

Miller has been one of Trump's closest advisers for more than a decade, dating back to his first presidential campaign in 2016. He has played a central role in shaping the administration's restrictive immigration policies, including its drive to carry out mass deportations during Trump's second term.

His promotion places one of the administration's most outspoken advocates of tougher immigration enforcement at the centre of White House decision-making.

The appointment also comes amid growing scrutiny of the administration's immigration operations, particularly following the fatal shootings of two protesters by immigration agents in Minneapolis in January, which triggered widespread demonstrations and criticism of federal enforcement tactics.

The personnel change follows a bruising midterm election for Republicans, with Democrats winning control of both chambers of Congress. The result represents a significant political setback for Trump and is likely to intensify scrutiny of his administration's domestic agenda.

Wiles had been widely regarded as an important organisational force within Trump's inner circle, helping manage competing interests and maintain discipline in the White House. Her departure also follows weeks of speculation about possible personnel changes, although the administration had previously rejected reports that she was about to be replaced.

By moving Wiles to his political operation and promoting Miller, Trump is reshaping his closest circle of advisers at a politically sensitive moment.

text:
HOUSTON (AP) — Houston's mayor on Friday directed police to limit cooperation with federal immigration authorities, signing an order that he called a direct result of Democrats reclaiming power in Texas for the first time in decades.

Watch the video in the player above.

The shift in the nation's fourth-largest city is one of the first actions to restrict U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations since Democrats' rout in Tuesday's midterm elections. It also is a sign that results are already having an impact in Texas, where Republican leaders have enthusiastically embraced President Donald Trump's mass deportation agenda.

The stunning victories included Democrat Gina Hinojosa ousting Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, which will make her Texas' first Latina governor and the first member of her party to hold the office in more than 30 years.

"I've said many times, elections matter," Mayor John Whitmire said.

ICE would only be contacted for jailable offenses

Whitmire, a Democrat, said the city would go after immigrants "that pose a danger, not those that are going about their family business, work and education." In the case of a traffic incident, "you write a citation or you warn them and they go about their way," he said.

Under the mayor's new directive, Houston police should contact ICE only if the person it stops is arrested on a charge that is subject to jailing or if ICE issues an administrative warrant, which is an order signed by a senior ICE official indicating that the person is wanted by immigration officials.

READ MORE: Democrats win full control of more state governments and the Texas House

"The fact that a person is, or is suspected to be, subject to immigration enforcement shall not, by itself, be a basis to contact ICE, to prolong any detention, or to take any person into or hold any person in custody," the two-page order states.

The Trump administration's immigration crackdown in Houston has sparked protests after an ICE officer fatally shot a Mexican homebuilder this summer and another struck a man with a car.

Spokespersons for ICE did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment on the mayor's announcement.

Cooperation with ICE has sparked protests in Texas cities

A grand jury last week indicted ICE officer Mario Alberto Morales on a charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon. Prosecutors say Morales intentionally rammed his car into Miguel Parra Hernandez, whose leg was broken. ICE has asserted that Parra Hernandez ran in front of the vehicle, an account that prosecutors say is contradicted by video.

Despite a one-time $75 billion infusion from Congress, ICE remains heavily dependent on local police to find people subject to deportation and turn them over. It has done so partly by signing about 2,600 agreements — many in Texas — to deputize local police and other state and local agencies to enforce immigration laws. Texas has been a primary target for ICE arrests.

Abbott has closely aligned the state with the Trump administration to collaborate on enforcing federal immigration laws. In April, he had threatened to take away nearly $200 million in public safety grants from Austin, Dallas and Houston after city officials in Houston tried to limit police officers' cooperation with ICE.

READ MORE: ICE officer charged with ramming man with SUV in Houston turns himself in

Houston's City Council passed an ordinance eliminating the requirement for Houston police officers to wait 30 minutes for ICE agents to pick up someone with a nonjudicial administrative warrant. If ICE agents didn't show up in time, police officers took a detained person's information and were able to release them.

Abbott said the ordinance violated the terms of millions of dollars in state grants Houston had received for police and security during the World Cup games the city hosted in June. Attorney General Ken Paxton filed a lawsuit, accusing the city of violating a 2017 state law that prevents cities from adopting policies that limit the enforcement of immigration laws.

The city changed the ordinance two weeks after passing it to delete language stating that administrative warrants — which ICE agents use to take individuals into custody, unlike warrants signed by a judge — are not enough for officers to arrest or detain an individual.

Advocate calls the change a 'sigh of relief' for immigrant communities

FIEL, an immigrant rights group in Houston that has been working with the family of Parra Hernandez, planned to hold a press conference Friday afternoon in light of the announcement.

Prior to the changes, immigration enforcement "looked like a complete collaboration between Houston Police Department and ICE," Cesar Espinosa, executive director at FIEL, said in an interview with The Associated Press. He said the collaboration paralyzed communities too afraid of getting stopped for a traffic ticket or getting referred to ICE when calling for help when witnessing a crime.

"It gives our community a sigh of relief in that we know of many people in the city of Houston that will not even go to the grocery store because they're afraid that they're going to get caught up by ICE or they're gonna get pulled over by HPD and HPD is gonna call ICE on them," Espinosa said.

Wilder reported from Austin, Texas, and Gonzalez reported from McAllen, Texas. Associated Press reporter Elliot Spagat in San Diego contributed to this report.

text:
On November 5, 2026, U.S. Customs and Border Protection (“CBP”) issued its interim final rule that would implement Section 2 of Executive Order 14411 by establishing heightened requirements for foreign importers of record (“IOR”) when making entry, new criteria to qualify as a U.S. IOR, and client verification responsibilities for licensed customs brokers (see Update of June 22, 2026). The rule becomes effective on January 5, 2027.

U.S. IORs

To qualify as a U.S. IOR, an entity must satisfy each part of a three-part test. It must be both located in, and organized under the laws of, the United States, and: (i) maintain at least 51% of beneficial owner(s) who are United States citizens or lawful permanent residents and have control of the entity; or (ii) direct ownership of a significant amount of unencumbered real property in the United States.

With respect to the location of the IOR, CBP will undertake a verification process. Accordingly, CBP may require U.S. IORs to demonstrate factors including but not limited to the entity’s principal place of business, physical presence in the United States, ownership of unencumbered property, whether the entity is sufficiently capitalized, and whether it is an instrumentality of a foreign manufacturer without substantial presence in the United States.

Foreign IORs

A foreign IOR is an IOR that does not meet the criteria of a U.S. IOR. A foreign IOR is prevented from being the IOR unless it becomes validated under the Customs Trade Partnership Against Terrorism (“CTPAT”) program. Currently, the only foreign country whose IORs can become CTPAT-validated is Canada. Except for Canada, the rules ban all foreign IORs from entering merchandise for consumption.

November 6, 2026 (SAINT PAUL) — Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison and a coalition of 23 states secured an important victory in court this week that stops the Trump Administration’s imposition of illegal immigration-enforcement conditions on Congressionally-authorized public safety grants, including grants intended to keep law enforcement officers safe and fight crime.

On November 4, District of Rhode Island Chief Judge John J. McConnell, Jr. declared the Trump Administration’s actions unlawful and permanently blocked any implementation or enforcement of these illegal conditions. The court’s order means Attorney General Ellison and the coalition have won their August 2025 lawsuit against the conditions.

“The Trump Administration has shown over and over that they’re willing to break the law and compromise Americans’ health and safety in order to impose their radical, un-American immigration enforcement priorities on us. I’m very pleased that the court has definitively ruled they cannot deny essential public-safety grants for these highly political purposes,” Attorney General Ellison said. “I’ll keep fighting to keep all Minnesotans safe from Trump.”

Last year, the Trump Administration, disregarding the clear letter of the law and intent of Congress, declared that states would be unable to access Victims of Crime Act (VOCA) funds unless they agreed to the Administration’s extreme immigration demands. In August 2025, Attorney General Ellison and coalition sued to block these conditions and in October 2025, succeeded in getting the federal government to remove them on more than $1.3 billion of VOCA funds, including $22 million for victims and survivors of crime in Minnesota.

However, earlier this year, the U.S. Department of Justice applied these illegal conditions to new grants, including funds dedicated to law enforcement and juvenile justice. Among the affected programs is the Edward Byrne Memorial Justice Assistance Formula Grants (known as the Byrne JAG Program). For decades, regardless of which political party held power, the Byrne JAG Program has been the leading federal source of criminal-justice funding to state and local governments.

Civil immigration enforcement is a federal responsibility and not a state government responsibility. The Trump Administration’s unlawful attempts to coerce states into doing their bidding conflict with core principles of American governance — the separation of powers and federalism. The Administration’s actions violated laws passed by Congress as well as the Spending Clause of the U.S. Constitution.

Joining Attorney General Ellison in this lawsuit, which was let by the attorneys general of California, Delaware, Illinois, New Jersey, and Rhode Island, are the attorneys general of Colorado, Connecticut, the District of Columbia, Hawaii, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Nevada, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Vermont, Virginia, Washington, and Wisconsin, as well as the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania.

text:
Even as a high school student, Stephen Miller knew how to make people listen, even if that meant irritating almost everyone in the room. During a speech to fellow students at his Santa Monica, California, high school, where he was running for student government, he argued that students should not have to pick up trash because janitors were paid to do that job.

He also declared that he would "say and do things that no sane person would say or do." More than two decades later, Miller, now 41, has become one of the most powerful figures in Washington following his appointment as President Donald Trump's new White House chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles after Republicans' sweeping defeat in the midterm elections.

Miller is among the few figures in Trump's orbit to have survived almost continuously since the president's first election campaign in 2016. He wrote speeches, shaped immigration policy and, perhaps most importantly, learned how to translate Trump's political promises and provocative statements into government action. While senior officials in Trump's first administration resigned, were fired or fell out with the president, Miller steadily consolidated his influence.

MAKE ynetGlobal MY TRUSTED SOURCE

During Trump's second term, he became deputy chief of staff and homeland security adviser, establishing himself as one of the few White House figures whose opinions Trump regularly seeks on a broad range of issues. His promotion to chief of staff places him in charge of managing the very administration whose policies he has spent a decade helping to shape.

The Jewish descendant of refugees who became an immigration hardliner

More than any other issue, Miller's name has become synonymous with Trump's restrictive immigration agenda. He was a driving force behind the administration's travel restrictions on several Muslim-majority countries, its controversial policy of separating migrant families at the Mexican border and efforts to limit legal immigration. During Trump's second term, he spearheaded efforts to expand mass deportations and accelerate immigration enforcement.

Critics accuse him of undermining human rights and the rule of law, while Miller presents his policies as necessary to defend America's borders and national security. His uncompromising approach has also created a deeply personal controversy within his own family, whose history stands in striking contrast to his political views.

Miller was born into a Jewish family with liberal political roots. His ancestors fled anti-Jewish pogroms in Eastern Europe, and one of his forebears arrived in the United States in 1903 with just eight dollars in his pocket. Yet Miller himself grew up far removed from the poverty his ancestors had escaped.

His father, Michael, a trained lawyer, expanded the family's wealth through real estate. Together with Miller's mother, Miriam, he managed a business that owned approximately 2,500 residential units in California. The family lived in one of Santa Monica's wealthiest neighborhoods and employed housekeepers born in Latin America, who cooked for the children and cleaned the home.

According to Miller's biographer, Jean Guerrero, he was once embarrassed when a housekeeper drove him to school in her old car because he feared classmates would think he was poor.

The family's financial circumstances changed in the 1990s amid legal disputes involving Miller's father and the damage caused by California's devastating 1994 earthquake. In 1998, when Miller was 13, his parents sold their home and moved to a more modest property. Their financial situation later improved, and the family donated tens of thousands of dollars to Israeli causes, including the American Friends of the Weizmann Institute of Science. His father also held senior positions in Jewish organizations in Los Angeles.

Miller's family background became a source of particularly sharp criticism from his uncle, David Glosser, who publicly condemned his nephew's immigration policies. Glosser argued that if the restrictions Miller championed had existed in the early 20th century, their Jewish ancestors might never have found refuge in America, and many family members could have perished in the Holocaust. The dispute was especially personal because Glosser himself had worked to assist refugees.

The emails that triggered outrage among Jewish organizations

Miller became the center of another controversy in 2019, when more than 900 emails he had sent to the right-wing website Breitbart were made public. Among other things, the correspondence showed him recommending coverage of a book depicting an immigrant takeover of Europe, a work popular among white supremacist groups. He also shared material from websites promoting racist narratives about immigrants and minority communities, particularly in relation to crime.

The revelations triggered condemnation from civil rights organizations and several prominent Jewish groups. The Anti-Defamation League and organizations representing Reform, Conservative and Reconstructionist Judaism called on Trump to dismiss Miller. The White House rejected the accusations and defended him.

The controversy illustrated the unusual position Miller occupies in American Jewish public life: a Jewish conservative whose family's history is rooted in persecution and migration, but whose policies have been condemned by Jewish organizations concerned about racism, immigration restrictions and the treatment of refugees.

From immigration enforcement to Israel, Iran and Greenland

Miller's influence has increasingly extended beyond immigration policy. He has been closely associated with the administration's hawkish approach toward Israel's regional adversaries and enthusiastically supported American-Israeli strikes against Iran.

He was also involved in the administration's crackdown on pro-Palestinian activists at American universities. Court testimony indicated that Miller participated in discussions concerning the cancellation of visas and deportation of foreign students over their political activities. Those measures drew criticism from civil liberties advocates and some Jewish organizations, which warned against restricting freedom of expression in the name of combating antisemitism.

In recent years, Miller has also emerged as one of the administration's most vocal advocates of projecting American power abroad. Following the U.S. military operation in Venezuela, he argued for the use of American force in other regions and even presented military action as a possible means of taking control of Greenland.

"We live in the real world, which is governed by force," he declared, encapsulating an approach to foreign policy that emphasizes power over diplomatic restraint.

Trump himself has occasionally appeared amused by Miller's intensity, joking in the past that he would prefer his adviser not to reveal every one of his true feelings, some of which might be excessive even by the president's standards.

‘Weird Stephen’ and the Voldemort comparison

Miller's appearance, demeanor and confrontational public style have also made him a frequent target of ridicule from political opponents. California's Democratic governor, Gavin Newsom, compared him to Lord Voldemort, the villain of the Harry Potter series. When reports emerged that an actor had been selected to portray Voldemort in the upcoming television adaptation but his identity was being kept secret, Newsom's office quickly offered Miller a sarcastic "Congratulations!"

According to Trump biographer Michael Wolff, even the president has privately referred to his longtime aide as "Weird Stephen." Yet such mockery has done little to weaken Miller's position. Unlike numerous other advisers who entered Trump's orbit only to depart amid public disputes or internal power struggles, Miller has remained consistently close to the president.

His appointment to replace Wiles, however, presents a different challenge. Wiles, a veteran political strategist who helped engineer Trump's 2024 election victory, was widely regarded as a disciplined operator who tried to impose structure on the sometimes chaotic White House. As chief of staff, she controlled access to the president, coordinated his schedule and sought to manage competing factions within the administration.

Miller, by contrast, is identified with its most ideological and confrontational wing. His promotion following the Republicans' midterm defeat suggests Trump is choosing to place one of his most committed political allies at the center of White House decision-making rather than turn toward a more conciliatory approach.

text:
Where substantial evidence supported the Board of Immigration Appeals’ findings that the petitioner failed to establish a nexus between his past or future persecution and his asserted particular social group of “imputed homosexuals,” it was affirmed.

Background

Mohammad Fawwaz Qaiymah, a native and citizen of Jordan, petitions for review of a final order of the Board of Immigration Appeals, or BIA, denying his application for asylum, humanitarian asylum, withholding of removal and protection under the regulations implementing the United Nations Convention Against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment, or CAT. Petitioner claims that two men in Jordan sexually assaulted him and that he fears persecution by his assailants if he were to return.

Persecution

Petitioner takes issue with the BIA’s factual finding that he failed to establish a nexus between his past or future persecution and his asserted particular social group of “imputed homosexuals.” He emphasizes that more than one reason may motivate a persecutor’s actions, that a persecutor’s motives may change over time or differ for separate acts of persecution and that “being young, poor, and vulnerable is not mutually exclusive with being perceived as a homosexual.”

This court does not doubt any of those premises. But they do not lead to vacatur or reversal here, because the agency did not run afoul of these principles and its findings are supported by substantial evidence.

The BIA found no clear error in the determination of the immigration judge, or IJ, “that Abdul was not motivated to target and sexually assault [petitioner] by imputed homosexuality.” Rather, “Abdul was motivated to target [petitioner] for sexual abuse because of [his] vulnerability of age, low self-esteem, and poor economic status.”

It did not treat these motivations and imputed homosexuality as mutually exclusive. Nor did it “fail[] to consider the intertwined reasons for the persecution.” Instead, the BIA and the IJ considered whether “Abdul believed [petitioner] was gay or . . . that belief was one central reason Abdul targeted” him and rejected those conclusions as unsupported by the factual record. Substantial evidence in the record supports that factual determination.

Petitioner argues that Abdul’s motivation changed after the first assault, as demonstrated by the fact that he filmed the abuse and then blackmailed petitioner with the recording even after he was no longer a minor. But this is not the only finding a “reasonable adjudicator” could reach, and sufficient evidence supports the agency’s contrary conclusion.

Petitioner next argues that the agency did not address whether unidentified “people in Jordan who might persecute [him] could become aware of his past sexual assaults and then perceive him as a homosexual.” The BIA found his argument “speculative” and not a basis “to disturb the [IJ’s] decision” that “record evidence does not indicate that [petitioner] would be persecuted in the future on account of imputed homosexuality.”

In this court, petitioner hypothesizes that Abdul might tell others about the assaults or they might learn about his report of “attempted” rape and “assume that [he] is gay.” The evidence, however, does not “compel[]” a finding that it is reasonably possible that unidentified people would become aware of petitioner’s past assaults, perceive him to be homosexual and persecute him on that basis.

CAT

Petitioner contends that the agency’s CAT analysis was deficient because it “never weighed” his “past torture claim, his inability to relocate or Jordan’s country conditions.” This court disagrees. Although petitioner would weigh that evidence differently than the BIA did, “we do not reweigh the evidence on a petition for review.”

As for country conditions evidence, the agency did not address it and did not need to do so. Petitioner raised the country conditions evidence only with respect to government acquiescence. Accordingly, the agency considered and addressed all of the CAT factors relevant to its decision.

Petitioner alternatively argues that “being sexually abused as a child created a permanent and continuing harm that entitle[s him], without more, to protection under [the] CAT.” But he does not identify any authority, from the BIA or any court, holding that the requirements for CAT protection can be satisfied by a showing of past torture regardless of the likelihood of future acts of torture.

The one Fourth Circuit decision petitioner cites reveals that his argument is more akin to a request for humanitarian asylum than CAT protection. The BIA therefore did not err in rejecting petitioner’s argument that his past abuse entitled him to CAT protection despite his failure to show that he likely would be tortured in the future if removed to Jordan.

Petition denied.

Qaiymah v. Blanche, Case No. 24-1099, Oct. 19, 2026. 4th Cir. (Rushing), from Board of Immigration Appeals. Joseph M. Colley for Petitioner. Anthony Jason Nardi for Respondent. VLW 026-2-368. 16 pp.

text:
MADISON, Wis. -- A 21-year-old Wisconsin State Trooper who came to the United States legally from South Africa as a child is now in federal immigration detention, according to his immigration attorney.

Carel Aaron Van Der Merwe, who lives in Onalaska and works out of the Tomah post, was detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents at an airport while waiting to board a domestic flight. His attorney Marc Christopher claims when Van Der Merwe showed agents his federal work permit and explained he had a pending asylum application, they told him they "did not care," before detaining and taking him to the Dodge County detention facility.

ICE's detainee locator shows a Carel Aaron Van Der Merwe, born in South Africa, is in ICE custody at the Dodge Detention Facility in Wisconsin.

In a statement to News 8 Now, a DHS spokesperson said ICE arrested Van Der Merwe on Thursday during a targeted enforcement operation at Dane County Regional Airport in Madison. ICE says Van Der Merwe entered the country in March 2019 with legal permission to stay until September 2019 but overstayed his admission. ICE added that Van Der Merwe will receive due process and remain in custody pending removal proceedings. ICE also noted that work authorization does not confer legal status in the United States.

Van Der Merwe's family claims they have followed the legal immigration process and waited seven years for an asylum interview. He is listed on his father's pending asylum application and holds a federal work authorization card through 2030, according to Christopher. Wisconsin State Patrol hiring rules allow noncitizens with valid work authorization to serve as troopers.

"Carel came here legally as a child. His family pursued asylum through the legal process. He holds federal work authorization and serves Wisconsin as a State Trooper," Christopher said. "Now the same government that authorized him to work has locked him up."

Christopher says he plans to seek Van Der Merwe's release on bond, a process expected to take about two weeks, and has called on the Department of Homeland Security and Wisconsin's congressional delegation to act.

text:
It also signals an aggressive doubling-down by the president, after losses of Republican majorities in the House and Senate that served as a rebuke of Mr. Trump’s handling of issues ranging from the economy to the war with Iran to tariffs to his push for a mid-decade redistricting effort.

“I wanted to make a change,” Mr. Trump told reporters as he departed the White House for a trip to Florida. She had done a “great job,” he said. “Sometimes in life you have to make moves,” he added.

Asked what he wanted Mr. Miller to do differently than Ms. Wiles, who he had previously claimed wasn’t going anywhere, the president said, “Just run things well.”

The Republican wipeout had further inflamed tensions within the administration, with officials bracing for a slew of congressional investigations by Democrats and turnover in the West Wing and the cabinet.

Mr. Trump’s decision elevates one of the most deeply ideological members of the White House, someone known for flexing his power, to a prime role. Mr. Miller is one of the few people in the current West Wing who spent years preparing for a second Trump term from the standpoint of executive power, and who knows how the levers of government function. He is also one of two top West Wing staff members to have been part of the first administration when the House majority flipped in 2018, prompting a blitz of subpoenas from Congress.

People familiar with his views say he is likely to steer the president away from his early instinct after Tuesday’s losses to seek deals with Democrats. That could involve leaning even more into culture war issues, such as hard-line immigration enforcement and efforts to target diversity initiatives.

“Stephen is and always has been the eternal flame of the MAGA movement — putting the president’s words and policy into action,” Hunter Morgen, who worked as a deputy to Mr. Miller during the president’s first term and is now a lobbyist at Ballard Partners, wrote in a text message. “Since the earliest days of the 2016 campaign, he has been a steadfast torchbearer of the president’s agenda.”

In the short term, Mr. Miller’s focus is said to be the Iran war, which has been viewed by the president’s base as a betrayal of the president’s campaign promises.

Mr. Miller has relationships with some of the key cabinet officials involved in Mr. Trump’s top priorities, such as Attorney General Todd Blanche, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. His arrival may help Mr. Hegseth, at least in the short term, as the president has heard myriad complaints about him from Republicans on Capitol Hill.

Mr. Hegseth celebrated Mr. Miller’s promotion with several posts on social media. “Huge CONGRATS,” he wrote, calling Mr. Miller “a true patriot and America First fighter.” He followed that up with a post that said, “Patriots in control,” and a subsequent one that included a picture of himself and Mr. Miller.

Mr. Trump, in his private conversations as well as his public remarks, has not accepted blame for the election results.

Instead, he repeatedly blasted Ms. Wiles and his other political advisers, insisting he was poorly served in the lead-up to the midterms. He criticized Ms. Wiles in front of several people at an East Room election watch party this week, according to people with knowledge of the incident, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe internal conversations.

Mr. Trump has also been privately critical of James Blair, Ms. Wiles’s ally, who ran the president’s outside political operation, people with knowledge of the comments said. And for the last several months, Mr. Trump has berated Ms. Wiles in front of other staff members about his frustrations that his administration has not moved faster to find people he brands as “leakers,” as well as the stalled prosecutions of his perceived political enemies, they said. In front of several advisers, he would accuse her of being among the leakers.

Allies of Ms. Wiles described her as prepared to leave her role. Her supporters saw the criticism of her as an effort to assign blame for a political strategy largely driven by Mr. Trump himself. And they faulted her detractors inside and outside the administration for spreading information meant to undercut her with Mr. Trump, including stories about her daughter’s lobbying work.

In her own statement posted on social media, Ms. Wiles described working for Mr. Trump in the White House as the “honor of a lifetime.”

“While my role may be changing, my commitment to the President and the mission never will,” she added.

Ms. Wiles, the first woman to hold the top staff job in the West Wing, helped steer Mr. Trump to his election victory in 2024, playing a central role in his return to power four years after his loss to Joseph R. Biden Jr.

She was diagnosed with breast cancer in early 2026. Ms. Wiles stayed in her role as she started treatment and recently announced that she was cancer free.

Ms. Wiles came into the job having established a rapport with Mr. Trump and a level of trust that none of his four first-term chiefs of staff had enjoyed.

Unlike some of Mr. Trump’s previous chiefs of staff, Ms. Wiles made clear she did not consider her job as trying to fundamentally change the president. But she tried to influence his decisions on core issues including his immigration crackdown, even if only on the margins, according to people with knowledge of her role. She pushed for the appointments of Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, and both have been seen by many outside the government as stabilizing figures.

But Mr. Trump has relied primarily on his own instincts this term, and few advisers have engaged him in the kind of direct confrontations over policy that characterized his first administration.

Mr. Trump has publicly expressed his confidence in Ms. Wiles in recent months. But behind the scenes, there were signs that her standing with the president was shaky, according to officials with knowledge of the dynamics.

Mr. Trump began cutting Ms. Wiles out of hiring decisions, including when he chose an inexperienced television pundit to replace the departing press secretary, Karoline Leavitt.

And Mr. Trump started to criticize his chief of staff in front of other staff members, including over decisions he had approved, according to people familiar with his remarks.

After the elections, Mr. Trump made it clear to some advisers that he was unhappy with Ms. Wiles and his political team, who persuaded him to sign off on his super PAC’s spending $400 million to help Republicans in the midterms. The president had been reluctant to approve the spending and agreed to it only in September.

text:
Stephen Miller, Donald Trump’s most controversial aide and the architect of his sweeping immigration crackdown, will become his new White House chief of staff days after Republicans lost control of the US Congress in US midterm elections.

The president announced the extraordinary appointment on Friday, confirming that Susie Wiles – his current chief of staff, and the first woman to serve in the role – had been ousted.

In a social media ‌post, Trump called Miller, 41, “one of ​my most trusted advisors” and praised Wiles for doing “an ⁠outstanding job”. Miller will begin on Monday.

Wiles, 69, reportedly handed in her resignation on Thursday night and said in a social media post that serving Trump “has been the honor of a lifetime”.

Holding an umbrella, Trump emerged from the White House South Portico on Friday for a trip to Florida. “I wanted to make a change,” he said. “I think Susie’s done a very good job ... Stephen’s been great, and we’ve got to make moves.”

“Stephen’s been with me from the beginning. He gets it,” the president said. “Very good politically and he’s a very good man. He’ll do a great job. Great manager.”

Trump then boarded the Marine One helicopter, followed by Miller, secretary of state Marco Rubio and close aide Natalie Harp.

In a statement, Wiles added: “I’m so proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First.”

She said her commitment to “the President and the mission” will not change.

Miller’s appointment is the first sign of a shake-up at the White House following Republicans’ catastrophic defeat in the midterms. His record as a far-right firebrand implies that Trump is preparing for an aggressive fight against congressional Democrats’ oversight and investigations.

Chris Whipple, author of The Gatekeepers: How the White House Chiefs of Staff Define Every Presidency, told CNN: “It’s almost a declaration of war by Trump … He [Miller] only knows one gear and that’s full-throttle, full steam ahead over the cliff.”

David Axelrod, a veteran Democratic strategist, added on X: “For those who hoped the @POTUS might pivot to work with the incoming Congress, the appointment of Miller is a bucket of ICE cold water.”

Miller is one of the most polarising figures in the administration and one of Trump’s closest and longest-serving advisers, having joined his 2016 presidential campaign as a speechwriter. He is a former aide to the former senator Jeff Sessions of Alabama, who would go on to serve as Trump’s first attorney general.

In Trump’s first term, Miller was the driving force behind policies such as family separation and a travel ban on Muslim-majority countries. More than a hundred Democrats in Congress signed a letter to Trump calling Miller a “documented white nationalist” and demanding his removal.

A biography of Miller, written by journalist Jean Guerrero in 2020, was entitled Hatemonger.

Miller has served as deputy chief of staff since Trump’s return to the presidency in January 2025. He had been hugely influential in hardline immigration policies and demanding an end to birthright citizenship. He is also one Trump’s most ardent, outspoken and pugnacious defenders.

Appearing on Sean Hannity’s Fox News show on Monday, just before the midterms, Miller said of the president: “He saved America from a corrupt political class. He saved America from open borders. He saved America from countries that want the American way of life to end, from foreign adversaries, from domestic adversaries.”

Miller added: “President Trump took a bullet for you, he bled for you, he faced life in prison for you. And what he needs from you tomorrow is your vote.”

Wiles is the longest-serving White House chief of staff for Trump, who cycled through four of them during his first four-year term.

Wiles led Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign to victory and was credited with bringing discipline to a chaotic effort and clamping down on leaks from his second administration.

The Florida operative generally shunned the limelight. At Trump’s 2024 election night victory party, she repeatedly shook her head and avoided the microphone as Trump tried to coax her to speak to the crowd.

But Wiles made headlines last year when Vanity Fair magazine published a series of interviews with her and other top Trump administration officials. Her comments stood out for their candour, including her observation that Trump has an “alcoholic’s personality”.

Her departure came months after she indicated she no longer showed evidence of breast cancer after she underwent months of treatment for the disease. She went public with the diagnosis in March.

Critics said Miller’s appointment showed that Trump had learned the wrong lessons from Tuesday’s electoral reckoning.

Becca Balint, a Democratic congresswoman from Vermont, posted on X: “On Tuesday, the American people rose up and overwhelmingly voted in opposition to the disgusting and inhumane policies of this second Trump administration. What does Trump do? He promotes Stephen Miller – the architect of some of this administration’s worst decisions. Sickening.”

title: Rights on the Ballot Alongside US Congressional Elections
description:
Alongside the high-profile congressional and gubernatorial races decided during the United States midterm elections on November 3, human rights were at issue in several state and local ballot measures across the country.
Vermont voters approved an amendment providing equal protection to individuals regardless of their race, ethnicity, sex, religion, disability, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression or national origin.
Ballot measures on transgender rights also showed mixed results.
Colorado voters rejected a measure that would have required state and local law enforcement to coordinate with federal immigration authorities in some circumstances.
The US Congressional elections may be the biggest story of the week, but voters took up some important human rights issues directly in these initiatives and the impacts will be felt for years to come.
text:
Alongside the high-profile congressional and gubernatorial races decided during the United States midterm elections on November 3, human rights were at issue in several state and local ballot measures across the country.

In Virginia, voters adopted a measure to automatically restore voting rights to people with felony convictions upon release from prison, ending a lifetime ban that had been in place since the Jim Crow era.

Arizona voters rejected and Wisconsin voters approved measures to end diversity, equity, and inclusion practices in education, employment, contracts, and administration, mirroring Trump administration initiatives to dismantle programs to address ongoing impacts of historical discrimination based on race and ethnicity. Vermont voters approved an amendment providing equal protection to individuals regardless of their race, ethnicity, sex, religion, disability, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression or national origin.

Meanwhile, Missouri voters rejected an effort to restrict the right to abortion care and measures to safeguard abortion rights were successful in Nevada and Virginia but failed in Idaho.

Ballot measures on transgender rights also showed mixed results. In Colorado, voters adopted a measure to ban gender-affirming surgeries for youth under 18. In Missouri, one of 27 US states to have a ban on gender-affirming care for youth, voters opted to keep the ban out of the state’s constitution.

Virginia voters approved an amendment formally lifting the state’s obsolete ban on same-sex marriage and affirming that two adults may marry regardless of sex, gender, and race.

Immigration-related measures were also on several ballots. Colorado voters rejected a measure that would have required state and local law enforcement to coordinate with federal immigration authorities in some circumstances. Voters in Honolulu, Hawaii were consulted on a measure requiring their police department to ensure the constitutional rights of all persons regardless of immigration or citizenship status, and work with federal agents only when required by statute or a court order, though the results are still to be decided. And voters in Chicago, Illinois, said they agreed that the city should seek financial compensation from the federal government for harm caused by immigration enforcement operations.

The US Congressional elections may be the biggest story of the week, but voters took up some important human rights issues directly in these initiatives and the impacts will be felt for years to come.

He also served as homeland security adviser at the White House, giving him a perch from which to coordinate with other agencies across the government.
In addition to Trump, Wiles also ran incumbent Sen. Rick Scott’s 2010 campaign for Florida governor and briefly served as manager of former Utah Gov.
The Wiles interviews stuck out for their candor, which is unusual for a sitting White House chief of staff.
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump said Friday that Stephen Miller was replacing Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff, installing as his closest adviser a loyal, combative bulldog for his “America First” agenda as the president prepares to stare down a newly empowered Democratic Congress next year.

Miller, long a key member of Trump’s inner circle, is a key architect of the administration’s hard-line immigration policies. He is one of Trump’s longest-serving aides, joining his long-shot 2016 presidential campaign as a speechwriter. He most recently has served as White House deputy chief of staff for policy and oversees a broad portfolio, though he is best known for his role in Trump’s immigration policy.

The staff shuffle signals that Trump, whose Republican Party was handed monumental defeats in Tuesday's midterm elections, is resisting a conciliatory approach to Democratic lawmakers who are eager to investigate the administration — including Miller himself as a top target. Miller, 41, is a dogged defender of Trump and has built a deep and sophisticated understanding of a president's executive power and how the federal government operates, portending a potential burst of executive actions in the final two years of Trump's presidency.

Wiles gave Trump her resignation on Thursday night, a person familiar with the events told the Associated Press, speaking on condition of anonymity to describe the private conversation. Trump praised Wiles and said she’d continue to work for his political organization.

Wiles, the steely political operator and longtime adviser to Trump, was the first woman to ever serve in that post and the longest-serving White House chief of staff for Trump, who cycled through four of them during his first four-year term.

“Serving President Trump in the White House has been the honor of a lifetime. I’m so proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First,” Wiles said in a social media post shortly after Trump’s announcement.

The departure also came months after Wiles indicated she no longer showed evidence of breast cancer after she underwent months of treatment for the disease, a diagnosis she went public with in March 2026.

Miller is tied to immigration policies that voters said went too far

During the midterm campaign, Miller took frequent partisan swipes at Democrats, calling them “extremists, freaks and America-hating lunatics” on social media and promoting unfounded theories about election fraud in California and Alaska.

He has been a major part of the Trump administration’s anti-fraud task force targeting benefit programs and a decision to suspend Microsoft and others from a green card program. He also served as homeland security adviser at the White House, giving him a perch from which to coordinate with other agencies across the government.

He joined Trump on Friday for his trip to Florida, and the president noted to reporters that "Stephen has been with me from the beginning.

"He gets it; very good politically," Trump said as he departed the White House. "He’ll do a great job. Great manager.”

But the immigration policies that Miller is so closely associated with were a major liability for Republicans during the just-wrapped election. The midterm AP Voter Poll found that most voters, about 6 in 10, said the administration’s immigration enforcement actions had gone too far and that they “somewhat” or “strongly” disapproved of how Immigration and Customs Enforcement had handled its responsibilities.

“Just days after the American people rejected his corrupt and lawless presidency, Donald Trump is doubling down,” said Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., who is set to become chairman of the powerful House Oversight Committee. “Stephen Miller is the architect of the unconstitutional ICE raids that have terrorized our communities and kidnapped and killed American citizens and immigrant families.”

In a statement, Garcia added: “Stephen Miller should lawyer up.”

Wiles brought order to Trump’s campaign

Trump on Friday praised Wiles, the veteran Florida operative who joined Trump’s team during his 2016 presidential bid, as having done a “very good job, great job.”

But he added, “Sometimes in life, you have to make moves.”

Wiles, 69, is the second woman to lead Trump’s presidential campaign to victory, although she never embraced the formal title of campaign manager.

She has been credited with steering the most disciplined of his three presidential bids, and Trump himself has said he was often told that Wiles led his “best-run campaign.” Often called the “ice maiden” by the president, she was seen as the no-brainer choice to serve as White House chief of staff at the start of his second term.

Wiles stuck with the job even after her breast cancer diagnosis. Deep into the midterm campaign, six months after having revealed her diagnosis, she said she was “cancer-free,” indicating she no longer showed evidence of cancer after her pathology results came back clear.

In a rare interview, Wiles told Fox News Digital last month that she hadn’t been planning on getting the mammogram that ultimately detected her cancer. Her doctor suggested she do the exam anyway, because a mammogram machine was available that day and her schedule was too busy and unpredictable.

Wiles, the daughter of the late NFL player-turned-broadcaster Pat Summerall, cut her reputation as someone who brought discipline to the president’s chaotic style and shunned the spotlight, so much so that at Trump’s 2024 election night victory party, she repeatedly shook her head and avoided the microphone as Trump tried to coax her to speak to the crowd.

In addition to Trump, Wiles also ran incumbent Sen. Rick Scott’s 2010 campaign for Florida governor and briefly served as manager of former Utah Gov. Jon Huntsman’s 2012 presidential campaign. She spearheaded Ron DeSantis ’ successful run for governor in 2018, but DeSantis would eventually urge the Trump campaign in 2020 to cut ties with Wiles, creating a rift that led to a particularly vicious effort by those in Trump’s orbit to mock DeSantis throughout his failed run for the Republican presidential nomination against Trump in 2024.

Wiles once said Trump had ‘an alcoholic’s personality'

But in December 2025, nearing the end of Trump’s first year back as president, Wiles became the headline when Vanity Fair magazine published a series of interviews with her and other top Trump administration officials conducted by the author Chris Whipple, an expert on White House chiefs of staff.

The Wiles interviews stuck out for their candor, which is unusual for a sitting White House chief of staff. She said Trump has an “alcoholic’s personality,” although the president does not drink, and said then-Attorney General Pam Bondi had “whiffed” in her handling of the Jeffrey Epstein files while remarking that Vice President JD Vance has been a “conspiracy theorist for about a decade.”

Trump and other administration aides rushed to defend Wiles, who, in turn, disparaged Vanity Fair for publishing what she called a “disingenuously framed hit piece,” though she did not deny making the comments.

In the interviews, which were conducted over a period of several months, Wiles also revealed a bit of her management style, saying she was “not an enabler.”

“I try to be thoughtful about what I even engage in,” Wiles said. “I guess time will tell whether I’ve been effective.”

___

Associated Press writers Michelle L. Price in Washington and Jill Colvin in New York contributed to this report.

A Wisconsin state trooper has been detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement and is facing deportation to South Africa, according to his lawyer.

Aaron Van Der Merwe, 21, was detained Thursday as he was waiting to board a domestic flight, according to a statement issued by law firm Christopher & De León.

Van Der Merwe told ICE officers he had a work permit and a pending asylum application.

“According to Van Der Merwe, the officers said they did not care, placed him in handcuffs and shackles, and transported him to immigration detention in Dodge County,” the law firm said.

An ICE database shows Van Der Merwe is currently being held at a detention facility in Juneau, Wisconsin.

According to the law firm, Van Der Merwe came to the U.S. legally from South Africa as a child and has waited seven years for an asylum interview. He has a valid work permit that expires in 2030, his lawyer said.

The Department of Homeland Security said ICE arrested him during a targeted enforcement operation at the Dane County Regional Airport in Madison. DHS said he came to the U.S. legally in March 2019 and only had permission to stay until September of 2019.

“In defiance of our nation’s laws, he overstayed his admission. This illegal alien will receive due process and remain in ICE custody pending removal proceedings,” a DHS spokesperson said in a statement.

“DHS reversed the horrendous Biden-era policy that allowed aliens in our country illegally to jet around our country. Under President Trump, DHS will no longer tolerate this. This administration is working diligently to ensure that aliens in our country illegally can no longer fly unless it is out of our country to self-deport,” the spokesperson said.

Attorney Marc Christopher said he will seek his client's release on bond.

“This is inhumane and despicable,” Christopher said in a statement. “Putting a Wisconsin State Trooper behind bars while his asylum case sits unresolved does not make our communities safer. Wisconsin’s congressional delegation should demand his release and demand answers.”
