text:
H.R. 1 compels states to enforce unprecedented new work requirements or lose all Medicaid funding — fundamentally changes Medicaid from a healthcare program to a work program that leverages healthcare for compliance

Changes Congress passed and Trump HHS is implementing constitute unconstitutional coercion of states — AG Ellison argues court should allow Minnesota to opt out of work requirements without losing Medicaid funding

Hundreds of thousands of eligible Minnesotans could lose healthcare coverage just because of Congress’s new red tape, straining Minnesota’s healthcare system and leading to more serious illness and deaths

November 6, 2026 (SAINT PAUL) — Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison late yesterday filed a lawsuit to block the Trump Administration from compelling Minnesota to enforce unprecedented new work requirements for receiving Medicaid or risk losing all Minnesota’s Medicaid funding. Strict new requirements, which Congress passed in H.R. 1 and are supposed to be implemented in 2027, would force more than hundreds of thousands of Minnesotans to cut through onerous bureaucratic red tape a regular basis to prove they meet the work requirements just to keep their health insurance, which Medicaid recipients have never been required to do before.

In the lawsuit, Attorney General Ellison and the attorneys general of New Mexico, Oregon, and Washington argue that the radical new requirements fundamentally transform Medicaid from a federally funded program to ensure that low-income people have access to healthcare into a federal work program that leverages access to healthcare for compliance. They argue that consistent with a significant 2012 U.S. Supreme Court decision, this dramatic change in the states’ 60-year Medicaid compact with the federal government means states cannot be compelled to comply with these eligibility changes and that the financial penalty Congress imposed for not complying with them — a loss of all Medicare funding — constitutes unconstitutional coercion on the states and exceeds Congress’s spending power.

In Minnesota, 1.2 million people — or about one every five Minnesotans — rely on Medicaid, known in Minnesota as Medical Assistance, for their healthcare. Medicaid’s coverage includes children and families, pregnant women, adults without children, seniors, and people who are blind or have disabilities. Its members include some of the most vulnerable residents in the state, such as those experiencing homelessness, living with significant disabilities, or who have a serious or complex medical condition.

The new work requirements, which have never existed in the six decades that Medicaid has helped ensure that low-income and vulnerable Americans can receive necessary healthcare no matter their economic circumstances, could lead to hundreds of thousands of Minnesotans losing their healthcare. This would produce enormous strain on the healthcare system throughout Minnesota, as well on strain on state and local governments, and would lead to more serious illnesses and more deaths.

“It’s bad enough that H.R. 1 robs one trillion dollars from Americans’ healthcare — one trillion — and gives it away to billionaires. It’s just as bad that this ugly bill’s unprecedented changes to Medicaid eligibility fundamentally transform the very nature of Medicaid from ensuring low-income can get healthcare into a system that withholds a person’s basic healthcare needs as a means to incentivize behavior. It’s a bait-and-switch and it’s unconstitutional,” Attorney General Ellison said. “This cruel bill, and the cruel former majorities in Congress that passed it, could push hundreds of Minnesotans off their healthcare and into ill health or worse — and that hurts us all. I’m determined to keep this from happening to people.”

Medicaid, Medicaid expansion, and impacts of H.R. 1

Congress created the Medicaid program in 1965 as a federal-state partnership. The program’s promise was straightforward: States that chose to participate would contribute administrative and financial resources, and the federal government would do the same, all with the goal of promoting healthcare coverage for the neediest among us. Over the next 40 years, every state joined, and the program was incrementally expanded to include new categories of eligibility in pursuit of its original objective.

Then in 2010, Congress enacted the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act (ACA), which marked a major change: it expanded Medicaid to include the nation’s entire non-elderly population below 133 percent of the federal poverty level. However, in a significant 2012 decision in National Federation of Independent Business v. Sebelius, or NFIB, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that Congress could not force states to participate in Medicaid expansion. Minnesota, however, did choose to participate in Medicaid expansion and has done so for the last 12 years.

As with the original Medicaid program, states like Minnesota that chose to participate in the ACA expansion opted into something like a contract: the states agreed to restructure their Medicaid programs and dedicate substantial administrative and financial resources to implementing the new program; in exchange, the federal government provided a large infusion of funding so that the states could increase the number of their residents covered by health insurance.

In 2025, the terms of these two deals took a dramatic turn when Congress enacted H.R. 1, commonly known as the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act.” H.R. 1 superimposes a new eligibility system on Medicaid that, for the first time in the program’s 60-year history, will make healthcare coverage contingent on work. H.R. 1 will also significantly shrink the Medicaid program by threatening to throw millions of beneficiaries out of it. This will happen either because those beneficiaries failed to work sufficient hours or, in many cases, because they simply failed to navigate the bureaucratic process of documenting their work or demonstrating an exemption. Since most of those disenrolled will lack any alternative source of healthcare coverage, they will lose access to treatment for chronic conditions, preventative medicine, and most other routine medical care. The inevitable results will include increasing strain on hospitals from uncompensated emergency visits, diminished public resources, higher rates of uncontrolled disease, and eventually, preventable deaths.

H.R. 1’s unprecedented new Medicaid eligibility system also puts States that signed up for Medicaid and the ACA expansion in a bind. Minnesota and the states — not the federal government — will tasked with enforcing this new eligibility system by finding beneficiaries subject to the requirement who cannot document whether they satisfied it. And Minnesota and the states, not Congress or the Trump Administration, will have to deliver the bad news to those disenrolled.

But Minnesota does not have a realistic option to decline this policy. If the state fails to implement it, then under H.R. 1, Minnesota will lose all Medicaid funding — a threat the Supreme Court previously characterized in its 2012 NFIB decision as “a gun to the head.” Nor could Minnesota realistically try to evade the work requirement by opting out of ACA expansion: in Minnesota, ACA expansion accounts for a large share of the state’s total federal Medicaid funding. Having already built up the expectations of residents who have come to rely on coverage from the expansion — and having also invested substantial administrative resources into implementing that policy — it is simply too late for Minnesota to back out, even if the state was willingto abandon the ACA’s promise of increasing health coverage.

Attorney General Ellison and the coalition argue therefore that the financial penalty accompanying H.R. 1’s work requirement is unconstitutionally coercive and exceeds Congress’s spending power. In NFIB, the Court held that Congress could not compel States to join the ACA expansion by threatening their existing Medicaid funding because that expansion was effectively a new program, not a mere alteration of the original one. That rationale applies here here: to quote from NFIB, H.R. 1’s work requirement will “dramatically” change Medicaid by “surprising” States with a “shift in kind, not merely degree” around Medicaid eligibility. Under the legislation’s new system, Medicaid “is no longer a program to care for the neediest among us,” but instead will be “transformed into a program” that, for the first time in its 60-year history, is designed to promote work by leveraging healthcare.

H.R. 1 therefore imposes a more radical transformation than even the ACA expansion: while the latter merely broadened eligibility, H.R. 1 requires state agencies to rebuild their eligibility systems to scrutinize beneficiaries’ occupations — a task that bears no relationship to the objective of Medicaid or the eligibility criteria that previously governed it. Again quoting the Supreme Court from its 2012 NFIB decision, Congress therefore cannot “penalize” States that decline implement this new eligibility system “by taking away their existing Medicaid funding.” Any other result would “threaten the political accountability key to our federal system,” because under these circumstances, States lack “a legitimate choice whether to accept the federal conditions in exchange for federal funds.”

For these reasons, Attorney General Ellison and the coalition are asking the court to rule that it would be unconstitutional for the federal government to withhold Medicaid funding from their states, including Minnesota, if they decline to implement H.R. 1’s work requirement. The court should rule that consistent with the Supreme Court’s finding in NFIB, state participation in H.R. 1’s unprecedented new eligibility system should be optional.

text:
Physicians for Human Rights (PHR) today called on the incoming U.S. Congress to protect fundamental rights through stronger oversight and science-based policymaking. The new Congress has both an important opportunity and a responsibility to act.

Our Mission

For 40 years, PHR has wielded medical evidence for human rights and justice. Across administrations and political circumstances, our mission has remained steadfast: to ensure that medical and scientific evidence informs decisions affecting people’s lives and to hold perpetrators of human rights violations accountable.

Priorities for the Next Congress

PHR calls on the next Congress to advance the following priorities:

Defend human rights and public health: Uphold the fundamental right to health, protect access to essential medical care, defend the independence of health professionals, and ensure that government policies are grounded in science, medical ethics, and respect for human dignity. Restore the scientific independence and decision-making capacity of health agencies, including the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

Protect asylum seekers and immigrants in detention: Strengthen oversight of immigration detention, including by investigating preventable deaths, medical neglect, and solitary confinement. Improve medical care in detention facilities and restore Department of Homeland Security (DHS) oversight mechanisms. End immigration enforcement actions that harm health and terrorize families and communities. Protect people from torture, including their right to seek asylum and protection from forced return to danger, while ending removals to third countries.

Protect the right to protest: Defend the right to peaceful assembly and expression, investigate excessive force by law enforcement, and establish stronger protections against the misuse of dangerous crowd-control weapons, including during immigration enforcement operations and public demonstrations.

Advance reproductive justice: Protect access to comprehensive reproductive health care, including emergency medical treatment and medication abortion. Ensure that patients can make decisions about their health and reproductive futures without discrimination or political interference, and that clinicians can fulfill their professional obligations without legal risk.

Protect civilians in conflict zones: Strengthen U.S. leadership in ending gender-based violence and protecting civilians, health workers, and medical facilities during armed conflict. Uphold and promote international humanitarian law, including in conflicts like Ethiopia, Gaza, and Ukraine. Support independent domestic investigations into violations of the laws of war, and where necessary, support regional and international accountability measures and advance accountability for attacks on health care, conflict-related sexual and reproductive violence, and other human rights abuses.

Restore U.S. global health assistance: Rebuild U.S. investments in lifesaving global health programs and restore essential services disrupted by funding cuts. Ensure that U.S. global health assistance prioritizes health outcomes and equitable access to care. Investigate and ensure accountability for the predictable harms of U.S. global health cuts to date.

End the assault on human rights and global health institutions: Reverse U.S. sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) and end interference in the ICC’s vital work for survivors of atrocities. Restore and strengthen U.S. engagement with multilateral organizations including the United Nations (UN) and World Health Organization (WHO).

Evidence for Action

PHR has spent the last two years and beyond gathering data and documenting harms in many situations where the U.S. government abdicated its long-standing role in monitoring and research. We have investigated violations ranging from the consequences of U.S. global health cuts to the injuries caused by law enforcement abuse during protests to the surging death rate in immigration detention. PHR’s unique data can now be harnessed for advocacy, accountability, and reform. In the months ahead, PHR will mobilize its community of medical, scientific, and legal experts to advance policies grounded in health, dignity, and rights.

Working Together

PHR stands ready to work with policymakers across the political spectrum and officials across branches of the U.S. and state governments to bring rigorous medical evidence, the expertise of health professionals, and the experiences of affected communities into the policymaking process. Effective oversight, independent investigations, and meaningful legislative protections can save lives, prevent abuses, and deliver sustainable improvements.

As a new Congress prepares to take office, PHR will continue mobilizing medical evidence for justice – and working to ensure that this moment of political change becomes an opportunity for meaningful human rights progress.

title: Belgium approves home raids for migration enforcement - InfoMigrants
description:
The government presents the measure as a narrowly targeted tool for enforcing removal decisions, but human rights groups say it risks turning private homes into sites of immigration enforcement.
The legislation is part of a broader push by Prime Minister Bart De Wever’s right-leaning coalition to limit migration and increase expulsions of people denied the right to stay in Belgium.
Rights groups argue that this makes the Belgian vote part of a wider European shift toward more coercive migration control.
Amnesty International argues that the law should also be understood in a social and economic context.
In its statement, Dissanayake said politicians should not use migration enforcement to divert attention from insecurity affecting the wider population.
text:
Belgium’s parliament has approved a law allowing police to enter private homes between 5 am and 9 am to detain foreign nationals facing deportation, after a debate that stretched into the early hours of Friday morning. The measure has reignited concerns over privacy, family life and due process at a time when the European Union is considering more coercive return rules.

The law allows the Immigration Office to ask an investigating judge to authorize police to enter a residence where a person may be staying who has been denied asylum, ignored an order to leave Belgium and is considered a threat to public order or national security. Police may search for identity documents and detain the person for removal, with immigration officials present.

The power also extends to homes where the person is staying with relatives, friends or other hosts. The government presents the measure as a narrowly targeted tool for enforcing removal decisions, but human rights groups say it risks turning private homes into sites of immigration enforcement.

Critics argue that the threshold of a “threat to public order or national security” is not defined clearly enough, creating uncertainty about how the power will be applied. The government, however, presents the measure as a narrowly targeted tool for enforcing removal decisions.

The legislation is part of a broader push by Prime Minister Bart De Wever’s right-leaning coalition to limit migration and increase expulsions of people denied the right to stay in Belgium.

Read Also

Brussels proposes turning Frontex into the EU’s central returns agency

A vote during a government crisis

The law passed while Belgium’s governing “Arizona” coalition faces one of its most serious tests since taking office, The Brussels Times reported. Earlier this week, De Wever submitted his government’s resignation to King Philippe after coalition talks on the 2027 budget and a package of fiscal measures worth about 10 billion euros by 2029 ended without agreement.

The King has kept the resignation under consideration while consulting the leaders of the five-party coalition -- De Wever’s conservative Flemish nationalist N-VA, the liberal MR, the centrist Les Engages, the social democratic Vooruit and the Christian democratic CD&V.

The governing coalition and the liberal opposition party Anders backed the law. Asylum and Migration Minister Anneleen Van Bossuyt told Le Soir that it fills a gap by providing a tool to execute certain removal orders, while Les Engages group leader Aurore Tourneur said the final text’s conditions are “strict and cumulative.”

Read Also

France confirms talks with Taliban to deport Afghan nationals

Amnesty International: ‘bound to sow fear’

Ahead of the vote, Amnesty International warned that the legislation would have consequences beyond the people directly targeted. Dinushika Dissanayake, the organization’s deputy regional director, said the proposals were “bound to sow fear and division.”

She warned of intrusions into private and family life "irrespective of whether children are present," saying the bill offered no effective means to challenge home-entry decisions.

Dissanayake also highlighted the potential effect on people who provide accommodation or other support to migrants, including friends and relatives.

“Belgium has a strong tradition of showing solidarity toward migrant communities, with many people opening their doors and homes to offer beds, food and support -- as is their prerogative. This will discourage people from doing so in future.”

In addition, she stressed that these proposals "will tear communities apart and make everyday life more dangerous, complicated and frightening for ordinary people” Amnesty urged lawmakers to reject the bill and any attempt to "scapegoat migrants."

Sotieta Ngo, executive director of CIRE, said the bill violated the constitutional principle that the home is inviolable. “It’s an attack against human dignity. It’s an attack against solidarity.”

Read Also

Germany deports 40 Afghans amid continued criticism from rights groups

The EU Return Regulation

The Belgian debate also has a European dimension. In October, EU governments adopted the Return Regulation, establishing a common system for returning third-country nationals who do not have a legal right to remain in the EU.

The regulation is intended to make returns more effective by strengthening cooperation with countries of origin and transit, expanding border surveillance and accelerating removal procedures. It forms part of a wider EU effort to reinforce external borders and increase Frontex’s role in returns.

Under the rules, detention can become the default for people issued deportation decisions, potentially for up to two and a half years. The regulation also expands obligations, surveillance and sanctions on people subject to deportation, including requirements that may be difficult to meet for people without identity documents or a fixed address.

Crucially for the Belgian debate, the regulation allows authorities to enter a person’s home or “other relevant premises” and seize belongings. Amnesty International says this could enable extensive surveillance, discriminatory policing and racial profiling.

Belgium’s law is national, but it reflects the direction of EU policy -- more enforcement, more home entry, more identity-document checks, and security-based exceptions to ordinary procedural protections. Rights groups argue that this makes the Belgian vote part of a wider European shift toward more coercive migration control.

Separately, the European Commission proposed expanding Frontex’s mandate on October 27, giving the EU border agency a larger role in coordinating deportations and supporting returns between non-EU countries. The plan would expand its standing corps to 30,000 officers and introduce social media monitoring; the Commission says it would improve operational effectiveness while maintaining rights protections. Amnesty International has warned that the proposed expansion could outpace human rights safeguards.

Read Also

Frontex’s new powers: more returns, less oversight?

More safeguards but concerns remain

The final text includes safeguards introduced after pressure from civil society and coalition partner Les Engages. Investigating judges have seven days, rather than five, to authorize a home visit, repeat requests require new information and judges may impose conditions where minors are present.

But the safeguards have not resolved concerns about how the law will operate in practice. Koen Dewulf, director of the Federal Migration Center Myria, told Le Soir that the definition of a threat to public order or national security remains vague and open to interpretation.

The Association of Investigating Judges has raised a separate objection. Its co-president, Jean-Louis Doyen, said authorizing home entry for an administrative deportation differs fundamentally from the criminal investigations that fall within an investigating judge’s usual remit.

Andrea Rea, chair of the board of CIRE, has also questioned the availability of remedies for undocumented migrants and the people hosting them. He warned that the legislation could face a challenge before Belgium’s Constitutional Court.

Belgium and the UK strike a deal to target Channel smuggling gangs

A wider political fight

The vote followed demonstrations across Belgium, including a human chain of around 3,000 people around Brussels’ Palace of Justice and more than 50 other gatherings nationwide.

Amnesty International argues that the law should also be understood in a social and economic context. In its statement, Dissanayake said politicians should not use migration enforcement to divert attention from insecurity affecting the wider population.

“At a time when the cost of living is soaring and economic insecurity is gripping millions across the country, politicians must not deflect attention by targeting one of the most marginalized groups in society.”

The law’s practical impact will depend on judicial interpretation, police guidance and possible constitutional challenges.

text:
GENEVA, November 6 (IPS) - A right under pressure No one disputes freedom of association. It is in the Constitutions of almost every country, the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Article 22 of the ICCPR, and in regional Articles in Europe, America, and Africa. What it has never had, at the universal level, is sincere implementation by governments.

Regional organisations and courts have filled that space in limited ways. Courts and human rights commissions have issued decisions that have not always been followed. States are left to interpret these obligations themselves for citizens and non-citizens in their jurisdiction.

Violations of the right to free association have risen 50% in two years, according to CIVICUS Monitor. The rise is not only a matter of scale. Governments are no longer relying mainly on administrative interference or political pressure to constrain civil society. They devise restrictive laws governing who can organise, on what terms, and access to resources. Restricting international funding for civil society, particularly through foreign agents’ laws, is now a global trend and poses unprecedented significant challenges. In 2025, restrictive laws affecting civic freedoms were recorded in at least 66 countries, the ninth most prevalent civic space violation worldwide.

The Committee is preparing to adopt General Comment No. 38 on Article 22 of the ICCPR, which guarantees everyone the right to freedom of association. General Comments are the Committee’s official interpretations of the Covenant. They clarify a right’s meaning and scope and set out how States may implement it. They serve as a reference point for national courts, litigators, and human rights institutions.

Rights and recognition for everyone

Article 22 clearly says everyone has the right to come together, but it does not specify who counts. On protest rights, General Comment No. 37 says all citizens and non-citizens hold the right, including migrants , asylum seekers, refugees and stateless people. Article 22 should follow the precedent.

Most of the world’s organising happens in grassroots movements, digital networks, and fluid conflict and humanitarian contexts, not with registered organisations. Restrictions fall hardest on those already excluded from decision-making and resources.

The article defines qualifications on national security, public order, and safeguards and rights of others. Without clarity, they have remained fluid since 1966. The Committee needs to clarify the scope.

States cannot be left to interpret the article. Amid rising authoritarianism and divisive politics impacting civic life and participatory governance, minorities and excluded people need strong freedom of association protection to defend their rights.

Registration is among the worst restrictions because authorities treat it as routine paperwork rather than a decision about whether a group may exist at all. The Committee should state plainly that registration means notifying the authorities, not asking permission, and that any procedure must be simple, quick, and free of official discretion. Organisations should not be required to comply with “national interest ” or meet disproportionate reporting demands. Penalties for administrative slip-ups should fit the offence, and only a court should be able to shut an organisation down, as a last resort.

Funding is critical for survival

Foreign agents’ laws have spread from a handful of states to dozens, with vague definitions of “foreign influence” and “political activity” that let officials choose their targets. These come with heavy reporting duties, frequent audits, and penalties ranging from fines to licence withdrawal and prison.

Other measures achieve the same effect without the label: prior approval for foreign grants, punitive taxes, or rules forcing funds through state-controlled accounts. Where foreign support is the only resource available, organisations will struggle to survive.

Funding is critical to securing freedom. The Committee should recognise the right to seek, receive and use resources from domestic, foreign and international sources, whether or not a group is registered.

Online and across borders

Groups now recruit, debate and organise online, so internet shutdowns and surveillance strike directly at freedom of association. Governments imposed a record 313 shutdowns in 2025, up from 304 the year before, according to Access Now, and people in 100 countries have lived through one since tracking began. Blanket shutdowns are disproportionate, even in conflict zones.

Governments increasingly pursue critics abroad through surveillance, harassment of relatives back home, misuse of Interpol and stripping of nationality, cutting exiles off from organisations at home. This transnational repression is also a restriction on association and should be named.

No justification without limits

In dozens of countries, counter-terrorism laws criminalise people for exercising basic freedoms. A government’s own definition of “security” cannot override its treaty obligations, and none of these grounds justifies criminalising organisations for lawful work. Emergency powers follow the same pattern.

At least 50 states restricted freedom of association during the pandemic, and many of those measures outlasted the crisis, as independent UN human rights experts warned they might. The Committee should set out categories of emergency and the limits each can justify, matching the real scale of the threat.

Enabling environment without

Governments must also create the conditions for civil society to thrive, including laws that meet international standards, access to information, a real say in decisions and lasting access to resources. A good law achieves little if officials publicly smear the groups it protects.

That means protecting people from intimidation, arbitrary arrest, smear campaigns, travel bans and reprisals for cooperating with the UN. Freedom of association cannot be separated from freedom of expression and peaceful assembly. According to the CIVICUS Monitor, just 7% of the world’s population lives in countries where these civic freedoms are broadly respected.

Building on regional courts

The European Court of Human Rights has built a rich body of case law treating freedom of association as essential to a pluralist democracy. In 2020, the EU’s Court of Justice struck down Hungary’s 2017 law on foreign-funded organisations as incompatible with freedom of association. The African and Inter-American human rights commissions have also set progressive standards.

But these rulings apply only within their regions, and even there, groups defending minority rights or exposing sensitive issues still come under attack. A universal standard would give everyone, everywhere, something to invoke.

Sixty years, one opportunity

Article 22 has waited, and the wait has had consequences. Restrictive laws survive because the standard is vague enough to accommodate them: a registration regime is presented as administration, a funding restriction as transparency, a ban as security. At the global level, nothing has tested those claims.

General Comment No. 38 can change that. It can give parliaments, courts and governments the detail they need to draft laws, interpret them and respect the limits of their power, at a moment when restrictions are spreading faster than the standards meant to contain them.

Freedom of association is a right that makes other freedoms enforceable. The Covenants turn sixty this year. At this critical juncture, the Committee must give it the clarity it deserves.

Sigrid Lipott is an international treaties specialist and the UN adviser at CIVICUS. Based in Geneva, Switzerland, she leads CIVICUS’s engagement with UN human rights mechanisms. CIVICUS is a global alliance of more than 17,000 civil society organisations and activists from 175 countries working to strengthen citizen action and defend civic freedoms worldwide.

text:
ALBANY, N.Y. — A federal judge has denied a request by 15 sheriffs, including the Wayne County sheriff, to block a New York State law that bans law enforcement from making agreements with federal immigration agents.

The sheriffs filed a lawsuit against Gov. Kathy Hochul’s administration in August over the “Local Cops, Local Crimes” Act. Wayne County Sheriff Robert Milby told News10NBC that he joined the lawsuit because he believes the law violates his independence as an elected sheriff.

U.S. District Judge Mae D’Agostino denied the sheriffs’ request for a temporary injunction, but the lawsuit itself can continue. The ruling says New York generally does not allow local government entities or their officers to sue the state over the constitutionality of state laws, except in narrow situations. According to the judge, the sheriffs’ lawsuit didn’t fit those exceptions. Read the full ruling at the bottom of this story.

“The Court has reviewed the cases cited by the parties, and, of course, conducted its own research,” the judge wrote. “In doing so, the Court has not found a case which supports Plaintiffs’ capacity to sue New York, its Governor, or its Attorney General for the alleged constitutional violations.”

More details on Local Cop, Local Crimes Act

In May, Gov. Hochul signed the law banning local governments from keeping immigration detainees in local correctional facilities on behalf of federal immigration investigators. It also bans police from entering or maintaining agreements with ICE, requiring all agencies that already had agreements to end them.

Hochul said the law aims to keep local police focused on combating crimes in their areas, not chasing undocumented immigrants. However, the lawsuit criticized the policy, saying it violates the constitutional rights of local police departments to collaborate with federal agencies and is an overreach of state oversight.

AG James sends letters demanding end to ICE contracts

New York Attorney General Letitia James says her office has sent letters to county executives and sheriffs across the state, reminding them to end any agreements involving federal immigration detention.

Local agencies must comply by Nov. 25, under the Local Cops, Local Crimes Act. After that date, the agreements are void under state law, according to James.

text:
A Nicaraguan asylum seeker who was living in Minnesota is fighting his deportation — which landed him across the world in the Central African Republic.

Federal judge Jeffrey Bryan ordered Kenis Lopez Gonzalez brought back home and released from detention last week, but U.S. attorneys are asking the court to delay that order. For now, he’s stuck in a country where he has no connections, no legal status and no protection from deportation back to Nicaragua, where he fears persecution.

In a phone call from the Central African Republic, Lopez Gonzalez said in Spanish that hearing the news of the judge’s order was a glimmer of relief.

“That made me feel good that they’re trying to comply with the law,” Lopez Gonzalez said.

He wants to come back to Minnesota.

He’d lived in Shakopee since 2022, where he owned a construction company. He had permission to stay in the U.S. as long as he attended scheduled check-ins with immigration authorities.

But in January, ICE agents arrested him outside his house. For the next seven months, he was flown from detention center to detention center, on a route that took him from Texas to Louisiana and back to Texas.

ICE couldn't fly him back to Nicaragua. A judge had previously granted him an order barring deportation there, because he fears persecution by the government. He’d participated in a wave of anti-government protests in 2018 and was jailed for several months because of that, he said.

He was being held in detention in Texas in late August, in a cell with about 40 other detainees, when officers in military gear rounded them all up and restrained them, according to a declaration he gave the court. They were put on a bus. It was several hours before agents told them where they were going: to board a plane to the Central African Republic.

At first, some detainees refused to get off the bus. So agents shot them with what Lopez Gonzalez said were rubber bullets. Photos filed in court show several dark purple welts those bullets left on his skin.

After days of flying, the plane dropped off the group of detainees in the Central African Republic’s capital city of Bangui.

Now, Lopez Gonzalez is staying in a defunct hotel there. He said daily life is a struggle.

“Constantly, the power goes out, the water goes out,” he said.

And he’s been sick more days than he’s been healthy. He blames the food. It has a strange smell, he said, and the deportees aren’t sure what kind of meat is in it.

“We have to eat it, because it’s the only option we have,” Lopez Gonzalez said.

Mosquitos buzz around the clock. He’s heard that other detainees have malaria. At night, it’s too hot to sleep.

The building is staffed, and guarded, by the International Organization for Migration, a UN affiliate.

Lopez Gonzalez said the IOM guards don't share much information. He said they’ve offered to help him get back to Nicaragua, but nowhere else.

He’s not sure if he’s technically a prisoner, or if he’s free. Either way, he's heard from guards and fellow detainees that it's dangerous to go out in the city.

“If they see me on the street and the police pass, the first thing they’ll do is ask for me for documentation. I don’t have that, so they’ll arrest me,” he said.

That’s in line with the U.S. government’s guidance on the country. A state department travel advisory warns people not to go there because of violent crime and civil unrest. Human Rights Watch has reported deportees facing extortion and imprisonment in Bangui.

Lopez Gonzalez’s attorney, Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, said he's worried that the Central African Republic will eventually send Lopez Gonzalez back to Nicaragua. He’s seen that happen before with other clients.

“It's all just a very inconvenient and very long layover on the way back to whatever country the U.S. has already been prohibited from deporting him to directly,” Sandoval-Moshenberg said.

Lopez Gonzalez is one of more than 25,000 immigrants deported to third countries under President Donald Trump’s administration, according to the U.S. Committee for Refugees and Migrants and Third Country Deportation Watch, two programs tracking the practice.

The Trump administration has struck deals with several countries around the world to accept deportees. Earlier this year, the Central African Republic entered one of these agreements, after the U.S. government gave $85 million to the IOM for operations there.

Sandoval-Moshenberg said third-country deportees land in a confusing situation.

“It's pretty unclear what's being done by the local government, what's being done by the federal government in the Central African Republic, what's being done by the IOM,” he said. “The U.S. government's position, of course, is once the person steps off the plane, we've washed our hands of it. None of it is our problem anymore.”

Sandoval-Moshenberg said he was glad to see Judge Bryan order Lopez Gonzalez sent back home. So were his friends at the Centro de Trabajadores Unidos en la Lucha, a Twin Cities labor advocacy organization that’s been keeping in touch with Lopez Gonzalez throughout his detention. Dozens of people gathered outside the St. Paul courthouse after the hearing to celebrate the order.

Judge Bryan’s order also included several deadlines for the federal government to arrange the trip and grant Lopez Gonzalez the appropriate travel documents, since ICE took his passport and ID. Sandoval-Moshenberg said he’s keeping a close eye on the government’s compliance with the timeline.

“Unfortunately, in many such cases, we've had to go back to the district court and say, ‘Look, the government's dragging their feet. They're not doing anything,’” Sandoval-Moshenberg said.

Even if the government complies with every deadline, it could be a couple of weeks before Lopez Gonzalez is back in Minnesota.

And it could be longer if the order gets stalled in court. The government has now appealed the order and requested to delay it. Judge Bryan has not yet ruled on that request. Until he, or an appeals court, issues another ruling, the order to bring him home stands.

U.S. Attorney Daniel Rosen argued that the judge should wait for a ruling on third-country deportations from the Supreme Court, which plans to hear a case on the issue in December. He also argued that courts currently allow for third-country deportations, in the interest of furthering the government’s goal of removing immigrants who don’t have legal status.

Sandoval-Moshenberg said Lopez Gonzalez should get a ruling sooner. He’s arguing that his initial detention was illegal, too, and that the government violated his rights to due process when they removed him.

For now, Lopez Gonzalez said he’s sticking to his daily routine inside his building: reading the Bible, exercising, and calling his daughter in Houston when he has power. That helps him get through, he said.

“Psychologically, it’s hard to be in this routine day after day,” Lopez Gonzalez said. “But truthfully, I’m doing fine — fine, fine and at peace.”

He’s holding on to that while he waits for more news — or a plane ticket.

ONALASKA, Wis. (WKBT) — A 21-year-old Wisconsin State Trooper who came to the United States legally from South Africa as a child is now in federal immigration detention, according to his immigration attorney.
Carel Aaron Van Der Merwe, who lives in Onalaska and works out of the Tomah post, was detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents at an airport while waiting to board a domestic flight. His attorney Marc Christopher claims when Van Der Merwe showed agents his federal work permit and explained he had a pending asylum application, they told him they "did not care," before detaining and taking him to the Dodge County detention facility.
ICE's detainee locator shows a Carel Aaron Van Der Merwe, born in South Africa, is in ICE custody at the Dodge Detention Facility in Wisconsin.
In a statement to News 8 Now, a DHS spokesperson said ICE arrested Van Der Merwe on Thursday during a targeted enforcement operation at Dane County Regional Airport in Madison. ICE says Van Der Merwe entered the country in March 2019 with legal permission to stay until September 2019 but overstayed his admission. ICE added that Van Der Merwe will receive due process and remain in custody pending removal proceedings. ICE also noted that work authorization does not confer legal status in the United States.
Van Der Merwe's family claims they have followed the legal immigration process and waited seven years for an asylum interview. He is listed on his father's pending asylum application and holds a federal work authorization card through 2030, according to Christopher. Wisconsin State Patrol hiring rules allow noncitizens with valid work authorization to serve as troopers.
"Carel came here legally as a child. His family pursued asylum through the legal process. He holds federal work authorization and serves Wisconsin as a State Trooper," Christopher said. "Now the same government that authorized him to work has locked him up."
Christopher says he plans to seek Van Der Merwe's release on bond, a process expected to take about two weeks, and has called on the Department of Homeland Security and Wisconsin's congressional delegation to act.

text:
Campaign Website:

https://jameswalkinshaw.org/

Candidate Questionnaire from WAMU:

1. Twenty thousand Virginians lost their federal jobs last year, including many in the 11th District. How would you support people in your district who are still recovering from those job losses?

In my first year in Congress, my top priority has been standing up to DOGE, defending federal workers and contractors, and protecting the public servants pushed out by this Administration. Immediately after being sworn in, I introduced the Limit on Sweeping Executive Reorganization Act to require congressional approval before any president can downsize agencies or eliminate federal positions. Neither the president nor an unelected billionaire should have the power to unilaterally dismantle federal agencies or slash federal jobs. I am also leading the Saving the Civil Service Act to stop efforts to replace nonpartisan civil servants with political appointees. I have met with impacted workers, rallied to reverse cuts, and assisted retirees in securing earned benefits. During last year’s shutdown, I helped stop the unlawful firing of 4,000 federal employees. If re-elected, I will keep fighting to reverse DOGE cuts and restore our civil service. As founder and co-chair of the Federal Workforce Caucus, I am committed to defending public servants while building a more effective, efficient federal government.

2. Companies are proposing to build several data centers in Fairfax County. Where do you stand on data centers in Northern Virginia? What guardrails and limits would you like to see on development?

While data centers are part of the modern economy, their rapid growth can strain the grid, increase energy costs, and create environmental and community impacts. During my time on the Fairfax County Board of Supervisors, we resisted the pressure to provide tax breaks and streamlined zoning for data centers. As a result, Fairfax County has far fewer data centers than our neighbors.

In Congress, I am pushing for data centers to cover their own energy costs, adhere to strict environmental standards, and give communities a genuine voice in siting decisions. I am also working to repeal the massive tax breaks granted to data center developers under the Big Beautiful Bill. It is also imperative that Congress regulate the advanced AI technology fueling the construction of new data centers.

3. What are your thoughts on the White House’s current position on immigration enforcement, and how specifically would you use your position in Congress to influence federal immigration policy?

An orderly, fair immigration system must uphold constitutional rights and reflect our values as Americans. Unfortunately, the Trump administration’s mass deportation policy has led to excessive force, racial profiling, and the targeting of U.S. citizens alongside immigrants, who are vital to Northern Virginia’s vitality and success.

ICE has lost the trust of the American people and must be rebuilt from the ground up or replaced with an agency focused on accountability, transparency, and civil rights. As a member of the House Homeland Security Committee, I have conducted unannounced oversight visits to ICE facilities and investigated enforcement incidents in Minnesota and Texas. I introduced the DHS Accountability Act of 2026 to mandate congressional notice and independent reviews of severe injuries or deaths involving DHS personnel. I support ending agent masking, protecting sensitive locations, enforcing strict use-of-force standards, and ensuring humane medical care. Additionally, I advocate for comprehensive immigration reform and the American Dream and Promise Act to create a pathway to citizenship for Dreamers and TPS holders.

4. Fairfax County has a housing crisis. What specific proposals to create more affordable housing in the district?

Rising housing costs and high interest rates strain working families. On the Board of Supervisors, I championed thousands of affordable homes, including redeveloping underutilized property into housing and childcare facilities. In Congress, I helped pass the ROAD to Housing Act to expand housing supply by reducing bureaucracy and incentivizing local development. Now that it has been enacted, the next Congress must conduct strict oversight to ensure its full implementation.

5. Where do you stand on the proposed Dominion Energy–NextEra merger?

I support Governor Spanberger’s intervention in the proposed Dominion-NextEra merger. Any deal must protect ratepayers, lower utility costs, and put Virginians first. If it fails to meet those standards, it should be rejected.

6. What is one issue you think the current Congress has failed to address?

Congress has failed to hold President Trump accountable for corruption and abuses of power, leaving working families to bear the burden. Virginians face inflated costs for groceries, utilities, housing, healthcare, and gas—with erratic trade policies costing the average Virginia household over $3,500 extra. While the President’s family profits from business ventures presenting massive conflicts of interest, his administration has raised prices through tariffs, cut healthcare and food assistance, and directed hundreds of millions toward building a White House ballroom. Rather than reasserting constitutional authority over tariffs or the unauthorized war in Iran to bring down prices, House Republicans passed the "One Big Beautiful Bill," enacting historic cuts to Medicaid and food assistance while adding $3.4 trillion to the national debt. In Virginia, this bill threatens healthcare coverage for up to 300,000 residents and cuts $1.8 billion to $2.6 billion annually in federal Medicaid funds.

With a Democratic House majority, we will deliver legislation that lowers costs for working families and stops administrative corruption.

7. In 20 words or fewer, what is your top campaign priority?

Fighting for working families by lowering costs, stopping Trump’s agenda, and delivering results for Virginia.

authors: Shannon Heffernan for The Marshall Project

The Department of Homeland Security and ICE did not respond to questions about children held in hotels.
But in reality, many people being arrested are vulnerable children who have viable paths to be in the United States legally.
text:
Immigration lawyers said they believe the government is arresting children because it wants to remove as many immigrants as possible, regardless of their age or vulnerability.

Elora Mukherjee, a lawyer and Columbia Law School professor, has represented more than 100 children and parents in ICE detention in the last year and said many of her clients were arrested while complying with immigration court instructions. “As a nation we shouldn’t be cruel to children. This is the time of year when children should be back in school in their classrooms,” Mukherjee said.

The Marshall Project analyzed data on ICE arrests and detentions obtained by the Deportation Data Project, a research collaboration between UC Berkeley and UCLA. Most immigration violations are civil, not criminal, and the vast majority of children counted in ICE’s arrest data have no criminal conviction or pending charges beyond the immigration violation.

The Marshall Project is tracking how many children have been pulled into the U.S. immigration system during Trump’s second term in office. A dashboard tracks the latest totals.

The Department of Homeland Security did not answer specific questions about the data. In a written statement, the agency said the data from the Deportation Data Project, which was supplied by ICE in response to information requests, was inaccurate. The department offered no evidence to support that claim and did not provide alternate figures.

Lawyers for immigrant families said many of the children being arrested have been in the country for years, and are traumatically torn away from friends, family, and homes.

A 16-year-old identified as J.A.I. said in a court declaration that he’d been living in Texas with his family for eight years. One morning earlier this year, around 5 a.m., he heard yelling and pounding on the door of his home. Suddenly, officers charged in, he said, and went to his 12-year-old brother’s room.

“They pointed a gun at my little brother; threw him against a wall; grabbed him by the hair; and then put handcuffs on him. They did the same thing with me,” he said.

ICE’s increased targeting of children was especially sharp in some states. In Massachusetts and Florida, more than twice as many children were arrested in the first seven months of the year as in all of 2025. In New York and New Jersey, the arrests tripled.

Nuala O’Doherty-Naranjo, an attorney and founder of the Jackson Heights Immigration Center in New York City, said the rise in arrests of families has created a chilling effect in immigrant communities. Outside her door, she sees ICE driving up and down the street, and when she visits high schools she senses a fearful mood. She said she used to tell immigrant families that they were welcome in New York City and should register students for school, go to English classes and join community groups. But she’s increasingly found herself shifting her message to: “I was wrong. Hide.”

Many children arrested by ICE wind up being detained, from less than an hour to several months. ICE has detained more than 8,750 kids since Trump retook office, slightly more than the number it arrested, because children can come into detention via various methods, like being apprehended by Border Patrol.

Children detained for long stretches are usually sent to the immigrant camp in Dilley. And throughout the year, hundreds of children continued to face long stints there.

But, children were also held for shorter stints in a wide range of locations, including hotels and hold rooms, where lawyers said their clients often lacked access to proper food or privacy. Becky Wolozin, a lawyer with the National Center for Youth Law, described these locations as black boxes, where families essentially disappear, with little to no contact with lawyers and relatives.

The ICE data obtained by the Deportation Data Project does not note when the agency detained children in hotels. But court filings in a class action lawsuit known as the Flores settlement, document 86 children who were held for more than three days in hotels in February and March.

The Department of Homeland Security and ICE did not respond to questions about children held in hotels. But in court filings, government officials said some hotel stays were necessary because of flight delays or challenges obtaining travel documents.

In February, a woman in Long Island, New York went with her two children to a scheduled check-in with ICE, planning to go to a favorite restaurant after the appointment. Instead, officers detained them. The mother, who asked to be identified only by her initials, M.S.P., because she fears retaliation from the government, said the family was taken far from New York, where they’d lived for nine years, and jailed in a hotel in Texas.

For nine days, she said they were not allowed to leave the room, or even look out the windows. M.S.P. said two guards were in the hotel room at all times, including sitting outside the bathroom door, making them uncomfortable using the toilet or sleeping.

Her teenager spent much of the time crying and worrying about failing missed classes. Her other child, age 12, worried about the cat they’d left behind at home.

M.S.P. said in Spanish that the guards told her they were private contractors hired by ICE. She said she was permitted two three-minute phone calls to her mother-in-law in New York. She said the guards warned her that if she told anyone where she was, her children would be taken away from her. Her attorney later wrote in court filings that he could not find them in ICE’s detainee locator and was left in the dark about their location – unable to provide legal advice.

In April, the federal judge overseeing the Flores settlement repeated an order for ICE to stop keeping children in hotels, with “a narrow exception for brief, one to two-night stays while in transit or prior to flights.” The judge has also appointed an independent monitor, who, among other things, can inspect hotels where children are held.

Children held in hotels are typically detained with family members, but ICE has also separated some children from their relatives and kept the children in hotels alone this year, said Michelle Brané, a former Homeland Security official under President Joe Biden and currently the executive director of Together and Free, an advocacy organization for families affected by immigration enforcement.

Brané described an 11-year-old who was kept in a hotel room for five days, while his father was sent to an immigrant camp for adults. The child was later transferred to the custody of the government’s Office of Refugee Resettlement, while his father pursued an asylum claim from detention. In another case, a baby and two other young children were kept in a hotel, without their mother for around 10 days, and no one in their family could locate them. The family later learned the children were kept in a hotel room, before they were reunited and placed on a flight to Venezuela.

Brané said the government argues it is removing “the worst of the worst,” in an effort to increase public safety. But in reality, many people being arrested are vulnerable children who have viable paths to be in the United States legally.

“The only reason this would benefit the government,” Brané said, “is to instill fear and chaos and cruelty and frighten people into getting their numbers of removed individuals up.”

title: Can Texas Democrats reverse Abbott's immigration crackdown? - The Texas Tribune
authors: Uriel J. García, Kayla Guo, Jaden Edison, Stephen Simpson, Megan Menchaca, Alejandro Serrano, Jessica Priest, Sneha Dey, Berenice Garcia, Terri Langford

text:
Over nearly 12 years as governor, Greg Abbott transformed Texas into a national model for state-led immigration enforcement, spending billions of dollars to deploy National Guard soldiers, arrest migrants and build border barriers while repeatedly testing the limits of state authority.

But on Election Day, voters ousted Abbott and elected two Democrats who have criticized his immigration policies: Gina Hinojosa, the first Mexican American elected governor of Texas, and Nathan Johnson, the first Democrat elected attorney general since 1994.

Johnson will succeed Attorney General Ken Paxton, whose office defended the governor’s immigration policies in federal court.

The historic Democratic wins across the country, including Texas, were a rebuke of the Trump administration’s economic policies and its immigration crackdown that has led to federal agents killing U.S. citizens and immigrants alike.

In Houston, where an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent fatally shot Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in July, people placed their “I voted” stickers at Salgado’s memorial.

Democrats also reclaimed support from voters in border counties, particularly the Rio Grande Valley, that had swung toward Trump just two years earlier when he campaigned on mass deportations of criminals. Leading up to the election, business owners said the arrests and deportations of undocumented people left some construction companies short of workers.

The election gives Democrats an opportunity to reshape Texas’ approach to immigration enforcement after years of Republican leadership. But Hinojosa and Johnson will inherit a system built through billions in spending, state laws, federal partnerships and court rulings that could limit how quickly they can change course.

“Obviously, a new state governor can’t rewrite immigration laws, but Texas can make a difference in terms of the choices they make about how it uses its state resources,” said Kristin Etter, director of policy and legal services at the Texas Immigration Law Council, a statewide nonprofit that advocates for immigrants’ rights.

Both Hinojosa and Johnson have been critical of Abbott’s approach to immigration. But on the campaign trail, they didn’t commit to fully dismantling the immigration framework the governor and Paxton have built for the past decade.

Abbott announced Operation Lone Star in March 2021, describing it as a collaboration between Texas Department of Public Safety troopers and National Guard members to combat human and drug smuggling into Texas. They deployed aircraft, boats and other personnel to assist in the mission. He said this was necessary because the Biden administration was implementing what he described as open-border policies.

Later that spring, he issued — and would later renew — disaster declarations that allowed the governor to mobilize resources and impose harsher criminal penalties on immigrants who crossed the border into the areas declared a disaster. Eventually, Abbott issued an executive order saying the state was being invaded and the federal government failed to defend the state, ordering troopers and National Guard members to apprehend migrants crossing the Rio Grande and return them to ports of entry so they would return to Mexico.

So far, Operation Lone Star has cost Texas $11 billion.

Later that summer in 2021, Abbott announced the state would fund and erect its own barriers along the Texas-Mexico border. Earlier this year, the Texas Facilities Commission, the state agency in charge of the building project, declared mission accomplished after the state installed about 82.2 miles of barrier. The state Legislature allocated $3.1 billion for the project as part of Operation Lone Star costs.

Hinojosa, who didn’t respond to questions from The Texas Tribune and didn’t bring up any policy issues during a news conference on Thursday, has previously said she would review the effectiveness of Operation Lone Star.

“Operation Lone Star needs to only exist to make us safer,” she said in an interview with KRGV-TV last month. “What has happened is we’ve spent billions of dollars in this state, billions of dollars to detain immigrants, to police for immigrants. That was not a plan to keep us safe. We need a review of Operation Lone Star.”

She has also described Operation Lone Star as “political theatre.”

“Public safety shouldn’t be a political stunt,” she said. “I will spend the money it takes to keep our community safe.”

The money behind Operation Lone Star isn’t permanent. The GOP-controlled Legislature last year approved nearly $3.4 billion for border security in the current state budget. Any funding to continue the operation into the next two-year budget cycle, which starts in the fall, would have to be renewed by lawmakers next session.

When the Legislature reconvenes in January, the House will be controlled by Democrats, many of whom, like Hinojosa, have condemned — and voted against — the state’s border security spending.

Hinojosa criticized Abbott for allowing state police to cooperate with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement deportation officers to find, arrest and deport undocumented Texans. She has also said that she supports having a secure border with Mexico.

“We need secure borders, absolutely, but targeting hard-working long-standing members of our community is not making us more secure,” she told CNN on Sept. 8.

Texas immigration lawsuits

Johnson has expressed similar sentiments while also blasting Abbott’s immigration policies. His campaign statements say that he supports cracking down on drug smuggling, human trafficking and “all forms of cross-border criminal enterprise,” and add that Texans “should reject policy and tactics that damage our sense of decency and fracture our communities.”

“We should not divert vital resources away from public safety to score political points. The attorney general has a role to play in assuring all of this: assisting with federal enforcement as appropriate, and blocking federal actions when they go too far.”

Etter said that one practical thing Hinojosa can do is stop renewing Abbott’s border security disaster proclamation, which has greatly expanded his powers without going through the state legislature.

Abbott has renewed it 69 times since first issuing the proclamation in 2021. It allowed him to justify sending National Guard members and state troopers to different parts of the Texas-Mexico border to apprehend people crossing the Rio Grande as part of Operation Lone Star.

Johnson didn’t respond to emailed questions from The Texas Tribune. As the state’s chief legal officer, Johnson will inherit decisions about whether to continue legal fights championed by Paxton or change the state’s position.

Paxton’s office helped shape national immigration policy by filing lawsuits challenging federal programs such as Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals — an Obama-era program that allows some immigrants with no criminal records to be temporarily protected from deportation.

Under Paxton’s leadership, the attorney general’s office also defended state enforcement measures such as Senate Bill 4, which allows police to arrest people suspected of crossing the Texas-Mexico border illegally.

Paxton filed more than 20 immigration-related lawsuits against the federal government that undermined the Obama and Biden administrations’ policies aimed at helping immigrants temporarily defer deportation or enter the country legally. Critics said Paxton was initially successful because he strategically filed the lawsuits in courts where judges were appointed by President Trump.

“Texas has led all of the major lawsuits attempting to end protections for immigrants in the entire country,” said Kathleen Martinez, an immigration attorney with an office in Dallas. “I think without Texas filing and leading the charge on these ridiculous federal lawsuits, it’ll help protect our programs on a federal scale.”

César Cuauhtémoc García Hernández, an immigration attorney from the Rio Grande Valley and law professor at Ohio State University, said Texas voters electing Johnson as attorney general is just as consequential as Hinojosa.

“Ken Paxton has been at the forefront of working hand-in-hand with Republican leaders of other states, and more recently with the Trump administration, to make Texas the model of harsh immigration policies,” he said.

Many of the court rulings didn’t give clear wins to Paxton, he said. In April 2026, the 5th Circuit Court of Appeals, which has a conservative majority reinforced by President Trump in his first term, ruled that Texas can enforce a law, known as SB 4, that allows police to arrest people suspected of crossing the Rio Grande.

The law says a magistrate judge can order people deported if they’re convicted of the state’s illegal entry statute. Still, the appeals court didn’t rule the law is constitutional, only that Texas can enforce it while the case is being litigated.

“The victories that Texas has won have basically allowed it to chart its own course using its own taxpayer funding to take a more aggressive approach,” García Hernández said. “But to say Texas has the permission to chart its own course is very different from saying that Texas is required to adopt that approach. So, the next batch of statewide leaders will have the opportunity to revisit how it is Texas taxpayers use their financial resources.”

Operation Lone Star arrests

Amrutha Jindal, who oversees indigent defense appointments for Operation Lone Star arrests as the director of Lone Star Defenders, expects Hinojosa to scale back Operation Lone Star but said the effects of the mission will be felt for years.

She said her organization has represented about 20,000 people who have been arrested on charges of trespassing, smuggling and a few illegal entry cases as part of Operation Lone Star. She said there are currently about 1,000 cases pending in state criminal courts.

“The program could end in name, but it wouldn’t end in practice in terms of the cases playing out,” Jindal said.

Advocates say the election results are a referendum on not just Trump’s immigration policies but Texas’ treatment of immigrants.

“Voters along the border and throughout the state sent a resounding message to Texas leaders: We have had enough, get ICE out of our communities,” said Osvaldo Grimaldo, policy strategist on border and immigrants’ rights at the ACLU of Texas.

Edna Yang, co-executive director of American Gateways, an Austin-based immigrant rights advocacy organization, said she interprets the Texas election results as a reaction to people being angry after “witnessing the cruelty towards immigrants that has been going on for the last two or so years.”

Yang added that regardless of the results, she wants to continue to put the focus on the immigrants who have been impacted by state and federal immigration policies. She hopes that with new leadership, policymakers can come up with a less punitive and more humane approach toward immigrants.

“There are still people in detention, families who are separated, asylum seekers who need representation, who are being denied access to due process,” Yang said.

text:
Dozens of people charged in connection to January's protest inside a Twin Cities church during the height of Operation Metro Surge returned to federal court on Thursday.

The group was protesting David Easterwood, a pastor who serves at Cities Church on St. Paul's Summit Avenue. Easterwood also leads the St. Paul field office of Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Thirty-nine people were charged with violating the FACE Act, which restricts "violence and intimidations targeting religious worship sites."

Among those arrested for the Jan. 18 protest were journalists Don Lemon and Georgia Fort, as well as lawyer and activist Nekima Levy Armstrong.

Defendants say they were peaceful and protected by the constitution. Inside the federal courthouse in downtown St. Paul Thursday, the judge heard from those who were involved.

For nearly an hour, lawyers spoke on behalf of two of the defendants, a couple who were arrested at their apartment a month after the protest by Homeland Security Investigation agents.

Lawyers pressed the HSI agent who arrested them about his process, specifically about why their phones were taken when only an arrest warrant — not a search warrant — was administered.

The agent said he was assigned to help HSI here for 30 days during Operation Metro Surge, and that he had probable cause to take the phones.

"The feeling among the defendants is positivity. We have hope," said defendant William Kelly. "We're going to win and I think the judge is going to give us a fair trial, if we get to trial. But he'll give us options on these motions. I think he'll make a fair ruling."

In a statement Thursday afternoon on social media, the head pastor of the church said "I saw these people scream in the faces of innocent worshipers, shut down our service, and terrorize children," adding that he wants a "fair ruling."

Later, in a statement to WCCO, lead pastor Jonathan Parnell said "The dangerous and unlawful invasion of our worship service on January 18 has harmed our church, and continues to negatively affect families and children."

"It was a shameful event that should never happen in any place of worship. We remain hopeful that common sense and justice will prevail," he continued.

This summer, St. Paul's city attorney dismissed the state level charges.

The next hearings are scheduled for Nov. 9 and 10.

When Huabing Xie told detention staff at an ICE facility in California that his chest hurt, neither of the supervising medical providers on site evaluated or treated him. Nearly two hours later, he died of a heart attack.

Delvin Rodriguez hanged himself with a bedsheet, a day after telling a guard at an ICE facility in Mississippi he didn’t want “to be on the earth anymore.” A correctional officer had removed the sheet from his cell, but another guard returned it.
