text:
SALINAS, Calif. —

The County of Monterey is demanding that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement stop using county property as a staging area for civil immigration enforcement, citing reported vehicle activity at several facilities and concerns about safety and access to services.

In a cease-and-desist letter dated Thursday, County Counsel Susan Blitch said ICE vehicles and personnel had been seen this week and last week at Natividad Medical Center, the Monterey County Jail, the Salinas Regional Soccer Complex and Juvenile Hall.

ICE agents were also reportedly seen outside the Monterey County Jail on Thursday.

The letter says vehicles were seen congregating in county parking lots and driveways, parking in red zones, blocking traffic and pedestrian access, and blocking employee parking at Natividad.

The county also said the reported activity created risks for employees and the public and was especially troubling when it could interrupt access to medical care.

The county demands that DHS and ICE immediately:

Cease any unauthorized use of County parking lots or other County property as a staging area, processing location or operating base for civil immigration enforcement activities.

Comply with all posted parking restrictions.

Comply with all applicable traffic laws and operate vehicles safely while on County property.

Refrain from conducting activities on County property in a manner or location that interferes with, intimidates or impedes individuals from seeking vital County services, particularly medical care.

Monterey County supervisors adopted a policy in September prohibiting the use of county property for ICE operations. The policy does not restrict lawful judicial warrants or criminal law enforcement.

The letter says ICE vehicles’ operations forced the jail to temporarily shut down last week. The Sheriff’s Office previously said the jail resumed normal operations after a lockdown that began as protesters gathered amid reports of federal immigration agents near the facility.

The county said it reserves its legal rights and may take action to protect county property, employees, the public and access to services if the conduct continues.

Monterey County Supervisors Wendy Root Askew and Luis Alejo addressed the cease-and-desist letter in social media posts Thursday.

“Today, I can say with confidence that the county is doing everything in our power to de-escalate the dangerous situation that immigration agents are creating in our community. Our County Counsel just sent this cease-and-desist letter to DHS,” Askew said.

Alejo said the county was demanding an immediate end to the unauthorized use of county property for immigration enforcement operations.

“Today, the County of Monterey sent a cease-and-desist letter to ICE demanding an immediate end to the unauthorized use of county parking lots, driveways and other property to stage or conduct civil immigration enforcement operations,” Alejo said.

“The letter cites ICE activity at four county sites in Salinas: Natividad Medical Center, the Monterey County Jail, the Salinas Regional Soccer Complex and Juvenile Hall. The county reported that ICE vehicles blocked access to employee parking at Natividad and that ICE operations forced a temporary shutdown at the County Jail.

“The county is demanding that ICE follow posted parking restrictions and traffic laws, drive safely on county property, and stop any activity on county property that intimidates people or interferes with access to essential county services.

“Everyone in Monterey County should be able to seek medical care without fear or obstruction. The County of Monterey stands with our immigrant workers and families and the county employees who serve them.”

text:
By Naveen Athrappully

Contributing Writer

Almost 24,000 illegal immigrants with criminal convictions or charges have been released into communities since Jan. 20, 2025, due to California’s refusal to honor Immigration and Customs Enforcement detainers, the Department of Homeland Security said.

“There are more than 81,000 criminal charges or convictions associated with these non-honored detainers,” the DHS said in a Monday statement.

This includes 3,295 burglaries, 1,097 assaults, 1,088 drug trafficking charges, 169 homicides, and 147 sexual assaults.

An ICE detainer asks a law enforcement agency to notify ICE before releasing a removable illegal immigrant from any prison or confinement facility, or to hold an illegal immigrant up to 48 hours past their scheduled release so DHS has time to take custody of the individual.

ICE typically issues such detainers in instances where an illegal immigrant has been convicted of crimes by a court or if they pose a public or national security threat.

Some of the ICE detainers in California include an El Salvador national who has been convicted of cruelty to a child and murder, a Cuban convicted of second-degree murder, an Armenian convicted of voluntary manslaughter, and a Libyan convicted of assault with a firearm on a person.

ICE had filed detainers for these individuals in 2025 or 2026. However, DHS said these detainers were not honored, and the individuals were released from jail.

“Sanctuary politicians have not only refused to cooperate with federal law enforcement to target and arrest the worst of the worst — but they’ve released nearly 24,000 criminal illegal aliens onto the streets of California to terrorize innocent Americans,” DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in the statement.

In California, state and local resources must not assist immigration enforcement activities unless they’re lawfully required to do so, according to guidance issued by California Attorney General Rob Bonta in July.

The guidance asks agencies to limit the collection, retention and disclosure of information that could help identify or apprehend people without lawful immigration status.

“Where there is no legal obligation to comply with a request from immigration authorities, agencies should require appropriate legal process — such as a judicial warrant, judicial subpoena, or court order — before complying,” the guidance said.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom justified his state’s sanctuary policies in a January podcast with conservative commentator Ben Shapiro. Newsom said that California does cooperate with federal immigration under certain circumstances, claiming that the state has coordinated more than 10,000 prisoner transfers. Newsom said he disagreed with calls from some Democrats to abolish ICE.

“California has cooperated with more ICE transfers probably than any other state in the country. And I vetoed multiple pieces of legislation that have come from my Legislature to stop the ability for the state of California to do that,” Newsom said.

In certain cases, individuals who face ICE detainers but are released from jail may go on to commit other crimes.

In June, an illegal immigrant from El Salvador was charged with murdering a veteran in Utah. ICE had previously lodged detainers for this illegal immigrant twice in California. But on both occasions, the state refused to honor the requests and released the individual, DHS said in a July 20 statement.

In addition to California, DHS has also criticized New York state for allegedly failing to comply with ICE detainers.

In an Oct. 9 statement, the department said New York did not honor 14,916 immigration detainers issued by ICE between Jan. 20, 2025, and Sept. 14, 2026. These detainers were associated with 47,750 criminal charges and convictions.

“Sanctuary politicians create an environment for criminal activity to thrive, not for American citizens to be safe. President Trump made it clear that he would restore law and order in our cities and in our states. When you have sanctuary cities and politicians, you endanger the safety of the public,” Mullin said in the statement.

text:
Amnesty International has urged Thailand to offer two Uyghur men sanctuary in a safe third country, warning that deporting them to China would endanger their lives and violate international law.

Secretary-General Agnes Callamard called on the Thai government to halt any plans to return the men, provide access to lawyers of their choice and find a safe third-country solution, saying their forced return would breach international law.

"Thai authorities must immediately halt any plans to forcibly return these two Uyghur men to China, where they face a real risk of torture, arbitrary detention and enforced disappearance," Ms Callamard said.

She warned Thailand against repeating its February 2025 deportation of 40 Uyghur men, whose whereabouts and well-being remain unknown despite subsequent visits by Thai representatives to China's Xinjiang region.

The two men are among five Uyghurs remaining in Thailand from a group of more than 300 detained without charge on March 13, 2014, after fleeing persecution and discrimination in Xinjiang.

On Oct 21, the two were released from prison under a royal pardon and transferred to Bangkok's Immigration Detention Centre. Amnesty said they had since been denied access to their lawyers, civil society organisations and the National Human Rights Commission of Thailand.

Both men have told their legal representatives that they fear for their lives if returned to China and do not consent to deportation. They have spent more than 12 years in Thai detention.

Ms Callamard said diplomatic assurances from Beijing could not override Thailand's obligation not to return anyone to a country where they face a real risk of torture or other serious human rights violations.

Amnesty also cited Thailand's obligations under the Convention against Torture and Article 13 of the Prevention and Suppression of Torture and Enforced Disappearance Act, which prohibits deportation where there are substantial grounds to believe a person would face torture, ill-treatment or enforced disappearance.

The organisation said its 2021 report documented crimes against humanity against Uyghurs and other Muslim ethnic groups in Xinjiang.

Chicago – Attorney General Kwame Raoul secured an important legal victory that protects Congressionally-authorized public safety grants, including grants intended to fight crime and keep law enforcement officers safe.

In August, Raoul co-led a coalition of attorneys general in filing a lawsuit challenging the Trump administration’s attempt to impose illegal immigration-enforcement conditions on public safety funding. On Wednesday, the District of Rhode Island Chief Judge John J. McConnell Jr. declared the Trump administration’s actions unlawful and permanently enjoined any implementation or enforcement of these illegal conditions.

“By targeting these funds, the Trump administration threatened to harm state and local law enforcement and put public safety at risk,” Raoul said. “This funding has no relationship to civil immigration enforcement, and I am pleased that the court ruled these conditions unlawful. I will continue to fight to protect public safety funding from overreach by this administration.”

Among the affected programs is the Edward Byrne Memorial Justice Assistance Formula Grants, known as the Byrne JAG Program. For decades, regardless of which political party held power, the Byrne JAG Program has been the leading federal source of criminal justice funding to state and local governments. Congress directed the U.S. Department of Justice to distribute funds based on a state’s population and violent crime rate, not the immigration priorities of the executive branch. The program provides crucial support for law enforcement, including funding for equipment and training. Over the last four fiscal years, Illinois has received a total of more than $25 million in law enforcement funds through this federal program.

This win comes after Raoul co-led a coalition of attorneys general that succeeded in getting the federal government to remove similar conditions on over $1.3 billion of Victims of Crime Act (VOCA) grants last year. Raoul also co-led a coalition that successfully blocked similar conditions on billions of dollars in annual U.S. Department of Transportation grants last year.

In July, Raoul co-led a coalition in filing a lawsuit challenging the administration’s attempt to impose unlawful conditions on billions of dollars in federal funds that Congress appropriated for states to use in preparing for and responding to emergencies and natural disasters, including acts of terrorism. Raoul filed this lawsuit after co-leading a coalition that successfully defended the same category of funding from unlawful conditions in 2025.

Civil immigration enforcement is a federal responsibility and not a state government responsibility. The Trump administration’s unlawful attempts to coerce states into doing its bidding conflict with core principles of American governance – the separation of powers and federalism. The administration’s actions violated laws passed by Congress as well as the Spending Clause of the U.S. Constitution.

Attorney General Raoul led the lawsuit along with California Attorney General Rob Bonta, Delaware Attorney General Kathy Jennings, New Jersey Attorney General Jennifer Davenport and Rhode Island Attorney General Peter F. Neronha. They were joined by the attorneys general of Colorado, Connecticut, the District of Columbia, Hawaii, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Vermont, Virginia, Washington and Wisconsin, as well as the commonwealth of Pennsylvania.

Now we need to hold our elected officials to keeping the promises they’ve made to us, the ones that influenced us to mark their names on our ballots.
We saw historically red states flip, and a progressive candidate was elected as L.A.’s first Asian mayor.

Here’s to the collective pressure we need to put on our elected officials.
L.A. TACO will be here beside our city, observing and reporting on whether change is truly on the horizon.
text:
Now that we’ve sobered up from our celebratory shots and pre-rolls, it’s time to cast a sharp eye on our local and national governments.

As a nation, the tremendous feat of tipping the scales in favor of progressives, the working class, and immigrants may have been the easier part of establishing the possibilities of change. Now we need to hold our elected officials to keeping the promises they’ve made to us, the ones that influenced us to mark their names on our ballots.

Tuesday’s election resulted in a deep blue-shaded shift across the country. We saw historically red states flip, and a progressive candidate was elected as L.A.’s first Asian mayor. This week’s elections also brought the country’s first Black and Native women governors into office. This is the same optimism that New Yorkers probably tasted when they elected Mamdani.

If these politicians are truly working in the best interests of their constituents, we’ll see the quick defunding and absolute abolishment of ICE, as well as better support for small businesses, working families, and improved resources for the homeless community.

In other news, ICE’s abuses continue.

Looking northward, last Friday, a 23-year-old Berkeley student and asylum seeker from Colombia named Paula Valentina Albornoz Hernandez was detained by ICE at San Francisco International Airport.

The young woman, who escaped “severe gender-based violence” in her home country, was about to visit Portland with her boyfriend when an ICE agent in plain clothes began interrogating her. AP reports that Hernandez’s asylum application is pending and that she currently has a valid work permit.

In August, we highlighted the Turkish chef behind Ararat Kebab in Culver City in our street kebabs guide. Sadly, he was recently detained by ICE. West Los Respuesta Rapida, a West L.A. rapid response group, helped get the truck towed to a “safe place,” and says they’re in touch with the only support systems he has in the U.S.

L.A. cannot keep suffering like this, lest we lose everything that makes L.A. the city we love: its people. Even though it has now been revealed that ICE was quietly ordered not to conduct any raids on Election Day, Aisha Wallace-Palomares was out in the streets ready to document any potential ICE activity at the polls.

Here’s to collective hope, a feeling that many of us have forgotten since Trump’s second term began. Here is to the encouraging development that a lot of younger, newer leaders are being given a chance to run things. Here’s to the collective pressure we need to put on our elected officials.

L.A. TACO will be here beside our city, observing and reporting on whether change is truly on the horizon.

title: 'We will not be intimidated': 3 anti-ICE protesters plead not guilty to federal charges - VTDigger
authors: Alan J. Keays, Emma White, Charlotte Oliver, Waterbury Record
description:
BURLINGTON — Three people have denied federal charges stemming from demonstrations where they allegedly blocked doors at a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement surveillance facility in Williston.
The filing of the federal charges is the latest prosecutorial turn following many anti-ICE protests and demonstrations in Vermont.
Vermont Attorney General Charity Clark, who also has the authority to bring state criminal charges in Chittenden County, has since filed trespass-related charges against protesters stemming from demonstrations at the White Cap facility.
Appel, the attorney for the three people who appeared in federal court Thursday, told reporters outside the courtroom that it is extremely rare for prosecutors to bring federal charges in such cases.
“A potential problem I see is that this is not a federal facility,” added Appel, a former head of the Vermont Human Rights Commission.
text:
BURLINGTON — Three people have denied federal charges stemming from demonstrations where they allegedly blocked doors at a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement surveillance facility in Williston.

Peter Booth, 58, of Jericho; Henry Prensky, 80, of Burlington; and Sherri Wormser, 57, of Colchester, appeared Thursday in federal court in Burlington for their arraignments on misdemeanor charges.

Attorney Robert Appel, representing all three, entered not guilty pleas on their behalf, and they were each released on a condition that they not violate any federal, state or local laws.

All three are charged with obstructing access to the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement National Criminal Analysis and Targeting Center at the White Cap Business Park in Williston during anti-ICE demonstrations earlier this year.

VTDigger has previously reported that, according to federal records, information at that facility is reviewed and collected from publicly available sources, such as social media, and assists ICE officers with investigations.

The U.S. attorney’s office in Vermont filed the charges in September against the three defendants as well as two other people — Lexington Kennedy, 22, of New York City, and Roan Wade, 23, of Red Hook, New York — in connection with the anti-ICE demonstrations in Williston.

Kennedy and Wade are to be arraigned on similar misdemeanor charges as the three arraigned Thursday.

According to charging documents, Booth, Prensky, Wormser, Kennedy and Wade went into the atrium of the White Cap building Feb. 9 and blocked the doors between the atrium and the federal facility with their bodies. They ignored orders to move, according to the documents.

Then on May 14, the documents say, Booth and Prensky blocked the doors again. Kennedy and Wade are charged with similar conduct on July 24, according to the documents.

By blocking the doors to the federal property, the defendants obstructed its “usual use, enjoyment and access,” according to the documents.

Each offense carries up to 30 days in prison and up to a $5,000 fine.

Appel, speaking to reporters after the hearing, said he was told by a prosecutor to expect an offer to resolve the cases that did not include jail time. Appel added that if he does receive a plea offer, he is obligated to present it to his client for their consideration.

Booth, Prensky and Wormser read a joint statement outside the federal courthouse to a group of about 30 supporters.

“The purpose of these prosecutions is to intimidate,” Wormser said, adding, “We will not be intimidated.”

Activists say they plan to continue protesting ICE’s presence in Vermont. Organizers have announced a mock funeral procession Friday starting at the Williston facility in remembrance of people who have died in ICE custody since the beginning of President Donald Trump’s second term in January 2025. The event will be followed by a sit-in, according to a press release.

The filing of the federal charges is the latest prosecutorial turn following many anti-ICE protests and demonstrations in Vermont.

Chittenden County State’s Attorney Sarah George has declined repeatedly to press state charges against anti-ICE protesters after their arrests at demonstrations in the county, contending that it didn’t serve justice to prosecute them.

Vermont Attorney General Charity Clark, who also has the authority to bring state criminal charges in Chittenden County, has since filed trespass-related charges against protesters stemming from demonstrations at the White Cap facility.

Appel, the attorney for the three people who appeared in federal court Thursday, told reporters outside the courtroom that it is extremely rare for prosecutors to bring federal charges in such cases. He said that he would seek to have the charges thrown out on several grounds, including that they violated his clients’ First Amendment rights.

“A potential problem I see is that this is not a federal facility,” added Appel, a former head of the Vermont Human Rights Commission. “It’s rented space in a public building that offers a variety of other services.”

Assistant U.S. Attorney Nathanael Burris, the prosecutor, requested a condition of release prohibiting the defendants from coming “within 50 feet of federal facilities or property occupied by the United States Department of Homeland Security” in Vermont, without prior court approval.

Magistrate Judge Kevin Doyle said he wouldn’t impose that restriction, adding that he was concerned the request was too broad and could result in violations for being at airports or ports of entry where Homeland Security may be located as well.

text:
The legal battle over a Nicaraguan immigrant deported from Minnesota to a potentially dangerous third country in Africa is escalating, as the federal government fights a judge's mandate to bring him back to the United States. Meanwhile, community advocates are rallying to demand his immediate return.

Sent to Africa

What we know:

The U.S. government had granted Kenis Lopez Gonzalez legal protection to live and work in Minnesota so he would not face torture in his home country of Nicaragua. He had lived in Shakopee, operated a construction company, and possessed a valid state driver’s license and work permit at the time of his deportation.

According to court records, Lopez Gonzalez was arrested outside his home in January during Operation Metro Surge. After being shuffled between several immigration detention centers for months, ICE deported him to the Central African Republic (CAR), a country that agreed to accept what are known as "third country" deportees from the United States.

The U.S. State Department currently maintains a Level 4 "Do not travel" advisory for the CAR, warning that the country suffers from a severe lack of government control and that foreigners are frequently targeted for violence and kidnappings. His legal team reports that Lopez Gonzalez is currently stranded in a guarded building in the capital city of Bangui where he relies on an international humanitarian group for "basic survival."

On October 30, U.S. District Court Judge Jeffrey Bryan ruled that the government likely violated federal regulations and constitutional due process by arbitrarily detaining and deporting Lopez Gonzalez. The judge ordered the government to immediately return him to Minnesota.

Government appeal

The other side:

The Trump administration is pushing back aggressively against the judge's mandate. Earlier this week, federal attorneys filed an emergency motion requesting an immediate stay to halt the return order. The government is appealing the ruling to the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals.

In their court filings, attorneys argue that judicial intervention in this case irreparably harms the government by interfering with U.S. foreign policy and delicate diplomatic negotiations with foreign sovereign nations.

Furthermore, the government claims the District Court's decision conflicts with actions taken by the U.S. Supreme Court. Attorneys noted that the Supreme Court has already paused a similar class-action lawsuit regarding third-country deportations, arguing that this precedent should squarely control and pause Lopez Gonzalez's case.

Advocates Demand Action

What's next:

As the government fights the order, grassroots organizations are stepping in to rally for Lopez Gonzalez's safe return. The Workers Circle and Centro de Trabajadores Unidos en la Lucha (CTUL)—of which Lopez Gonzalez is a member-- have scheduled a Friday news conference to call for his immediate return.

Judge Bryan has yet to issue a follow-up ruling on whether he will pause his return orders to give the Eighth Circuit time to respond. Stay with FOX 9 for the latest developments in the case.

As President Donald Trump’s administration prepares for a flurry of congressional investigations into shootings by immigration agents and the Jeffrey Epstein files, the top official in charge of the United States Department of Justice’s civil rights division has resigned.

US Attorney General Todd Blanche on Thursday confirmed Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon’s departure in a post on social media.

Recommended Stories

list of 3 items

list 1 of 3Former US Justice Department staff says civil rights division ‘destroyed’

list 2 of 3Ex-US Attorney General Pam Bondi testifies in Epstein files probe

list 3 of 3US Justice Department denies whistleblower claims on anti-Semitism probes

end of list

“Today, I accepted the resignation of Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon,” Blanche wrote on X. “She has defended the civil liberties of every American and enforced the law without fear or favor.”

A top Trump ally, Dhillon was confirmed to her role in April 2025 and has overseen a dramatic overhaul of the Justice Department’s civil rights division, which is tasked with enforcing anti-discrimination laws. Hundreds of former Justice Department officials penned a letter last December decrying the “destruction” of the agency division under Trump.

Dhillon is the first high-ranking official to resign from the Trump administration since US Democrats swept both chambers of the US Congress in the country’s pivotal midterm elections on Tuesday.

Democratic congressman Robert Garcia, who will likely become the new chair of the powerful House of Representatives Committee on Oversight and Accountability, pledged on Wednesday to take on four major investigations, including abuses of power by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents and the Epstein files.

Dhillon reportedly told her staff earlier this year that her office, which has typically been charged with investigating law enforcement killings by police officers, would not be looking into the fatal shootings of two US citizens – Renee Good and Alex Pretti – who were gunned down by ICE agents in Minneapolis.

In May, Garcia accused the administration of continuing to shield Trump from scrutiny related to unreleased documents tied to the Epstein investigation

During a closed-door hearing in which Blanche’s predecessor, Pam Bondi, was asked by lawmakers about the case, the California Democrat Garcia alleged Dhillon repeatedly intervened to block questions about the president’s connection to the release of the files.

The Justice Department referred Al Jazeera to Blanche’s social media post when asked when Dhillon submitted her resignation. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

text:
More than 10 people were apprehended on the morning of Nov. 5 as federal agents conducted an immigration operation with the assistance of nearby agencies, a local official said.

At 7:47 a.m. that day, the Putnam County Sheriff’s Office released a Facebook statement advising people of a heavy law enforcement presence due to a traffic stop 17 minutes earlier in the Round Lake Park neighborhood, which is near the intersection of Silver Lake Drive and State Road 19 in Palatka.

At 3:30 p.m., however, the sheriff’s office updated its Facebook post to say there had been a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement operation at a construction site near that area.

“Due to the proximity to a school and the possibility one individual was armed with a gun a modified lockdown was (triggered) at Palatka Intermediate School for several hours,” sheriff’s office officials said in the updated post.

While ICE has not released information about its operation, the sheriff’s office post stated that the county agency, as well as the Palatka Police Department and Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, assisted the feds with a “mutual aid request to assist in locating the individuals who ran.”

The sheriff’s office’s post didn’t list exactly where the ICE operation took place, but a video posted on Facebook shows law enforcement officials leading at least 13 handcuffed people from the construction site of Palatka Primary School on Kelly Smith Road.

In a text message to the Daily News, Superintendent Rick Surrency said he was alerted of the operation at about 8 a.m. Nov. 5.

Surrency said he spoke with the construction manager and learned construction was halted for three to four hours.

While the construction manager is in charge of the goings-on at the site, Surrency said, local law enforcement agencies and the Putnam County School District must adhere to state mandates to assist federal agents when required.

“I’m not really worried about these operations at our construction sites because our construction managers are responsible for the workers who are on the site,” he said Nov. 5. “My reaction about today is that I know law enforcement needs to do their job, and as a school district, we will cooperate in any way that we are required.”

There have been numerous ICE operations in Putnam County. Surrency said immigration agents conducted a raid at a South Putnam construction site last year but that “it created no issues.”

Allison Waters-Merritt, the sheriff’s office’s public information officer, said ICE was in Putnam County on Nov. 4 and received assistance from the Florida Highway Patrol. She did not know how many operations took place that day, but she said the sheriff’s office helped with one stop in the area of Point of Woods Trail and S.R. 19 in Palatka.

text:
Muslim civil rights groups’ advocacy and legal services for Floridians are suspended in the state while they appeal

November 5, 2026 2:25 pm

Media Contact

125 Broad Street

18th Floor

New York, NY 10004

United States

TALLAHASSEE, Fla. — The Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR) and its Florida chapter, CAIR-Florida, will appeal a Wednesday night ruling by the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Florida that denies their request to reverse Florida officials’ “terrorist” designation of the two civil rights organizations. According to Chief Judge Allen C. Winsor, the plaintiffs are unlikely to succeed at this stage on their claims that the designations under HB 1471, a new and unprecedented state law, violate their due process and First Amendment rights. However, the judge issued a narrow form of preliminary relief, holding that Florida prosecutors cannot enforce the law’s penalties against plaintiffs, their employees, or third parties with respect to the provision of legal services to the groups.

While Chief Judge Winsor’s ruling does not resolve the case, address all claims in it, or make factual findings about Florida officials’ allegations against the Muslim civil rights groups, which the groups maintain are baseless, the designation takes effect today, November 5. As a result, CAIR and CAIR-Florida are forced to shut down their advocacy and operations in the state.

“Florida’s new law has profoundly disturbing parallels to authoritarian states, in which political leaders silence and punish dissent without due process,” said Hiba Rahim, executive director of CAIR-Florida, before the shutdown went into effect. “Governor DeSantis and other officials have unilaterally branded Muslim nonprofits as ‘terrorist’ with devastating consequences for our rights, our supporters, and the communities we serve. CAIR-Florida categorically rejects Florida officials’ baseless designation of us. Nevertheless, we are heartbroken that we have no choice but to close our doors to protect our staff and people of all faiths who support our work. Years ago, when Alabama banned the NAACP from operating in the state, the U.S. Supreme Court ultimately issued a landmark decision protecting every American’s freedom of association. We trust that the courts in our case, too, will ultimately uphold the fundamental rights we are entitled to as Americans and the constitutional freedoms that protect every one of us.”

The impact on the Floridian communities CAIR and CAIR-Florida serve will be immense. CAIR-Florida provides a range of pro bono legal services to Florida residents, including those who suﬀer government and workplace discrimination in violation of their civil rights, as well as those navigating the immigration system.

As the ACLU explained in court last month, CAIR and CAIR-Florida’s devastating designation under the new Florida law is unjustified. Neither group has ever been charged, let alone convicted of, any crime. If Florida tried to do so, it would fail. The reason is simple: neither CAIR nor CAIR-Florida is engaged in terrorist activity, and the state would be unable to prove its case to a jury in a court of law.

“Today’s ruling is deeply disappointing and we are appealing it. Our clients’ challenge to Governor DeSantis’s grave abuse of authority continues,” said Ashley Gorski, senior counsel with the ACLU’s National Security Project. “Today’s decision upholds state officials’ sweeping power to punish American organizations they brand as ‘terrorist,’ without due process and in violation of the First Amendment. Florida officials have been relentless in seeking to silence our clients’ civil rights work and advocacy, damaging not only them but also their community. We cannot allow this dangerous and sweeping censorship regime to stand.”

Under HB 1471, five Florida executive officials have the power to designate and debilitate U.S. groups — including nonprofits engaged in First Amendment-protected advocacy — without filing charges, initiating judicial proceedings, proving their case beyond a reasonable doubt, submitting the case to a jury, or complying with any of the other required constitutional protections of the criminal legal system. Once a designation becomes effective, an organization’s lawful, constitutionally protected speech and association are immediately rendered illegal and impossible. An elaborate set of prohibitions makes it a serious crime for the targeted American organization to do virtually anything in the state, and for others to work for or otherwise actively associate with or support the designated group. The consequences of violating these prohibitions are severe, including up to life imprisonment.

According to Chief Judge Winsor, while the groups did not succeed in demonstrating that their freedom of association had been unconstitutionally restricted or that the designation regime was an unlawful “prior restraint” on speech, the state’s attempt to criminalize the provision of legal advice to CAIR and CAIR-Florida was a content-based restriction of speech that likely violated the First Amendment. “The State has no meaningful interest in denying Plaintiffs’ legal counsel,” the court said.

Concerning due process, the court recognized that Florida’s new designation regime is “novel—and perhaps unprecedented,” but said that the plaintiffs had not demonstrated that the state-level appeal procedures were constitutionally inadequate. The court also held that the plaintiffs did not show that the designation was a form of criminal punishment, as opposed to a civil remedy.

“Today, for the first time in over twenty years, Florida Muslims cannot call their community’s leading civil rights organization for help if they experience a hate crime at their mosque, illegal discrimination in the workplace, violent bullying in school, or any other acts of bigotry,” said Edward Ahmed Mitchell, National Deputy Director at CAIR. “The Constitution’s guarantees of free speech and due process apply to every inch of our nation, including Florida. The unprecedented notion that Governor DeSantis has the power to punish an American civil rights organization for its speech and unilaterally force the closure of its doors without due process is an affront to the Constitution. We look forward to appealing this initial ruling so that we can protect the rights of everyone in the State of Florida. Although this is a tragic day for the people of Florida, our struggle to protect the U.S. Constitution is just beginning and we are confident that the rule of law will ultimately prevail, God willing.”

“We are dismayed by this ruling,” said Scott McCoy, deputy legal director, Southern Poverty Law Center (SPLC). “A law that allows officials unjustly to brand a civil rights nonprofit with such a grievous label and expose it, and anyone who supports it, to life in prison with no hearing and no trial, threatens every Floridian’s constitutional rights. Our commitment to CAIR, CAIR-Florida and the communities they serve has not changed, and we will continue fighting this unconstitutional law throughout this case and on appeal.”

“The court’s decision at least recognizes that an organization cannot be prosecuted for participating in its own legal defense, contrary to the state’s dystopian law,” said Daniel Tilley, legal director of the ACLU of Florida. “CAIR-FL has already been forced to shut its doors in Florida, cutting off Floridian Muslims and others who relied on its services. No nonprofit engaged in First Amendment-protected activity should face this kind of harm without due process. We stand with CAIR and CAIR-FL and will appeal this decision. Our commitment to challenging this dangerous and arbitrary designation has not wavered.”

On Wednesday night, the defendants also stipulated that they would not prosecute (a) employees, board members, and third parties for their good-faith and reasonable involvement in the groups’ two legal challenges to Florida officials’ designations, or (b) good-faith and reasonable actions undertaken to comply with state and federal legal obligations. As a result, these legal and compliance activities may continue as the litigation moves forward.

CAIR and CAIR-Florida are represented by the ACLU, ACLU of Florida, the SPLC, and Bondurant Mixson & Elmore LLP.

title: 2026 midterm election live updates as Democrats prepare to take Congress, GOP grapples ...
authors: Joe  Walsh, Kathryn  Watson, Stefan  Becket, Kaia  Hubbard, Caitlin  Yilek, Caroline  Linton, Melissa  Quinn
description: After Democrats' sweeping House and Senate victories, the party is laying out how it plans to wield power, while President Trump and Republicans react to their midterm losses.
text:
The U.S. Senate race in Mississippi remains a toss-up between incumbent Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith and Democrat Scott Colom, with Colom leading by fewer than 2,000 votes.

According to Mississippi Secretary of State Michael Watson , there are approximately 3,600 outstanding mail ballots and an unknown number of affidavit ballots, or provisional ballots, from voters whose eligibility needs to be confirmed. Absentee ballots must be received within five business days, while affidavit ballots must be processed within the 10-day window that counties have to certify results, which ends Nov 13.

Both parties are keeping a close eye on the process. CBS News has confirmed the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee has deployed lawyers and resources to the state to monitor the count.

"I'm confident that ultimately Mississippi has decided to go in a new direction," Colum told reporters after greeting campaign volunteers Thursday morning in Jackson.

The National Republican Senatorial Committee and Hyde-Smith campaign filed a request for all counties to separate and preserve all affidavit ballots. The Colom campaign called the move a "desperate stunt."  His counsel also sent a new letter to Mississippi's 82 counties asking them to respect election procedures.

Hyde-Smith predicted that she will represent Mississippi for another six-year term, posting on X : "We believe thousands of votes remain to be counted from dozens of Republican counties, and we are confident those votes will reinforce her path to victory."

At a news conference Thursday, Mississippi Republican Party Chair Mike Hurst insisted the election "is far from being over" and noted the state party has attorneys and observers throughout the state to ensure all legally cast ballots are counted.

Mississippi does not allow recounts, so a winner will be decided based on a plurality of votes.

Democrats won control of the House of Representatives by picking up perennial swing districts and seats that were once considered deep red. The party's wins ranged from suburban areas in the northeastern United States to areas of South Texas that were once viewed as increasingly GOP-friendly.

So far, 42 districts have shifted to Democrats and two have shifted to Republicans. Winners in dozens of races have yet to be projected.

Read more here .

GOP Rep. Anna Paulina Luna narrowly won her race in Florida's 13th District, CBS News projected. With 99% of the votes counted, Luna was leading by less than one point.

She faced Democrat Leela Gray.

Democrat Cait Conley defeated two-term Republican Rep. Mike Lawler, winning a highly competitive seat in New York's Hudson Valley region, CBS News projected.

Lawler's loss is another setback for Republicans. CBS News has projected that Democrats will take control of the House in January with a wide majority.

Lawler called Conley to concede Tuesday.

Read more here .

Rep. Ted Lieu of California announced his bid for Democratic Caucus chair in a dear colleague letter on Thursday.

"I am now running for Chair of the Caucus because I want to work with all of you to seize the opportunity the American people just gave us. If we do this right, we can build an enduring majority, one that will win not just the next one or two election cycles, but many more," he said.

House Democrats are on pace to win 256 seats, according to the latest CBS News estimate.

It's quite an increase from the 214 seats they hold in the current Congress.

The estimate includes several races that CBS News has not yet projected.

GOP Rep. Richard Hudson, the chair of the GOP's House campaign arm, lost to Democrat Richard Ojeda in North Carolina's 9th District, CBS News projected.

Hudson conceded the race on Wednesday.

Ojeda was previously a state senator in West Virginia, and in the last decade ran unsuccessfully for the House, Senate and president before moving to North Carolina.

Democrat Kristina Knickerbocker defeated GOP Rep. Mike Turner in Ohio's 10th District, CBS News projected.

Turner has represented the district since 2003 and won reelection in 2024 by more than 18 points.

Widespread Republican losses in the midterm elections are roiling the GOP, prompting soul-searching over what went wrong and a brewing blame-game that's expected to heat up as the party looks toward the next election.

From House and Senate races to governors' mansions, Republicans saw striking losses, both in battlegrounds and in places where the party saw significant support just two years ago. The victories dramatically shifted the balance of power in Washington, delivering Democrats a sizable majority in the House far beyond what was expected heading into Election Day, as well as a Senate majority larger than what the GOP has enjoyed for the last two years.

As Republicans process the results, including some GOP officials who have ambitions of their own in 2028, they're offering frank assessments of the shortcomings — and laying the groundwork for where the party heads next.

Read more here .

Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa gave her first press conference since Democrats' stunning wins in the state on Tuesday, with every statewide seat flipping to Democrats.

"This is a transition for the whole state of Texas," Hinojosa said as she announced members of a bipartisan transition team.

"This is not about being a Democratic administration, I'm not going to be the governor just for Democrats, I'm going to be the governor for all the people of Texas," Hinojosa said.

Hinojosa said Gov. Greg Abbott, who she defeated on Tuesday, is being "gracious" and said they are both committed to a "smooth transition."

When asked about Republicans at the state Capitol who may try to undermine her power, she said "the people of Texas have spoken." Democrats are on track to have a majority in the state House of Representatives, but Republicans will continue to have a majority in the state Senate.

L.A. Mayor Karen Bass released a statement on Thursday morning conceding to Nithya Raman, saying she called her to congratulate her on the victory.

"While this is not the outcome we hoped for, the people of Los Angeles have spoken. I have called Councilmember Nithya Raman to congratulate her on her victory, and I have committed to ensuring a smooth and seamless transition," Bass wrote.

Bass thanked her supporters and other leaders who helped during her campaign. She added that she will continue to "ensure the promise of a better life belongs to all of us."

Democratic Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez won a third term in Washington's 3rd Congressional District, CBS News projected.

Gluesenkamp Perez's victory, in a district President Trump has won three times, comes as she's flexed her independence over party loyalty. Democrats will take control of the House of Representatives in January, with stunning wins across the country .

The congresswoman beat Republican state Sen. John Braun to win reelection in the rural district in the southwestern corner of the state. Braun, the top Republican in the Washington state Senate, was a more mainstream Republican than Gluesenkamp Perez's prior opponent, far-right conservative Joe Kent, who went on to become Mr. Trump's counterterrorism chief before resigning in protest over the Iran war. But Braun, who was endorsed by Mr. Trump, also distanced himself from the president on some issues, including on tariffs, the Iran war and affirming that Joe Biden won the 2020 election.

Read more here .

Democratic Rep. Joe Neguse of Colorado on Wednesday announced his bid for assistant speaker when Democrats take the House majority in January.

"With our decisive and overwhelming victory this week, it is more important than ever for the House Democratic Caucus to be unified in the 120th Congress, and to repay the faith that the American people have put in us to lower costs, end corruption, and deliver for working families. To that end, and as we embark on that road together, I write to respectfully request your support for Assistant Speaker," he wrote in a letter to his Democratic colleagues on Thursday.

"If elected Assistant Speaker, my goals would be straight-forward — to prioritize direct member services for every member of our diverse and talented caucus, and to assist Speaker Jeffries and our incredible Democratic Leadership team," he said.

The leadership hierarchy could be a point of tension as both Neguse and Rep. Ted Lieu of California seek to claim the No. 4 spot. Neguse currently holds the No. 5 spot in the minority as assistant Democratic leader. A source familiar with the matter told CBS News that assistant speaker is the No. 4 spot in the majority.

Lieu, who currently holds the No. 4 spot in the minority as Democratic Caucus vice chair, will run for Caucus chair. Another source familiar with the matter told CBS News that the leadership hierarchy will be the same as it is now — with Lieu as No. 4 and Neguse as No. 5.

Sen.-elect Annie Andrews told CNN on Thursday that she has spoken to Republican Sen. Tiim Scott, the chair of Senate Republicans' campaign arm, and they scheduled a longer call for next week. Andrews did not say if Scott apologized for calling her "Trany Annie," but said she is focused on working "productively" with the senior senator from South Carolina moving forward. On the campaign trail, Darline Graham called Andrews "batshit crazy."

"You know, I understand politics is a dirty business, and name calling is sometimes part of it," Andrews said on CNN. "But it's not really about my hurt feelings or the way that they operated in the campaign. It's about Sen. Tim Scott and I finding a way to work productively together. And I really do have a lot of hope that we can do that."

Andrews also addressed reporting that she had internal polling showing she was winning, but declined to share it publicly.

"We were on track to win and we didn't want anything to disrupt the path that we were on," Andrews said. "And we knew if we kept showing up everywhere, talking to local media, talking about the issues, like I said, in addition to those issues, the data center issue that became really hot at the end of the race, we knew we could bring this across the finish line, and we didn't want this to become a national race because it's not about national politics."

Progressive Democrat Nithya Raman, a democratic socialist, defeated incumbent Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass in the mayoral race, CBS News projects.

Read more at CBS News Los Angeles .

Harmeet Dhillon, the assistant attorney general in charge of the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division, resigned on Thursday, Attorney General Todd Blanche said.

"Today, I accepted the resignation of Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon, who led the Civil Rights Division with conviction the past 18 months," Blanche wrote in a post on X . "She has defended the civil liberties of every American and enforced the law without fear or favor. The Department is grateful for her dedicated public service, and we wish her every success in her future endeavors."

Dhillon oversaw a mass exodus from the Civil Rights Division last year, with more than 75% of its staff departing. She upended many of the division's traditional priorities that focused on combating discrimination against some of the nation's most vulnerable and historically marginalized groups.

Read more here .

President Trump is scheduled to attend the Army-Navy game, one of the longest rivalries in college football, U.S. officials told CBS News.

The stands at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey on Dec. 12 will be filled with active-duty troops and veterans.

Mr. Trump has made an appearance at the game several times as commander-in-chief, including last year. The game is known for its military flyovers and patriotism.

Read more here.

House Democratic Whip Katherine Clark has launched her bid for majority leader in the next Congress.

"Today with pride in what we've achieved and confidence in what we will deliver, I ask for your support," Clark wrote in a letter to fellow Democrats obtained by CBS News.

The Massachusetts Democrat pledged to make affordability a top priority, give rank-and-file members a "seat at the table" and harness the party's "collective power."

If elected by her caucus, Clark would become the first woman to serve as House majority leader.

Rep. Erin Houchin of Indiana is challenging Rep. Lisa McClain of Michigan for the role of GOP conference chair in the next Congress.

In a letter to colleagues on Thursday, she wrote, "The road back to a Republican House Majority runs through our message and our ability to communicate it effectively. The American people are asking for something different. Our Conference should be willing to do the same."

On Wednesday, McClain released a list of 35 Republicans who are backing her to remain as conference chair. She was elected to the leadership position in 2024.

"We can spend the next two years licking our wounds and waiting for the political winds to shift, or we can get off the mat and go on the offensive. I know which path I'm taking," McClain said in a statement.

As Alaska continues to count its ballots cast in the midterms, President Trump posted on Truth Social that he believes votes for retired teacher Daniel J. Sullivan and Republican candidate Gerald Heikes should be given to Sen. Dan Sullivan, a Republican who is running for reelection.

"The vote totals for the Fake Dan Sullivan, plus the other 'slug' that the Dems put on the Ballot, should be immediately given to the REAL Dan Sullivan, and the Election is over - He easily wins. There is no other fair solution!" Mr. Trump wrote on Truth Social.

CBS News has rated the Alaska Senate race a toss-up.

Alaska uses ranked-choice voting , where voters rank candidates in order of preference, instead of selecting a single candidate. Under the system, if no candidate is ranked as the top choice for more than 50% of voters, the count goes to a second round. The candidate with the least amount of votes is eliminated, and votes from that candidate's supporters are redistributed to their second pick.

The process continues until a candidate wins a majority.

Days before the election, the Justice Department filed a lawsuit and asked a federal judge to block certification of the Alaska Senate election if Sullivan, the incumbent, lost. But a judge tossed out the suit on procedural grounds. The Justice Department has appealed.

ABC News' Jon Karl posted on X on Thursday morning that he had spoken to President Trump, who told him "I have every intention" of keeping Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

Karl said Mr. Trump said "I get these calls, you know, about him. I don't understand why." But Karl said Mr. Trump also acknowledged that it would be easier to get a new defense secretary confirmed by the Senate before the Democratic majority takes over in January.

Multiple sources told CBS News on Wednesday that Mr. Trump was asking advisers if Hegseth should stay in his job. Vice President JD Vance, meanwhile, publicly blamed the Iran war for the GOP's losses on Tuesday.

Outgoing Republican Sen. John Cornyn, who lost a primary earlier this year to Attorney General Ken Paxton, wrote an op-ed in the Wall Street Journal criticizing Republicans for their decisive losses in the midterms.

Cornyn wrote that an "epic blame game had begun" before the polls even closed, but he writes that "both sides miss the point" because "this week's beat-down wasn't only foreseeable, it was foreseen — because our party forgot four basic rules of coalition politics."

Cornyn said that Republicans shrunk their coalition after making gains with Hispanic voters in 2024, noting that some Republicans obsessed over "RINOs." He said Texas Republican Bo French "poisoned the well even further with blatant bigotry against Indian-Americans."

Cornyn also outlined other mistakes he feels the GOP made: the Republican candidates weren't likeable enough, and the Trump administration didn't follow through on its promises.

But ultimately, Cornyn wrote, "character and integrity still matter."

"Pre-election polls showed that corruption had surged toward the top of voter anxieties, thanks to flawed midterm candidates and a parade of unsavory headlines out of Washington," Cornyn said. "Voters won't trust Republicans to cut fraud and scams out of government programs until we cut them out of our own ranks. Party leaders have to stop excusing the inexcusable and police our side of the aisle—or voters will continue to police it for us."

As President Trump prepares for the final two years of his presidency, he is expected to devote more attention to his presidential library, which has become a growing destination for money from companies and allies, according to current and former advisers who spoke on the condition of anonymity.

"He undoubtedly recognizes that the library development season opens now, and he will go for it," said a senior administration official. A second administration official said that in this lame-duck period Mr. Trump will focus on "all things he can control, which means: Building."

With Democrats taking control of Congress in January after a sweeping victory in the November elections, lawmakers have pledged investigations into the library's finances.

Read more here .

House Democrats will start 2027 with a sizable majority, but their exact margin isn't clear, as votes are still being counted in key races in Maine, Montana, Florida, Alaska and elsewhere.

Here's how many House seats CBS News projects for each party:

CBS News still rates two Senate races as toss-ups: Alaska and Mississippi.

The Alaska race between GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola is still tight, and vote-counting could take some time , partly due to the state's ranked-choice system. The race was shaken up last week by allegations that Peltola-linked operatives helped recruit a candidate with the same first and last name as Sullivan — which Peltola's campaign denied.

The Mississippi race between GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde Smith and Democrat Scott Colom wasn't expected to be competitive, but  is razor-thin. State officials say thousands of ballots still need to be counted, including outstanding absentee ballots that aren't due for a few more days and "affidavit" ballots from voters whose eligibility needs to be confirmed.

Here's where control of the Senate stands:

Democrats won control of the House of Representatives on Tuesday by flipping more than two dozen Republican-held seats, picking up perennial swing districts and seats that were once considered deep red. The party's wins ranged from suburban areas in the northeastern United States to areas of South Texas that were once viewed as increasingly GOP-friendly.

Read more here on the districts that are changing hands.

Republicans undertook a historic effort to redraw several states' Congressional districts mid-decade in an attempt to maintain control of the House. That effort was rebuffed on Tuesday night as the GOP was on track to lose all of the districts it tried to gerrymander.

There were several reasons that states undertook what had previously been a rare practice of mid-decade redistricting. Republican efforts started when President Trump ordered Texas lawmakers to redraw their map to net up to five seats for the GOP.

But despite the all-out effort, Democrats won control of the House on Tuesday, with CBS News estimating Democrats could end up with 251 to 268 House seats.

Read more here .

Republicans have begun trying to pick up the pieces from Tuesday's midterms, with top GOP voices pitching themselves for leadership roles and offering theories on why the party lost.

House Speaker Mike Johnson announced on a call with his staff that he won't run for minority leader next year, a source familiar with the matter told CBS News .

House Majority Leader Steve Scalise announced he plans to run for Republican leader. He told his colleagues : "We will need to be honest with ourselves about what happened."

House Judiciary Chair Jim Jordan also threw his hat in the ring, calling it a "staggering day for our Conference." He said he's "battle-tested" after brawling with Democrats on investigations.

Others offered diagnoses on what went wrong. Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas, whose state shifted hard toward Democrats, called the results an "ass-kicking" and a "Watergate-level repudiation."

On his podcast, Cruz argued his party didn't address a "real economic disconnect" and that many GOP politicians "seem like they didn't understand or they didn't care" about the cost of living.

In what could be a looming intraparty debate, Vice President JD Vance said the "reason we lost is the war." He said many Trump 2024 voters flipped to Democrats in order to end the Iran war, address cost-of-living issues, "Put America First" and change the U.S.-Israel relationship.

The likely presidential contender wrote that "everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there."

(The president's son, Donald Trump Jr., reacted to Vance's post with "💯💯💯.")

Former Republican National Committee chairwoman Ronna McDaniel told CBS News' "The Takeout with Major Garrett" that Tuesday's results were a "red rebellion" that she linked to people's frustrations with the economy. She said the GOP needs to do some "soul-searching."

"You don't win Texas, you don't win Kansas, you don't win South Carolina without Republican voters actually crossing over and voting for the Democrats," she said.

President Trump's first public appearance since the midterms was at the construction site for his White House ballroom, where he lauded the contractors and signed a steel beam.

In remarks to reporters, Mr. Trump again blamed Republican candidates for the party's massive losses Tuesday night, saying there was so much "love" at his rallies.

"If I was on the ballot, we would have won," he said. "But they just — you couldn't transfer that love. There was such love at those rallies, it was incredible. And we weren't able to transfer the love to candidates."

He also said it's "largely true" that the GOP lost the House and Senate because of the Iran war's impact on energy prices, agreeing with Vice President JD Vance, but he argued it was worthwhile, saying: "If I had to do it again, I'd have to do it again."

"You have no choice; you have to do it. You can't let Iran have a nuclear weapon or everything that you see here some day might not exist," the president said.

President Trump has been asking advisers around him and on the phone whether Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth should stay in his job, following Republicans' catastrophic losses Tuesday night, multiple sources familiar with the matter told CBS News on Wednesday.

Some White House aides have predicted some of the blame for GOP midterm losses will be trained on Adm. Brad Cooper, the head of U.S. Central Command, and Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine, who both played big roles in guidance on the Iran war.

One source told CBS News that GOP Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis is being floated as a possible replacement for Hegseth, arguing he could go through Senate confirmation in the lame-duck period before Democrats take control of Congress.

Still, other sources said Mr. Trump hasn't decided to replace Hegseth.

White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly said in a statement that the president "has full confidence in Secretary Hegseth." Asked if he is considering replacing Hegseth, Mr. Trump told reporters: "No, I think he's doing a very good job."

Read more here .

Rep. Robert Garcia of California, who will chair the House Oversight Committee next Congress, laid out four areas where the panel will focus its investigative efforts.

The overarching investigations include the Trump family's business dealings, corporate corruption, actions of the Department of Homeland Security and Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and the Jeffrey Epstein scandal.

"I think folks that need to be concerned first are administration officials that have caused real harm. We're going to investigate the abuses," Garcia said at a news conference Wednesday, singling out Stephen Miller, Corey Lewandowski, Kristi Noem and Trump family members.

Garcia acknowledged the Justice Department is unlikely to prosecute people who refuse to cooperate, but said House Democrats could sue in civil court.

Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer, meanwhile, called the midterms a "generational remake of the Senate map," but said his party's most important task is to respond to the mandate from voters by "prov[ing] ourselves worthy of their trust."

Previewing the party's plans starting next year, the minority leader said: "Whenever Trump defies the will of the American people or the law, we will launch investigations, take him to court, and entangle him in legislative razor wire."

Many congressional Democrats are likely to be enthusiastic about investigating the Trump administration. But one moderate incoming Democratic senator, Adam Hamilton of Kansas, told CBS News he wants to spend more time on cost-of-living and other issues than investigations or impeachments, saying: "I do not want to spend the next two years in trials."

Asked about the potential for Democrat-led investigations, White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said: "As the President has said, he's willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans. If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people."

Democrat James Talarico on Wednesday said his win over Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton in the Texas Senate race delivered a message to Elon Musk, who spent more than $150 million to boost Paxton's candidacy: "Texas is not for sale."

Hours after his projected win over Paxton, Talarico told "CBS Mornings" that his victory is an opportunity to get big money out of politics "for good."

"The people of Texas delivered a crystal-clear message to the world's first trillionaire: Texas is not for sale," Talarico said. "The power in this state, in this country, belongs to the people and we've got to make sure it stays that way."

Read more here .

text:
Voters delivered Democrats decisive control of the U.S. House of Representatives and Senate in the 2026 midterm elections, giving years of oversight interest a path to investigative action. When the 120th Congress convenes on January 3, 2027, the incoming majority will have the power to compel document productions and testimony in pursuit of inquiries into the Trump Administration, companies, other organizations and individuals. Those drawn into these inquiries can face significant reputational, legal and financial consequences well before any future legislative risks.

For private companies, Democratic control of the U.S. Congress will have several immediate and longer-term implications:

Existing Inquiries Will Gain Force. Companies should expect renewed or expanded document and testimony requests, backed by the incoming majority's authority to hold hearings and issue subpoenas.

Corporate Relationships with the Administration Will Face Increased Scrutiny. Government contracts, waivers, regulatory approvals, loans and policy changes may become subjects of investigation, bringing companies' communications with administration officials and the benefits they received into focus.

Companies May Become Sources of Evidence When Their Conduct Is Not the Focus. Where executive branch agencies resist or delay disclosure, investigators may turn to private parties for corresponding emails, messages, meeting notes and other records concerning government decisions.

Likely Investigative Priorities and Committees to Watch

Long before the midterm elections, Democratic members and oversight staff laid the groundwork for a return to the majority. The election now gives that work a path to compulsory process and other committee action. Affordability and scrutiny of the relationship between private interests and government decisions will drive much of the agenda, while leadership choices will help determine which inquiries move first and how aggressively they proceed.

Reps. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.) at the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) at the House Committee on the Judiciary and Frank Pallone Jr. (D-N.J.) at the House Committee on Energy and Commerce are positioned to advance inquiries they have helped develop from the minority. Other gavels remain contested. At the House Committee on Financial Services, Rep. Maxine Waters (D-Calif.) faces challenges from Reps. Bill Foster (D-Ill.) and Sean Casten (D-Ill.), with implications for the committee's approach to financial regulation, digital assets, housing and consumer protection.

Senate leadership choices are also interconnected. Sen. Maggie Hassan (D-N.H.) is positioned to succeed retiring Sen. Gary Peters (D-Mich.) at the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, while Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) is positioned to lead its Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations. An anticipated move by Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) to the Senate Committee on the Judiciary following the retirement of Sen. Dick Durbin (D-Ill.) could open the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works gavel to Sens. Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) or Ed Markey (D-Mass.), depending on other leadership selections.

At the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs, Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) is positioned to chair, although Sen.-elect Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio) has also been discussed as a contender; his prior chairmanship does not automatically restore his seniority under Democratic Conference rules. These selections remain subject to party processes and organizational decisions and will help determine which inquiries receive sustained attention.

Not all oversight efforts will be exclusively partisan. China, healthcare and consumer prices, energy costs, artificial intelligence (AI) and data centers are likely to attract bipartisan interest and potential cooperation. The following chart maps the principal areas of anticipated scrutiny and committees positioned to pursue them.

The incoming majority could also create select committees or dedicated subcommittees to pursue particular priorities. Recent Congresses have used these bodies to investigate the coronavirus pandemic and competition with China. Affordability or AI could provide a focus for a similar effort in the 120th Congress, creating additional avenues for scrutiny of private companies.

Considerations for Organizations Facing or Preparing for Congressional Scrutiny

The change in control warrants a fresh assessment by organizations already responding to congressional inquiries and those anticipating future scrutiny. Prior correspondence and staff reports offer useful indicators of likely priorities. Organizations should review outstanding requests, commitments and submissions and assess applicable preservation obligations – including where they have received preservation letters – as well as prepare for expanding document demands or witness testimony.

Leaders of legal, government affairs, communications and relevant businesses should establish response objectives, identify relevant records and personnel, and confirm procedures for escalating inquiries. Counsel should help structure this work to preserve applicable privileges and work-product protections, recognizing that congressional committees may challenge those protections.

Response decisions should account for parallel litigation, enforcement matters, government contracts and pending approvals. name: Human Rights
title: A Catholic immigration agenda for the new Congress: Accountability for ICE and a long ...
description:
Any “overreach” in the near term could create a backlash at the ballot box in 2028 and jeopardize the church’s ultimate goal of humane and comprehensive immigration reform.
To interpret the outcome as some sort of mandate on the passage of positive immigration reform would be a mistake.
For the long term, we need to lay the groundwork for humane immigration reform.
Catholic leaders should also hold internal discussions about what a successful immigration reform bill might look like and what concessions are inevitable.
They should keep in mind that in past immigration reform debates, the “perfect” bill has been the enemy of the good.
text:
The midterm election’s “blue wave” has changed the political landscape in Washington, particularly when it comes to the hot topic of immigration. With Democrats in control of both houses of Congress beginning in January, Catholic immigration advocates have an opportunity to play offense on this crucial issue, rather than scrambling to block punitive policy initiatives.

In assessing what the Catholic community, including the U.S. bishops, should pursue, a long-term strategy is required—one that should extend beyond the presidential election in 2028. Any “overreach” in the near term could create a backlash at the ballot box in 2028 and jeopardize the church’s ultimate goal of humane and comprehensive immigration reform.

The election results were the product of several issues (most prominently the high cost of living), of which immigration was only one. To interpret the outcome as some sort of mandate on the passage of positive immigration reform would be a mistake. Nevertheless, the excesses of Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents in the administration’s mass deportation campaign did seem to play a part in electing the new Congress, especially among Latino voters and other voters of color, who, according to early estimates, turned out in high numbers.

However, President Trump still maintains control over immigration policy and will certainly use his veto power to defeat any immigration legislation that runs counter to his mass deportation agenda. As such, Catholic immigration advocates should pursue immigration priorities that have at least some bipartisan support in Congress, if only to raise the profile of these issues for a future time when they can become law.

A sound immigration agenda the church could pursue for the new Congress would feature three priorities.

First, we need oversight and accountability for ICE. With the majority, the Democrats have the power of the gavel and the purse and can use them to ensure that ICE conducts enforcement in concert with legal norms. They can hold oversight hearings that require ICE to explain its enforcement actions, including the shootings of both U.S. citizens and immigrants.

Second, issues of specific importance to the church can be highlighted, including limits on the pastoral access to detainees, the separation of families, the detention and deportation of pregnant women, children and the disabled, and the weakening of asylum protections at the border. The new Congress could require reforms to enforcement through the appropriations process, conditioning any new funding for the Department of Homeland Security on their implementation. A statement signed by 20 Catholic bishops in February provides a blueprint for possible reforms to immigration enforcement.

Finally, advocates of immigration reform can pursue the passage of legislation that has bipartisan support. Legislation that could, realistically, be passed by both chambers of Congress would help draw attention to important immigration issues, even if it were vetoed by the president.

For example, the American Dream and Promise Act, introduced in the current Congress, provides a path to citizenship to undocumented youth who entered the country as children, known as Dreamers, and members of groups that had Temporary Protected Status before it was stripped away by the Trump administration, including Haitians and Afghans. These are groups who most Americans believe should not be sent back to their home countries.

The church could also push for passage of the Religious Workforce Protection Act, legislation that would facilitate the permanent status of foreign-born pastoral workers, including Catholic priests and religious, who have legally entered and worked in the United States.

For the long term, we need to lay the groundwork for humane immigration reform. Advocates may first need to spend time convincing Democrats to back positive immigration reform, as opponents have been successful over the past 10 years in pushing the debate in a more restrictionist direction. And any passage of a comprehensive immigration reform bill, including a path to citizenship for the undocumented, would certainly be met with a veto by President Trump (and the bill might be severely weakened during the legislative process at any rate). Passing a humane and fair immigration reform bill requires a president—either Democratic or Republican—who is willing to spend political capital on its passage.

In the meantime, Catholic immigration advocates should pursue a more prudent path and join with labor and business leaders to push for congressional hearings that highlight how mass deportations have hurt the nation, both economically and socially, and reveal how the current legal immigration system is severely broken and needs repair.

Advocates should also work to shape public opinion among the Catholic faithful. Catholic IMMpact (the Catholic Immigrant Prophetic Action Project), an initiative of the Catholic-based Center for Migration Studies of New York and Hope Border Institute, was launched to help (arch)dioceses educate Catholics and prepare them for the immigration reform debate that is to come.

Catholic leaders should also hold internal discussions about what a successful immigration reform bill might look like and what concessions are inevitable. For example, advocates may face the decision of whether to accept a form of legal status for the undocumented that does not include a pathway to full citizenship. They should keep in mind that in past immigration reform debates, the “perfect” bill has been the enemy of the good.

The Trump administration’s mass deportation campaign has revealed the ugly underbelly of the U.S. immigration system and how it can undermine human dignity and violate human rights. It has also taught us that the removal of hard-working immigrants and their families can harm the U.S. economy and weaken the social fabric of local communities. These lessons provide hope that out of the darkness of the current period of mass deportation a dawn of opportunity may emerge to pass humane immigration reform legislation, for which the church must be patient yet prepared.
