text:
The Justice Department filed a lawsuit on Thursday against Pennsylvania State University over its policy of giving in-state tuition to illegal immigrants.

The DOJ alleged that Penn State violated "federal law by prioritizing the needs of illegal aliens over U.S. citizens in defiance of Congress’s commands."

The university's policy allegedly "grants in-state tuition to illegal aliens while denying reduced tuition to U.S. citizens," the DOJ said. "This policy unconstitutionally discriminates against U.S. citizens who are not afforded the same reduced tuition rate, in direct conflict with federal law."

The lawsuit seeks to enjoin Penn State from enforcing the policy and "from enacting any new tuition policies that favor undocumented students over U.S. citizens," according to the DOJ.

“The Department of Justice today continues its efforts to ensure that no state law or university policy gives preferential treatment to illegal aliens over our Nation’s own citizens,” Associate Attorney General Stanley E. Woodward, Jr., said in a statement. “Congress long ago made clear that states, through their public universities, cannot give reduced tuition to illegal aliens not available to all Americans.”

With Thursday's lawsuit, the DOJ has filed 27 total complaints against states and Washington, D.C., over in-state tuition for illegal immigrants. Of the 27 lawsuits, six of them — involving Texas, Kentucky, Oklahoma, Nebraska, Illinois, and Kansas — had resulted in favorable court orders permanently blocking and declaring unconstitutional the challenged provisions. Other cases remained pending.

According to Penn State's website, "Undocumented students, with or without [Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals], can be eligible for in-state tuition if they meet Penn State’s residency requirements. These requirements include attending an accredited Pennsylvania high school for at least four years and graduating from an accredited Pennsylvania high school or receiving a Pennsylvania General Educational Development (GED) certificate."

Under the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996, which is codified as 8 U.S.C. 1623, a person who is not lawfully present in the United States cannot receive a postsecondary education benefit based on state residency unless U.S. citizens are eligible for a benefit of at least the same amount, duration, and scope regardless of whether they live in that state.

Supporters of in-state tuition policies for illegal immigrants counter that many recipients have lived and attended school in their states for years, that expanding access to higher education can increase graduates' earning potential and tax contributions, and that denying resident tuition can make college financially inaccessible.

text:
Where a habeas corpus petitioner has challenged his detention following the revocation of his release, his petition should be granted because the government revoked his release without complying with the applicable legal requirements.

“This is a habeas petition that concerns a noncitizen’s challenge to his detention following the revocation of his release. Petitioner … is a citizen of Brazil who illegally entered the United States in 2021, was ordered removed, and was released on an order of supervision. He was on supervision for more than five years without apparent incident.

“In September 2026, he was arrested and his release was revoked. In revoking his release, the government failed to comply with its own procedural regulations. Because those regulations are intended to provide notice to the arrestee and a meaningful opportunity to be heard, the failure of the government to follow them violated [the petitioner]’s right to due process of law. The Court will therefore grant the petition and order [the petitioner]’s release and return to supervision.

“The Court recognizes that the government may have the authority to re-arrest [the petitioner], and if the government complies with its regulations before revoking his release, [the petitioner] will likely receive the due process to which he is entitled. Nonetheless, the government cannot simply ignore the law, and if it does, it must live with the consequences. For his part, [the petitioner] contends that he plans to file a motion to reopen his removal proceedings and stay his removal. The Court cannot, however, base any part of its ruling on that representation. Instead, the Court will issue its ruling based on the circumstances as they now exist, without regard to possible future events. And because the government revoked [the petitioner]’s release without complying with the applicable legal requirements, it will be ordered to release him from custody pending further developments. …

“In short, nothing in the revocation notice puts [the petitioner] on notice of the ‘reasons for revocation,’ as the regulation requires, and that would permit him to meaningfully contest his revocation during his informal interview. 8 C.F.R. §241.4(l)(1). …

“… Because ICE violated its own regulations and thereby impaired [the petitioner]’s right to due process, the revocation of his [Order of Supervision (OSUP)] is invalid and his detention is unlawful. …

“For the foregoing reasons, the petition for writ of habeas corpus is granted. Respondents shall release [the petitioner] no later than 5:00 p.m. local time on October 23, 2026. …”

Modolo v. Wesling, et al. (Lawyers Weekly No. 02-574-26) (8 pages) (Saylor, J.) (Civil Action No. 26-14411-FDS) (Oct. 22, 2026).

text:
The Trump administration held secret talks with Iran on deporting Iranians even as the war there dragged on, court documents obtained by the Associated Press show.

The court documents unsealed on Thursday show the Republican administration as recently as mid-October said it had plans to deport the Iranians through an unnamed third country, although it was unclear when it intended to do so.

The judge in the case ordered the government to give the court 24-hour notice of any finalized plans to deport Iranians to Iran or to any other country and five days’ written notice before any such deportation is carried out.

“We are at war with a country where the president of the United States has said, as recently as two or three days ago, if not yesterday, that it is essentially lawless … A country that is an enemy of the United States, according to the current president. A country that, according to our president, murdered tens of thousands of protestors,” the judge, Ana Reyes, said according to the 15 October transcript that has now been unsealed.

“And what you’re telling me is that the United States of America is going to send individuals back to that region, facing what you and I and everyone who would ever look at this would know would be, at a minimum, a serious threat of certain death.”

“Yes, your honor,” justice department attorney Dimitar Georgiev-Remmel said. “The government is executing lawful orders of removal.”

Georgiev-Remmel told the court there was no specific date set to carry out any removals. A legal group representing Iranians held by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) said a dozen Iranian detainees had been given notice over the past week that they would be deported to Iran. The legal group, the Iranian American Legal Defense Fund, brought the lawsuit in which the transcript was released.

The court documents show that the administration maintained contacts with Iranian officials during the war over the removals, specifically for submitting travel documents and figuring out “possible avenues for removal”.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), ICE’s parent agency, and the state department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The development emerged from an ongoing lawsuit that alleges the Trump administration’s immigration agencies have been sharing confidential information about Iranian asylum seekers with the Iranian government, violating national immigration regulations and endangering countless Iranians, court filings argue.

The Iranian American Legal Defense Fund said on Thursday at least 12 Iranian detainees have been contacted by the Iranian Interest Section, an Iranian representative office in the Pakistani embassy in Washington that handles consular affairs, in the past week and notified of an upcoming deportation flight to Iran through Pakistan. The group did not say when the deportation would occur.

One of those detainees attempted suicide once he learned he might be returned to Iran, according to Yasmine Chubin, the executive director of the organization. He was one of two people who were subsequently moved across state lines to a detention center in Texas, where detainees are often relocated immediately preceding a removal.

None of the detainees who have been contacted have been provided any information in writing from immigration authorities, the legal group said.

Activists abroad have expressed concern about deportees returning to Iran, whose theocracy has been cracking down on intellectuals and where the government vociferously cracks down on any dissent.

The lawsuit depicts a coordinated campaign between the US and Iranian governments to identify Iranians in ICE custody and pressure them to return to Iran – a marked departure from decades of diplomatic hostility between the two governments. The DHS has denied that it is sharing asylum application records with the Iranian government.

Hundreds of emails exchanged between US immigration officials exposed how the two countries worked together to arrange for more than 100 Iranians to be flown back to Iran on three immigration flights in September and December 2025 and January 2026.

During the 15 October hearing, Reyes warned government attorneys that she would initiate contempt proceedings if the administration violated her order to give the court advance notice of any planned deportation flights.

“We are talking about sending individuals in our care and custody to a country that we have bombed and we may continue bombing, and is a declared enemy of this country,” Reyes said.

In a court filing on Wednesday, the justice department said the judge’s order effectively served as an injunction against the government “given the possibility of sanctions and contempt dangling overhead”.

Deportations of Iranians back to their home country are historically rare, owing to the lack of diplomatic relations between the US and Iran and the possible persecution they could face there.

But under the Trump administration, which is carrying out a broad immigration crackdown, ICE has aggressively pushed to deport people even from countries that have typically been reluctant to take people back or with whom the US has had icy or no diplomatic relations.

Sometimes that has meant sending people back to their home country, but it has also meant deporting people to other countries they have no connection with.

name: Policy
title: What a Democratic Congress Means for Oversight in 2027 | Morrison Foerster
authors: Carlos Felipe Uriarte, Kimberly Hamm, Joseph Charles Folio III
description:
Democrats’ Oversight Agenda Voter sentiment will shape Democrats’ oversight agenda in 2027.
Key committees: House Energy and Commerce Committee, House and Senate Judiciary Committees, Senate Banking Committee, and Senate Finance Committee Federal power and civil liberties.
Key committees: House Oversight Committee, House Judiciary Committee, House Natural Resources Committee, and Senate Finance Committee The Pentagon, national security, foreign donations, and foreign business.
Key committees: House Foreign Affairs Committee, House Armed Services Committee, House Intelligence Committee, and Senate Armed Services Committee AI and data centers.
Key committees: House Energy and Commerce Committee, Senate Banking Committee, Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, and Senate Commerce Committee Takeaway: Expect Democratic investigations into alleged corruption paired with legislative reform proposals.
text:
Democrats will control both chambers of Congress in 2027 following a sweeping midterm election victory on Tuesday. While votes are still being counted in several states, Democrats are on track to hold at least 54 Senate seats and a House majority of more than 250 seats, the largest in nearly two decades.

Within hours of the results, the incoming chairs of two of the most powerful investigative congressional committees signaled what comes next: “Lawyer up.” and “Subpoenas.”

Key takeaways

Investigations will be wide-ranging and move quickly, driven by four issues: affordability, federal power and civil liberties, alleged corruption, and national security. Against this backdrop, artificial intelligence (AI) and data centers will feature prominently in investigations across committees and chambers.

Parallel investigations will multiply, as Congress, state attorneys general, and potentially the Trump administration act on the same issues.

Subpoenas may be ubiquitous, but litigation could be selective. Democrats have threatened the robust use of subpoenas, but enforcement is challenging and accommodations are the preferred method of resolution.

The clock is already running. Letters can arrive now, and subpoenas are likely early next year.

“Lawyer Up”: The Signal Is Clear

On election night, House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform Ranking Member Robert Garcia (D-CA) issued a two-word statement: “Lawyer up.”

This message follows Democratic committee leaders’ 2026 preview of their investigative agenda, sending hundreds of letters requesting records and information from the Trump administration and private parties alike. Representative Jamie Raskin (D-MD), in line to chair the House Judiciary Committee, has been meeting with House Democratic leadership to divide the oversight work among committees and expects to spend November and December setting priorities for public hearings.

Takeaway: Democrats are in the minority until the 120th Congress convenes on January 3, 2027, but incoming chairs can send letters and preservation requests now. Subpoenas are likely early next year, once committees organize and adopt their rules. How a company responds to an informal request today will shape the record later, and declining to engage is rarely a sound strategy.

Democrats’ Oversight Agenda

Voter sentiment will shape Democrats’ oversight agenda in 2027. On key concerns that dominated the exit polls, Democrats spent 2026 sending the letters that will become 2027 investigations.

Affordability, market power, and consumer protection. Three in four voters said the economy is in bad shape, and at least 85% were concerned about the cost of gas, food, utilities, and healthcare. Expect scrutiny of pricing practices, drug-pricing arrangements, energy costs, the impact of tariffs on consumers, and industries Democrats argue are raising costs or shifting risk onto consumers.

Key committees: House Energy and Commerce Committee, House and Senate Judiciary Committees, Senate Banking Committee, and Senate Finance Committee

Federal power and civil liberties. A majority of voters said immigration enforcement has gone too far. Democrats are poised to investigate the administration’s immigration enforcement and deportation efforts, as well as government contractors and companies whose products and services may have been used to support the administration’s immigration enforcement actions.

Key committees: House Oversight Committee, House Judiciary Committee, House Homeland Security Committee, Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee and its Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations

Corporate engagement with the Trump administration and Trump family members. About nine in 10 voters called corruption a major factor contributing to their vote, and both parties will want to demonstrate to voters they can be trusted to address the issue. Democrats will attempt to tie this concern to Trump family businesses, donations to Trump-aligned projects, and corporate interactions with the administration. Expect probes into corporate donations, government financial support of certain industries, government contracts, and corporate ties to Trump family-aligned businesses or industries.

Key committees: House Oversight Committee, House Judiciary Committee, House Natural Resources Committee, and Senate Finance Committee

The Pentagon, national security, foreign donations, and foreign business. Nearly two-thirds of voters (63%) were opposed to military action in Iran. Ranking Member Gregory Meeks (D-NY), in line to chair the House Foreign Affairs Committee, has promised investigations into the administration’s Iran war decision-making, as well as Venezuela operations and military strikes in the Caribbean and Pacific. These probes include inquiries into energy companies, government contractors, and financial services companies. Democrats have also highlighted possible national security risks of foreign donations to Trump-aligned projects, foreign investment in sensitive technology, and foreign business entanglements with Trump family businesses.

Key committees: House Foreign Affairs Committee, House Armed Services Committee, House Intelligence Committee, and Senate Armed Services Committee

AI and data centers. Three in four voters (76%) oppose a data center in their community, and 57% believe AI will do more harm than good. Expect committees across Congress to hold hearings with technology and AI leaders, along with scrutiny of data-center energy costs and chip exports.

Key committees: House Energy and Commerce Committee, Senate Banking Committee, Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, and Senate Commerce Committee

Takeaway: Expect Democratic investigations into alleged corruption paired with legislative reform proposals. AI cuts across all four issues, and with comprehensive legislation unlikely, congressional action will shift toward hearings and other oversight requests.

Parallel Investigations

Congress rarely investigates alone. Democrats flipped attorney general offices in Texas, Georgia, Iowa, and Kansas. Texas elected its first Democratic attorney general since 1994, who has pledged a focus on consumer protection and anti-corruption. These offices join states such as California and New York that already lead multistate litigation. Meanwhile, the administration may want to show that it is protecting consumers too, with the Federal Trade Commission and Department of Justice (DOJ) pursuing visible enforcement of their own, including partnering with state attorneys general.

With Democrats in the majority, expect committee reports to serve as road maps for state attorneys general, and potentially as source material for plaintiffs’ attorneys.

What this means for companies:

Be prepared for multi-front fights with Congress, state, and federal authorities. While congressional committees in the past may have simply referred concerns of misconduct to state or federal authorities, or declined to press agencies about open criminal investigations, companies are unlikely to see such restraint next Congress.

Assume anything produced to Congress will become public. Committees control their own records and can release documents, quote them at hearings, or publish them in reports. Caution should be observed if committees demand copies of records provided to state or federal authorities.

Be mindful of privilege concerns. Committees do not consider themselves bound by attorney-client privilege or work-product protection, but in practice accommodations can be reached.

Keep one fact record. Inconsistent statements across forums become the story and criminal false-statement liability extends to congressional inquiries.

Democrats’ Subpoena Authority

On election night, President Trump had a simple message: “VETO.” Senate Finance Committee Ranking Member Ron Wyden (D-OR) posted his own one-word message: “Subpoenas.”

Despite the confrontational rhetoric, expect both the administration and a Democratic Congress to pick and choose their battles, with accommodations reached on both sides.

The White House has added legal staff to prepare for oversight and a recent DOJ Office of Legal Counsel opinion suggests the administration may assert executive privilege over certain presidential communications with private parties. But contesting every request across dozens of committees would consume time and capital the administration will need elsewhere in its final two years.

Despite the focus on potential subpoenas next Congress, the use of congressional subpoenas is now a commonplace occurrence. Since 2021, nearly 600 subpoenas have been issued by congressional committees, but Congress has brought just three civil enforcement actions during that time. Document demands and subpoenas may be broadly worded to seek “any and all” documents, but narrowed responses are typically negotiated. Litigation risks for House committees mean negotiation is the preferred resolution.

Why understanding subpoena threats and litigation matters:

The threat of a subpoena no longer carries the weight it once did. Subpoenas are common and rarely enforced, through litigation or criminal contempt of Congress.

The legal arguments shape leverage. Legislative purpose, pertinence, breadth, burden, and constitutional defenses all bear on how much room a company has to negotiate scope.

Companies may be caught in the middle. If the White House asserts privilege over its communications with a company, the company should consider its exposure on each side as it considers whether to produce, withhold, or seek an accommodation.

Congress will enforce subpoenas selectively. Committees will choose the strongest candidates for litigation – subpoenas narrowly written, with a clear legislative purpose, seeking clearly non-privileged materials, and in support of an investigation with a compelling narrative. Criminal contempt requires a DOJ prosecution, which rarely follows when Congress is led by the opposing party.

Takeaway: Expect widespread subpoena threats, but behind-the-scenes negotiations to resolve disputes. Disputes that reach court will be chosen carefully to win and to set precedent. Knowing which category a matter falls into should shape strategy from the first letter.

Looking Ahead: Key Dates

November 10, 2026: Republican leadership elections to take place.

November 18-19, 2026: House Democratic leadership elections to take place. Senate Democrats hold leadership elections in December.

December 11, 2026: Government funding expires, an early signal of how each side will approach the 120th Congress.

January 3, 2027: The 120th Congress convenes, and the House adopts its rules package.

January 2027: Committees set organizational meetings and finalize internal rules.

Early 2027: The first subpoenas are possible, along with opening hearings.

We will continue to monitor developments as the new Congress takes shape. For questions, please contact the Congressional Investigations team.

Alec Bartishevich, a Policy Advisor in our Washington, D.C. office, contributed to this alert.

text:
A private prison company that has raked in billions by selling immigration detention centers to the Trump administration wants the government to “move quickly” on more deals, days after a Democratic landslide in the midterms.

CoreCivic has sold four detention centers to the Department of Homeland Security this year for $2.2 billion and has been touting plans for future sales. But its new CEO faced questions Thursday during an earnings call from investors wanting to know if that would continue under Democratic control of Congress starting in January.

“We can’t predict what will happen one way or the other on timing or really on whether they will happen at all,” CEO Lucibeth Mayberry said of the negotiations for additional sales. “We would urge the ICE administration to move quickly. They have a need for capacity. We have the capacity. There’s no reason to wait.”

Mayberry, who took over as the head of CoreCivic in September, emphasized that Congress had given DHS billions for immigration detention — $45 billion in 2025 and $31 billion last year — available through fiscal year 2029. She said she saw no reason DHS wouldn’t continue entering into contracts until that funding is gone.

Trending

But the massive cash influx Congress gave to Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and the contracts with CoreCivic and its main competitor, Geo Group, are set to come under scrutiny once Democrats take back the gavel.

Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-Washington), the ranking member of the House Judiciary subcommittee dealing with immigration, said the heads of the companies can expect to be called to testify. She’s been closely tracking immigrants’ deaths in detention.

“The gravy train is over,” Jayapal said.

And Rep. Rosa DeLauro (D-Connecticut) is seeking to chair the House Appropriations Committee, saying the party must “claw back” billions of dollars Republicans gave to ICE and Border Patrol outside of the regular appropriations process.

Geo Group is expecting to sell four detention centers to DHS by the end of the year, but those sales won’t materialize if the company can’t secure long-term agreements to manage the daily operations, CEO George Zoley told investors Thursday.

The company announced last month the sale of a complex of more than 2,600 beds in Adelanto, California, to ICE for $950 million and a new 10-year contract to run the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma, Washington, that will generate $140 million in annual revenue.

The day before the election, Geo Group announced another 10-year contract to manage a 2,329-bed detention center in Big Spring, Texas, though it does not own the land.

CoreCivic acknowledges in its quarterly reports that its contracts with ICE can be terminated. “We can provide no assurance that we will continue to manage these facilities in the future, or that the terms of the management agreements will remain the same,” the most recent report states.

The detention center sales have already raised questions about federal waste and how the federal government is agreeing to pay hundreds of millions of dollars for detention centers that, in most cases, ICE was already using.

For example, ICE paid more than $495 million for a vacant 1,600-bed lockup in Appleton, Minnesota, that CoreCivic had offered to the state government for $75 million a year prior, an investigation from KARE 11 found.

Both companies and the Trump administration have said the value is calculated based on how much it would take to replace the buildings, adjusted depreciation and land value, among other factors.

“Why are both of those things happening in the order that they’re happening in?” Jayapal said of the sales and long-term management agreements. “It seems like somebody is making a lot of profit off of these sales and purchases, and we need to understand that.”

text:
BANGKOK—Two Uyghur men held in Thailand for more than a decade are pleading to not be sent back to China, fearing abuse or torture.

Human rights activists and some Thai politicians warn the men could be sent to China following their release from prison in late October.

Uyghurs are a Turkic, majority Muslim ethnic group native to Xinjiang in China’s northwest. After decades of conflict with Beijing over discrimination and suppression of their cultural identity, the Chinese government launched a brutal crackdown on them that some Western governments have called a genocide.

The two men were among more than 300 Uyghurs fleeing China detained by Thai authorities in 2014 near the Malaysian border. China has consistently pushed for their return, saying they were terrorists.

The two men, ages 26 and 35, told the Office of the National Human Rights Commission on Wednesday that they do not want to be sent back to China, according to a source with direct knowledge of the meeting who requested anonymity for fear of retribution. They made the same plea in a letter published last week.

In response to the concerns, Thailand said Wednesday that China must make a formal extradition request if it wants the two Uyghur men returned.

National Security Council chief Chaipruak Doungprapat said the courts would decide on whether to deport the two, unlike the case of 40 Uyghur men sent back to China last year, and that the men would be able to defend themselves. A ruling in their favor could allow them to resettle in another country.

“But if the court rules against them, they will be extradited according to the treaty. This is the judicial process,” he said.

China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Mao Ning didn’t comment on whether China had sent an extradition request.

“China and Thailand’s cooperation in combating cross-border crimes, including illegal immigration, is in accordance with the laws of both countries, as well as international law and international practice,” Mao said Wednesday.

Of the group of more than 300 Uyghurs detained over a decade ago, Thailand sent mostly women and children from the group to Turkey. In 2015, Thailand deported 109 to China against their will, prompting an international outcry. The Thai embassy in Turkey was ransacked in protest.

In February 2025, Thailand sent back another 40 despite pleas from the men themselves, Thai lawmakers and U.N. officials not to.

Today that fear is front and center for the two men.

“Every time we are worrying from China to take back us,” one of the Uyghur men wrote in English in the letter shared by Kannavee Suebsang, a former lawmaker and founder of the Peace Rights Foundation, a human rights group that represents them. “We aren’t terrorist,” he wrote.

Sasinan Thamnithinan, a lawmaker from the opposition People’s Party, said Thailand is obligated by both domestic and international law to ensure that no individual is returned to a country where they could face torture or inhumane treatment.

“Maintaining international relations is important, but it must not take precedence over human rights and the rule of law. No one should be sent back to face danger simply because the government wants to end a problem,” Sasinan said in a statement Tuesday.

Up until the very last moments before the previous group was deported, the Thai government denied they would be sending the men to China.

The Thai government said the men had signed forms in Chinese to return voluntarily. China then took select Thai media groups on an official tour, but they did not have independent access to speak to the individuals who were returned.

Thailand’s Office of the National Human Rights Commission said last year that Thai officials involved failed to provide evidence that the men consented to be sent back or an assurance of the group’s safety upon their return.

“The assertion that the Uyghurs returned voluntarily remains a one-sided claim ... despite reports assessing human rights concerns in the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region, which document instances of torture and cruel treatment against the Uyghur population,” the office said in a statement.

Kannavee said he made official attempts while still in office to determine what happened to the 40 men but received no reply. He said Thailand’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and others also attempted to follow up. The ministry declined to comment.

text:
The Trump administration said during a court hearing that it has been making plans to deport Iranian immigrants back to Iran while the U.S. is at war with that country, earning a rebuke from a federal judge, court documents show.

According to an unsealed transcript of a hearing held on Oct. 15, a Justice Department attorney disclosed in federal court that the Trump administration was making plans to deport Iranian nationals to Iran through third countries.

The hearing was part of a lawsuit brought by the Iranian American Legal Defense Fund against the Trump administration alleging that the government is sharing confidential information about Iranian asylum seekers with the Iranian government.

During a heated two-hour hearing, U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes blasted government lawyers after learning that Department of Homeland Security officials were working on removal logistics to send individuals back to Iran.

"Your Honor, one of the questions that you had asked is whether there are any planned removals to Iran," said DOJ attorney Dimitar Georgiev. "The answer in August was no. Today that answer has changed and it is yes".

"I'm sorry, I just want to make sure I understand this correctly," Judge Reyes said. "We are going to remove people in our custody to a country with which we are at war?"

"We are at war with a country, where the president of the United States has said as recently as two or three days ago, if not yesterday, that it is essentially lawless ... and what you're telling me is that the United States of America is going to send individuals back to that region facing what you and I and everyone who would ever look at this would know would be at a minimum a serious threat of certain death?" Reyes said.

A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment from ABC News.

The transcript shows the U.S. government has been holding talks and coordinating with representatives of the Iranian government to arrange removals.

According to court documents, the Iranian Interest Section in Washington, D.C., sent officials to U.S. detention centers to meet with detainees. Iranian detainees in California and Arizona were offered meetings with officials, but they refused and no meetings took place, according to the transcript.

During the hearing, Georgiev said the U.S. will "facilitate the travel" of the Iranian detainees to a third country and that the government of Iran will facilitate the travel from the third country into Iran.

Judge Reyes ordered the government to provide at least five days' advance notice before any individual is "placed on a transport vehicle or plane bound for removal," and 24 hours' notice of any finalized removal plan.

"If anything happens that violates either of those two orders, I will hold every single person associated with violating it. I will start contempt proceedings," Reyes said.

"We are talking about sending individuals in our care and custody to a country that we have bombed and we may continue bombing, and is a declared enemy of this country," the judge said. "It is like saying we have individuals in 1942 in this country that we are going to send back to Nazi Germany. That is the equivalent of what you are telling me."

title: After the Midterms: Defending Health Care, Building a Better Future
authors: Jennifer Cannistra, Geraldine Doetzer, Abigail Coursolle
description:
The 2026 midterms have opened a door, as voters made clear that rising health care costs and threats to their coverage demand action.
What we do next will determine whether that opening becomes meaningful change for people who need health care.
We have fought to protect their access to health care, defend their civil rights, and advance health equity.
In California, we continued to lead efforts to protect the health care system that millions of people rely on.
And rebuilding must mean reaching the people our health care system failed long before this administration took office.
text:
The 2026 midterms have opened a door, as voters made clear that rising health care costs and threats to their coverage demand action. What we do next will determine whether that opening becomes meaningful change for people who need health care.

For the last two years, the National Health Law Program has stood as a bulwark against the Trump administration’s unlawful and harmful actions. Our responsibility was clear: stand with low-income families, people with disabilities, people struggling to make ends meet, and everyone this administration has left out, maligned, or targeted. We have fought to protect their access to health care, defend their civil rights, and advance health equity.

Support our Work

We challenged the administration’s purge of the federal government and joined allies determined to preserve the expertise and public institutions our communities depend on. We also welcomed public servants driven out by those attacks onto our own team, putting their knowledge to work in defense of health care.

We fought to stop the so-called One Big Beautiful Bill Act. We continue to contest its implementation and equip advocates to protect people from its harms.

We sued to demand transparency about the administration’s sharing of Medicaid enrollees’ personal information with immigration enforcement.

We joined amicus briefs defending the rights of people with disabilities and immigrants, access to ACA insurance plans, and funding for sexual and reproductive health clinics.

This fall, we filed the lawsuit Taylor v. Kennedy to challenge federal Medicaid work requirement rules that unlawfully narrow protections for people who are medically frail or have special medical needs, threatening health coverage for people with serious health conditions, including cancer, diabetes, HIV, and substance use disorders.

We strongly opposed the administration’s use of “waste, fraud, and abuse” as a pretext to freeze Medicaid and other social service funding. These actions sowed fear among working-class and low-income communities, immigrants, LGBTQ people, and people with disabilities, threatening essential services that help people stay healthy and make ends meet.

In states across the country, we defended sexual and reproductive health rights and helped expand access, including in Maryland and Virginia.

In California, we continued to lead efforts to protect the health care system that millions of people rely on.

This work has demanded resolve, expertise, and extraordinary partnership. It has also demanded the conviction that a better future is possible and a concrete plan to make that future real.

Now we must turn that conviction into action.

We will work with our partners and the new congressional majorities to advance legislation that reverses the trillion-dollar Medicaid cuts and restores the expired Affordable Care Act insurance subsidies. We will demand accountability for the harm already done and continue to challenge unlawful actions in court.

The most urgent work starts now. Federal law requires most states to launch Medicaid work requirements by January 1, 2027, and some already have. New governors taking office in January will shape how they are carried out. We will work with state partners and Medicaid applicants and enrollees to make sure no one who is eligible loses coverage to red tape. And we will hold states accountable when implementation fails the people it is meant to serve.

We continue our ongoing work to develop a proactive agenda for health reform, both internally and with partners.

We are also developing a Medicaid Repro Roadmap to expand access to sexual and reproductive health care. This spring, we will bring that vision to Capitol Hill and statehouses across the country, with practical proposals that move us toward a future where everyone can get the care they need.

An election does not restore someone’s coverage, reopen a clinic, eliminate discrimination, or erase the fear of seeking care. Those changes take sustained work. And rebuilding must mean reaching the people our health care system failed long before this administration took office.

NHeLP is ready for that work. We have defended the possibility of a better future. Together, we can build it. Join us in that future!

For audio listeners, you can listen to our audio version of the News Digest here. You can also join our Immigration News Digest Newsletter here.

Ninth Circuit Temporarily Pauses Reinstatement of Venezuela TPS

UK Confirms Major Settlement Reforms With New 10-Year Standard Pathway

Canada Introduces New Penalties for Immigration Fraud and Unauthorized Representation

Ninth Circuit Temporarily Pauses Reinstatement of Venezuela TPS

A federal appeals court has temporarily blocked a district court order that would have reinstated Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Venezuelan nationals, adding to ongoing uncertainty surrounding the country’s TPS designation.

On November 3, 2026, the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals granted the Trump administration’s request for an administrative stay, reversing its earlier denial of temporary relief. The stay pauses implementation of the lower court’s reinstatement order while the appeals court considers the government’s request for further relief.

The dispute centers on the Department of Homeland Security’s decision to terminate TPS for Venezuela. The district court had ordered reinstatement of TPS, but the latest appellate action temporarily prevents that order from taking effect.

The administrative stay is not a final ruling on the legality of the TPS termination, and further court decisions could affect beneficiaries’ status and employment authorization. The ruling also creates uncertainty regarding employment authorization for Venezuelan TPS holders. Employers should not assume that the district court’s reinstatement order currently provides a basis for extending employment authorization without supporting USCIS guidance.

Impact: The temporary stay extends uncertainty for Venezuelan TPS beneficiaries and their employers.. Organizations should closely monitor USCIS announcements, review affected employees’ documentation, and ensure Form I-9 reverification decisions reflect current government guidance and applicable court orders.

UK Confirms Major Settlement Reforms With New 10-Year Standard Pathway

The UK government has published its response to the Earned Settlement consultation, outlining plans to increase the standard qualifying period for permanent settlement, or Indefinite Leave to Remain (ILR), from five to 10 years. The reforms would introduce a contribution-based framework allowing certain individuals to qualify sooner based on earnings, occupation, and immigration history.

Under the proposed framework, settlement timelines would vary depending on individual circumstances:

Three years: Certain exceptional talent applicants and individuals earning at least GBP 125,141 for three of the preceding four years.

Five years: Individuals earning at least GBP 50,271 for three of the preceding five years and certain qualifying public-sector healthcare and education workers.

10 years: The standard pathway, generally requiring earnings of at least GBP 12,571 for five of the preceding seven years, subject to exemptions.

Up to 20 years: Certain individuals with immigration violations or a history of claiming public funds.

The government has also proposed greater flexibility for families, including combining qualifying couples’ earnings and allowing certain dependent children to settle with their parents.

Limited transitional protections would preserve a five-year pathway for qualifying care, healthcare, and education workers who entered or switched immigration routes before the May 2025 Immigration White Paper.

Importantly, the reforms are not yet legally effective. The government is expected to publish a Statement of Changes outlining the final requirements and implementation dates.

Impact: The proposed framework could extend settlement timelines for many sponsored workers while offering accelerated pathways for higher earners and certain occupations. Employers should review affected employees’ settlement plans, anticipated sponsorship costs, and family circumstances as they prepare for potential changes to the Immigration Rules.

Canada Introduces New Penalties for Immigration Fraud and Unauthorized Representation

Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) has introduced new financial penalties for unauthorized immigration representation and fraudulent or misleading information in immigration applications. Effective October 28, 2026, the new framework allows authorities to impose combined penalties of up to CAD 1.5 million for violations.

The regulations apply to individuals providing paid immigration or citizenship advice and representation, including licensed consultants, lawyers, and unauthorized service providers operating within or outside Canada.

Under the new enforcement framework, penalties may include:

CAD 5,000 for providing paid immigration or citizenship advice or representation without proper authorization.

CAD 15,000 for knowingly submitting or facilitating false or misleading information on behalf of an applicant.

Additional penalties for more serious or repeated violations, including cases where applications are approved based on fraudulent information.

The government has also announced plans to establish a public registry in 2027 identifying penalized representatives and detailing their violations.

The measures aim to strengthen oversight of immigration service providers, protect applicants from fraud, and reinforce the importance of accurate documentation and authorized representation.

text:
WASHINGTON —

President Donald Trump is facing a new political reality after voters handed Democrats control of Congress, leaving him to decide whether to compromise with the opposition party or fight to preserve his agenda.

"I'll get along probably with the Democrats unless they want to be destructive," Trump said Wednesday.

His White House is already warning the incoming majority against using its power to investigate his administration.

"If crazed Democrats want to abuse their power and politicize their process of investigations, subpoenas, and destroying lives, they should be reminded that we still control the federal government and all of its powers," a White House official said.

The warning comes as some Democrats are already promising investigations into Trump and his administration.

Rep. Robert Garcia, D-California, who is expected to lead the House Oversight Committee, had a two-word message after his party won control of the House: "Lawyer up."

Garcia has outlined plans to investigate the administration's handling of the Jeffrey Epstein files, Trump's family business dealings, immigration enforcement and government contracts.

Democrats will gain the power to launch congressional investigations, compel testimony and demand documents when they take control of both the House and Senate in January.

Democrats outline their agenda

That confrontation is already taking shape as Democrats outline plans to reverse parts of the president's domestic agenda and pressure him to end the war in Iran.

"The first thing we're going to do is reduce people's costs," Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, D-New York, said.

Democratic leaders have signaled a desire to restore expired Affordable Care Act premium tax credits and reverse Medicaid cuts Trump signed into law.

Both proposals would require Trump's signature or enough support in Congress to override a presidential veto, which requires a two-thirds vote in both chambers.

Before the election, Hearst Television asked Interior Secretary Doug Burgum whether a Democratic victory should prompt the administration to reconsider its policies or priorities.

"No, I don't think so. I think it would be a reflection of short-term frustration about, you know, the moment of time that we're in right now," Burgum said. "But long term, if you think about having lower taxes, lower regulation, more affordable energy, you know, a secure border, add up all the things that President Trump is doing. That is the pathway to a stronger economy."

Burgum argued that the administration's policies would produce long-term economic benefits, even if voters were frustrated with current conditions.

Iran war becomes a political and legislative challenge

One of the most consequential confrontations could center on the war in Iran. Democrats want to use Congress's authority over federal spending to pressure Trump to end the conflict.

Asked Wednesday when the war could end, Trump said, "Whenever I wanted to. But it's got to be done right."

The war has already emerged as a point of discussion within the administration following Republicans' election losses.

Both Trump and Vice President JD Vance acknowledged that the conflict hurt Republicans politically.

Vance went further, saying, "the reason we lost is the war," as he questioned whether the conflict was worth the political cost of losing control of the Senate in a post on X.

Asked Wednesday whether he would have done anything differently in regard to the Iran war, the president said no.

Republicans still control Congress for several more weeks, giving them a final opportunity to advance legislation before Democrats take over.

Legislation that needs to be addressed includes a government spending bill, as lawmakers face a Dec. 11 deadline to once again avoid a government shutdown.

text:
On September 30, 2026, a judge in the District of Oregon denied our motion for a preliminary injunction and motion for class certification in CLEAR Clinic et. al. v. Noem. Both motions had been pending for over ten months. While the court did not grant the requested relief, the case showed the many ways that ICE is blocking people’s access to due process. Documenting ICE’s disregard for the fundamental right to an attorney is a win that we can build on.

We filed the CLEAR Clinic case with organizational plaintiffs CLEAR Clinic and Pineros y Campesinos Unidos del Noroeste (PCUN), and an individual plaintiff who proceeded in the case as Leon X, at the height of ICE’s 2025 invasion of Oregon. During this surge, known as Operation Black Rose, federal agents detained over a thousand Oregonians as part of the Trump administration’s efforts to effectuate the largest deportation program in history. To achieve this goal, agents made a practice of denying people subject to immigration arrest access to counsel, and attempted to move people out of the state of Oregon (and away from their lawyers) very quickly. In practical terms, this meant that officers routinely refused to allow attorneys, including attorneys from CLEAR Clinic, to meet with people held at the Eugene and Portland ICE offices after immigration raids and warrantless arrests. When officers did allow attorney meetings, they often cut them short after only a few minutes; in some cases, attorneys were not even let past the lobby of the Eugene field office despite having representational agreements with clients held there.

Why does access to an attorney soon after arrest matter? As part of the Trump Administration’s xenophobic and racist campaign to deport as many immigrants as possible, regardless of the law and the Constitution, ICE agents are routinely pressuring the people they arrest to waive their rights and agree to deportation. Even US citizens have given into the pressure and signed for removal. ICE often engages in retaliatory transfers of immigrants from local detention centers to remote holding facilities in less favorable jurisdictions where attorney access is even more limited. Moreover, agents interview arrested persons to elicit information relevant to the decision to detain or release them, and that may be relevant to their immigration proceedings. Due process and federal law require access to counsel under such circumstances. But for ICE, due process and attorneys are merely barriers to achieving their arrest and deportation quotas. When people have access to legal representation, they can assert their constitutional rights and fight their unlawful arrest. As another case in this District has recognized, for every person who has been “fortunate enough to find counsel at the eleventh hour” in spite of the barriers ICE’s places to accessing counsel, “countless more people . . . have been rounded up, . . . remain in detention, or have [been] “voluntarily” deported” because of ICE’s unlawful detention campaign.

While this case did not result in the relief sought, we are extremely proud of the extensive evidence surfaced, both in writing and during two evidentiary hearings, regarding ICE’s interference with Oregonians’ access to counsel. Now that ICE has begun yet another attack on Oregon and other sanctuary states around the country, early access to an attorney is more crucial than ever.

All of the plaintiffs continue to work for justice. CLEAR Clinic continues to provide zealous representation for detained immigrants, including through the filing of habeas corpus petitions and in representation before the detained immigration court in Tacoma, Washington. PCUN ensures that its members both know their rights and are prepared to use them in any ICE interaction, especially when access to an attorney may be delayed by several days or longer. Leon X continues to be a brave Oregonian, who shows up everyday for his community, even when it's hard and even when he is scared. And we will continue to advocate for more just outcomes through federal litigation, individual representation, and advocacy for the state’s universal representation program, Equity Corps of Oregon, and state-level policies to defend all Oregonians.

text:
GW Law student attorneys in the Immigration Clinic helped a client and domestic violence survivor obtain asylum in the Annandale Immigration Court in October, marking a second major win for the clinic in a single semester.

Current and former student attorneys Mikaela Black, Caroline Peters, Olivia Russo, Angelica Salazar, and Maria Villalobos, wrote a 46-page brief, compiled over 1,200 pages of documents, and argued the client’s case in court.

The Immigration Clinic, led by Clinic Director Paulina Vera, JD ‘15, Distinguished Professorial Lecturer in Law, is one of 21 clinics offered through GW Law’s Jacob Burns Community Legal Clinics Program. The asylum result follows another success in which the clinic helped a 72-year-old grandmother avoid deportation by obtaining a rare writ of coram vobis to waive decades-old shoplifting convictions.

“Professor Vera and the student attorneys in the Immigration Clinic are truly living out GW Law’s mission to make an impact on the law,” said Dean Dayna Bowen Matthew. “Not only did they gain invaluable real-world experience in these two cases, they were able to make an undeniable difference in the lives of their clients, using law as a tool to achieve impactful results.”

The client in the asylum case is originally from Pakistan and a mother of two children, both United States citizens. She moved to the U.S. with her now ex-husband. For over 10 years, the client endured psychological and physical abuse from her ex-husband, leading to multiple hospital visits, Vera said. After initiating a divorce, which came with social and familial stigma, the client feared for her life if she were to return to Pakistan.

Student attorneys in the clinic wrote a 46-page brief and compiled over 1,200 pages of documents in support of the claim for asylum. Their work culminated in a hearing at the Annandale Immigration Court in Annandale, Virginia. After hours of testimony, led by Peters, Class of 2027, the Department of Homeland Security attorney waived appeal and the immigration judge on the case granted humanitarian asylum.

According to research from the Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse, the national asylum denial rate reached 94 percent over the summer with just 771 people obtaining asylum in June.

“I cannot emphasize enough how hard it is to get a result like we did,” Professor Vera said. “By design, asylum cases, especially gender-based asylum cases, are very difficult to win these days.”

From Briefing to Trial

The case required an all-hands-on-deck approach from a team of five student attorneys across two academic semesters. Professor Vera directed the student attorneys to try three approaches at once: applying for a U visa, which is granted to victims of crimes in the U.S. who cooperate with law enforcement; applying for a T visa, which applies to victims of trafficking; and applying for asylum. Villalobos and Black, both JD ‘26, worked to apply for the U and T visas in October of last year.

“Our client came to us and told us her story involving domestic violence and how she ended up in the United States,” Villalobos said. “We were starting from scratch. We sat down–me and [Black] with Professor Vera–and she laid it out and said, ‘We’re going to try absolutely everything that would be applicable, that would fit her situation, and it’s going to be a lot of work.’”

Ultimately, it was the asylum case that ended up being the quickest path to success. Last Spring, Peters and Salazar, class of 2027, took on the mantle to prepare for the client’s hearing in immigration court. Peters and Salazar compiled the 46-page brief and an affidavit for their client with the help of Professor Vera’s guidance and feedback. Peters then practiced the case in moot trial sessions with her client, honing her oral argument skills.

Prior to the trial on Tuesday, October 6, Peters sat in on other cases presided by the judge in the case.

“[The judge] was tough to say the least,” Peters said. “I was really confident and prepared when I walked in but also a little bit nervous because I didn’t know how the judge and opposing counsel would react to my arguments. I didn’t know how my opposing counsel was going to react to my arguments”

When the Immigration Clinic team received their decision that afternoon, they were thrilled.

“For me, it was especially rewarding because I wasn’t simply researching a hypothetical legal issue for class,” Salazar said. “The work I was producing was being an advocate for a person whose future depended on the outcome.”

Combining Passion with Legal Education

All of the students involved in the Immigration Clinic said they first became interested in doing this work because of a passion for helping others.

Both Salazar and Villalobos have personal experiences with the immigration system. For them, working in the clinic was not only an opportunity to improve their legal skills; it provided the means to make a real difference for clients who have had similar life experiences.

“I was born in Colombia and I immigrated to the United States with my family when I was 7 years old,” said Villalobos, adding that her experience filing her citizenship application and becoming a citizen when she was an undergraduate student made her want to go to law school. “I was really excited when I got accepted [into the clinic]. It felt like a full circle moment to represent clients that went through similar things that my family and I did.”

Professor Vera’s mentorship has also been an extremely valuable experience, the students said.

“I was super very intimidated by this whole process–by doing a trial on my own,” Peters said. “But Professor Vera was so knowledgeable and really supportive the whole time.”

Professor Vera is not just a mentor, Salazar said, she is a role model.

“I’ve never had a Latina professor,” Salazar said. “Seeing her and learning from her, and then also seeing how she is as a lawyer and trying to be more like her, it made a really big difference for me.”

The case is just one example of how experiential education offered to students through GW Law's clinical program serves the strategic goals of both the university and GW Law, fulfilling the mission to be a global law school that exists to have an impact on the law.

text:
The Department of Homeland Security is expected to face reinvigorated oversight and scrutiny in the next Congress, as top Democrats pledge to pursue investigations into the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement approach, allegations of corruption and other issues at DHS.

With their new majorities in the House and Senate following Tuesday’s midterm elections, Democrats are previewing plans to pursue aggressive oversight and investigations at DHS, ranging from Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s rapid expansion to staffing cuts at the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.

Rep. Bennie Thompson (D-Miss.) will seek the chairmanship of the House Homeland Security Committee, a position he previously held from 2019 through 2023. In a statement, he said the Trump administration “will finally be faced with real oversight” next year.

“We will have much on our plate after congressional Republicans have sat on their hands doing nothing for two years, but we will not shy away from what the American people demand of us,” Thompson said. “We will investigate the administration weaponizing DHS against Americans, its out of control immigration policies, and its blatantly corrupt self-dealing. The American people expect nothing less, and we will deliver.”

In a letter to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on Wednesday, Thompson demanded written confirmation that DHS would comply with records preservation requirements. He also pushed DHS to provide by Dec. 2 all information and documents sought by the committee over the last two years.

Meanwhile in the Senate, with Sen. Gary Peters (D-Mich.) retiring, Sen. Maggie Hassan (D-N.H.) is anticipated to take the gavel at the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee.

“The new majorities in Congress must focus on affordability and accountability for the American people,” Hassan said in a statement. “We must use every tool at our disposal to rein in this President, end this illegal war in Iran, and reverse his tariffs. And as part of my new role on the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, we will investigate and expose the corruption that is hurting taxpayers and Americans.”

Hassan has already posted job openings seeking “investigators and oversight counsel to lead investigations” at the homeland security committee. Open positions include an anti-corruption counsel and a policy advisor for AI security and safety issues.

Democrats’ oversight activities in the minority over the last two years offer a preview of what they may do next year with the power to call hearings, issue subpoenas and advance legislation.

Immigration enforcement is expected to be the top issue. Democrats on the House Homeland Security Committee have repeatedly pushed back against the Trump administration’s aggressive deportation agenda.

Democrats, including those on the appropriations committees, have raised repeated questions about how DHS is spending an influx of funds from the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act, as well as this year’s Secure America Act. Much of that funding went to ICE and Customs and Border Protection.

Thompson and Democrats on the homeland security committee have also sought investigations into ICE’s hiring practices, as the agency has more than doubled in size by hiring 12,000 new personnel under the Trump administration.

Democrats on the house committee have also pledged to investigate what they have called “the weaponization” of DHS, including reports on the department’s use of watchlists, biometric tools, data collection, social media monitoring, and other intelligence capabilities.

Kristina Moore, a former congressional investigator who now advises companies as partner at Womble Bond Dickinson, said “it’s pretty predictable” that ICE will be at the top of list of targets within DHS.

“In terms of, how are decisions made, who facilitated in making those decisions, who was hired, and then within that, is there any waste, fraud, and abuse?” Moore told Federal News Network. “Was a contract obtained because of a kickback? Was a contract obtained because of a relationship? Was it a no bid contract?”

Democrats are expected to target companies tied to allegations of corruption, including at DHS. Lawmakers have raised repeated questions about spending decisions at DHS, including many issues stemming from former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem’s tenure at DHS. In October, for instance, Thompson and his colleagues sent a letter to DHS seeking more information about the department’s purchase 10 luxury jets from a company owned by a political donor connected to Noem.

Moore said she advises companies that believe they might be swept up in any DHS-related inquires to be prepared to respond to congressional investigators and engage before lawmakers feel compelled to flex their subpoena powers.

“I would advise clients that you don’t want to be that company that Congress feels like they have to make the example out of,” Moore said.

Beyond ICE and immigration enforcement, meanwhile, House and Senate Democrats have also put a spotlight on staffing cuts at other DHS components, in particular CISA and the Federal Emergency Management Agency.

Democrats and Republicans have also introduced a slew of bills in recent months aimed at strengthening the government’s approach to AI security, including efforts within DHS.

Tonya Ugoretz, a cybersecurity leader at consulting firm PwC and former senior cyber official at the FBI, said she expects lawmakers in the new Congress to closely examine cybersecurity capacity across the federal government, not just at CISA.

“We’ll see more congressional scrutiny overall, both on the cybersecurity resourcing and preparedness within the federal government, as well as clarity around which government agencies will have a role when it comes to being the main interfaces with some of the developers of the new frontier AI capabilities,” Ugoretz told Federal News Network.

title: What a Democratic Congress can (and can't) do on immigration - America Magazine
description:
I went to Washington before the election to speak with the leaders of think tanks and advocacy groups influencing immigration reform across the political spectrum to find out how much a Democratic Congress could change immigration policy over the next two years.

Mr. Krikorian said he does not expect much to change on immigration policy now that Democrats will control Congress.
Mr. Krikorian would prefer to see more compromise over immigration policy in Congress, but he does not believe the Democratic Party will work with Republicans on the issue.

text:
Few issues strike an American nerve like immigration. Fewer galvanize the U.S. bishops to such a fervent and morally resolute response.

Tuesday’s blue wave—flipping Senate seats in Republican strongholds like Texas, Iowa and South Carolina—returned the Senate and the House of Representatives to the Democrats, who take control in January.

But with Immigration and Customs Enforcement already funded at historically high levels through 2029, and with President Donald J. Trump’s strong executive control still intact, there are limits on what Congress can do.

I went to Washington before the election to speak with the leaders of think tanks and advocacy groups influencing immigration reform across the political spectrum to find out how much a Democratic Congress could change immigration policy over the next two years.

The Advocates

Gaby Pacheco, president and C.E.O. of TheDream.US, the nation’s largest college and career success program for undocumented immigrant youth, said she expects to see some long-overdue oversight once the Democrats take control in January.

“There’s going to be hearings. There’s going to be Democrats calling in certain leaders, secretaries, heads of departments to … hold them accountable for what is happening right now,” Ms. Pacheco said.

She also said that while ICE already has “astronomical” amounts of funding, she’s hoping to see the agency slow down over the next two years as those funds finally begin to dwindle.

Democrats could also use spending bills as leverage.

“We just saw earlier this year a government shutdown over D.H.S. specifically,” said Eric Rodriguez, senior vice president for policy and advocacy at UnidosUS, the nation’s largest Latino civil rights and advocacy organization.

“Are we likely to see a reaction like that, that says we’re going to just shut this down until we get a vote on guardrails, things that represent some restraint on Homeland Security and ICE? Yes, that’s possible.”

There are also possible avenues for bipartisan work that don’t involve a full shutdown, he said, like bills designed to streamline legal immigration for specific industries suffering from recent enforcement sprees.

“There may be sector-specific bills that would be advanced to try and provide some stability to those in the workforce,” Mr. Rodriguez said.

Ms. Pacheco said that while she fears the next few months may actually bring more deportations, she is hopeful that people are interested in finally addressing immigration in some permanent capacity.

“We have seen, in these last 30 years, the great experiment of doing nothing on immigration. We have seen super-enforcement, which is what’s happening now. We’ve seen, from the Biden administration, the opposite, a more generous ‘Let’s let people come in,’” Ms. Pacheco said. “Now we have to figure out how to actually get something done.”

The Centrists

Cecilia Esterline, senior immigration policy analyst at the Niskanen Center, a centrist think tank, believes immigration reform will have to wait until the 2028 election cycle. Given that changes over the last two years have happened through executive order, she said the new Congress may not be able to change a lot.

The Supreme Court declined to intervene on Oct. 27 in a legal fight over a Biden-era policy that let immigration judges pause deportation cases, which could add to already crowded immigration dockets. Democrats could exert some power, Ms. Esterline said, over the funds needed to hire immigration judges.

“What I think is arguably the most impactful and most detrimental part of what’s happening right now is the cuts to legal immigration,” Ms. Esterline said. The decrease, she said, stems from executive restrictions, travel bans, growing application backlogs and steep hikes in visa fees.

She holds out tempered hope that the 2028 elections might change that—so long as both parties do some soul-searching in the meantime.

“I don’t think either party is really equipped for a post-Trump era in terms of an actual immigration plan,” she said. “I think that both parties do need to come to a real conclusion over what it is that they want their immigration system to look like, because neither party benefits from the pendulum-swinging, executive-branch-driven immigration policy.”

The Restrictionists

The office at the Center for Immigration Studies is home to every miniature Statue of Liberty depiction imaginable—Lady Liberty rendered as Mickey Mouse, Bugs Bunny, the green M&M. Mark Krikorian, executive director of C.I.S., said he began the collection because he thought liberals had co-opted the Statue of Liberty as a symbol of unlimited immigration.

C.I.S. is a small but prominent immigration restrictionist group, which describes itself as “low-immigration, pro-immigrant.” Mr. Krikorian has been its executive director since 1995.

Mr. Krikorian said he does not expect much to change on immigration policy now that Democrats will control Congress.

“Their own voters are going to be demanding that they do something, and in fact, they’re going to have to be extra strident, precisely because they have no ability to change what the administration is going to do,” Mr. Krikorian said.

Mr. Krikorian would prefer to see more compromise over immigration policy in Congress, but he does not believe the Democratic Party will work with Republicans on the issue.

Mr. Krikorian predicts that most politicians will tread water with immigration policy over the next two years, but that the potential presidential candidates for 2028—Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Representative Brandon Gill of Texas, Senator Eric Schmitt of Missouri and Vice President JD Vance, Mr. Krikorian’s choice—might push back against legal immigration as well as illegal.

“They’re not just about enforcement,” Mr. Krikorian said. “And so, when Trump moves off the political scene, you’re going to have a debate that is both somewhat less hysterical—just because Trump’s a unique hate figure for the left—but also more constructively and explicitly restrictionist.”

The Church

The U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops headquarters in Washington, D.C., impresses not only with its size but also with its vacancy—the conference laid off about a third of its migration staff in 2025 after the Trump administration halted funding for its refugee resettlement work.

David Spicer is the director of policy and engagement for the U.S.C.C.B.’s Secretariat of Migration, a forward-facing role that often involves managing relations with Congress on behalf of the conference.

“I wish I could tell you that on a weekly basis I’m having serious policy discussions with members of Congress and their staff about possible changes to the immigration system, but I think the real issue right now—and this has been the case for some time—is that we’re not having discussions about policy,” Mr. Spicer said. “It’s really just an exchange of rhetoric and things that are meant to alienate one group or another.”

Until cross-communication improves, it will be difficult to make headway with any immigration reforms, he said, much less to build reforms that reflect Catholic social teaching.

While Catholic social teaching does not exist to prescribe specifics on immigration policy, it does offer important guideposts for navigating it: targeted and proportionate immigration enforcement, maintaining family units, expanding access to legal immigration and addressing the causes of forced migration.

“Obviously, it’s perfectly reasonable for people to be treated differently based on things such as immigration status, but there comes a certain point where that treatment can infringe on people’s God-given human dignity, and that’s where it becomes problematic from the perspective of the church,” Mr. Spicer said.

Mr. Spicer emphasized that the church does not simply dismiss the legal and political considerations surrounding immigration. But for the church to hold legal considerations above all moral considerations, he said, would be impossible.

While Mr. Spicer does not expect an immediate change in immigration policies or practices to come from the midterms, he remains hopeful that the bishops can help bridge divides.

“That’s what I would say the bishops are hopeful for and what the bishops have long strived to do,” he said, “to create opportunities for that meaningful conversation and dialogue and to build bridges in that way.”

text:
As previously reported, the FY 2027 DV Lottery will remain on pause once more. On October 29th, 2026, the Ninth Circuit stayed a lower court’s order requiring the State Department to open DV-2027 registration and administer the DV Program. The appeal remains pending, but for now the government does not have to do anything.

Background

In August 2026, Red Eagle Law, L.C. filed suit against Secretary of State Marco Rubio for failing to open the FY 2027 DV Registration period. Red Eagle Law is a San Diego County law firm that specializes in helping DV winners. They alleged that by not opening the DV Program, they were losing money because many of their clients are DV Winners.

Judge Jinsook Ohta of the US District Court for the Southern District of California entered a Preliminary Injunction requiring the State Department to open DV-2027 registration and adjudicate DV-2027 cases. The order included several deadlines, including notifying DV Winners by December 3rd. The Government quickly filed an appeal.

Ninth Circuit Stays Lower Court’s Decision

A panel of judges consisting of Judge McKeown, Judge Smith, and Judge Thomas determined that the government was likely to prevail on appeal. One reason why was who filed the lawsuit. Congress created the Diversity Visa program to encourage immigration from countries with low admission rates, and the panel found that a law firm’s revenue from representing selectees falls outside the interests the statute protects. Notably, the only Plaintiff was Red Eagle Law. There were no prospective applicants or DV winners who filed suit. Judge Smith concurred that the law firms’ injuries were too hypothetical to file a suit.

The panel did make one thing clear. Granting the stay doesn’t mean it endorses the State Department’s decision to leave the program closed.

What Happens Next?

The DV-2027 registration will remain closed until further notice. There is currently no ETA for when the DV Program will be reopened. The injunction deadlines will be paused until the appeal is resolved. Red Eagle Law stated they will continue to fight and can petition the entire Ninth Circuit or the Supreme Court to hear their case. We may also see more lawsuits filed against the government.

No one can apply for the FY 2027 DV Lottery since registration has not opened. If any website or person tells you that they applied for you, please be aware this is not true. Keep an eye on the travel.state.gov website for updates.

“Today, I accepted the resignation of Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon,” Blanche wrote on X. “She has defended the civil liberties of every American and enforced the law without fear or favor.”

A top Trump ally, Dhillon was confirmed to her role in April 2025 and has overseen a dramatic overhaul of the Justice Department’s civil rights division, which is tasked with enforcing anti-discrimination laws. Hundreds of former Justice Department officials penned a letter last December decrying the “destruction” of the agency division under Trump.

Dhillon is the first high-ranking official to resign from the Trump administration since US Democrats swept both chambers of the US Congress in the country’s pivotal midterm elections on Tuesday.

Democratic congressman Robert Garcia, who will likely become the new chair of the powerful House of Representatives Committee on Oversight and Accountability, pledged on Wednesday to take on four major investigations, including abuses of power by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents and the Epstein files.

Dhillon reportedly told her staff earlier this year that her office, which has typically been charged with investigating law enforcement killings by police officers, would not be looking into the fatal shootings of two US citizens – Renee Good and Alex Pretti – who were gunned down by ICE agents in Minneapolis.

In May, Garcia accused the administration of continuing to shield Trump from scrutiny related to unreleased documents tied to the Epstein investigation

During a closed-door hearing in which Blanche’s predecessor, Pam Bondi, was asked by lawmakers about the case, the California Democrat Garcia alleged Dhillon repeatedly intervened to block questions about the president’s connection to the release of the files.

description:
