text:
5 November 2026

Responding to reports that two Uyghur men recently moved to an Immigration Detention Centre in Thailand face imminent forcible deportation to China, Amnesty International’s Secretary General Agnès Callamard said:

“Thai authorities must immediately halt any plans to forcibly return these two Uyghur men to China, where they face a real risk of torture, arbitrary detention and enforced disappearance. Thailand must not repeat last year’s unlawful deportation of 40 Uyghurs, who were forced back to danger in China.

“Thai authorities must now allow them access to a lawyer of their choice and, together with the international community, urgently find a safe and voluntary third-country solution for them and the other Uyghurs still detained in Thailand.”

Amnesty International’s Secretary General Agnès Callamard

“These two men fled persecution only to spend more than a decade detained in Thailand. Amnesty International has documented crimes against humanity against Uyghurs and other predominantly Muslim ethnic groups in Xinjiang. Returning them would expose them to the abuses they sought to escape.

“Both men have previously made clear to their legal representatives that they fear for their lives if returned to China and do not consent to being sent back. Thai authorities must now allow them access to a lawyer of their choice and, together with the international community, urgently find a safe and voluntary third-country solution for them and the other Uyghurs still detained in Thailand.

“No amount of diplomatic assurance from China can override Thailand’s obligations not to return anyone to a real risk of torture or other serious human rights violations. After more than a decade in detention, these men must be released and given the chance to rebuild their lives in safety and freedom “

Background

The two men are among five Uyghurs remaining in Thailand from a group of over 300 who were apprehended without charge by the Thai authorities on 13 March 2014 after they had fled persecution and discrimination in China’s Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region.

On 21 October 2026, two of the five men were released from prison under a royal pardon and transferred to the Immigration Detention Centre in Bangkok. Since then, Thai authorities have denied the two men access to their lawyers, as well as blocked access to the men by civil society organizations and the National Human Rights Commission of Thailand.

The two men have spent more than 12 years in Thai detention. In June 2015, Thailand allowed 173 women and children from the group to travel to Türkiye but unlawfully deported at least 109 people to China.

A document obtained by Amnesty International shows that, on 7 January 2025, the Chinese embassy in Thailand sent a letter to Thailand’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs requesting the “repatriation” of 45 Uyghur men who remained in the country. In February 2025, Thailand forcibly deported 40 of them, in breach international law. Five remained in a Thai prison to serve sentences related to an attempt to escape the Immigration Detention Centre.

Following the deportations, Thai authorities made two visits to Xinjiang in February and March 2025 at China’s invitation, as part of its efforts to provide diplomatic assurances. NGOs monitoring the case reported that Thai authorities were able to meet fewer than 10 deportees and that no subsequent updates have established that all are alive and safe; their whereabouts and wellbeing remain unknown. Amnesty International previously called on both governments to disclose the whereabouts of all 40 men.

Amnesty International opposes any use of diplomatic assurances that a person transferred would not be subjected to torture or other ill-treatment as it undermines the universality of the prohibition of torture and cannot be considered reliable. Thailand is bound by the Convention against Torture, and the principle of non-refoulement under international law, which prohibits States from returning or transferring anyone to a place where they would be at real risk of persecution or other human rights violations. Article 13 of Thailand’s Prevention and Suppression of Torture and Enforced Disappearance Act, in force since 2023, prohibits deportation where there are substantial grounds to believe a person would face torture, cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment, or enforced disappearance.

Amnesty International issued a groundbreaking report in 2021 documenting crimes against humanity of imprisonment, torture and persecution against Uyghurs, Kazakhs and other predominantly Muslim ethnic groups in Xinjiang. Despite similar UN findings released in an assessment report in August 2022, China has taken no steps to implement recommendations, remedy documented violations or investigate and hold accountable perpetrators. Instead, the government continues to silence criticism from those within and beyond its borders, issue counternarratives denying abuse and maintains its discriminatory and assimilationist policies.

Amnesty International is a global movement of more than 10 million people who take injustice personally. We are campaigning for a world where human rights are enjoyed by all – and we can only do it with your support.

text:
The Trump Administration continues to claim U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents are targeting the "worst of the worst" offenders during ongoing immigration enforcement operations across the country.

During Operation Metro Surge in Minnesota earlier this year, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) — stated repeatedly that they were detaining rapists and murderers who were roaming the streets of Minnesota after being released from custody.

But those claims quickly fell apart last winter when state officials released detailed records proving many of the "worst of the worst" offenders were already in custody, had been transferred to ICE, or had no criminal records in Minnesota.

"Thin I.C.E.", a new docuseries from FOX 9 Documentaries, details one state official's efforts to expose what he called "propaganda" from the federal government.

‘This became a propaganda game’

What they're saying:

"Every name was checked. Every record was checked," said Paul Schnell, Commissioner of the Minnesota Department of Corrections.

Schnell, a long-time police chief, said he tried to explain to DHS officials that the information released on social media and at press conferences was inaccurate.

"Even when they were checked, they continued to push it," Schnell said in an interview. "You can only assume that this became a propaganda game."

Video of ICE transfers

Why you should care:

Schenell said his department coordinates the transfer of any inmate into federal custody if they have what’s known as an ICE detainer.

Yet, DHS repeatedly claimed several offenders were detained after being released from prison by Gov. Tim Walz.

Schnell eventually held a press conference in which he showed video of offenders being physically transferred to federal agents.

"I think showing the video became just a clear indication of what's happening and how what was being said by some in the federal government and what was being shared with Minnesotans, simply didn't match up to reality," Schnell said in the upcoming documentary.

Gov. Tim Walz said Schnell’s decision to release the video was a "big turning point" during the surge.

"It became very clear that this was about retribution," Walz said.

ICE detainers

The other side:

The Trump Administration also claimed that county jails were releasing violent offenders instead of holding them for ICE agents.

"The root cause of it was the refusal to cooperate with federal law enforcement in the first place," Rep. Walter Hudson (R-Albertville) said in an interview for the documentary.

ICE claims undercut by prison and jail records

Dig deeper:

However, records analyzed by the FOX 9 Investigators undercut DHS claims that ICE agents were picking up people recently cut loose by county jails.

Dozens of the "worst of the worst" offenders did not have criminal records or had not been incarcerated in Minnesota in years.

"They're giving us names that have, in some cases, have never even been arrested in our state," Schnell said.

Schnell and Walz said communication with the federal government improved once Border Czar Tom Homan took over immigration operations.

"I said, ‘you're asking, are we cooperating?’ You have just found out that we have always cooperated with you in our state prisons, and he acknowledged that," Walz said.

Watch Thin I.C.E. documentary series

What's next:

Thin I.C.E. is a three-part series by FOX 9 Documentaries detailing the Trump Administration's immigration operations in Chicago and Minneapolis that resulted in constitutional challenges, violent tactics and deadly shootings.

Thin I.C.E. Part I: "Worst of the Worst" premieres Wednesday, Nov. 4 at 10:35 p.m. on FOX 9 and streaming on FOX LOCAL and the FOX 9 YouTube channel.

title: Outcry after ICE violently detains US citizen walking to high school - The Guardian
description:
“ICE agents illegally assaulted Mr Zepeda and then issued a false public statement to cover it up,” the attorneys said.

Two ICE vehicles were stopped alongside a Santa Maria road as agents questioned a driver.

text:
The violent ICE detention of a US citizen with disabilities as he walked to his high school has sparked outrage in California where leaders are condemning the incident as racial profiling and calling on authorities to investigate.

Erik Zepeda, a 20-year-old high school student, was stopped by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers last month in the small agricultural city of Santa Maria, famed for its strawberry harvest, where 79% of residents are Latino. His wrist was broken and later required surgery.

Zepeda, who has disabilities that affect his physical reflexes and ability to communicate verbally, told the Guardian in writing that he was “walking to school the same way I do every day” when the ICE agents “tackled me and handcuffed me (and) hurt me”.

“I thought they were going to kill me,” Zepeda said. “I did not do anything wrong, and they should never have done that. I don’t want this to happen to anyone else.”

An ICE-watch observer who witnessed the incident unfold on 21 October told the Guardian that masked ICE agents approached Zepeda from behind, pinned him face-down on the ground and put him in a car. The agents then drove the student around for a while before letting him out. With a black eye and his wrist in severe pain, Zepeda walked the remaining half mile to his school, where staff called an ambulance.

The observer, who volunteers with a local rapid response network to document ICE activity, asked not to be named due to fears of retaliation from federal officials. To independently verify the observer’s account, the Guardian reviewed dashcam and phone videos that the observer recorded of the incident.

Local activists and US lawmakers are calling the ordeal the latest example of ICE brutality.

“ICE’s assault and wrongful detainment of Erik Zepeda was grotesque and heartbreaking,” said Adam Schiff, a Democratic US senator from California, in a statement to the Guardian. “There must be accountability for what happened to Erik.”

Democratic representative Salud Carbajal, whose central coast district includes Santa Maria, said during a press conference that he was “outraged” by the incident, calling the ICE agents’ conduct “thuggish” and racial profiling “rampant”.

In an Oct. 29 letter to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and ICE, Carbajal called for “a full, transparent investigation” into Zepeda’s detention.

The incident comes amid a surge of ICE activity in California that started in early October and has led to multiple hospitalizations. Days earlier, agents broke the arm of Ricardo Gonzalez, also a US citizen, in Long Beach. In videos, Gonzalez appears face-down in a gutter crying out for help while officers kneel on his back.

In the Bay Area, two separate ICE arrests also led to hospitalizations, sparking anti-ICE protests outside of an Oakland hospital.

Santa Maria police chief Christopher Williams told the Guardian that an investigation into the incident was “ongoing” and confirmed that he reported the incident to the county district attorney, the California department of justice, and DHS.

In a statement, Santa Barbara county district attorney John Savrnoch called the incident “deeply troubling.” He said his office was “coordinating with the appropriate authorities to gather information and determine the appropriate next steps.”

JP Cooney and Molly Gaston, former federal prosecutors who are now senior attorneys at legal nonprofit Democracy Forward, are representing Zepeda. They told the Guardian in a statement they “look forward to vindicating Mr Zepeda’s rights in court”.

Glenn Goldin, is a retired special education teacher who formerly taught Zepeda and remains a close mentor to him. He described Zepeda, who lives in a group home for adults with disabilities, as quiet, sensitive and a caring housemate, who loves the Golden State Warriors and likes to spend time scrolling TikTok.

After Zepeda’s terrifying encounter with ICE, Goldin said that he remains shaken and doesn’t plan to return to school for at least several weeks.

Goldin said Zepeda had worked up the courage to begin walking to school by himself last year.

“He’s felt very proud of himself, you know, he’s independent,” Goldin said. “I feel like they took that away from him.”

‘You’re hurting me’

In response to questions from the Guardian about the incident, an ICE spokesperson said its officers were conducting “a targeted enforcement operation” when they encountered Zepeda, who “they believed matched the description of the criminal illegal alien target”, and that their use of force was justified.

“When the individual resisted officers, refused lawful commands, and assumed a fighting stance with clenched fists, they relied on their training to safely control the situation until they could confirm his identity, whereupon he was released,” the spokesperson said. “Claims that the individual suffered broken bones are FALSE. He never requested medical assistance.”

Cooney and Gaston, Zepeda’s attorneys, said that his hospital discharge records confirmed that he received surgery for his fractured wrist after the incident.

“ICE agents illegally assaulted Mr Zepeda and then issued a false public statement to cover it up,” the attorneys said.

The volunteer observer’s testimony and videos call key aspects of ICE’s version into question. Rather than a targeted operation, the ICE officers’ actions leading up to Zepeda’s detention point to a pattern of spontaneous immigration stops.

In the 20 minutes before ICE officers detained Zepeda, they had already pulled over two separate dark-skinned drivers and then let them go, according to the observer, who provided videos of both encounters to the Guardian.

The first ICE stop occurred around 7:08 am. Two ICE vehicles were stopped alongside a Santa Maria road as agents questioned a driver. After the agents drove away, the driver – who the observer said was a Hispanic man – can be heard saying to the observer, “I’m a US citizen” in a video reviewed by the Guardian.

About 10 minutes later one of the same ICE vehicles pulled over a truck with two people inside and then let them go, the observer’s video shows. The observer said they appeared to be Latino men.

The observer said they continued monitoring the ICE agents, who came to a sudden stop after they drove past Zepeda a few minutes later. Videos reviewed by the Guardian do not show the entire encounter but capture key moments of what unfolded next.

In the observer’s dashcam footage, two masked agents are seen hopping out and quickly approaching Zepeda from behind as he walks along a sidewalk wearing a hoodie as a light rain falls. Zepeda appears to notice the masked officers for the first time when one touches his arm; he immediately shakes his arm loose, just as the dashcam frame shifts away.

The observer estimates that 10 to 20 seconds later they started recording on their phone. In the footage, Zepeda is seen lying face-down on a patch of grass as two officers restrain him. Three additional officers arrive and appear to help handcuff Zepeda. At one point, a voice can be heard shouting: “You’re hurting me.” The officers load him into a second government vehicle and then drive away.

The observer said that during the roughly 10 to 20 seconds not captured on video, Zepeda did not appear to resist at any point. “He looked like he was just astonished,” the observer said.

Two days after the incident, a federal judge blocked immigration agents from stopping people solely on the basis that they appear to be “low-income or working-class and Latino” across the central district of California, which spans seven counties and includes Santa Maria.

The ruling stems from a class action lawsuit over racial profiling during immigration stops. The judge pointed to ICE bodycam footage and text messages – in which federal immigration agents used racial slurs to identify people to target – as evidence of the pattern. The Trump administration has appealed the preliminary injunction.

National Day Laborer Organizing Network staff attorney Lauren Michel Wilfong is part of a legal coalition representing plaintiffs in the case and has been tracking reports of alleged racial profiling by ICE in southern California. Wilfong said that Zepeda’s detention appeared to match several common patterns – masked agents quickly surround a person in a public space, use force to get them into a vehicle before asking questions, and later claim that they matched a target.

“It’s part of an approach of ‘grab first, justify later’. [They] detain people because they appear ‘suspicious’ – and here ‘suspicious’ just means Latino,” Wilfong said.

‘Any brown person is at risk’

Rapid response groups first reported the California ICE surge in early October, with ICE arrests as far north as Sacramento and as far south as San Diego.

The nonprofit 805 UndocuFund, which coordinates a rapid response network across three central coast counties, tracked more than 280 arrests in October, up from roughly 150 arrests per month on average during the previous nine months. More than 100 occurred in Santa Maria.

805 UndocuFund executive director Primitiva Hernández said the network had received numerous reports of ICE pulling over Latino drivers.

“We knew it was only a matter of time before something like this happened,” Hernández said of Zepeda’s experience. “Any brown person regardless of their legal status is at risk of being pulled over, stopped and questioned.”

The fact that Zepeda’s detention occurred a half mile from Santa Maria high school has put parents and students on edge, regardless of their immigration status, said Santa Maria city councilmember Gloria Soto.

Last Friday, hundreds of students at Santa Maria High and nearby Lompoc High organized a walkout to protest what happened to Zepeda. The students – some in halloween costumes – chanted “Chinga la migra” and held signs that read “ICE out of 805” in reference to the local area code.

“Their actions send a powerful message,” Soto said. “Our students do not want to live in fear.”

text:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detains noncitizens in facilities across the U.S. Entities within the Department of Homeland Security inspect these facilities to ensure they meet standards for humane detention.

The numbers of facilities and detained noncitizens have increased since FY 2024. At the same time, the frequency of inspections has changed—decreasing in some cases—with more reliance on facility self-inspections.

ICE depends on inspections to find problems in areas like medical care and food service. But, ICE hasn't determined how changes to its inspections have affected its oversight.

Our recommendations address this issue.

ICE Detention Facility in Louisiana

The outside of a detention facility with three flag poles centered in front of the entrance and cars parked on both sides.

What GAO Found

Department of Homeland Security (DHS) detention facility inspections have changed at the same time that the number of immigration detention facilities and the size of the detained population have increased. From April 2025 to April 2026, following a January 2025 Executive Order, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) added over 40 detention facilities that detain noncitizens for over 72 hours. The average daily population of detained noncitizens grew by over 50 percent, to 61,817 individuals, over the timeframe. From fiscal year 2024 to July 2026, three of the four DHS entities that conducted inspections changed the frequency (decreased or increased) or stopped conducting inspections.

Changes to Inspections Conducted by DHS Entities from Fiscal Year (FY) 2024 to July 2026

ICE relies on these inspections to identify deficiencies in its facilities and ensure compliance with its detention standards. However, the frequency of inspections has in some cases decreased, there is an increased reliance on self-inspections, and processes for these inspections have changed. ICE has not used evidence, such as data on deficiencies identified through inspections and performance information such as the extent to which facilities are in compliance with their contracts, to determine the effects of these recent changes on facility conditions. By using evidence to determine these effects and applying the results to improve oversight, ICE could ensure that facilities provide sound conditions and care for noncitizens, in accordance with its standards.

Why GAO Did This Study

ICE is authorized to detain noncitizens apprehended for violations of immigration law pending removal proceedings or execution of a removal order. ICE guidance states that ICE must detain noncitizens in the most humane manner possible. ICE has established detention standards that dictate how facilities should operate. ICE relies on various DHS entities within and outside of ICE to assess compliance. These inspections identify deficiencies related to medical care and food service, among other areas.

GAO was asked to review compliance with detention standards and related oversight. This report examines (1) changes to DHS inspections of detention facilities since GAO’s last report on this topic (GAO-25-107580) and (2) ICE's use of evidence to inform its oversight of detention facilities in light of the changes. GAO reviewed documentation on DHS’s various oversight mechanisms and how they changed between fiscal year 2024 and July 2026. GAO also analyzed ICE data on the number of facilities that detain noncitizens for over 72 hours and the average daily population from April 2025 to April 2026. GAO interviewed officials responsible for conducting oversight from various offices within DHS.

title: Violating human rights when DHS sends immigrants to third countries - MV Times

Among the most striking cases before the Supreme Court is one that may well affect immigrants on Martha’s Vineyard.
The question is whether those six justices are sensitive to human rights abuses, especially those recognized in international law.

These third countries could and may well send the immigrants back to their home country, where they have already endured persecution and torture.

text:
Among the most striking cases before the Supreme Court is one that may well affect immigrants on Martha’s Vineyard. The case, Department of Homeland Security v. D.V.D., asks the court to continue to allow the Trump administration to send undocumented immigrants to a country where they have no ties, and where they may be in danger of torture, imprisonment, or death (known as “third countries”). These removals are often undertaken without a hearing in violation of due process of law.

Boston District Court Judge Brian E. Murphy initially ruled against the administration, and placed a nationwide injunction to stop these removals. Six conservative Supreme Court justices allowed the administration to continue this practice after an emergency appeal by the administration. The case is terribly troubling and frightening to the four litigants, who now may face dreadful consequences if the U.S. deports them.

The question is whether those six justices are sensitive to human rights abuses, especially those recognized in international law. For many generations, jurists, political commentators, and lawyers have debated whether American law is subject to international law and norms. Some have said yes, others no. Dean Harold Koh of Yale University Law School once wrote an article, for example, titled, “International Law Is Part of Our Law.” Justice Antonin Scalia objected, saying that he does “not use foreign law in the interpretation of the United States Constitution.”

This case raises the issue of international human rights abuses: the plaintiffs argue that they may well be in danger in some countries that will not recognize their individual needs. One plaintiff needs psychiatric care, and is fearful of being deprived of it should his host country ignore his problems. Another is outwardly gay, and was beaten and raped in his home country before he traveled to the U.S. A third is a woman whose husband beat and abused her, and she is frightened that he will locate her in a third country and kill her. A fourth person was severely beaten by local police in his own country after he refused to deliver illegal drugs for them. They all fear that they may be deported back to the country from which they fled.

The problem is amplified because Homeland Security officials do not tell immigrants the name of the third country where they’re sending them. Nor do they give them an opportunity to contest their removal to these places. These failings directly violate the Convention Against Torture and Inhuman Treatment and Punishment (known as CAT), to which the U.S. is a party.

When President Ronald Reagan submitted the treaty to the Senate for ratification in 1987, he stated that “the core provisions of the convention establish a regime for international cooperation in the criminal prosecution of torturers relying on so-called ‘universal jurisdiction.’ Each state party is required either to prosecute torturers who are found in its territory or to extradite them to other countries for prosecution.”

But the Trump administration, in violation of the convention’s provisions, ignores the convention’s key element when it disallows undocumented immigrants to ask Homeland Security officials where they are being sent, and inform them why they should not have to go to these places. These third countries could and may well send the immigrants back to their home country, where they have already endured persecution and torture. The removal of these four plaintiffs, and others who follow them, also implicates another U.S. law, the Foreign Affairs Reform and Restructuring Act, which President Bill Clinton signed in 1997. The act states that it is U.S. policy “not to expel, extradite, or otherwise effect the involuntary return of any person to a country in which there are substantial grounds for believing the person would be in danger of being subjected to torture, regardless of whether the person is physically present in the U.S.”

The bottom line is whether the U.S. has become a lawless nation regarding international human rights in areas that are deeply ingrained in federal law. We won’t know until the Supreme Court hears this case on Dec. 9, but even then, we will have to await the court’s final ruling sometime next year in June or July. Meantime, those living on the Island who are picked up by Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers may well find themselves suddenly herded off to some foreign country to which they have no ties and where they may find they face horrible forms of persecution. This is not the U.S. we have long believed in.

Jack Fruchtman, who lives in Aquinnah, taught constitutional law and politics for more than 40 years.

text:
Rep. Robert Garcia has a two-word message to the Trump administration: “Lawyer up.”

With Democrats claiming control of the House of Representatives and Senate in Tuesday’s midterms, the Long Beach congressman is on track to lead the House Oversight Committee, which brings powerful tools to investigate almost anything in government.

From a seaside hotel in Huntington Beach, Garcia told reporters to expect a flurry of investigations launched on “day one” once he takes the chair in January, starting with alleged corruption within the Trump family and the president’s administration.

“They are stealing your money, and they’re stealing your hard-earned labor, giving it to themselves and their billionaire donors and friends, while you and your family are having a hard time filling a gas tank or paying the mortgage bill,” Garcia said.

As the minority chair, Garcia has only been able to pursue inquiries and question witnesses. With the new seat, he will be able to issue subpoenas and call hearings regardless of Republican support.

The congressman said he will target a number of other issues: allegations of pay-to-play in contracting with the Department of Homeland Security, congressional stock trading, corporate profiteering, and issues and delays with the release of the Jeffrey Epstein investigation files.

Despite the “thousands of women that have come forward,” Garcia pointed out that there has not been a single public hearing on the Epstein investigation. “I’ve talked to numerous survivors who are looking to come forward to [testify] in front of Congress,” he added.

Garcia said he will also investigate former DHS Secretary Kristi Noem and aide Corey Lewandowski, whom he accused of engineering a corrupt and inhumane immigration crackdown. This comes with increasing urgency locally after federal agents descended upon North Long Beach last month and detained a U.S. citizen, allegedly breaking his arm in the process.

When asked about his two-word warning to “lawyer up,” Garcia said he was referring to any “administration official that caused harm,” including Stephen Miller, Noem and Lewandowski, as well as the Trump family.

He said investigations will encompass anyone involved in the abuses of ICE, including agents on the ground but also administrators who train them and “created the system” for a culture of impunity. He plans to hold field hearings, starting early next year with one in Long Beach on “abuses of ICE and DHS.”

“I think the American public, regardless of party, are sick of it,” Garcia said.

Garcia said he also wants to focus on corporate corruption, including cryptocurrency schemes, dynamic pricing, Jared Kushner and his conflicting interests as a businessman and U.S. peace envoy. He also listed insider trading (by Congress members and the Trump administration alike) — tying them to the tabletop issues, like groceries and gas prices.

A major concern, he said, is the behind-the-scenes push along the state’s coast, including “the coast of Huntington Beach and Newport and Long Beach,” of oil companies trying to expand offshore drilling. “We’re going to stop them,” he said. “It’s not acceptable in this new majority.”

Polls show the congressman won his re-election Tuesday with more than 60% of the vote, in a district that now extends into Huntington Beach, Costa Mesa and Newport Beach.

“The days of Huntington Beach being a MAGA city are over,” Garcia said. “This is a community that is diverse. Folks just want good services. People want good representation, and I’m excited to represent the entire community. It’s clear that this city voted for change.”

text:
Dominican authorities detained 44,414 Haitians with irregular migration status in October, expelling 40,521 of them as part of intensified immigration enforcement operations across the country.

The General Directorate of Migration (DGM) said the operations were conducted in coordination with the armed forces, National Police and other security agencies, targeting several provinces and commercial and agricultural establishments.

Dajabón recorded the highest number of detentions during the month, with 6,700 cases, followed by Elías Piña with 4,961 and Santo Domingo with 4,845.

The Dominican Republic Army handed over 10,872 people to the DGM during the operations, while the National Police accounted for 4,895. Other agencies involved included the Specialized Corps of Land Border Security, which handed over 3,289 people; the National Environmental Protection Service, with 151; and the Dominican Republic Navy, with 43.

Immigration inspections were also conducted at agricultural holdings and agro-industrial projects in San Francisco de Macorís, Moca and San Juan, where nearly 700 Haitians with irregular migration status were identified during October.

Authorities also carried out operations at commercial establishments in Duarte, Peravia, San Pedro de Macorís and La Romana, as well as the National District and several areas of Santo Domingo. The inspections were intended to verify the immigration status of foreign workers and assess their employment conditions.

In a separate update, the DGM reported that 2,102 people unable to demonstrate regular immigration status were detained during operations on October 31 and November 1. A further 2,234 people were deported through border control points in Dajabón, Elías Piña, Jimaní and Pedernales.

The agency said it would continue conducting joint operations with the armed forces and National Police throughout the country as part of efforts to enforce Dominican immigration laws.

The DGM also reported initiatives to strengthen training for its operational and administrative personnel, with support from national and international organizations. The training is intended to improve the monitoring and verification of foreign workers' immigration status and the services provided to those affected.

text:
By Silvia Higuera

November 4, 2026

Summary

Luis Galeano fled Nicaragua and was detained by U.S. immigration authorities. Now that he has been granted asylum, he is more determined than ever to keep reporting on his country.

For Nicaraguan journalist Luis Galeano, the U.S. government's approval of his and his family’s political asylum application represented a victory not only for them personally but also over the repressive government of Daniel Ortega and Rosario Murillo, which forced them to flee their homeland.

Galeano spoke with LatAm Journalism Review (LJR) after spending 11 days in detention at the Krome Detention Center in Miami and nearly a month awaiting a decision on his immigration status.

He said the ruling had renewed his determination to continue working against the news blackout gripping Nicaragua for nearly a decade.

“When I left the detention center, I did my program and said, particularly to the dictators [Ortega and Murillo], that what happened to me here in the United States was their responsibility because I should be in Nicaragua, doing my program without any problems” Galeano said. “If they thought they were going to silence me [...], they were wrong. I am coming back with more strength, more commitment and more drive to keep doing my work.”

Galeano was detained on Sept. 14 in Orlando, in central Florida. He had migrated to the United States in 2018 and had a pending asylum application after an arrest warrant was issued against him in Nicaragua.

Since his detention, Galeano's case has drawn attention because of what it could mean for Nicaraguan journalism surviving in exile.

The case highlights the precarious situation of other Nicaraguan journalists seeking protection after being forced into exile because of their work. Those who have sought refuge in the United States have faced not only continued attacks from the Ortega-Murillo government in Nicaragua but also uncertainty over the immigration policies of the Donald Trump administration, which has increased deportations, denied a large number of asylum applications and eliminated humanitarian protection programs for migrants.

José Carlos Zamora, regional director for the Americas at the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ), welcomed the approval of Galeano's application.

“It is essential protection that allows him to continue reporting from exile,” Zamora told LJR. “The persecution he has faced for practicing journalism is well documented.”

“A path of hope”

Galeano said he believed his asylum application was approved because of the strength of his case: He had extensively documented the persecution he experienced because of his work, both in Nicaragua and while living in exile in the United States.

Immigration Judge Daniel Dowall approved his application after U.S. immigration authorities acknowledged that there were grounds to grant him protection, according to a report by Miami's Telemundo 51 news station.

Since arriving in the United States eight years ago, Galeano had sought ways to continue his work through his program “Café con Voz,” driven by a “moral commitment” to report on what was happening in his country. While already in exile, he learned that journalists Miguel Mora and Lucía Pineda — who ran the 100% Noticias television channel, where he hosted his program — had been detained and that the country already had at least 600 political prisoners.

“I couldn't abandon what was happening or pretend not to know about it,” Galeano said, adding that his work further angered the dictatorship. The persecution and attempts to silence him continued, he said.

“I am a journalist. I am visible, and my work can be scrutinized every day,” he said. “I am on my program every day, doing the same thing every day, receiving threats and insults every day. I can demonstrate that I have remained active and that this activity is a source of irritation for the regime, and that the danger is persistent, ongoing and has not ended.”

Reporters Without Borders included Ortega and Murillo on its 2026 list of “Predators of Press Freedom,” citing the exile of hundreds of media workers and the closure or confiscation of dozens of news outlets during their rule. The government has also stripped journalists such as Galeano of their property and Nicaraguan citizenship.

Galeano's asylum approval, however, was not guaranteed. In fact, approvals of such cases in the United States have become uncommon.

According to an analysis by Syracuse University's Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse (TRAC), immigration judges denied 94.1% of asylum applications in June 2026.

Following Galeano's detention in September, immigration authorities said he had overstayed the period of authorized stay granted when he first arrived in the country. Authorities have said that having a pending application for an immigration benefit does not confer legal status to remain in the country, a position that several legal organizations have disputed.

Meanwhile, the Trump administration has repeatedly condemned the Ortega-Murillo regime, in part for silencing and exiling journalists.

Zamora, who has not been able to review the legal ruling in Galeano's case, said it was not possible to determine whether the asylum approval reflected a broader shift in the U.S. government's position toward Nicaragua or journalism. Still, he said, the decision was positive.

“There must be consistency between standing up against the repression of the press in Nicaragua and protecting those forced to flee it,” Zamora said. “That has been our call. The United States must offer refuge and ensure that immigration measures are not used to silence journalism.”

Supporting Nicaraguan journalism

When Galeano was detained, international organizations and several U.S. politicians called for his release and urged authorities to prevent his deportation.

María Elvira Salazar, a Republican congresswoman from Florida, issued a statement calling for an immediate review of his case.

“The United States must always know how to distinguish between a criminal and a political exile,” the congresswoman wrote in her statement. “Luis is a highly respected journalist who paid a very high price for telling the world the truth about the Ortega-Murillo dictatorship [...] Luis cannot end up in the hands of the same dictatorship that persecuted him.”

Mario Díaz-Balart, another Republican congressman from Florida, said the United States must continue to be a beacon of light for people fleeing tyranny.

“We must uphold that tradition and ensure that Luis Chavarría-Galeano and other political exiles receive the protection and due process they deserve,” he wrote.

The Inter American Press Association and Reporters Without Borders also spoke out.

Tifani Roberts, a Nicaraguan journalist who works for the Univision network in the United States, said journalists in exile are essential to reporting on what is happening in their country.

“The responsibility to inform is in their blood, and their conscience allows them to do nothing else but report. That is what it means to love a country,” Roberts said. “Nicaraguans owe a debt to these journalists who have lost everything because of their work. They did not sell their conscience; they chose to pay the price of informing the public, and that price was enormous.”

Galeano has also called for greater protection for Nicaraguan journalism. He emphasized the courage of those who remain in the country and continue reporting clandestinely, as well as the need to support those doing the same from exile.

Beyond the persecution that follows journalists across borders, Galeano said, practicing journalism in exile brings greater economic challenges. At the time of his detention, Galeano was driving for the ride-hailing app Uber, a job that helps support his family.

“The fact that these voices have not been silenced is already significant,” he said. “But support must be provided to sustain the few platforms that remain. [...] Any resources are welcome if they help keep a voice alive, one that can overcome the obstacles to denouncing injustice and violations of human rights and freedom.”

text:
In the run-up to Tuesday’s elections, the Trump administration would not dismiss the idea that federal immigration agents could show up to polling places, or that the president could invoke a national emergency to seize control of elections from individual states after failing to do so in Congress and in courts.

In the end, though, immigration officers didn’t patrol the polls. The president didn’t invoke the Insurrection Act or some other emergency action. Feds didn’t seize any ballots or voting machines. Instead, more than 124 million Americans cast their ballots in midterm elections this year, according to preliminary results, marking the second-highest turnout rate for a midterm election in modern American history.

State election officials and voting rights groups who sued to stop the administration from sending federal agents to the polls have attributed those figures to the hard work of poll workers and others who run the nation’s elections free of interference.

But Donald Trump took unprecedented steps this year to insert himself into how elections are run, an effort that merged his crusade against “fraud” with his administration’s mass deportation efforts. By Tuesday night, the Republican president admitted his party’s defeat — without incident.

“Any stolen election nonsense is gonna fall flat in the face of a blowout,” former Arizona elections official Stephen Richer summed it up.

But it wasn’t merely the work of a “too big to rig” blue wave or the president’s empty threats that stopped it, according to election law expert Rick Hasen at the UCLA School of Law.

“The risk that Trump would interfere with our democracy in a way that made 2020 look harmless was quite serious, and it took laborious work of thousands of lawyers, election administrators, and key parts of civil society to neutralize the threat from materializing,” he wrote.

For months, the president and administration officials were being encouraged by close advisers and influential Republican figures to send Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents to poll sites or to invoke emergency authority to investigate fraud on Election Day.

Trump as well as now-former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt, Attorney General Todd Blanche and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and other top officials never publicly shot down the ideas.

And a series of close calls between ICE agents and election workers raised serious alarms for voting rights groups paying close attention to potential election interference incidents this year.

ICE agents were spotted making an arrest in the parking lot outside a polling place in San Antonio, Texas, earlier this year, and agents also showed up to polling places in California and New York, where agents questioned an election worker about her social media posts about the ICE officer who fatally shot Renee Good in Minneapolis.

The administration’s failure to shut down questions about ICE’s involvement in this year’s elections prompted several groups and state officials to file lawsuits to prevent it.

The Department of Justice tried to toss the cases. In one lawsuit, after election officials said they were scrambling to adjust for the potential for ICE agents at polling sites in their already-busy Election Day planning, the Justice Department called their efforts “voluntary, self-directed operational change” in response to speculative fears.

The Justice Department, however, did end up deploying more than 900 agents to observe polls in all 50 states.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom said his state deployed its own election monitors to watch the ones sent by the feds so they could “hold the line against Trump’s goons,” he wrote on X.

A coalition of civil rights groups also deployed their own counter fleet.

The Vote Safe program from the Save America Movement — joined by the Rev. Al Sharpton’s National Action Network and the American Federation of Teachers union, among others — dispatched observers to several battleground states.

“Whether or not a federal agent ever showed up, the fear was the point,” said Mary Corcoran, co-founder of the Save America Movement.

“It was built to keep people from voting in the communities this administration most wanted to silence," she said. “So we worked alongside those communities and reached out through trusted voices to turn fear into defiance and intimidation into preparation.”

There were some “routine challenges” throughout election night, but “the 2026 midterm elections have thus far demonstrated the resilience of our election system,” according to Michael McNulty, senior policy director with nonpartisan pro-democracy group Issue One.

“Despite unprecedented executive branch efforts to interfere in election administration, state and local officials responsible for running our elections have continued to do their jobs and uphold the process,” he said.

The real test of the nation’s election system isn’t whether the votes are processed quickly but whether “the votes counted, the results are certified, and the rules hold,” he said.

A relatively smooth process of election administration “demonstrates that overall the guardrails are holding, and a massive amount of planning and pre-work to prevent problems and ensure voters can keep voting has paid off,” according to Pamela Smith, president of nonpartisan election security group Verified Voting.

Election officials must be allowed to “complete the careful, multi-step work of tabulating remaining ballots, reconciling records, and conducting post-election audits to verify that every eligible vote is certified accurately,” she said.

Much of the anxiety stemmed from the possibility of armed federal agents or service members of the polls on Election Day — but the administration has launched a government-wide effort to investigate voter data and root out alleged noncitizen voters that is expected to continue well past the results of this year’s midterms.

Mullin told reporters on Tuesday that he did not send ICE agents, and there were no reports of troops, either, telling Fox News that he “made it very clear that ICE agents aren’t going to be around polling places unless there’s a threat.”

But he said his agency isn’t done scrutinizing voter data.

“After this election we’ll be gathering all the data,” he continued. “We’ll be gathering the voting logs, and we’ll be going through those and making sure that no illegals voted.

Trump, meanwhile, after spending years raging against “fake” polls and “rigged” elections when he doesn’t like the results, conceded Tuesday night that he is willing to accept the outcome.

text:
article

Federal agents arrested five people during a targeted criminal operation outside a Mesa grocery store on Election Day, setting off fierce backlash from community advocacy groups who accused federal authorities of voter intimidation near polling locations.

The Tuesday operation unfolded outside the Food City near Southern Avenue and Mesa Drive.

What we know:

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement confirmed that special agents carried out the enforcement action on Nov. 3 as part of an active criminal probe.

"Special agents with Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) conducted a targeted enforcement operation that resulted in the arrests of five illegal aliens," Fernando Burgos, a public affairs officer for ICE in Arizona, told FOX 10. "These arrests are part of an ongoing criminal investigation."

The operation occurred at the supermarket located about a half-mile from a vote center at The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints and less than a mile from a second polling site at Progressive Baptist Church on Horne.

‘Direct attack on immigrant communities’

What they're saying:

Civil rights organizations, including the San Francisco-based Asian Law Caucus and Arizona Asian American Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islanders for Equity, sharply condemned the federal action, describing it as an immigration raid that netted between six and eight people.

"This took place less than a mile away from two polling sites," the groups said in a joint statement under the campaign banner This is Our Mesa! Keep ICE Out of Our Streets! "For the last year, the Trump administration has threatened communities across the nation with ICE’s presence at the polls. This action is a direct attack on immigrant communities and sends a message of intimidation for voters and residents of Mesa."

"Mesa voters have the right to vote without the fear of ICE’s interference and intimidation," the statement continued. "We demand accountability from ICE and the City of Mesa on why this raid occurred on Election Day."

The other side:

The Mesa Police Department firmly rejected claims that local officers helped coordinate or execute the arrests, captured on video by a witness and later shared with FOX 10.

"The Mesa Police Department was notified that HSI was in the city today," Detective Jose Aguirre said on Tuesday. "There was no other contact with HSI nor did PD provide operational support to their activity."

Department officials directed the public to the city's immigration transparency page, which states local police do not enforce federal civil immigration law on patrol.

Federal officials have not released the names, ages or nationalities of the five individuals taken into custody. ICE has also declined to disclose the specific criminal allegations at the center of the probe, noting only that "no additional information is available for release at this time."

While Arizonans took to the polls Tuesday, volunteer constitutional monitors volunteering were watching out for federal interference and other issues.

ICE and other armed federal personnel are not legally allowed to be at polling sites. But for months, rights groups worried a federal deployment might still happen — especially after Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said ICE agents may go to polls for specific threats.

In the lead-up to the the midterms this week, Democratic lawmakers argued the move was meant to sow fear among voters, and the ACLU of Arizona sent out letters to election officials outlining the laws prohibiting such an effort.

Karime Rodriguez, an organizer with the progressive political action group LUCHA, says about 70 volunteers were sent to nine polling sites in Maricopa County and Tucson to monitor that activity.

The afternoon on Election Day, Rodriguez said no agents were reported at polling sites, but enforcement activity was reported near one site in Mesa.

"There was a raid happening less than 10 minutes from the location they’re at. And even then, we’re still seeing people showing in huge numbers," she said Tuesday afternoon.

Rodriguez said ICE agents made arrests around noon on Tuesday at a shopping plaza parking lot near the polling site at Mesa Community College. and that unmarked vehicles had been seen in the area in the days beforehand.

She said her group sent personnel to verify the enforcement after receiving a tip that it underway through a rapid response line.

"And then the volunteers at the polling place stayed behind and they were on standby with Know Your Rights cards, just in case," she said. "So this was the whole idea all along, is that the only way we’re able to respond as quickly as we need to is with neighborhood relationships and neighborhood organizing."

Rodriguez said her group would not have been able to respond as quickly as they did without having the deployment of volunteer monitors, and despite the enforcement, the polling site still saw huge voter turnout.
