text:
A version of this article was originally published on the Border Criminologies blog at the University of Oxford. It is part of a two-part series on the new EU Return Regulation.

The EU migration management framework is increasingly centred on control and securitisation – an approach which goes hand in hand with the growing use of digital technology for immigration enforcement. The recently implemented EU Return Regulation takes this further. New rules expand the powers available to member states to restrict people’s movements, search their homes and belongings, collect biometric data and monitor compliance with return procedures.

The new regulation formally introduces provisions on investigative measures (a new addition to the 2008 directive), restrictions of movement, and alternatives to detention. These measures will effectively extend surveillance and control into people’s everyday lives and communities.

Challenging the neutral-sounding term ‘return’, The Platform for International Cooperation for Undocumented Migrants (PICUM) has dubbed the Return Regulation the “Deportation Regulation” and draws attention to the deeply punitive and coercive nature of the legislation – an approach that we take forward in this blog post.

A broader framework for control

The ‘Deportation Regulation’ introduces a new framework for “measures to promote returns and alternatives to detention” (included in Chapter IV), which includes:

movement restrictions (under Article 20)

investigative measures (under Article 21)

consequences for non-compliance with the obligation to cooperate (under Article 22)

alternatives to detention or ATDs (under Article 23).

In the new regulation, these measures are grouped together under the same chapter, which effectively expands the possibility for EU member states to locate and control undocumented migrants subject to return, even where there are no detention grounds.

Restrictions on freedom of movement and sanctions for non-cooperation

The new provisions restrict the freedom of movement of people subject to a return decision, to encourage “compliance with the obligations to leave and cooperate” and to prepare “an effective return”. To this end, state authorities can require people to remain within a geographical area, reside at a specific address, and report to competent authorities at specific times. They may also impose “other measures” provided for in national legislation, a framing that remains vague and open to broad interpretations. These measures allow continued control over where people live, where they can go and how frequently they must report to authorities, even when they are not detained.

The regulation links these measures directly to detention. Failure to comply with movement restrictions can itself contribute to a finding of a risk of absconding, which in turn can constitute a ground for detention. These measures can also be imposed on people not complying with the obligation to cooperate, while Article 22 adds further sanctions, including the refusal or reduction of benefits and allowances; exclusion from return and reintegration assistance; refusal or withdrawal of a work permit; extensions of entry bans; criminal sanctions, including imprisonment; financial penalties; and “other measures”.

New investigative powers

The provision on investigative measures (under Article 21) gives member states new powers to carry out raids and other vaguely defined “investigations” at private homes or “other relevant premises”, search and seize personal belongings, and collect biometric data, including fingerprints. These measures can be carried out without the consent of the person concerned and allow for the use of “means of coercion” in cases of non-compliance to obtain biometric data.

These powers raise serious concerns about how immigration enforcement will reach into homes, workplaces and other spaces where people live and seek support. There are justified fears that the measures will lead to more racial profiling – a practice already entrenched within EU border practices. There are also concerns about invasive investigations within the homes/offices of people and organisations suspected of sheltering undocumented migrants.

Healthcare workers and schools could additionally face pressure to cooperate with immigration authorities during investigations. Over 110 organisations have warned that these provisions will trigger policing of public services, thus preventing people from accessing medical care and other important services for fear of persecution and imprisonment.

PICUM and its member organisations have collected extensive evidence on the far-reaching consequences that these practices – already existing in some member states – lead to in everyday life across EU member states.

Changed understanding of ‘alternatives’ to detention

Under the 2008 Return Directive, member states were required to consider “less coercive measures” as alternatives to detention (ATDs) before applying detention. However, there was no definition of what the less coercive measures might actually look like.

In 2018, the international community and member states within the UN adopted a definition of alternatives to detention in the Global Compact on Migration (Objective 13). The definition stated that these measures should be prioritised over detention, be non-custodial and allow the individual to remain in their community with human rights standards in accordance with international law.

In the new ‘Deportation Regulation’, the definition of ATDs (under Article 23) includes the deposit of a financial guarantee; the use of electronic monitoring; or “other measures” when provided in national law. These measures can be applied to any third country national subject to a return procedure. However, the new rules remove an explicit obligation for states to consider ATDs before deciding to apply detention.

Beyond this, while the regulation sets maximum periods for detention, it does not establish a specific time limit for ATDs. Crucially, Article 30(4) expressly provides that the expiry of the maximum detention period does not prevent member states from applying measures under Articles 20 and 23. This means that reaching the legal limit on detention does not necessarily mean the end of restrictive controls: a person may instead remain subject to movement restrictions, reporting obligations, financial guarantees or electronic monitoring.

Digital surveillance

By explicitly referring to “electronic monitoring”, the regulation will likely expand existing national practices that embed the use of technology within “alternatives to detention”, such as through the use of GPS tagging and mobile phone surveillance.

The use of surveillance methods and digital technologies as “alternatives to detention” has been highly criticised for extending the harms of detention and hindering migrants’ access to rights and dignity. Digital rights experts have warned that these technologies are highly stigmatising, violate rights to privacy and freedom of movement, and may amount to de facto detention.

Research shows that the use of electronic monitoring engenders feelings of shame and criminalisation and has deeply negative mental health impacts for those subjected to it. Rather than being a genuine “alternative”, it ultimately represents another tool of coercive control that extends into the community, lacks external oversight, and leads to discrimination, exclusion, and broad violations, including of privacy and data protection rights.

Such models show how digital surveillance can become embedded in migration infrastructure, with technologies that monitor movement and access becoming part of the everyday experience of people subject to immigration control.

What’s next: enforcement

On 1 October 2026, the Council of the EU took the last institutional step needed for implementation through formal adoption. The regulation will apply in its entirety 12 months after its publication in the Official Journal of the EU. Certain provisions, including those relating to the possibility of developing “return hubs” and agreements with third countries, will apply from the date of publication. However, the majority of the regulation, including articles related to detention and alternatives to detention, will only be applicable from autumn 2027. This means that over the course of the next 12 months, EU member states will prepare for implementation through national legislation and other arrangements.

text:
Colorado voters have spurned a conservative group’s effort to force police and prosecutors to aid the Trump administration’s mass deportation agenda.

Amendment 81, which failed to receive 55% of the vote on Tuesday, would have required Colorado’s law enforcement agents to notify federal immigration authorities if individuals accused of violent crime were not lawfully present in the US or if their legal status was undetermined.

The mandate also included a 72-hour deadline for law enforcement to alert the Department of Homeland Security after filing charges for crimes, such as murder, assault and arson, against possibly undocumented individuals.

Proponents for the measure, including the conservative non-profit Advance Colorado, reportedly argued it would ensure public safety by removing undocumented people who had committed crimes, or repeat offenders, from the country.

Critics of amendment 81 panned the measure, saying it took charges as evidence of criminality rather than as allegations.

“Being accused of a crime is not the same as being convicted, and our laws need to respect that distinction,” Shad Murib, the Colorado Democratic party chair, said in a Wednesday statement.

The reports to the Department of Homeland Security may have put individuals at risk of deportation before they received a trial. Concern also mounted over whether racial profiling would factor into how people’s citizenship status was questioned.

“We’re grateful to the advocates and community members who stood up for their neighbors. Colorado can hold people accountable for crimes without giving ICE more power over families who deserve fair treatment,” Murib said.

description:

Increase your impact this year by organising your own Write for Rights event!

The Manly Action Group also hosts a Write for Rights event each year at their local surf club, featuring speakers, raffles, and food.
text:
Welcome to Amnesty International’s Write for Rights letter-writing kit. Here you will find everything you need to successfully take part in the Write for Rights 2026 campaign. Write for Rights changes lives and your words matter.

The people featured in this year’s campaign are from all around the world, like Owen Chow jailed in Hong Kong simply for standing up for democracy, and Rokiatou Doumbia in Mali, detained for daring to ask why food was too expensive on TikTok.

You’re here because you want to make a difference. You want to speak truth to power. Whether you do this with a group of friends, classmates, your family or by yourself, your words can change lives.

Quick links: 2026 Cases, Rainbow Case, How does W4R work, Key Dates, Organise your own Write for Rights event, Helpful Resources, Young Activists & Schools, Let us know how it went!

What is Write for Rights?

A letter can change someone’s life. That’s the idea behind Write for Rights, our global letter-writing campaign. In 2001, a small group of activists in Poland decided to run a 24-hour letter-writing marathon for 10 December – Human Rights Day. The idea took off and this year marks the 25th anniversary of people taking over 50 million actions against injustice, writing letters and signing petitions in support of people whose human rights have been denied.

Every December, for 25 years, supporters across the globe write millions of letters, cards and tweets, and sign petitions for those whose basic human rights are being attacked. These supporters form a vibrant community of people like you, continuing a long tradition of writing letters to right some of the world’s biggest wrongs.

Together, Amnesty International’s global Write for Rights campaign has supported more than 200 people and groups, and over 100 people featured in our Write for Rights campaign have seen a positive outcome in their situation. People unlawfully detained have been released, families have been reunited and justice achieved. Just as important – individuals have been reminded that they have not been forgotten.

Real change happens because of your letters and actions. People wrongfully imprisoned are released, abusers are brought to justice, and those in prison are treated more humanely. You can read more about our wins over 25 years or watch the inspiring story of Sasha Skochilenko, a Russian artist imprisoned for her peaceful anti-war protest – whose case shows the true power of solidarity.

How does Write for Rights work?

2026 Cases

Right now, all around the world, human rights are under attack. This year we’re taking action for individuals and communities from around the world, who are courageously speaking truth to power.

You can check out videos of all the cases here.

For all the cases, in one printable PDF, see our Helpful Resources

Rainbow case

Alongside the cases, above, Amnesty International Australia has included another action that we think will be of interest to people taking part in Write for Rights 2026, wanting to take powerful written actions for human rights and justice.

Helpful Resources

Download and print our Letter Writing Kit (includes all Case Cards)

Print with bleed available here

W4Rs cover sheet for reporting actions – please fill in this sheet, instead of filling out your details across all the individual letters. This will help us ensure that your letters get to the right place efficiently to maximise our collective impact.

PDF petition for Write for Rights: One signature, Eight times the impact!

Print Case Cards from Letter Writing Kit to display alongside PDF petition form

Young Activists and Human Rights Education in Schools Resources

Log your event so it’s promoted on our website and so we can provide additional support and resources.

If you are part of an Amnesty Action Group log your event through SupporterBase

For further questions, or if you are not part of an Amnesty Action Group, please let us know about your event, by emailing: activism@amnesty.org.au

Use our handy Events & Tactics Checklist when organising your Write for Rights event!

Campaigning for human rights can be difficult. Burnout and vicarious trauma can happen and it’s important to keep a look out for the signs in yourself and your friends. You can check out our Sustainable Activism & Self Care guide and workshop here. It examines how we can better take care of ourselves as activists and what you can do to make sure your activism is sustainable!

Monday, 9 November 2026 – Write for Rights 2026 Launches.

Thursday, 10 December 2026 – Human Rights Day!

Sunday, 31 Jan 2027 – Deadline for all offline actions to be sent back to us at ”Amnesty International Australia, Gadigal Country, Locked Bag 23, Broadway NSW 2007, Australia”

Organise your own Write for Rights event!

Increase your impact this year by organising your own Write for Rights event!

You can organise a general Write for Rights event and take action for all of the cases, or focus on one or two cases that particularly resonate with you and your group. You could aim for something big and ambitious like a screening of a film or documentary that strongly relates to one of our Write for Rights cases, followed by an action taking blitz by all attendees. Or you could plan something simple like a gathering of friends and family at the local library or at your favourite café to collectively take action together.

The key thing for any Write for Rights event is taking action. Your event can focus on gathering petition signatures, writing letters calling for justice for our 2026 Write for Rights cases, or writing solidarity messages of hope or any combination of these actions!

You can host your event anytime before the end of January 2027 – just remember that any offline actions collected like physical petitions, letters, and solidarity messages need to be sent back to us by the 31st of January 2027

Big or small, Write for Rights events are an amazing way to increase action and, ultimately, increase our impact. They raise community awareness about important human rights issues happening around the world, and demonstrate just how much of a difference collective action and solidarity can make!

No matter what kind of Write for Rights event you decide to host, we’re here to support! Log your event so it’s promoted on our website, and so we can provide additional support and resources, through SupporterBase. For further questions, contact: activism@amnesty.org.au

How you can promote your activities with SupporterBase

Are you hoping that Write for Rights will help expand your impact and reach more people?

SupporterBase is here to help you grow your group, promote your Write for Rights events, and engage supporters through text and call functionality – all in one easy-to-use platform. Many of our activists have already been using this platform but if you haven’t had a chance to login and use it yet, Write for Rights is the perfect opportunity!

What SupporterBase can help with:

Create and Manage Events: Add your Write for Rights events to the platform, ensuring you’re covered by our public liability and have the event resources you need to make it a success!

Automatic Website Promotion: Your events will automatically be published to our Amnesty Australia website, making them accessible to a broader audience across the country.

RSVP Management: People will then be able to register directly for your event. You can track RSVPs and manage attendee lists in real-time, ensuring you’re prepared for the day.

Bulk SMS Campaigns: You can send out (or schedule) important updates or reminders to your event RSVPs with a few clicks.

Call Campaigns: If you have the time and interest you can also call any RSVPs who may be new to the group providing that more personal touch to build relationships and encourage them to attend.

Advanced Audience Filters: Finally you can use advanced filters to segment your supporter list and email specific groups based on their interests or past involvement. For example you can ask your existing group members to volunteer on the day while tailoring a different communication to newer sign ups. This helps to make your communications more impactful and relevant.

Everything you need to know about SupporterBase is here including how-to guides and handy video tutorials. You can also email activism@amnesty.org.au should you need any help getting set up.

Check out events happening around Australia here.

Let us know how it went!

Please fill out the Event Evaluation Form to let us know how your event went—evaluations enable us to report on events, recognise your work and address any issues.

Send all your letters and petitions back to the Sydney action centre at: Amnesty International, Locked Bag 23, Broadway NSW 2007 OR scan and email them to supporter@amnesty.org.au and we’ll post them to the targets, and ensure that your solidarity messages are delivered!

Young Activist & Schools Guide

Are you a passionate young person looking to get involved in our Write 4 Rights Campaign but not sure where to begin?

How many letters could your school community write to help others?

Put pens to paper during Term 4 for the world’s biggest human rights event, Write for Rights!

How can my school participate in W4R?

Host a Letter Writing Marathon (during lessons or home room, over lunch, or at dedicated events any time at all during Term 4) with groups of students (Year 9 to 11), staff, and/or members of the wider community to:

Cultivate compassion;

Discuss human rights issues;

Foster an inclusive, rights-respecting community;

And challenge injustices by writing as many letters as possible!

What support and resources will Amnesty provide?

To be a part of this important campaign, simply register your school’s interest via our form (anyone in your community can do it – with school permission, of course) and we will send you our digital School W4R Pack, which includes instructions, letter templates, and a wealth of resources to guide you.

If you have any questions, please email Caroline (caroline.wells@amnesty.org.au) – we’re here to help!

Inspiration from previous years

In 2022, the Amnesty Chermside Group held a Write for Rights event at their local library, hosting a screening of the documentary The Troublemaker, which explored the global wave of civil protest in response to the climate crisis. They invited a speaker from Extinction Rebellion and took action together for two Write for Rights cases focused on climate justice and environmental activism.

In 2021, the Victorian Activism Leadership Committee celebrated Amnesty’s 60th birthday and Write for Rights with their #LightUpYellow project, arranging for major landmarks across Victoria to be lit up in yellow on Human Rights Day.

Last year, the National Iran Network hosted a Write for Rights art workshop in collaboration with local artists, providing a space for participants to slow down, reflect, create artworks, and take meaningful action for human rights.

The Manly Action Group also hosts a Write for Rights event each year at their local surf club, featuring speakers, raffles, and food. In 2023, they collected 251 letters, 86 messages of support, and 85 petition signatures at their event.

These are just a few examples to get you started. Be creative and think of a fun, engaging way to take action for Write for Rights in your community! If you have any questions, please reach out via activism@amnesty.org.au—we’d love to help!

Although some races haven't yet been called, and key Democrats such as House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, a New Yorker likely to become the next speaker, don't support shifting the United States to a universal public healthcare system, the Democratic "tsunami" on Tuesday still revived hope that the results could help the fight for Medicare for All.

Democrats reclaimed both the US Senate and House of Representatives after Trump and congressional Republicans last year used their budget package, the so-called One Big Beautiful Bill Act, to slash Medicaid spending and allow Affordable Care Act subsidies to expire—which has already led to millions of Americans losing health insurance coverage.

The wave of Democratic wins also came nearly five months after a coalition of over 325 organizations argued that "now is the time to organize" for Medicare for All, given that "we may face a once-in-a-generation opportunity to legislate on healthcare in 2029."

While—as the coalition suggested—passing federal Medicare for All legislation would likely require not only a Democrat-controlled Congress but also replacing Trump with a progressive president in 2028, the midterm results are still being seen by voters and elected officials alike as "a mandate to deliver big change" over the next two years.

"Wins by progressive candidates will jumpstart a national discussion of Medicare for All," said Larry Levitt, executive vice president for health policy at KFF. "Medicare for All isn't going to pass in the next two years. But, newly prominent advocates will have a platform to make sure it's part [of] the discussion, carrying through to the 2028 primaries."

Even without support from party leaders and the White House, Democrats may still push for congressional hearings or even votes on single-payer policies before the 2028 elections.

Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.), lead sponsor of the Medicare for All Act in the House, told Punchbowl News this week that she wants to mark up the bill next year and fight for a vote on the floor: "I want to make sure we have the requisite number of co-sponsors, and I’m hoping that our leadership is part of helping to make that happen."

As Forbes reported:

Several Democrats who won seats in the US Senate and the US House of Representatives made Medicare for All or a public option key parts of their winning campaigns. Such ideas will likely get more airtime now that Democrats control both houses of Congress in a rebuke of Trump administration policies that have slashed healthcare spending.

Exactly what form a "public option" would take [is] unclear, but such a choice being offered to Americans alongside private and existing health insurance coverage would seem more achievable than replacing the existing health insurance system with Medicare for All.

The American Prospect pointed out that Medicare for All supporters who emerged victorious on Tuesday include Rep.-elects Claire Valdez, Brad Lander, and Darializa Avila Chevalier in New York's 7th, 10th, and 13th districts, along with "Democratic Georgia state Rep. Dr. Jasmine Clark, who won more than 81% of the vote to represent Georgia's 13th District; Democrat Melat Kiros, who beat nearly 30-year incumbent Republican US Rep. Diana DeGette to represent Colorado's 1st District; and Democratic socialist Janeese Lewis George, who will be Washington, DC’s first new mayor in more than a decade."

Among the victors in the US Senate were Democrats Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan and Troy Jackson of Maine, also both vocal backers of Medicare for All. Jayapal highlighted that "Abdul was up against millions of dollars in dark money from Republican donors—and today Michigan voters sent a clear message that their state and their votes are not for sale."

"Abdul ran a strong campaign on Medicare for All, refused corporate [political action committee] money, and stayed focused on working families from day one to Election Day," she added. "I am so proud to have stood with him throughout his campaign and I cannot wait to work with him in Washington to deliver for you."

From leading a border blockade to protect loggers' wages, to the state legislature and President of the Maine Senate, Troy has spent his life fighting for working Mainers. We look forward to organizing with Sen.-elect Jackson to pass Medicare For All and secure a federal right to abortion.

The leading voice for Medicare for All in the upper chamber, Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), worked to elect both El-Sayed and Jackson, as well as several leftist House candidates who won. He wrote on social media Wednesday that "last night saw some of the greatest progressive victories in modern American history. All across the country, in rural and urban areas, Americans said NO to oligarchy, and YES to an agenda that fights for the working class."

Sanders, who caucuses with Democrats, is expected to chair the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions when the party takes over in January, and Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), another Medicare for All backer, will likely lead the Finance Committee, as STAT Washington correspondent John Wilkerson noted Wednesday—predicting that "the wins that Democrats amassed on Tuesday night could breathe life into efforts to create some type of a single-payer system."

Yale University researchers estimated in August that Sanders' related legislative proposal could save over 114,000 lives and $1 trillion annually. In response to those findings, the senator said that "at a time when 15 million Americans are being thrown off the healthcare they have and 20 million Americans have already seen their premiums double, on average, as a result of Trump's so-called 'Big Beautiful Bill,' we need Medicare for All now more than ever."

A KFF survey released last month found that 66% of Americans—including 84% of Democrats, 72% of independents, and 34% of Republicans—support Medicare for All, the highest level of support since the organization began tracking the proposal.

Sharing KFF data on how the average US family's health insurance premium has soared over the past quarter-century, The Tennessee Holler declared on social media Wednesday: "Medicare for All. Now. We can't afford not to do it. It isn't radical to support it. It's radical to oppose it."

"Voters just overwhelmingly repudiated the most anti-environmental, pro-fossil fuel administration in US history," Jamie Henn, the director of Fossil Free Media, told Common Dreams. "This was a historic climate victory in disguise. Voters across the country supported candidates who pledged to cut energy costs, end corruption, and take on corporate greed. That’s the exact framework we need to push a bold clean energy and polluter pays agenda."

"Climate politics are back on the table, and we plan to fight for them."

"Last night’s election opens the door for plenty more states to pass climate legislation, like climate superfund bills, and block industry attempts to hold back clean energy or immunize themselves from climate damages," Henn said.

Affordability and Corruption Are Climate Issues

While climate and the environment took a backseat in election rhetoric and reporting to issues like affordability and corruption, many winning candidates who champion reducing inequality and challenging corporate greed—such as Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) and Reps.-elect Chris Rabb (D-Pa.), Claire Valdez (D-NY), and Melat Kiros (D-Colo.)—also back policies such as a Green New Deal and holding polluting industries accountable. Also in Michigan, Democratic Rep.-elect Will Lawrence was a co-founder of the climate focused Sunrise Movement.

"Ardent advocates of climate and environmental action and justice who loudly rejected Trump and the Republican attack on both are now heading to and returning back to Congress and to offices across the nation," environmental investigative journalist Antonia Juhasz wrote on social media. "It’s officially a Green Wave too."

Kidus Girma, Sunrise Movement's campaign director, told Common Dreams that on Tuesday, "Young people proved that progressive ideas like the Green New Deal are just as popular in central Michigan as they are in Brooklyn."

"Working people in America no matter where they live want the same thing—good green jobs, a pause on data centers, and a system that works for people, not billionaires," Girma said. "Climate politics are back on the table, and we plan to fight for them."

Climate advocates pointed out that issues such as the high price of gas due to Trump's illegal war on Iran are intimately connected with the dependence on a fossil fuel industry that is empowered to profit from energy crises.

"Climate change may not have dominated the election, but the consequences of our dependence on fossil fuels certainly did," said Cassidy DiPaola, the communications director at Fossil Free Media and spokesperson for the Make Polluters Pay campaign, in a statement. "Americans are struggling with high gas prices, rising energy bills, and mounting climate disaster costs while Big Oil rakes in record profits and spends millions buying influence in Washington."

Further, the backlash against the AI data centers build-out, reflected in massive wins for data centers moratoriums and anti-data center candidates, is also a major climate victory, as the Sierra Club projects that the use of fossil fuels to power new data centers will increase power sector emissions by 42% by 2030 when compared with 2025 levels, undoing 15 years of climate progress in electricity generation.

"Millions of voters cast their ballots in frustration over data centers, corporate greed, and Trump’s egregious giveaways to fossil fuel CEOs and other industry cronies," Brett Hartl, the national political director at the Center for Biological Diversity Action Fund, said in a statement.

Elizabeth Bast, executive director at Oil Change Action, said in a statement that "voters send a clear message: They’re fed up with Trump’s agenda of fossil fuel giveaways, illegal and immoral wars, and unchecked data center expansion that makes their lives more expensive while lining the pockets of Big Oil and Big Tech,"

Bast continued: "Affordability and accountability were voters’ top concerns this election cycle. Both are inseparable from fossil fuel dependence. Americans have spent an additional $101 billion on gas since the start of Trump’s war on Iran, highlighting the dangers of fossil fuel reliance. Meanwhile, Trump increased his wealth by tens of millions through stock trades made profitable by his war—a blatant example of this administration’s corruption."

Big Oil Bet and Lost

One major theme of the midterms was the ability of the "many" to beat the "money," as El-Sayed put it in his victory speech. Big spending by the American Israel Public Affairs Committee and Big Tech oligarchs including Elon Musk failed to force their preferred candidates over the finish line.

This was equally true of Big Oil, as Emily Atklin detailed in a race-by-race breakdown for Heated. On the national level, Chevron, Koch, Energy Transfer, and the American Petroleum Institute gave a combined $25 million to keep Republicans in charge of Congress, only to see the Democrats retake both the House and Senate. Chevron also gave $200,000 each to losing GOP candidates Ken Paxton in Texas and Sen. Susan Collins in Maine.

Lawrence, the Sunrise Movement alum, triumphed over the combined forces of Musk and other GOP insiders in what was the nation's most expensive House race.

"Lawrence mobilized voters and volunteers by his long-standing commitment to putting working-class families over billionaire polluters and data center developers. His campaign estimates it knocked more doors than any other House Democratic race," Oil Change's Bast said.

Mya Lega, a Lawrence campaign spokesperson, told Common Dreams: “Michiganders want our land, air, and water protected from AI data centers, polluters, and corporate oligarchs. Will Lawrence built his career on standing up to them. In the House, he’ll be a leading voice against the Trump administration’s rollbacks on environmental protections and handouts to corporations and oligarchs.”

The victory of people over money was true of more local races as well, as in Georgia where voters flipped the Georgia Public Service Commission to Democratic control despite fossil fuel spending on behalf of Republican candidates, while voters in Colorado rejected an industry-backed attempt to enshrine a right to use or sell natural gas in the state constitution.

"Fossil fuel money is one of the most powerful forces in American politics. It is the biggest obstacle we face in preserving a livable climate for everyone on Earth," Atkin wrote. "But it is not invincible. Not even close."

Further, the appetite for getting money out of politics was reflected in votes on energy and climate issues. In Michigan, voters approved Proposition 2 to bar publicly regulated utilities from giving funds to state and local candidates. And nationwide, more than 65 congressional candidates who had signed the No Fossil Fuel Money Pledge won their races.

“Big Oil and Big Tech have poured enormous amounts of money into this election to protect their power and profits," Bast of Oil Change wrote. "Across the country, candidates who refuse fossil fuel money have won elections, proving that Big Oil's money is no match for the power of organized communities."

A Win for Wildlife

Beyond climate and energy concerns, Defenders of Wildlife celebrated Tuesday's results as a check on Trump's gutting of protections public lands and endangered species.

“For those of us working to protect America's wildlife and wild places, this is a moment of renewed hope and possibility," the group's president and CEO, Andrew Bowman, said in a statement. “Over the past two years, we have faced extraordinary challenges, including relentless efforts to weaken the Endangered Species Act, roll back protections for public lands, and undermine decades of conservation progress."

Bowman continued: "A new Congress offers opportunities to defend bedrock environmental laws, strengthen congressional oversight, and advance conservation priorities that have faced significant political headwinds. It also creates new possibilities for bipartisan cooperation around something we know transcends political divisions: America's shared commitment to wildlife and our natural heritage."

'Rallying Cry'

Following Tuesday's win, climate and environmental campaigners urged victorious candidates to consider their election as a mandate to protect public health and the environment and to hold polluters accountable for harm and corruption.

They also urged current members of Congress to reject the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), a bill that advocates argue would gut current regulations to clear the way for more fossil fuel and data centers projects.

“The midterm results are a rallying cry for Democrats to use their newfound power to rein in Trump. Democrats must not cut deals in the lame duck that bolster Trump and give Republicans wins but instead lay the foundation to end Trump’s corrupt anti-environmental crusade for good," the Center for Biological Diversity's Hartl said.

“Voters gave Democrats control of Congress to advance policies that uplift communities, not offer sweetheart giveaways to corporate polluters and data centers, like the Senate permitting reform bill,” Hartl continued. “Trump has done so much damage to our public lands, wildlife habitats, and clean air and water protections in the last two years. Democrats must take ownership of their new mandate right now and start changing the conversation in Congress.”

"For newly elected leaders looking to establish themselves as champions of the working class, taking on Big Oil is an obvious place to start."

Earthworks policy director Lauren Pagel warned: "In the coming weeks this administration and current Congress will treat the lame-duck session like a fire sale on essential environmental and health protections and the rights of tribal governments. It is critical we stop them before they do even more damage to our air, water, land, sacred places, and the health of our communities."

She argued that this started with rejecting BAAJA: "This legislation that the Senate will likely consider next week would permanently undercut the ability of communities to say no to dangerous oil, gas, and mining projects in their backyards."

Bast of Oil Change agreed, saying: "Democrats have a clear mandate to rein in Big Oil and Big Tech. They must seize the opportunity to do so, first by rejecting the currently proposed permitting deal... and then by taxing Big Oil’s windfall profits in the incoming Congress."

The Environmental Protection Network (EPN), an organization made up of more than 800 former employees of the Environmental Protection Agency, called on the new Congress to hold Trump's EPA to account for failing in its mission to protect people and the environment from pollution and to restore it to its prior function and scientific rigor.

“Americans understand that when corporations aren't held accountable for their pollution, ordinary families end up paying the price,” EPN's senior director of public affairs, Marc Boom, said in a statement. “Our polling shows that 81% of registered voters surveyed believe the costs of pollution are being shifted onto families. The incoming Congress has an opportunity and a responsibility to hold EPA and the rest of the federal government accountable and make sure they're doing their jobs to protect public health and leave families safer, not sicker.”

Others urged the new Congress to take the opportunity to hold Big Oil accountable as well.

"Americans are struggling with high gas prices, rising energy bills, and mounting climate disaster costs while Big Oil rakes in record profits and spends millions buying influence in Washington," DiPaola said in a statement. "Voters made clear they're fed up with corporate greed and politicians who put wealthy donors ahead of working families. Now Democrats have a chance to prove they're serious about changing that. For newly elected leaders looking to establish themselves as champions of the working class, taking on Big Oil is an obvious place to start."

She continued: "We want to see oil executives hauled before Congress to answer for their profiteering and political influence. We want a windfall profits tax that puts money back in working people's pockets, climate superfund laws that make polluters pay for the damage they've caused, and an end to Big Oil's push for special legal immunity. Democrats have won the power to take on one of the wealthiest and most politically connected industries in America, and we expect them to use it."

Aaron Regunberg, who directs Public Citizen’s Climate Accountability Project, agreed.

"Democrats across the country ran on a pledge to lower the costs of essentials and take on corporate corruption. They just won a massive mandate to do just that. And you can't achieve those goals without fighting for Big Oil accountability," he told Common Dreams.

He continued: "Democrats have an opportunity to crack down on fossil fuel profiteering and haul Big Oil CEOs in to investigate their corrupt dealings with Trump. It would be a huge mistake to not seize this huge opportunity."

Even on a night when Democrats clobbered the GOP up and down the map and won decisively in states as red as Texas, South Carolina, Kansas, and Iowa, very few analysts believed Mississippi—where President Donald Trump won by nearly 23 points in 2024—would be competitive, let alone a nail-biter that dragged into the next day.

But NBC election analyst Steve Kornacki explained Wednesday morning that with thousands of votes left to count in overwhelmingly Democratic Hinds County, “Colom could absolutely win this.”

In a 5-4 decision that now looms large, the US Supreme Court shot down Republican efforts to stop the counting of mail-in ballots postmarked on or before Election Day that arrive afterward. Those ballots, which can continue arriving until November 10, may ultimately decide the election.

Even if Colom falls short, his strong showing was evidence of what the NAACP, the nation’s oldest civil rights organization, described as "historic voter turnout" in Black communities, in response to Republicans' attack on the Voting Rights Act.

Following the Supreme Court's Louisiana v. Callais decision earlier this year, several GOP-controlled states, including those in the Deep South, moved to redraw congressional and state legislative districts in ways that voting rights advocates warned would dilute Black voting power.

On the campaign trail, Colom described Callais as "a threat to our democracy" and said Republican Gov. Tate Reeves, who proposed legislative maps that would have drawn Black lawmakers out of their districts, was seeking to stop Black voters from "being able to pick leaders they want."

When the court’s conservatives kneecapped the Voting Rights Act, they inspired a fierce backlash among Black voters across the South," explained reporter Jim Saksa in an analysis for Democracy Docket. "Massive Black turnout helped Democrats coast to victory in Georgia and made the Senate races in Mississippi and Louisiana the tightest seen in decades."

Voter turnout in Mississippi is on pace to be about 40% higher than in the last midterm election in 2022. In majority-Black Hinds County, which contains Jackson, unofficial results showed nearly 76,500 votes for the two leading US Senate candidates alone, about 44% more than the total number of ballots cast four years ago.

"The story of this election is not just about who won," said Dominik Whitehead, chief of field for the NAACP. "It's about the Black wave of voters who understood what was at stake and made their voices heard."

Democratic US Senate candidate Scott Colom of Mississippi stands outside the home of slain civil rights leader Medgar Evers in Jackson, Mississippi, in a video posted on November 1, 2026. (Screenshot from a video by Scott Colom)

Colom didn’t have to water down his platform much to achieve tremendous gains, even in a deep-red state. As political strategist Paul Hilder explained, he “ran on a ‘commonsense’ economic populist platform aimed at daily life: gas, groceries, healthcare, and closing hospitals, plus Medicaid expansion.”

In the nation’s poorest state, where nearly 1 in 5 residents rely on Medicaid or the Children’s Health Insurance Program, this message was potent. It was especially effective against Hyde-Smith, who has comfortably won her previous elections and was relentlessly criticized for dismissing voters’ concerns about high prices.

For example, in DeSoto County, which Trump carried by 24 points in 2024, Colom led Hyde-Smith by more than six points in early returns.

"[Colom] won many switchers, and the Republican vote collapsed," Hilder said. "Swing voters are more volatile than ever, especially when they’re economically hard-pressed. They respond to common sense, and they’ve decided Trump and the Republicans are not on their side."

Mississippi has not elected a Democrat to the US Senate since Sen. John C. Stennis, a conservative segregationist, won his seventh term in 1982. And although it has the highest proportion of Black residents of any US state, Mississippi has not sent a Black senator to Washington since Reconstruction, when Republican Blanche K. Bruce, who was born into slavery, was elected by the state Legislature.

Colom told NPR last week he’s always believed change was possible and that it has failed to materialize only because of neglect by national Democrats, who have long written the state off as unwinnable.

"The reality is, Mississippi has never been a lost cause," he said. "We've been a betrayed cause."

"What a night for the movement Bernie has been building for decades," said Jeremy Slevin, Sanders' senior adviser and communications director, listing dozens of the candidates who were endorsed by the senator and ran on platforms demanding Medicare for All, housing justice, civil rights, and an end to the influence of powerful corporations on US politics.

RoseAnn DeMoro, a labor organizer and former executive director of National Nurses United and the California Nurses Association, recalled how, as her organization campaigned for Sanders in 2016 and 2020, "we educated, agitated, organized, gained the most principled allies, incredible people, like Abdul El-Sayed."

"And last night—we won!" said DeMoro.

She added: "Thank you, Bernie Sanders, for working your heart out to change this country. Your 'long game' should be very gratifying today."

A decade after he first ran for president, the proposals Sanders pushed in 2016 have been embraced by large majorities of Democratic voters, and even Americans across the political spectrum. His signature proposal, Medicare for All, dismissed then by former presidential candidate Hillary Clinton as something that would "never, ever come to pass," is supported by 66% of US adults, according to a KFF poll taken last month, with 52% of respondents still supporting the idea if it would "eliminate private health insurance companies."

The US House held its first-ever hearings on Medicare for All in 2019, and some of the Democratic Party's most popular members—Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY), elected in 2018, and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, elected in 2025—are outspoken proponents of the plan.

On Tuesday night, said Josh Orton of Demand Justice, "across the country, in red states and blue, Democratic candidates adopted the fight Bernie led for years: for the people against the powerful. You lead that fight and welcome everyone to join you, you win."

Even candidates who did not campaign alongside Sanders, such as Democratic Sen.-elect James Talarico and Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa in Texas, put forward platforms that showed clear signs of Sanders' influence on US politics. Hinojosa told The New York Times that "the one fight in this country is about economic power" as she explained why she identifies as a "populist" rather than a progressive, and Talarico spoke out against "the billionaires who own the social media platforms, who own the cable news networks, who own the politicians fighting on our screens."

"The people at the top work so hard to keep us angry and divided because our unity is a threat to their wealth and their power," Talarico said, suggesting a call for the working-class solidarity Sanders has urged at his Fighting Oligarchy rallies.

Will Steakin of Politico said he was "not sure any Democratic surrogate campaigned as hard as Sanders this cycle," counting 58 rallies since the Fighting Oligarchy Tour, attended by 340,000 people, and "20 rallies in October alone."

Posting a montage of the rallies, set to David Bowie's "Starman," the senator himself said that Americans "across the country, in rural and urban areas," had "said NO to oligarchy, and YES to an agenda that fights for the working class."

"I am so happy that Bernie Sanders is with us today to be able to see the fruits of his labor. He cultivated a whole generation of young leaders through the movement he spawned who are now winning seats everywhere," historian Asad Dandia said of the 85-year-old senator. "Thank you, Bernie."

"Deliver on the big change people are demanding," Casar wrote in a message to his fellow Democrats. "End the war. Stop ICE’s reign of terror. Root out corruption. Raise wages. Stop price gouging. Get money out of politics. Strengthen unions."

"No complacency," he added.

Top Democrats signaled in the immediate aftermath of the party's midterm rout of President Donald Trump's Republican Party that they would not hesitate to begin investigating alleged corruption—a major issue for voters, according to exit polls—and other wrongdoing by the White House and its allies.

House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY), who is in line to become speaker in the new Congress, said Wednesday that his caucus would also work to "make significant and decisive progress on addressing the affordability crisis"—though legislative efforts could by stymied by Trump's veto power.

Progressives—bouyed by victories in key races across the country—implored Democrats to use every bit of power that voters gave them to pursue bold change and lay the groundwork for retaking the White House in 2028, warning against a return to the status quo politics that delivered the country into the grasp of Trump and the GOP in the first place.

"Use every committee, hearing, and budget negotiation. Follow the contracts and conflicts of interest. Put executives and administration officials under oath," Joseph Geevarghese, executive director of the advocacy group Our Revolution, said in a statement Wednesday. "Fight for concrete gains and make Trump answer for what he blocks. We know we won’t win everything at once. People need to see Democrats using every bit of power they have to fight for them."

Geevarghese also called on Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-NY) to step aside as leader of the Senate Democratic caucus, arguing that the fight ahead "requires leadership ready to meet the moment."

"The blue wave was powered by a progressive wave. We are the center of gravity in this party, and we intend to drive the agenda. People deserve a new New Deal: a $25 living wage, stronger unions, affordable housing, taxes on billionaires and a sustained fight for Medicare for All," said Geevarghese. "If Democrats retreat into caution and fail to improve people’s lives, they will rebuild the distrust Trump exploited. The people organized for change. We organized to win. Now we organize to make Democrats deliver."

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani also weighed in on the implications of Tuesday's election results, saying at a press conference that "what last night told us is that Americans are tired of being told that their needs are unrealistic, by politicians who have been bought by the wealthiest people in the country."

"This country has elected a new generation of leadership, a generation with a mandate to lower the cost of living, to build not bomb, to never betray the working people who entrusted them with power," said Mamdani. "And I hear often that the politics that we're fighting for here in New York City are not possible outside of city limits. And what last night showed us is that working people are the majority, whether we are speaking of Austin or Ann Arbor or Astoria. It is time to put those same people first in our politics."

"There will be a lot of infighting and arguing over what happened and why that is," Vice President JD Vance said Tuesday in a lengthy social media post. "One of the pollsters I really respect told me that our economic messaging wasn’t sharp enough down the stretch. I’m sure that’s true."

"But the real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone," the vice president continued. "The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night."

Indeed, Trump acknowledged that the war harmed Republicans, telling Fox News, "I think a part of it was Iran," but nevertheless defended the 35-week military campaign, insisting that "people understood the importance of what I've done with Iran."

In an interview with The Wall Street Journal, Trump was similarly unapologetic, declaring: "I did the right thing. I would have done it again."

Numerous observers contended that Tuesday's results offered an opportunity for Democrats to do more than simply capitalize on Republican mistakes.

"Among other things, this is an absolute rebuke of the war in Iran. Democrats would be wise to heed that lesson and truly become the anti-war party," said commentator Ben Rhodes—who, while serving as a senior national security adviser to then-President Barack Obama, supported US intervention in countries including Iraq, Libya, and Syria, as well as Obama's wider drone war campaign.

Geopolitics scholar Van Jackson opined on social media that "if Democrats remain the party of the national security state, they will lose everything in 2028. If they become the anti-war party, they’ll consolidate this wave with the presidency."

A Wednesday analysis on the libertarian site Reason by Matthew Petti argued that Democrats now have an opportunity to exercise Congress' constitutional power over the war, including by withholding military funding.

Petti noted that Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) told Fox News last week, "The House and the Senate should stop the funding for any further actions in the Iran War," just like "we did to stop the Vietnam War."

However, Petti cautioned that Democratic electoral victories usually don't lead to anti-war foreign policy.

"Party leadership that is willing to attack Republicans' execution of the war may not share a principled anti-war commitment," he wrote, recalling how Democrats who swept the 2006 midterms over public anger with the Iraq War but then struggled to use their control of both chambers of Congress to end it.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) wants his party to cut off funding for Trump's war and said Democrats can do so by demanding explicit restrictions on war spending as a condition of supporting the fiscal year 2027 government funding bill that expires next month.

"Right now, the continuing resolution goes through December 11," Van Hollen told The Lever on Tuesday. "And my view is that Democrats should not advance spending to continue to fund this war."

"The Vietnam War ended only when Congress defunded it," he added. "This is an illegal war, and we need to make sure that taxpayer monies are not used to continue an illegal war."

Institute for Middle East Understanding executive director Margaret DeReus pleaded on social media, "For the love of all that is good, Democrats, do not squander this."

"The voters have given you a mandate. Use it. Be the party of working people. Be the anti-war party. Be the anti-corruption party," she added. "We cannot go back to business as usual."

Matt Duss, a former top aide to US Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) who serves as executive vice president at the Center for International Policy, noted that "Trump ran and won as an anti-war candidate in 2024 because Democrats left that lane wide open for him."

"Voters have just brutally punished him and the GOP for breaking that promise. Will Democrats finally get it?" Duss added. "Americans are tired of war. They want a new foreign policy."

Nixon refused to back off her progressive platform after her primary win, continuing to campaign on Medicare for All, free childcare, paid family and sick leave, a national rent freeze and eviction moratorium, a universal jobs program, ending wars, getting big money out of politics, and taxing billionaires in a state written off by the Democratic Party throughout the 21st Century.

"I'm proud of the race we ran. We helped drive turnout and broke the supermajority in the state House and Senate. 2028 is around the corner. LFG!" Nixon said on social media late Tuesday. "We invested in grassroots organizers and partnered with candidates down ballot. I'm so proud of the work we did helping to flip 17 House seats. Many of whom were candidates we partnered with in the primary. Imagine what would have happened if we had more investment early on."

As people across the country took note of her close race—and some called out the national Democratic Party and its leadership for not pouring into the contest—Nixon added early Wednesday, "Invest in the South."

Jonathan Cohn, political director of the group Progressive Mass, said on social media that "Angie Nixon sadly didn't win, but for a race the national party did not invest in, she did damn well."

Amanda Litman, president of Run for Something, which recruits and supports young Democrats to seek elected office, said that she's "not sure there's a federal candidate in the country who worked as hard—with as little national help—as Angie Nixon. What a star."

Stressing that Florida, now Trump's home state, "is the absolute epicenter of MAGA," political commentator Kyle Kulinski highlighted that "a democratic socialist nearly pulled off one of the biggest upsets in political history. What a tremendous campaign from Angie Nixon."

WFP national director Maurice Mitchell said in a statement that "we are incredibly proud of Angie's campaign and our part in it. But there is no hiding our anger, because this race was winnable."

"In the face of outsized spending and racist attacks, Angie's people-centered campaign came within inches of defeating an incumbent senator," he emphasized. "The Democratic establishment failed to invest in Angie, because she wasn't their preferred candidate."

"The Working Families Party is proud to have been the first national organization to endorse Angie," he continued, "and we're committed to recruiting and running powerful leaders like her all across the South."

Some critics directly called out Senate Minority Chuck Schumer (D-NY), who's expected to lead the chamber again when Democrats officially reclaim their majority in January.

"Never forget that Angie Nixon lost by three points after being snubbed by Schumer and the Dem establishment for running on a progressive, DSA-backed platform this cycle," said Jack Petocz, senior director of programs and communications at Gen-Z for Change.

Although Schumer didn't bother with the race, Nixon was endorsed by national leftist leaders, including Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY), and Congressional Progressive Caucus Chair Emerita Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.).

As the results rolled in late Tuesday, Jeremy Slevin, Sanders' communications director and senior adviser, pointed out that "Bernie held four rallies for Angie Nixon, had four staffers on the ground, contributed $330,000 to support her directly, and raised another $266,000. She's currently within about 2 points. Imagine if the establishment hadn't written this race off."

Jayapal said late Tuesday that "even though Angie Nixon did not pull it out, she ran an incredibly competitive race, and drove up votes down ballot for other candidates. She was underestimated and overspent at every step, but she never stopped being who she was and running on bold, progressive values. Thank you, Angie!!"

At The American Prospect, Naomi Bethune and James Baratta noted that "Moody will have to run again for a full term in 2028. Given how close the matchup between Moody and Nixon ended up, the energetic progressive insurgent is expected to try again."

title: Arizona assistant AG asks judge to dismiss federal lawsuit over in-state tuition - KJZZ
description:

text:
Lawyers for the state are telling a federal judge it's none of the business of the Trump administration who gets reduced tuition at Arizona's public universities.

In new court filings, Assistant Attorney General Hayleigh Crawford acknowledges that Arizonans voted in 2022 to change the law for who qualifies for in-state tuition and is eligible for certain kinds of financial aid. And it allows the lower tuition for those who meet certain requirements, "regardless of residence and lawful immigration status."

That led to the Trump administration filing suit earlier this year claiming that the policy runs afoul of both a 1998 federal law and an executive order issued last year by President Donald Trump.

But Crawford told U.S. District Court Judge Murray Snow he should send the attorney from the Department of Justice packing.

"The government lacks standing," she wrote.

Crawford said the only people who can sue in federal court to overturn Arizona's law are those who can show an injury that "concrete and particularized, and actual or imminent." Yet the administration's lawsuit nowhere claims such an injury to the federal government.

"Instead, the government points to alleged economic harm suffered by Arizona universities," she said, a figure the Department of Justice put at $10.5 million for the last school year.

Aside from the fact that Crawford told Snow the amount of reduced tuition is wrong -- she does not say what it actually is — she said it's irrelevant.

"Any alleged economic harm from reduced tuition payments to state universities accrues to Arizona and its institutions, not the United States," Crawford said.

She also sniffed at the claim that the federal law was designed to ensure that those who are not citizens would not become "public charges." She said what voters approved are "state education policies intended to promote self-sufficiency through educational attainment and training."

And if those arguments don't work, Crawford has several others.

The issue of tuition for those who are not citizens traces its roots back to the Obama administration which created the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program in 2012. It allows people who arrived in this country illegally as children before 2007 — colloquially called "Dreamers'' — to remain and even to work if they meet certain conditions.

Based on that, the Maricopa community college system and, later, the Arizona Board of Regents agreed to let DACA recipients pay in-state tuition. But the Arizona Supreme Court ruled in 2018 that is precluded by Proposition 300, a 2006 ballot measure that denies various public benefits to those not in the country legally — including any form of subsidized tuition.

Proposition 308, approved in 2022 by a margin of 51.2% to 48.8%, was crafted to say that no longer applies to tuition and scholarships.

A 1998 federal law says someone who is not lawfully present in the United States can't get any postsecondary benefits based on residency in a state unless the same benefits are available to citizens of any other state.

But it was not until 2025 when Trump when Trump issued an executive order directing the Department of Justice to take action against any state that has practices that give benefits to aliens that are not available to all American citizens. That, the order says, includes "state laws that provide in-state higher education tuition to aliens but not to out-of-state American citizens."

There is no question but that Prop. 308, the 2022 ballot measure, allows certain individuals who have graduated from a high school in Arizona and meet other conditions to pay the same tuition available to state residents, regardless of immigration status. At the same time, U.S. citizens from another state can be required to pay the higher non-resident tuition.

More to the point, none of what is in Prop. 308 is linked to the student's legal status. In fact, one provision in that voter-approved law specifically says that "persons without lawful immigration status are eligible for in-state tuition."

The financial difference is significant.

At the University of Arizona, for example, in-state undergraduate tuition is $13,906 a year. That compares with the out-of-state cost of $43,068.

Crawford, in her new court filing, acknowledged that Congress has "broad, undoubted power" over immigration and the status of those who are not here legally.

"But the regulation of education remains a core state prerogative,'' she said. "Indeed, education is perhaps the most important function of state and local governments."

What the Trump administration is doing, Crawford said, is attempting to use immigration law "to curtail a state law that has no connection with immigration law."

"There is no conflict between Arizona's classification of who pays in-state tuition and any federal immigration classification," she told the judge.

Even if Snow doesn't accept all that, Crawford said there's another reason why the lawsuit against the state fails.

She says that Prop. 308, strictly speaking, isn't based on whether a person resides in Arizona. Instead, the law says in-state tuition requires meeting two conditions.

First is that the person attended any public or private high school or is home schooled "while physically present in this state for at least two years."

Second is having graduated while physically present.

"Those requirements do not mention a student's 'principal, actual dwelling place,'" Crawford said, the language used in the federal law that Arizona is accused of violating.

For example, Crawford said, a student who crossed into Arizona daily from another state would be a resident of that state but could qualify for in-state tuition by attending and graduating from an Arizona high school.

She also said someone from elsewhere who graduated from an Arizona boarding school could qualify to pay the lower-in state rate even though that person, strictly speaking, is a resident of the state where her parents lived.

And anyone who met the conditions but later moved to another state also could qualify, even after being gone for years.

Conversely, Crawford said someone whose family moves to Arizona in a final year of high school does not qualify. Ditto an Arizonan who attends and graduates from a boarding school or private school out of state.

She said rulings in favor of the Trump administration in Illinois, Texas and Nebraska are irrelevant because the wording of the laws in those states are different.

Snow has not said when he will consider the arguments.

name: Human Rights
title: Illegal immigrants didn't 'jump ahead' of any line. 'America First' means path to legal status
description:
The U.S. government fixes the number of immigrants it will admit each year.
But opportunities for people to come to America legally are limited, and those who are not selected have not suffered any injustice.
Every country has a sovereign right to select the immigrants it wishes to admit.
However America decides to punish or legalize those who have entered our country illegally, it owes no debt of justice or fairness to people it has chosen not to admit.
As for “dreamers,” 81% of people prefer a path to citizenship for immigrants brought to America illegally by their parents as children.
text:
A common argument for the current mass deportation policy tells us that those immigrants who have come to the United States illegally must be deported because they “jumped ahead of the line” and that it wouldn’t be fair to those would-be immigrants around the world who have waited for years or even decades to get a legal visa. The reasoning behind this claim needs further consideration. In fact, no line exists, and no fairness issue enters the picture.

The U.S. government fixes the number of immigrants it will admit each year. Our government offers many different types of visas, and the requirements vary. But opportunities for people to come to America legally are limited, and those who are not selected have not suffered any injustice. While the Universal Declaration of Human Rights recognizes that everyone has the right to emigrate, no one has the right to immigrate to any country they choose. Every country has a sovereign right to select the immigrants it wishes to admit. However America decides to punish or legalize those who have entered our country illegally, it owes no debt of justice or fairness to people it has chosen not to admit.

Recommended Stories

What to do with the millions who have immigrated outside the law remains a political question that Congress must resolve in dialogue with the public. The latest Gallup poll shows that 73% of people believe immigration is a good thing for our country. As for “dreamers,” 81% of people prefer a path to citizenship for immigrants brought to America illegally by their parents as children. A large majority, 75%, supports “allowing immigrants living in the United States illegally the chance to become citizens if they meet certain requirements over a period of time.” As for the mass deportation of illegal immigrants back to their home country, only 39% of people support the policy. Voters clearly prefer a legalization process for illegal immigrants.

title: Six Democrats Who Voted to Fund ICE Hold Off Republicans to Win - Newsweek
description:
Seven House Democrats voted for a Department of Homeland Security (DHS) appropriations bill on January 22.
Four of the seven Democrats again crossed party lines on March 5 to support a similar DHS funding measure.
The results underline divisions among Democrats over how to approach ICE funding and immigration enforcement.
Democrats could use control of the House to pass legislation seeking to restrict ICE funding when the new Congress takes office in January.
The House-passed January funding bill, meanwhile, did not become law in its original form.
text:
Six Democratic members of Congress who voted for a Department of Homeland Security (DHS) funding bill that included money for Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) were projected to retain their seats after facing Republican challengers in Tuesday's midterm elections.

It comes as Democrats prepare to take control of the House and Senate following the midterms, renewing the question of whether the party can use its majorities both chambers of Congress to restrict or repeal ICE funding.

The results came on a bruising night for President Donald Trump and Republicans, as a Democratic wave cost the party control of the House and Senate. The shift represents a major political setback for Trump, whose second-term agenda has faced growing scrutiny, particularly over his administration's aggressive immigration crackdown.

Read More on News

With Democrats now poised to control both chambers, the election could give the party renewed leverage to challenge the administration's immigration policies, scrutinize ICE operations and seek limits on the agency's funding. The results also drew fresh attention to the six Democrats who backed DHS funding that included money for ICE but still survived Republican challenges at the ballot box.

Don Davis of North Carolina led Republican Laurie Buckhout in the 1st Congressional District by 10,305 votes, according to unofficial results from the North Carolina State Board of Elections. With all 290 precincts reporting, Davis had 156,564 votes to 146,259 for Buckhout. Libertarian Tom Bailey received 9,880 votes.

Vicente Gonzalez held Texas' 34th District, defeating Republican Eric Flores. The latest AP-supplied results show Gonzalez with 112,667 votes, or 55.6 percent, to Flores' 80,572, or 39.8 percent, a margin of 32,095 votes, with about 99 percent of the vote counted.

Henry Cuellar won reelection in Texas' 28th Congressional District over Republican Tano Tijerina. The latest Texas Secretary of State figures reported Wednesday showed Cuellar with 113,315 votes, or 65.8 percent, to Tijerina's 51,065, or 29.6 percent, a margin of 62,250 votes.

Tom Suozzi secured another term in New York's 3rd Congressional District, defeating Republican Michael LiPetri. The latest figures sourced from the Associated Press (AP) showed Suozzi with 144,174 votes, or 55.1 percent, to LiPetri's 117,001, or 44.7 percent, a margin of 27,173 votes, with counting continuing.

Laura Gillen won reelection in New York's 4th Congressional District over Republican Jeanine Driscoll. AP-supplied results showed Gillen with 160,234 votes, or 56.1 percent, to Driscoll's 124,259, or 43.5 percent, a margin of 35,975 votes, with about 97 percent of the vote counted.

Marie Gluesenkamp Perez was called as the winner in Washington's 3rd Congressional District against Republican state Senator John Braun. AP-supplied results showed Gluesenkamp Perez with 143,417 votes, or 55 percent, to Braun's 115,271, or 44.2 percent, a margin of 28,146 votes.

Seven House Democrats voted for a Department of Homeland Security (DHS) appropriations bill on January 22. The measure passed 220-207, with seven Democrats joining 213 Republicans in voting in favor. A total of 206 Democrats voted against it, while Republican Thomas Massie of Kentucky was the only Republican to oppose the bill.

The bill included funding for ICE alongside appropriations for other federal agencies, including the Federal Emergency Management Agency, Coast Guard and Transportation Security Administration.

Jared Golden of Maine announced in November 2025 that he would not seek reelection. His 2nd Congressional District remained too close to call Wednesday afternoon, with Republican former Governor Paul LePage leading Democrat Matt Dunlap by 1,686 votes, 155,230 to 153,544, with roughly 87 percent of the vote counted.

Four of the seven Democrats again crossed party lines on March 5 to support a similar DHS funding measure. Gillen, Suozzi and Gonzalez voted against it.

The vote sparked backlash from progressives who argued that the measure did not do enough to constrain the Trump administration's immigration enforcement operations.

Several of the Democrats said at the time their votes were intended to protect funding for agencies such as FEMA and the Coast Guard rather than endorse ICE's enforcement tactics.

“Congress has an obligation to fund federal agencies that provide essential public services and resources to all Americans," Gonzalez said in a press release on January 22.

Davis defended his vote by pointing to the importance of disaster relief and Coast Guard funding in eastern North Carolina.

“Strong, reliable support for disaster relief is non-negotiable,” he said, adding that the region also depended on a well-resourced Coast Guard.

Gluesenkamp Perez said ICE would continue operating with existing funding even if DHS were shut down, while other agencies and local communities would bear the consequences. Gillen similarly cited funding for FEMA, the Transportation Security Administration and the Coast Guard, while calling for then Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem's impeachment.

Cuellar, the top Democrat on the House Appropriations Subcommittee on Homeland Security, defended his vote by arguing that the bill provided greater oversight of ICE while protecting funding for other agencies, including FEMA and the Coast Guard. In a speech on the House floor, he said the measure was “better than the alternatives of either funding the Department under a continuing resolution or shutting down the government.”

Golden defended the need to fund federal law enforcement, pointing to provisions for body cameras and de-escalation training. Suozzi later expressed regret, saying he had failed to recognize that the vote would be viewed as a referendum on ICE's conduct in Minneapolis, where two U.S. citizens were shot to death by federal authorities in January. He said he heard his constituents' anger and accepted responsibility.

The results underline divisions among Democrats over how to approach ICE funding and immigration enforcement. Some lawmakers have argued that funding DHS is necessary to maintain essential federal services, while progressives have pushed for tighter restrictions on ICE and greater accountability for immigration agents.

Can the Democrats Now Defund ICE?

Democrats could use control of the House to pass legislation seeking to restrict ICE funding when the new Congress takes office in January. But changing the agency's funding would be more complicated than simply refusing to approve another annual appropriations bill.

Congress has already approved substantial multi-year funding for immigration enforcement. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act, signed by President Trump on July 4, 2025, provided approximately $75 billion for ICE and $65 billion for Customs and Border Protection, which includes the U.S. Border Patrol. Both agencies have been on the front lines of President Trump's mass deportation campaign.

That money was separate from the annual DHS appropriations legislation the House considered in January.

A separate reconciliation law, the Secure America Act, was signed on June 10. It provided nearly $70 billion in additional funding for ICE, Customs and Border Protection and DHS, available through September 30, 2029. The law means significant funding has already been appropriated and remains available beyond the current fiscal year.

To claw back or restrict that money, Democrats would need Congress to pass legislation rescinding previously appropriated funds or limiting how they can be used.

Under the normal process, legislation could pass the House with a simple majority, generally 218 votes when all seats are filled. In the Senate, however, most legislation would require 60 votes to overcome a filibuster. Any measure would also require the president's signature or enough support in Congress to override a veto.

Budget reconciliation offers another potential route because qualifying legislation can pass the Senate with a simple majority and is not subject to the usual 60-vote threshold. But reconciliation is governed by strict budgetary rules and cannot automatically be used to enact any policy change a congressional majority wants.

The House-passed January funding bill, meanwhile, did not become law in its original form. The Senate removed annual appropriations for ICE and the U.S. Border Patrol from the revised legislation that Trump signed on April 30.

However, the agencies retained access to substantial funding Congress had previously approved.

That leaves Democrats with a significant legislative and procedural challenge even with control of both chambers. Blocking future annual appropriations could restrict new funding for ICE, but it would not, by itself, eliminate money Congress has already made available to the agency.
