end of list

But Democrats won’t take control of Congress until January. Even then, there’s only so much they’ll be able to do without Republican cooperation.

Most bills need 60 votes to get past a filibuster in the Senate, and even if Democrats manage that, Trump can still veto their legislation. He has already threatened to do just that, telling a podcast on Monday, “I’ll veto everything.”

But the Democrats now also have other tools at their disposal, including power over Senate confirmations and control over committees that can launch investigations.

So what can Democrats realistically accomplish over the next two years, and where might they struggle to make good on their promises?

Can Democrats bring down the cost of living?

Affordability was one of the biggest issues for voters heading into Tuesday’s midterm elections, and Democrats seized on that, promising to bring down the costs of energy, housing, healthcare and groceries.

Dean Baker, an economist and cofounder of the Center for Economic and Policy Research, a US-based think tank, said one of the most effective things Democrats can do to bring down costs is push for an end to the war on Iran.

Since February, the conflict has driven up energy prices, as Iran has restricted commercial traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway for the oil and gas trade.

Baker argued that Democrats could use congressional investigations and oversight to pressure the Trump administration to end the war, potentially helping to give consumers relief.

Foreign policy is an area where some Republicans could find common cause with Democrats, said Baker.

Another area, he added, might be healthcare, an issue that similarly hits voters in the pocketbook.

The expiration of enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies in 2025 has left many Americans facing higher insurance premiums.

With their new congressional majorities, Democrats could push to restore those subsidies and reverse cuts to Medicaid, the government healthcare programme for low-income Americans.

A possible path to accomplishing that goal would be to include those measures in government spending bills that Congress needs to pass, according to Baker. That would also make them harder for Trump to reject.

“Republicans living in a post-Trump world, I don’t think they want to be on the side of preventing people from getting healthcare or basically paying more for healthcare,” Baker said. “They can make the politics such that he doesn’t want to veto it.”

Trump’s tariff campaign is another factor driving up consumer costs. But Baker warned that they could be tougher to reverse, without substantial support from Republicans to override a Trump veto. Even if they do manage that, prices could take a while to actually drop.

“Prices are like rockets and feathers. They shoot up like rockets; they come down like feathers,” said Alex Jacquez, chief of policy and advocacy at Groundwork Collaborative, a progressive economic think tank.

Jacquez, however, pointed to another path Democrats could take that wouldn’t need Trump’s approval.

With majorities in Congress, Democrats could wield congressional committees to investigate companies that have been raising the prices of everything from groceries to electricity bills.

“There’s a lot of precedent for getting some real material outcomes just through having the gavels and being able to subpoena CEOs and haul people in front of Congress,” Jacquez told Al Jazeera.

While there’s no guarantee these investigations would bring down prices, they could put pressure on companies to explain or adjust their decisions.

Could a Democratic Congress hold Trump accountable?

Laura Blessing, a senior fellow at Georgetown University’s Government Affairs Institute, expects Democrats to make extensive use of their new investigative powers.

“In terms of time spent and newspaper ink spilled, this is where you’re going to see the most action from Dems, by a mile,” she told Al Jazeera in an email.

Congressional investigations do not require White House approval. But they could make life harder for Trump by scrutinising his actions both within and outside of government.

Many Democrats have signalled they plan to investigate the source of the Trump family’s wealth as part of January’s incoming Congress.

Trump’s personal wealth has soared by about $2.2bn since the start of his term, according to financial disclosure forms released earlier this year.

His family’s business empire has likewise expanded over the last two years into everything from cryptocurrency and drones to artificial intelligence and prediction markets — industries his government has favoured in its policies.

Democratic senators have already been laying the groundwork for potential investigations, sending letters to companies and government departments demanding that they preserve records.

Among the issues they could examine are whether donors to Trump’s White House ballroom received favourable treatment from the government, and whether the Justice Department targeted his political opponents.

There is no guarantee, however, that everyone will cooperate.

Trump administration officials could challenge subpoenas in court, delaying investigations. But while Blessing doesn’t expect “Trump’s nuclear family to show up to a subpoena”, she said Democrats could still question government employees and others connected to Trump’s inner circle.

Even if they uncover wrongdoing, however, there is no guarantee of legal consequences, since it’s Trump’s own Justice Department that would have to decide whether to take up the cases.

Impeachment is another possibility. Lawmakers have already introduced articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth for multiple reasons, including allegations that he waged war against Iran without seeking congressional approval first.

Republican Representative Thomas Massie has said he will try to force a House vote on Hegseth’s impeachment when the outgoing Congress returns to session next week.

Trump, who was impeached twice during his first term, however, dismissed the prospect of facing a third impeachment himself, telling reporters on Wednesday that he was “not even a little bit” worried.

“I think it would destroy the Democratic Party if they did that, because it would be impeachment for no reason,” he said.

Trump also defended Hegseth, saying he was doing “a very good job”.

Even if the House of Representatives votes to impeach a government official, the case must still be weighed in a Senate trial.

Removing an elected official would require a two-thirds vote in the Senate, meaning many Republicans would need to get on board to oust a figure like Trump or Hegseth. No president in US history has ever been removed from office as a result of an impeachment proceeding.

Could Democrats end the war on Iran?

With less than two months until the 120th Congress is sworn in, experts anticipate Trump will use his final weeks with the outgoing Republican majorities to push through any remaining legislative priorities.

It also leaves Trump a critical window in which to escalate the war on Iran, according to Trita Parsi, the executive vice president of the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, a foreign policy think tank.

“He has shown a pattern in which, in the face of humiliation and defeat, he becomes more reckless,” Parsi told Al Jazeera.

Democrats could pursue a binding resolution to wind down the war. After all, the US Constitution assigns Congress the sole authority to declare war, and laws like the War Powers Act of 1973 give lawmakers a path to ending unauthorised conflicts past the 60-day mark.

But there is no guarantee that those efforts would work, given the possibility of Trump vetoing their proposed measures.

Experts, however, say there is another way that Democrats could rein in Trump’s war powers. One of their most powerful tools will be control over government spending.

The Trump administration can continue using money already allocated for military operations, but Democrats could try to block additional funding for the war.

“It creates a limitation for how long he can pursue the war,” Parsi said. “If he needs more funding for it, we’re not talking about small sums that he can just reallocate from other places easily.”

With control of congressional committees, Democrats could also investigate the administration’s conduct during the war, including whether its military operations complied with US law.

“Rigorous oversight would not restrict military operations by itself but could raise the political costs of the war beyond what the president or other key officials are willing to endure,” said David Janovsky, a policy analyst at the Project on Government Oversight.

How much political will Democrats have to end the conflict, however, is an open question.

Blessing, the government affairs fellow, noted that the party has historically been reluctant to withhold military funding out of fear of being accused of undermining US troops.

But Parsi warned that failing to act would be politically unsustainable — and could be seen by the party’s base as a tacit endorsement of US military involvement in the Middle East.

“It will no longer be just Trump’s war,” Parsi said. “They will also co-own it, because they will be complicit, because they have the ability to stop it.”

Could Democrats rein in Trump’s immigration crackdown?

Another target for the incoming Democrat-led Congress could be Trump’s hardline immigration crackdown.

His pledge to oversee the largest mass deportation in US history has sparked widespread public backlash. A public opinion poll earlier this year found that 65 percent of Americans believe Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has “gone too far” in its efforts.

With control of both chambers of Congress, Democrats could launch investigations into ICE and other agencies involved in the crackdown.

Their probes could seek information about conditions inside detention centres, allegations of abuse and how taxpayer dollars are being used for immigration enforcement, said Heidi Altman, the vice president of policy at the National Immigration Law Center.

Altman argues Congress could also claw back the roughly $240bn already given to the Trump administration for immigration enforcement over the past two years.

That amount of money, she explained, has allowed ICE to operate with few constraints, without having to prioritise which communities to go into or who to detain.

“The only way to force a slowdown and actual sort of decision-making and prioritisation and enforcement is to dramatically curtail their budget by taking back the funding from the last session,” she said.

Doing so would require passing legislation that Trump could eventually veto. But Altman argued that Democrats should push ahead anyway.

“The worst possible thing we could do is throw up our hands and say we have limited power,” she said.

“Pass the bills, see what happens, put them on the president’s desk, and dare him to look at the American people and say he’s not signing something that they overwhelmingly demanded.”

text:
Colorado voters Tuesday rejected a ballot measure that would have amended the state constitution to force police and prosecutors to work more closely with federal immigration agents.

The Associated Press called the race against Amendment 81 at 1:20 p.m. on Wednesday, when 45% of the votes tallied were in favor of the amendment and 55% were opposed. The initiative needed the support of at least 55% of voters to pass since it adds language to the state constitution.

Amendment 81 would have changed Colorado’s constitution to require police officers, sheriff’s deputies and prosecutors to alert the U.S. Department of Homeland Security if they formally charge someone whose immigration status is in question under certain circumstances — if that person has a prior felony conviction or if the charge is for an alleged violent crime, like murder, first-degree assault, kidnapping or aggravated robbery.

The Department of Homeland Security houses the nation’s federal immigration agencies, including U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Customs and Border Protection.

The constitutional amendment would have overridden recent laws passed by Colorado lawmakers to limit cooperation between ICE and local law enforcement. Those laws, including one that makes it illegal for state and local government agencies and their employees to share personal information with ICE unless ordered by a judge, will remain intact.

Advance Colorado, a conservative political nonprofit that doesn’t disclose its donors, filed the initiative. Another conservative political nonprofit that doesn’t disclose its donors, A Common Sense America, spent hundreds of thousands of dollars to collect voter signatures to get the measure on the November ballot.

Brighter Colorado, an issue committee that backed several conservative ballot measures this year, including Amendment 81, raised about $6.1 million, most of it from conservative political nonprofits that don’t disclose their donors.

Colorado Communities First was the main issue committee that battled Amendment 81. It raised about $560,000 during the election cycle.

The group’s major donors included the Colorado Immigrant Rights Coalition, the ACLU of Colorado and the Rose Community Foundation.

Registered agent for Colorado Communities First Henry Sandman celebrated Amendment 81’s defeat.

“Colorado voters have made it clear, ICE overreach has no place in our state,” he said in a statement. “By rejecting this ballot measure, Coloradans have prevented ICE from getting more power in our state and have helped to ensure that ICE’s lawlessness does not get enshrined into our state constitution.”

Vote Common Sense, another issue committee, fought Amendment 81 and other conservative ballot measures this year. It raised about $1.1 million, much of it from the Green Advocacy Project; Denver philanthropist Merle Chambers; and the Colorado Fund for Children and Public Education, which is tied to the state’s largest teachers union.

Colorado Sun staff writer Jesse Paul contributed to this report.

text:
Orders for what one official called a “national no enforcement day” began circulating on Monday inside U.S. Immigrations and Customs Enforcement.

Handed down through ICE’s Enforcement and Removal Operations division through internal group chats and verbal commands, the directive called for a halt to all immigration enforcement operations on Election Day, according to ICE officials across the country who spoke to The Intercept.

“We were told all operations are canceled for Election Day,” said one ICE immigration official, who operates in the south and requested anonymity to protect their livelihood. “Word of mouth from our first-line supervisors, no official email notice.”

According to multiple ICE officials who spoke to The Intercept, the orders were handed down quietly to avoid media attention.

“Yesterday was the least amount of activity observed from ICE ERO throughout the entire year so far,” said Sherman Austin, the creator of StopICE.net, a crowdsourced platform tracking reported ICE activity across the United States. “You can kind of tell like from the morning. Usually, ICE gets started really early, and there’s a huge spike in activity between 5 a.m. and 10 a.m. That spike wasn’t there on Election Day.”

Another ICE official, who works in the Great Lakes region, confirmed the orders ahead of Election Day, referring to it as “National No Enforcement Day.”

“We were told to do ‘admin’ shit,” the official said. They said that ICE deportation officers who regularly do street-level operations were diverted to administrative office work: “I’ll be drinking coffee at the office for the first time in a year.”

In total, ICE officials working in four areas of responsibility — ICE’s jurisdictional regions — coving parts of the northeastern, midwestern, northern, and south-central U.S. regions told The Intercept that they had received orders to stand down on Election Day.

“Something Unusual Was Going On”

StopICE, the tracking website, which has roughly half a million subscribers, did record some ICE activity on Election Day, according to Austin, although most of the reports stemmed from sightings unrelated to any immigration enforcement activities.

“There were a few reports that came in about ICE being at usual spots like the jails,” Austin said, “or seen driving in certain areas in in the city, but it wasn’t the same type of activity that’s usually seen on the site. It was pretty clear that something unusual was going on.”

AntiFreeze, another crowdsourced ICE-tracking platform that allows users to report and receive real-time alerts about ICE raids, also saw abnormally low levels of ICE activity on November 3, according to Josh, the creator and developer behind the site, who requested to keep his last name anonymous.

“On Election Day, our network only logged about 56 reported ICE sightings nationwide, which is one of the quietest Tuesdays we’ve ever seen,” Josh said. “We did get about three sightings that did report ICE activity near polling stations, but most of the reports were observations of vehicles associated with ICE. We barely got any reports about actual ICE arrests yesterday.”

Local activists also observed a low level of ICE activity on the street level.

“There was no evidence of street abductions,” said an activist working with the rapid-response network in Minnesota’s Twin Cities.

“ICE, in some capacity, was still out and about, but we did not see any reports of off-the-street detainments by ICE or attempts at detainments,” said the activist, who said they got word of ICE arrests at jails, but not targeted operations among the general public. “There were a lot of folks, probably more than usual, observing, and so I think we can be pretty confident that this wasn’t due to lack of observation.”

Leo Martinez, who volunteers with VC Defensa in Southern California, told The Intercept that no one in his rapid-response group reported any sightings of ICE activity on Tuesday.

It is still unclear exactly where the orders to halt immigration enforcement operations on Election Day originated from, although some ICE officials believe the orders stemmed from ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations leadership — and not directly from the White House.

“Nobody from the SDDO level” — a reference to Supervisory Detention and Deportation Officer, part of ICE’s upper management — “expected it to happen until the very last moment,” said another ICE official familiar with the matter. “But I think some of us caught on that senior leadership was making this call with fears of us being at the polls.”

The official said, “It’s crazy that The White House didn’t catch on.”

Attorney General Dan Rayfield won a court order today protecting federal money that helps at-risk youth turn their lives around. A federal judge ruled the Trump Administration broke the law when it tried to force states to help with immigration enforcement in order to get grant funding. The judge threw out the immigration requirements and permanently blocked the federal government from using them as a condition for the funding.

“Youth intervention programs can make all the difference in a kid’s life, giving them skills and tools to create a bright future for themselves,” said Attorney General Rayfield. “Congress set this funding aside to help kids, not as leverage to advance a partisan, anti-immigrant agenda.”

In Oregon, the grant funding goes to Youth Development Oregon, a division of the Oregon Department of Education. This year, the program is expected to receive $667,119, paying for programs that keep young people from getting into trouble in the first place, improve youth probation, and support kids in the justice system and their families. Today’s ruling clears the way for Oregon to receive this year’s funding.

This is the latest example of states pushing back against the federal government’s attempts to attach illegal conditions on critical funding. Last year, the Trump administration told states they couldn’t get funds for crime victims unless they agreed to its immigration demands. A group of states pushed back, and the federal government dropped those requirements on more than $1.3 billion in crime victim funding.

In today’s case, AG Rayfield and 22 other attorneys general argued the Trump Administration can’t add strings that Congress never approved and can’t use federal money to coerce states into doing its work.

Alongside Attorney General Rayfield in filing this lawsuit were the attorneys general of California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia, Washington, Wisconsin, and the District of Columbia, as well as the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania.

Huntington Beach (KABC) -- In a two-word statement released late Tuesday after the Democrats were projected to take control of the House, Rep. Robert Garcia, the presumptive chairman of the House Oversight Committee, stated: "Lawyer up."

On Wednesday, he expanded on that terse statement during a news conference in Huntington Beach, which is part of the district he'll represent in the next Congress.

"We should be very clear that the American people have spoken loudly and clearly - they want change," Garcia told reporters. "They are tired of the destruction and the corruption of Donald Trump and this administration."

Garcia pointed to Democrats' electoral victories nationwide as a mandate. He said the Oversight Committee will be focused on four areas.

"The first is: We're going to take on the Trump crime family," Garcia said. "The amount of grift and corruption is unprecedented in American politics."

Garcia is expected to seek to interview Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner along with other Trump family members about their alleged business dealings.

"Our second investigation is focused on DHS and the abuses of ICE," the congressman said, referring to the Department of Homeland Security and Immigration and Customs Enforcement. "What we see on the streets -- across the country, but I want to talk about California - whether it's been here in Orange County, in Long Beach, in Los Angeles.

"When people are being kidnapped and detained, thrown to the ground, arms broken, people snatched up on their way to immigration appointments that we the government gave them - that's inhumane, it's wrong, and I think the American public - regardless of party - are sick of it.

Garcia said he plans to investigate corporate donors to the White House ballroom, no-bid contracts like the Reflecting Pool contractor and companies he has said are "ripping off" the American public.

"While you're struggling, CEOs and companies across this country are making record profits," he said. "They're putting in systems of surveillance pricing, so that when you go to the supermarket, you might be paying a different price than you're neighbor."

As it relates to the Epstein investigation, Garcia said that he wants to hold public hearings, which would replace the interviews that occurred behind closed doors when Republicans were in control.

Garcia, whose congressional district includes parts of Long Beach, Huntington Beach, Costa Mesa, Santa Ana, Seal Beach and Newport Beach, said he is "proud to represent all of Orange County."

text:
A federal judge in Colorado launched an inquiry on Wednesday into U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s repeated violations of court orders, telling ICE and the government’s lawyers that their conduct amounted to contempt.

Before a packed courtroom of observers, U.S. District Court Judge Charlotte N. Sweeney said she would not tolerate ICE’s practice of releasing people from immigration custody in response to judges’ orders, only to immediately arrest them again.

Recommended Stories

▶

“It appears to me we have a problem of monumental importance,” she said, addressing the government and a man who ICE immediately re-detained last week. “We are now in a situation where this court’s order, and the orders of other judges of this court, are frankly being made a mockery of. And that cannot be. This gentleman was ordered released, period. There was no take-him-out-to-the hallway-and-let’s-do-this-process-again.”

Sweeney, a Joe Biden appointee, added that, to her knowledge, ICE had released and immediately rearrested 10 people in a week despite judges’ orders.

“You are usurping this court’s very scarce judicial resources,” she said. “We are handling thousands of these cases. And I assure you, we are not going to handle them twice when we’ve got a binding court order in place. This appears to be some weird game of hide-and-seek. This will stop.”

Sweeney set a follow-up hearing for Monday, ordering ICE’s Denver field office director, Nathan Rasper, to appear and speak to the agency’s conduct.

For more than a year, Colorado’s federal trial court has faced a flood of “habeas corpus” petitions from those in immigration detention, pushing court filings to unprecedented levels. The most common allegation is that the government is improperly denying bond hearings to people who are eligible by law to be released while their immigration proceedings unfold. The Denver-based federal appeals court recently handed down a binding interpretation of the law confirming the government’s interpretation of its authority is incorrect.

In the case at hand, Ramon Quintero Alvarez of Wyoming filed a habeas petition seeking release from Aurora’s privately operated detention center. The court assigned Alvarez’s case to Sweeney on Oct. 20, and she gave the government seven days to respond. If the government did not honor the deadline, she ordered Alvarez’s release within 24 hours.

The government did not respond. Instead, on Nov. 3, Assistant U.S. Attorney Andrew Soler told Sweeney that Alvarez was released, immediately re-detained, and remained detained.

The government “will not be submitting a brief that argues that the current detention is lawful. Because habeas relief has been effectuated,” Soler wrote, “Respondents respectfully submit that the Court should close this case.”

Sweeney immediately scheduled a hearing for the next day, ordering ICE to be present and ensure that Alvarez would also attend.

“I like to refer to this courtroom not as my courtroom, but as the courtroom of the people of Colorado. Today, I feel that statement rings particularly true because I am here to effectuate the rights of the people in Colorado,” Sweeney said at the outset, addressing Alvarez, who sat by himself without an attorney. “And I have some concerns with what has occurred in that past week with respect to you.”

Sweeney first grilled Soler about his filing. Soler responded that he was on duty last week at the U.S. Attorney’s Office and received around 100 habeas cases.

“Of those cases, there’s an understanding of ones we will or will not have the ability to respond to. This is one of the ones we will not have the ability to respond to,” he said. “We would inform ICE of the duty to release within the 24-hour response deadline.”

Soler continued that he informed ICE on Oct. 26 that it needed to release Alvarez by Oct. 28. Afterward, he learned ICE had released and re-detained Alvarez on the spot.

“If you’re not defending that, and there is no lawful basis to detain him, that by definition means his current detainment is unlawful. Are you following?” Sweeney asked.

Yes, said Soler.

Sweeney asked “how many of these” re-detention cases there are, considering Alvarez’s was at least the tenth in a week. Soler did not know. Sweeney then questioned whether the U.S. Attorney’s Office planned to “simply come into this court and indicate to me that their client is acting in defiance of this court’s order and unlawfully, and there is nothing going to be done about it.”

She added that ICE’s conduct was “contempt of my court order.”

Sweeney then heard testimony from Nichole Black, the assistant field office director for ICE.

“I received a direct order,” Black said, “to re-detain habeas releases that had some kind of criminality.”

In Alvarez’s case, she said ICE re-detained him outside the public lobby of the Aurora facility. The directive came from Deputy Field Office Director George Valdez, who in turn received the order from Rasper, the director.

In response to Sweeney’s questions, Black said she understood “at the time” that Alvarez had a domestic battery conviction and an arrest for domestic violence.

“And do you believe that as you sit here today?” Sweeney asked.

“I was told that charges were not filed,” said Black.

Sweeney asked if Black had concerns that she would be violating the order by re-detaining Alvarez. Black said no, and that she believed ICE was empowered to immediately re-detain someone under the circumstances.

“Do you still maintain that belief?” asked Sweeney.

After a long pause, Black said yes.

Alvarez also testified that, on Oct. 27, an ICE officer he knew “fist-bumped me and said I was being released.” Employees took Alvarez and other detainees to the Centennial office. Once there, he overheard a phone conversation where someone said “bring them back” to Aurora.

The officers “just didn’t know what’s going on,” he said.

Sweeney told Black that ICE’s re-detention protocol was a violation of her order.

“Frankly, I am unclear how anyone can argue with a straight face that what you believed was appropriate and could lawfully occur,” Sweeney said. “Releasing somebody momentarily is not releasing somebody at all.”

She also told Soler and Kevin Traskos, the head of the U.S. Attorney’s Office’s civil division who was also present, that they were “walking a very fine line” that is “bordering on unprofessional conduct.”

Sweeney ordered Alvarez’s release by 2 p.m. She set a hearing for Monday morning with the field office director and ordered the government to give her a list of all people in Colorado who were re-detained immediately after being released pursuant to court orders.

“A habeas petition is one of the most important tools people in this country have to fight unlawful detainment. It will not be allowed to be stepped on and abused in the way that it is currently being used,” she concluded.

text:
After seeing a University Christian Ministry post online about protests at the Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility in Broadview, Illinois, Weinberg senior Chandler Vargas said he decided to join the organization.

“With everything that’s been happening in the country, ICE included, it’s been very easy to feel sort of helpless to be frank,” Vargas said. “So finding an organization where I can find community with like-minded people and find a connection with God of course, has really been instrumental for me in terms of caring forward during these trying times.”

Since Operation Midway Blitz, a federal immigration crackdown targeting undocumented immigrants across the Chicago area, began in September 2025, student groups like UCM have supported the Northwestern community by hosting Know Your Rights trainings and speaker events.

UCM, for instance, sponsored a training in October for volunteers accompanying undocumented immigrants to hearings.

While Vargas said he is “a bit scared,” he said it was important for him to volunteer as a U.S. citizen and the son of immigrants. He added that people need to have compassion for those going through the immigration system, especially because that system is “more convoluted than it’s ever been before.”

“So, I feel like as a citizen, I have the privilege to put myself in the situation, even though it might potentially be dangerous,” Vargas said. “The worst thing that could ever happen to me is nowhere near as bad as what could happen to the person who’s undocumented.”

Purple Sanctuary, a group of NU students, grad workers, faculty and staff focused on protecting campus from ICE, was created to call on NU to take action against federal immigration enforcement, according to eighth-year physics and astronomy doctoral candidate Jorin Graham.

“Purple Sanctuary formed because we believe that Northwestern should be a place where people can study and research and teach and work and feel safe doing so,” Graham said. “And so far, Northwestern, we feel, has really failed to uphold their responsibilities in this regard.”

Graham said Purple Sanctuary’s current focus is publicizing a petition that urges NU to institute policies that provide “meaningful protections” on campus and recognize the “harm and anxiety immigration agents have caused” on campus and within the surrounding community.

In a statement to The Daily, a University spokesperson wrote that NU “closely monitors federal immigration developments and provides updates to the community as necessary,” while encouraging “members of our community to familiarize themselves with the published guidance for what to do if approached by a federal officer.”

The spokesperson wrote that the Office of International Student and Scholar Services provides regular updates and links to resources for members of the international community.

Purple Sanctuary hosted an event in October comparing NU’s response to ICE activity with institutions in the Chicago area and other private, highly-ranked universities, Graham said. They added that, unlike NU, peer institutions had policies outlining areas where ICE agents could legally enter or trainings for students to understand their rights.

The event and UCM’s volunteer training were both part of NU Disorientation Week, which aimed to highlight students to the work of activist and organizing groups on campus, Medill junior Kylie Chen said.

“Part of the importance of coalition building and solidarity is that we all, at the end of the day, share the same values,” she said. “We’re all, at the end of the day, kind of fighting against the same entity, which for us in the immediate sense is Northwestern and the administration, and trying to get them to change so that our community can be better for everyone, safer for everyone.”

Some of Purple Sanctuary’s most important work is “talking to our neighbors, talking to other groups that are working on these issues,” Graham said.

SESP senior Alaina Parr, a member of Students Organizing for Labor Rights, a group of undergraduate and graduate students in solidarity with campus workers, said the group is open to coalition building to organize against ICE and protect community members. SOLR will mobilize its membership to support other organizations that are hosting events and taking other anti-ICE actions, she added.

SOLR “didn’t want to reinvent the wheel” since there were other organizations working on this issue, but the group still wanted to help, Parr said.

“We wanted to find how we could close the resource gap between workers that may not be able to access current resources for whatever reason, and also try to see what we can do to hold Northwestern itself accountable for the fact that it was not giving any clear guidelines or any actual commitment to protecting its immigrant community,” she said.

Closing the gap included distributing whistles and Know Your Rights resources to campus workers around Halloween last year, Parr said. SOLR also created a workers’ Know Your Rights guide in partnership with the James B. Moran Center for Youth Advocacy and hosted a Know Your Rights training with the Moran Center and Illinois Workers in Action in April, she added.

Even though Operation Midway Blitz has “quieted down,” the recent detention of an NU alum and presence of immigration agents in and around Evanston indicates that ICE remains a “threat to our community,” Graham said.

“When institutions like Northwestern fail to step up to protect us, or when people feel like there’s danger in their communities, people have to have others, neighbors, colleagues, friends, classmates they can turn to when they need help,” Graham said. “That can only happen if we have relationships already built, relationships that are built on trust, relationships that are built on safety, where information can be shared and people can go to seek help.”

text:
(Washington, DC) – The newly elected US Congress should prioritize respect and protection for human rights both within the United States and around the world, Human Rights Watch said today. Voters elected a majority of Democrats to control both the House and the Senate in the November 3, 2026 midterm elections.

“This newly elected Congress will convene at a critical moment for human rights domestically and globally,” said Michael García Bochenek, interim US program director at Human Rights Watch. “Lawmakers should challenge the Trump administration’s many abuses, embrace the oversight authority provided to Congress, and act decisively to respect, protect, and fulfill human rights.”

Lawmakers should address the widespread abuses in immigration enforcement by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and its agencies, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Patrol (CBP), which have resulted in arbitrary detention, serious injuries, and unlawful killings. The new Congress should reconstitute and strengthen transparency and oversight mechanisms, put in place meaningful protections against excessive force, and pursue accountability for officials and enforcement agents responsible for the many serious human rights violations of the last two years.

The incoming chair of the House of Representatives oversight committee, Rep. Robert Garcia, has said that his focus will include “DHS and ICE abuses,” warning responsible officials to “lawyer up.”

“The incoming Congress should prioritize rigorous oversight over the Department of Homeland Security, the Department of Justice, and the Department of Defense,” Bochenek said. “Congress should restore gutted oversight bodies to full force. Without comprehensive oversight and accountability, abusive practices will most likely continue with impunity.”

The new Congress should also mandate actions to repair and provide a remedy for harm and abuses committed by the Trump administration in its second term, Human Rights Watch said. These harms should include discrimination in voting, policing, discrimination, education, and housing.

To begin rebuilding the federal civil rights infrastructure necessary to tackle discrimination, which has been dismantled, Congress needs to conduct oversight hearings on the collapse of enforcement capacity at the Department of Justice, the Department of Education, the Department of Housing and Urban Development, and the Equal Opportunity Employment Commission. It should provide appropriations for these agencies that are explicitly directed to civil rights enforcement and pass legislation to allow private individuals to file suit under the Civil Rights Act to address disparate impact claims of harm that government actions have caused them.

Congress has failed to implement adequate safeguards or oversight of the Trump administration, including as the administration has committed serious violations of the laws of war in Iran and continued unlawful lethal strikes on boats in the Pacific and Caribbean that have resulted in over 240 extrajudicial killings. Congress also oversaw the gutting of US foreign assistance and approved a bill allowing the government to claw back approximately $9 billion of previously approved aid, including critical support for human rights. The new Congress should look at opportunities to restore foreign assistance funding, particularly for human rights programs, in future appropriations processes.

The new Congress should also demand that the Department of Defense release its report on an unlawful strike on a primary school in Minab in southern Iran that killed over 150 people, most of them children, and analyze whether dismantled civilian harm mitigation structures contributed to other unlawful strikes, Human Rights Watch said.

The Trump administration has also removed tens of thousands of third-country nationals to other countries where they have faced human rights violations and a risk of onward return to countries where they are at risk of persecution. It sent Venezuelan nationals to El Salvador’s CECOT prison, where they were tortured systematically and subjected to other abuses, including sexual violence. The new Congress should reassert scrutiny over foreign policy and security cooperation, Human Rights Watch said.

“Incoming members of Congress should strengthen the institution’s commitment to protect human rights for every person in the United States,” Bochenek said. “Congress should also embrace the guidance these protections offer for a rights-respecting foreign policy.”

Federal officials and employees who violate the FRA (Federal Records Act) are subject to criminal penalties.

“The Committee intends to closely observe the compliance of the Department—and all its components—with these preservation requirements. The Committee expects to receive by November 11, 2026, assurances, in writing, that Departmental records, documents, data, and information have not been and will not be destroyed, modified, removed, transferred, or otherwise rendered inaccessible,” wrote Ranking Member Thompson.

“The Department’s repeated refusal to cooperate with the Committee’s oversight requests—which are essential to effectuating the separation of powers established by the U.S. Constitution—stands in direct contravention of the legal obligations of the Department. In the 120th Congress, the Committee intends to address the Trump administration’s assault on the rule of law and hold those responsible accountable.”

text:
A Scripps News viewer from the Detroit area texted this question to us when it became clear Democrats would control both the U.S. House and Senate next year:

“What accountability measures will be put in place to ensure ICE agents who abuse their authority/violate constitutional rights are investigated and prosecuted?”

While affordability and the economy propelled Democrats to victory, candidates also campaigned on a promise of being a check on ICE.

“We have masked men in unmarked vehicles kidnapping people off our street,” said James Talarico, hours after becoming the first Texas Democrat to win a Senate seat since 1988. “We have to take action.”

RELATED STORY | DNC chair says Democrats must deliver on promises after midterm wins

Even with full control of Congress next year, Democrats will find their power to restrain ICE will have its limits.

Congress sets ICE spending levels and could withhold future funding, but under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Republicans approved major funding increases for the agency that will keep it with flush with money through the rest of President Trump’s term. Any attempt to claw back dollars would almost certainly meet a presidential veto.

Democrats' most powerful tool is likely to be their authority to direct investigations as the majority party in power. After their victory on election night, Democrats quickly made clear they planned to launch inquiries related to DHS and ICE.

“LAWYER UP,” posted the likely incoming chairman of the House Oversight Committee.

When former homeland security secretary Kristi Noem wrote on social media, "...we were too successful the first year of the trump administration,” the Democrat on deck to lead the Senate Homeland Security Committee fired back, “Want to say that under oath?” cc’ing Noem senior adviser Corey Lewandowski.

For more than a year, the Scripps News ICE Inc. investigation has exposed DHS awarding lucrative immigration contracts to corporations, sometimes without opening up a standard competitive bidding process. The government deals have led to record revenues at for-profit companies, including owners of private immigration detention centers.

The GEO Group, owner of the most ICE lockups, poured more than $7 million into the election in an effort to keep Republicans in office.

Democrats ended up winning, and with subpoena power, could get to the bottom of who is behind some of the more obscure companies given taxpayer-funded contracts. That includes a deal worth more than $1 billion for Acqusition Logistics LLC, run out of a suburban house, to stand up the Camp East Montana detention center in Texas last year. Three detainees have died there, including one whose death was ruled a homicide.

ELECTION RESULTS | Key races for Senate, House and governor

DHS on Wednesday accused Democrats of being more interested in “political shenanigans” than governing.

“Rest assured, however, that we are well prepared to deal with this nonsense so Secretary (Markwayne) Mullin can continue focusing on protecting the homeland,” said James Percival, DHS general counsel.

The White House will also be able to slow-walk investigations, attempt to defy congressional subpoenas and claim executive privilege, tactics used by presidents in the past to stall congressional inquiries.

text:
The midterm losses could delay, but not prevent, another Iran escalation

Trump’s policies toward the Middle East undoubtedly contributed to Republicans’ midterm defeats, and he appears to recognize that. Trump has already publicly acknowledged that his war with Iran contributed to his loss. Moreover, his surprising announcement early on Election Day that he would end US financial support to Israel’s military in two months suggests that he sees that issue as a pressing political problem on the right and left. In Israel, Trump’s statement was seized upon by Gadi Eisenkot who will likely get the first chance to form a new government in the wake of last week’s elections. The growing threat to the bilateral relationship will be a top priority for the next Israeli prime minister.

The Iranian regime will undoubtedly see the results as another example of their form of “regime change” in Washington. If they make this view public, they risk encouraging a Trump decision to escalate. Before the elections, Trump had already reviewed war plans and ordered additional military forces to the region. Thus far, encouragingly, statements from Iran about the US election results have generally been de-escalatory.

That respite may prove temporary. Iran has a relatively consistent track record of miscalculation and overplaying its hand, and while a Democratic Congress has the power to stymie Trump’s domestic legislative agenda, it doesn’t have much ability to stop a president from exercising his powers as commander in chief.

Trump may eventually surmise that a diplomatic agreement along the lines of the previous Memorandum of Understanding would only reinforce perceptions that his war was an unmitigated disaster that damaged US national security, the Republican Party’s electoral prospects, and his personal legacy. The only way out, Trump may therefore conclude, is to win the war. That could lead to a decision to restart major combat operations, if not immediately, then in the months to come.

Trump may double down on energy policy

With Democrats having gained control of Congress, Trump is likely to lean more heavily on his substantial executive and foreign policy authority. Despite mounting legislative headwinds, the president faces a narrowing window to translate his priorities into durable policy and investment decisions before the 2028 presidential race takes hold.

Affordability dominated the run-up to yesterday’s elections, with a Reuters/Ipsos poll finding that 48 percent of registered voters identified the cost of living as their top voting issue. Retail gasoline and diesel prices have also risen sharply this year, reinforcing the political pressure on the administration. But with the midterms behind him, Trump may increasingly weigh near-term consumer-price concerns against longer-term strategic objectives. The tension will be particularly apparent in energy policy, where foreign policy ambitions, domestic industrial priorities, and consumer affordability do not always align.

That starts with Iran, where Trump may place greater weight on his long-term objective of preventing a nuclear-armed Iran than on short-term electoral considerations. His behavior before the 2025 and 2026 strikes demonstrates that diplomatic rhetoric and military escalation can coexist. Sustained economic pressure remains a likely course, with renewed military escalation a viable alternative, even at the expense of regional stability and energy prices.

Presidential power has its limits, however. Trump may seek an energy-centered resolution to the war in Ukraine in negotiations with Moscow, but achieving one is another matter. Bipartisan congressional resistance to sanctions relief on this side of the Atlantic and Europe’s determination to eliminate its dependence on Russian gas—backed by a legally mandated phaseout through 2027—present formidable obstacles. And this doesn’t even account for the fact that restoring Russian energy flows to Europe would undercut US liquefied natural gas export interests and Trump’s broader energy dominance agenda.

Beyond foreign policy and diplomatic ambitions, the president has considerably more latitude to advance his domestic energy agenda without the cooperation of foreign governments or Congress. Expect a renewed push to expand conventional energy production, export capacity, and the infrastructure needed to power the United States’ artificial intelligence (AI) and manufacturing ambitions. These priorities may offer limited near-term consumer-price relief, but they present the administration with an opportunity to translate executive authority into long-term infrastructure investment and commercial commitments that will be harder for future administrations to unwind.

Markets are unsure what to make of the Democratic sweep

Two years ago, as Trump was reelected to the presidency, bond yields shot up—as markets expected higher tariffs and more deficit spending. They were right. Two years later, as Democrats swept Congress, bond markets initially reacted in the opposite direction—on the belief that AI-related infrastructure spending would have to slow down and gridlock would mean fewer spending deals. This time, the markets may be mistaken.

The Democrats are planning a hundred-hour legislative blitz in January on a range of their priorities, including rolling back tariffs—which, based on exit polls, were among the least popular policies of Trump’s second term—and restoring cuts from Medicaid and the Affordable Care Act. All of that would increase the deficit.

The markets assume Trump will veto the full package. But it’s not so simple.

The strength of the Democrats’ majorities in both the House and Senate means they will enter two major fiscal fights in a strong negotiating position. First up will be federal government appropriations, as current funding only runs through December 11. The lame-duck Congress may pass a continuing resolution, but in 2027 a budget fight will almost certainly take place. It could happen at the same time that the US hits the debt ceiling—the $41 trillion limit is projected to be breached sometime in the first half of the year. The Democrats will insist on their spending priorities as a condition of reaching an agreement. Don’t be surprised to see some deals in the coming year—ones where both sides get their spending priorities met and the debt continues to pile up.

Tariffs, meanwhile, are not likely to change. Voters delivered a clear message about how they felt about Trump’s trade policies and the impact they have on prices. But Trump will reject any attempt to limit the use of his favorite tool. The Democrats’ legislation will be important because it will show where the party wants to head on trade in 2028 and beyond. But for those countries looking for a break on tariff rates after the midterms, the wait will be at least a little longer.

The one exception may be China. Trump’s trade détente with Beijing was driven in part by the series of summits the two leaders had this year (with two more expected before year-end). Once those pass, Trump may refocus in his final two years on what has been the core animating economic idea since he first ran for president—China’s unfair trading practices. On that issue, he may find a rare area of bipartisan consensus.

The power of the purse will be the route to shaping US NATO policy

As long as Trump is in office, questions and concerns about US engagement in NATO will remain. It was not Congress, but rather the president, who created a transatlantic crisis by repeatedly threatening to annex Greenland, make Canada the fifty-first state, and withhold protection from NATO allies that do not spend enough on defense. It was also the administration, not Congress, that bypassed all efforts to build European support for (or even awareness of) its war with Iran. The administration took not only Europeans but also Congress by surprise when it canceled troop deployments to Europe earlier this year. Now that Democrats control the legislative branch, many on both sides of the Atlantic will be looking to see if the party can wrestle some degree of control away from the executive branch in foreign and security policy.

Democrats who favor a robust US presence in Europe and a strong commitment to NATO are starting from a solid foundation. Despite the administration’s unwieldy approach toward allies, support for NATO in Congress already crosses party lines—and to meaningful effect. In the fiscal year 2026 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), Republican majorities passed multiyear security assistance for Ukraine, as well as limits on the administration’s ability to enact troop cuts in Europe, and required the US military commander of European Command to retain the supreme allied commander Europe role in NATO.

Despite this already strong bipartisan support for NATO, Democratic control of Congress will still have a recalibrating effect on transatlantic security. Come January 2027, Democrats will chair every committee and subcommittee in the House and Senate, including the appropriations committees and those important for European security and foreign policy (the Senate Armed Services Committee, Senate Foreign Relations Committee, House Armed Services Committee, and House Foreign Affairs Committee). Democrats will decide which bills get hearings, control investigations, and oversee about two-thirds of committee staff and budgets. We will see the effects of this shift in the 2027 NDAA negotiations and hearings regarding US force posture in Europe. While Trump maintains broad executive privileges in the foreign policy arena, Democrats will start paving the way for a new approach to working with US allies.

Public trust is driving politics—and perhaps now policy—on AI

For the United States to compete effectively in the age of AI, the country must address the significant trust deficit the American public has toward the technology. This was a key finding of the Atlantic Council’s Commission on AI earlier this year, which brought together bipartisan members of Congress, industry leaders, and civil society experts.

The deep anxiety Americans feel about the technology and skepticism of the titans building it were on full display throughout the midterm elections and in the results. For example, an NBC News exit poll found 56 percent of voters said AI and associated infrastructure were a “crucial or major factor” in their vote for Congress. There is little reason to believe these concerns won’t remain on full display in the next Congress and at the state level in California, Texas, Ohio, and elsewhere.

Despite the significant Democratic gains in the election, AI skepticism transcended partisan lines, with many Republican candidates—from Michigan to Texas—advocating for slowing down the AI infrastructure buildout or increasing the regulation of the tech sector. Likewise, there are an increasing number of bipartisan policy proposals on AI safety in the current Congress—such as the FRONTIER ACT or the AI Kill Switch Act—which will likely reemerge in some form in the next Congress.

The bottom line is that, despite the increasing use and integration of AI in daily life around the country, polling as recent as last month shows that 75 percent of Americans view AI with fear or concern rather than excitement, especially when it comes to affordability, employment, education, the environment, safety and security, and many other issues. These concerns are especially prevalent among young people.

The election comes one week after one of the largest tech-driven sell-offs wiped out nearly one trillion dollars in market value due to subpar earnings reports across the AI industry. Much of that sell-off was driven by shaky confidence in whether the record borrowing and spending fueling the AI industry will translate into sustainable revenue, even as the infrastructure buildout takes time and has become a political flashpoint. Either way, the US economy is extremely dependent on whether the huge bets being placed on AI will pan out. Taken together, we’re likely in for continued market and policy adjustments related to AI.

AI is here to stay as a general-purpose technology, but it is also increasingly a determinant of geopolitical competition. As AI development outpaces institutions’ ability to manage it, we’re past due for a coherent national dialogue on AI’s impact and what US leadership in AI should look like. That debate will be on full display in the coming Congress.

US-China AI safety talks could be back on the agenda

Democratic control of Congress could strengthen political support for US-China coordination on AI safety, particularly around frontier-model risks, incident reporting, and crisis communications. The election comes at a consequential moment: During their September 2026 summit, Trump and Xi agreed to establish a bilateral AI dialogue and a communication channel for AI-related incidents, with follow-up talks scheduled for November.

Congressional Democrats have already articulated a more ambitious agenda for bilateral engagement: In September, representatives Gregory Meeks, Ami Bera, and Sara Jacobs, along with twenty-six of their colleagues, urged the administration to pursue shared AI safety standards, establish crisis communications mechanisms, address the proliferation of advanced capabilities, and facilitate exchanges between American and Chinese AI researchers. A separate initiative led by Senator Chris Van Hollen and sixteen Democratic colleagues went further, calling for a formal agreement on frontier AI testing, oversight, human control, and verification. The senators also proposed considering a mutual pause in frontier AI development, highlighting growing congressional interest in managing the risks of an accelerating technological competition.

With control of both chambers, Democrats could use committee hearings, appropriations, and legislation to press the administration to operationalize the new dialogue. Potential priorities could include defining which AI incidents trigger bilateral notifications, establishing protocols for information sharing, and supporting technical exchanges on model evaluations and catastrophic risks.

There is some bipartisan support for this approach. In September, members of the bipartisan Problem Solvers Caucus also called for US-China coordination on AI testing and incident reporting. Growing public backlash against current AI policy—including data center buildouts, permissive AI self-regulation, and growing concerns about the impacts of AI on employment—could also add momentum to renewed engagement on AI.

However, significant constraints remain. The executive branch controls diplomatic negotiations, while disagreements over semiconductor restrictions, technology access, and verification complicate cooperation. Democratic lawmakers also differ significantly on how far bilateral commitments should extend, with more national-security-oriented Democrats expressing greater skepticism about such a process.

The election’s most immediate effect may be to make implementation of the existing AI safety dialogue a more prominent congressional priority. Whether this develops into formal agreements will depend on the administration’s willingness to negotiate and Beijing’s readiness to accept reciprocal safeguards—a tall order, considering that Beijing has previously rejected Washington’s efforts to frame AI safety talks around US-defined priorities.

Democrats could extract some concessions on Ukraine, but don’t expect a sea-change on Europe

Europe can expect the Democrats in the next Congress to signal a more constructive US reengagement in transatlantic relations, on Ukraine, and even on trade issues. But European decisionmakers are right to have tempered expectations about how much a Democratic Congress will translate into substantial US policy changes on what matters most to the continent: support for Ukraine, US commitments to European security, and greater stability in trade and tariff policies.

Even with a strong majority in both chambers of Congress, Democrats will struggle to impose meaningful limits on Trump’s conduct of foreign policy, given his constitutional powers and willingness to push the envelope. Democrats may put him and Republicans on the record with messaging bills on items such as the Russian diesel deal and waived Russia sanctions. They can put supplemental funding for Ukraine on the agenda and leverage must-pass legislation such as the NDAA to try to extract concessions on Ukraine support or US security and troop commitments in Europe related to the administration’s ongoing force posture review. The new majority will also try to claw back trade and tariff powers that Congress has ceded to the executive branch in Trump’s second term. But Trump has stated a willingness to use his veto, and hard limits on the president’s power are unlikely.

Much will also depend on where congressional Republicans go politically in response to the midterm rout. The remaining Reaganite hawks in the Senate may not continue to mute their opposition to the president’s dealings with Moscow and Beijing or his pressure on Kyiv and allied European capitals. Large Democratic majorities in both houses of Congress may make it easier to assemble the two-thirds majorities needed to override a presidential veto. Republican hawks will have more leverage to confront the White House, even if they will have to pick their battles.

Complicating matters, Europe will have to navigate two poles of power in Washington. Europe will, on the one hand, confront a Democratic Congress that wants to drive a reengagement agenda with European allies but will not be able to deliver significant policy changes on key areas of concern, at least not on its own. And on the other hand, Brussels and national capitals must be prepared to counter continued disruption from the president on trade and Ukraine, while avoiding antagonizing him with overly partisan approaches.

NATO and EU countries will continue to confront a mercurial US president who may double down on foreign policy as he is likely to come under significant pressure at home from congressional investigations, budget fights, and political gridlock under divided government. Unshackled from having to face voters at the ballot box again, Trump may shift into deal-making overdrive to cement his legacy. In doing so, he will lean into the instincts that have defined his foreign policy Weltanschauung—one of sphere-of-influence arrangements among supposedly great powers, personalized leader-to-leader dealings, and hard power realism. Trump’s deal-making mode carries both risks and opportunities for Europe and its adversaries.

Moscow and Beijing will now have to contend with a more boxed-in Trump administration. Trump’s instincts may still be to look for deals with Putin and Xi. So Europeans should assess which opportunities and deals they can shape, from Ukraine to European security and trade, even if these may turn out to be more tactical than strategic, as broader initiatives with this White House may remain elusive. But Europe simply cannot afford to fatalistically write off the next two years given the president’s powers and what is at stake for the continent in US foreign and defense policy.

Congress will double down on defense and intelligence oversight

Democratic leaders in the House and Senate will need to focus immediately on essential foreign policy issues such as Iran and Ukraine, but equally important will be the possibility of renewed oversight of core defense and intelligence issues. Expect Democrats to press on issues such as the Pentagon’s force posture plans around the globe and getting numbers on critical munitions stockpiles and associated defense production issues. Democrats are also likely to look into reports of inappropriate business practices within the department and seek out accountability on recent military actions against targets in the Caribbean and Iran. Trump’s programmatic priorities such as Golden Dome, and broader issues of personnel readiness, promotions, and recruitment, are also likely to be on the agenda.

On intelligence issues, we may see a revived bipartisan core of members who will want baseline information on how layoffs and retirements have affected US collection capacity, where AI offers expanded risks and opportunities, and how adversaries may be working together in new ways against US interests and those of the international community.

These fundamental issues won’t be easy to address. They will require urgent bipartisan attention and rapid coordination across several committees before the new Congress is even sworn in this January. Much more work lies ahead.

It’s time for bipartisan progress on immigration policy

Opinion polls have consistently made clear that the American people want an immigration system that is both just and fair, and they are prepared to vote against those who fail to deliver on that objective. Concerns about the US immigration system helped elect Trump president in 2016. Trump’s child-separation policy helped elect Joe Biden president in 2020. Chaos at the border helped elect Trump president in 2024. Cruelty in Trump’s immigration enforcement over the past two years helped create last night’s electoral triumph for Democrats.

Trump’s border adviser Tom Homan had it right two years ago: If Trump had focused on deporting only those unauthorized migrants with criminal records, he might have kept the support of the majority of Americans on this issue. Instead, Trump’s immigration policy appears to have lost the trust of the American people. As of early Wednesday morning, Democrats are expected to win in every single congressional district along the US-Mexico border, including in formerly deep-red (now looking purple) Texas.

With their new power, expect congressional Democrats to start investigations into the Trump administration’s immigration detention system.

The lesson Republicans and Democrats should learn is that only a bipartisan approach on border security and immigration will get the lasting support of the American people. The United States needs a solution along the lines of the 2023–2024 bipartisan Senate compromise or the bipartisan Dignity Act. The 120th Congress should update the 2024 compromise legislation, reallocate existing appropriations from Immigration and Customs Enforcement to other priorities, mandate a major shift in detention and asylum policy, and send it to the White House attached to whatever Trump considers must-pass legislation. Even if bipartisan immigration reform does not pass in 2027, it will help set the agenda for 2028.

Expect tougher scrutiny of Israel and Iran, and potentially more support for Ukraine

Last night’s resounding loss for the Republican Party will have some immediate impacts on foreign policy. First, the new Congress will be without a slew of experienced Republican national security voices, who either lost last night, retired, or passed away. Senators Susan Collins (ME), Thom Tillis (NC), John Cornyn (TX), Lindsey Graham (SC), and Mitch McConnell (KY), and representatives Mike Lawler (NY), Michael McCaul (TX), Ann Wagner (MO), Don Bacon (NE), and Brian Fitzpatrick (PA) have been advocates for American strength and strong alliances, including with Ukraine. That is a significant loss of expertise and experience for the Republican conferences in both chambers that will take years to rebuild.

Israel is also facing a brand-new world this morning—one with a Congress far less supportive of its causes and far more likely to cut military aid. The Israeli government and its supporters in the United States would be wise to begin immediate outreach to Democrats open to mending fences and attempt to rebuild support. Trump himself announced Tuesday that he would cut off four billion dollars in annual aid to Israel, but he will need Congress to agree, since it is actually responsible for appropriating that money. He now likely has a Congress that will.

On the war in Iran, which drove many voters to turn on Republicans, the next Congress is likely to prioritize legislation to halt, or at least significantly curtail, US military action. Still, it is unclear what that would look like beyond a resolution of disapproval, because Iran has been unwilling to have any reasonable discussions to end the conflict.

The new Congress also injects a measure of uncertainty into Ukraine policy. While Democrats have been generally solid in supporting Ukraine militarily and financially during the conflict, voters sent a resounding message in this election to focus on domestic policy and affordability. It’s unclear whether this new crop of Democrats will be interested in sending money and weapons overseas—regardless of the destination. In good news for Ukraine, the likely chairs of national security committees—particularly Representative Adam Smith (D-WA) at House Armed Services and Senator Chris Coons (D-DE) at Senate Foreign Relations—have a strong record of support. They will be powerful allies for Ukraine in the new Congress, as Kyiv fights for access to much-needed weapons.

Venezuela oil deals and military operations will come under scrutiny

Latin America policy wasn’t on the ballot yesterday, and Democrats are expected to focus on affordability and other pocketbook issues. But the Democratic-controlled House and Senate, especially with more seats flipped than expected, are likely to bring hearings, oversight, and investigations into some of Trump’s marquee policies in Latin America in at least four priority areas.

Top of that list will be Venezuela. There, investigations could stretch from looking at who benefits from oil agreements to how revenues are managed and the legal authority for those arrangements, as well as greater scrutiny of the extent to which a pathway to a democratic transition is taking shape. Senator Tim Kaine, a potential new chair of the Western Hemisphere Subcommittee in the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, may push the administration on the exact timing and plan for an election.

Expect possible involvement from the House Foreign Affairs and Oversight committees, and the Senate Foreign Relations, Banking, and Finance committees. Democrats have long been asking for more information on these issues, including in a September letter from Representative Gregory Meeks and Representative Robert Garcia to Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Attorney General Todd Blanche requesting more information on the management of Venezuelan oil revenue and the September oil deal announced by Trump.

But it won’t only be about Venezuela. Representative Adam Smith, in line to chair the House Armed Services Committee, has stated that, with enough backing, he would push to investigate the boat strikes and the overall military campaigns that the United States has deployed across the region since the Trump administration took office. Hearings could include the legal basis for US actions, the costs, and the casualties. Global tariffs will also be on the congressional agenda, with the implications for countries like Mexico, Washington’s largest trading partner, likely to receive greater attention.

Hearings and investigations are not the only tools available to Congress. Ahead of elections in 2028, both parties will be pressed to show concrete results through legislation—and hopefully through bipartisan alignment—on the issues that will define the continued expansion of the US presence in the hemisphere.

text:
But Trump’s handling of immigration enforcement also remains at the forefront of that conversation. In the two years since he took office, the Trump administration’s increased crackdown on immigration has seen ICE agents shoot two American citizens dead in Minneapolis and leave hundreds of others involved in enforcement operations either injured, incarcerated or both.

Here in the Big Apple, 26 Federal Plaza’s immigration court became a powder keg in the summer of 2025, as journalists’ ability to enter the facility gave the public a rare glimpse into ICE arrests and subsequent family separations that saw children left in tears as they were torn from their parents’ arms.

Peter Melck Kuttel, detention coordinator for Father Fabian Arias’ Saint Peter’s Church, has worked with immigrants detained in the courthouse since the summer of 2025. In his mind, he does not doubt that the suffering in plain sight at 26 Federal Plaza and operations across the country had a major impact on how the country voted Tuesday.

“I think those images and the stories of those images played a huge role in Americans’ rejection of the administration’s spin on immigration and their enforcement on immigration. I don’t think it was just Iran,” Kuttel told amNewYork. “Many saw them as their neighbors, their friends, even employees.”

While Kuttel stated that a vote for Trump two years prior may have been to close the border, he says that is something different from voting for what he says is the cruelty of breaking apart families.

Over the course of his work, Kuttle noted that he has seen very few immigrants with serious criminal records, and did not see “the worst of the worst” that Trump Border Czar Tom Homan claimed to be targeted by ICE, as masked agents pulled families away in the halls of Federal Plaza and other courthouses across the country.

ICE agents’ actions in New York since 2025

In the end, he believes American voters also saw this and took action with their ballots.

“I think Americans, by and large, saw through that, and the images that they would see out of Minnesota, the images that they would see out of the courts, the images that they would see out of California or even Texas or even just in their own backyards. With the agents being masked up, being so unprofessional and so filled with hate, it didn’t even seem like an organized government operation. It just seemed like cruelty,” Kuttel added.

For almost one year, amNewYork gave the city a firsthand look at the drama unfolding in the halls of 26 Federal Plaza, from the arrest of then-Mayoral candidate Brad Lander to journalists being roughed up by masked ICE agents and children left in tears.

While enforcement in the courthouse continued, the scope of ICE operations eventually moved out into the streets of New York, including the apprehension of Canal Street vendors in Chinatown in October 2025.

In June, a hunger strike at New Jersey’s Delaney Hall also drew nationwide attention and weeks of protests that saw demonstrators doused in pepper spray, beaten with nightsticks, and thrown into oncoming traffic.

Then, in October of this year, ICE agents shot and wounded Oscar Belgal, a Dominican native, during a confrontation in Marble Hill. He was hospitalized, but ICE later took him into its custody; Belgal would be detained at the Metropolitan Detention Center with a bullet still lodged in his neck more than a week later. As of Oct. 23, he was still listed in ICE custody.

For Murad Awawdeh, President and CEO of the New York Immigration Coalition, the sights of ICE agents acting brutally inside Federal Plaza and beyond all contributed to what he called a rejection of Trump on Nov. 3.

“Voters across America and New York have resoundingly rejected Trump’s war on immigrants. The courthouse arrests at 26 Federal Plaza represent the extreme unlawfulness of this administration, as families have been systematically separated because they tried to follow our immigration procedures. New Yorkers want ICE out of our communities once and for all,” Awawdeh told amNewYork. “We call on the new Congress to conduct aggressive oversight hearings on ICE, including their unlawful abductions and detentions at 26 Federal Plaza, to take back enforcement slush funds and reinvest in programs that help all New Yorkers, and to provide a real pathway to citizenship.”

Meanwhile, religious leaders like Midtown pastor Father Fabian Arias, who has spent decades fighting for the rights of immigrants, says he hopes these vote results will allow for new discourse around immigration.

“I hope that new paths of dialogue and reconciliation will open, so that our immigrant families may live without fear of ICE raids, deportations, and family separation,” Arias said.
