text:
November 9 marks a tragic milestone: 100 days since the Trump administration cut off competent legal support for tens of thousands of children who are going through the immigration courts alone, abandoning them to the whims of ‘deportation judges hired to carry out Stephen Miller’s mass deportation agenda.’

The immigration court data already show the effects of these policies. Acacia’s October 15 fact sheet, The Data Behind a Due Process Crisis, found that 69 percent of unaccompanied children’s cases completed in the first eight months of 2026 ended in a removal order, up from an average of 28 percent from 2021 through 2024. Voluntary departures for children also climbed, reaching 1,831 in those eight months, compared to 527 in all of 2024. The immigration courts haven’t just become a deportation machine for adults in the system, they’re a deportation machine for kids, too.

To ensure that these children are not forgotten and to push for practical solutions that protect them, I am hosting a virtual conversation this Monday, November 9 at 1:00 PM Eastern, with three of the most recognized subject matter experts: Dr. Marsha Griffin, President and CEO of Community for Children; Katie Fleming, Director of Public Education and Engagement at Acacia Center for Justice; and Neha Desai, Managing Director of Children’s Human Rights and Dignity at the National Center for Youth Law.

Together, they will help us understand what has gone wrong for children in court in the past 100 days. While more Americans are aware of the shocking fact that kids are going to court alone, few people truly understand what that means and just how consequential this is for these children.

Dr. Marsha Griffin, Katie Fleming, and Neha Desai will share new findings and firsthand stories from courtroom observation that reveal how dangerous courts have become for children. The government is offering unrepresented children $3,000 to accept voluntary departure, even when it is not in their best interest and before they have a chance to have their case heard. Hearings are being shuffled around and added to virtual videoconferencing dockets that make it even harder for children to know what’s going on. So far, the multi-million dollar contract has gone to a firm with ties to the Trump administration, then to an organization called Our Rescue founded by a former ICE agent. And HHS is now attempting to send its own attorneys to represent children, a move that six senators called a “clear conflict of interest.”

We will also discuss real solutions, especially putting pressure on states to do their part to ensure that children have basic access to legal counsel. California is one example. Its 2026-27 state budget renewed the Children’s Holistic Immigration Representation Project, which pairs unaccompanied children with legal and social service teams, for more than 1,000 children, and created a new Immigration Counsel Access Pilot Program. In August, New York committed $7.25 million in new state funding for legal services for about 1,400 unaccompanied children in removal proceedings.

Moreover, with the stunning results of the midterms now in, this 100-day retrospective on the loss of competent legal services for children in court is also a forward-looking appeal to the incoming representatives of the 120th Congress to prioritize real fixes to the Trump administration’s sabotage of due process for children.

title: Roxbury turns Democratic after ICE detention center fight - New Jersey Globe
description:
In 2022, Kean carried Roxbury by more than 19 percentage points against then-Rep. Tom Malinowski (D-Ringoes); he won Roxbury by 5,611 votes – more than half of his 9,309-vote margin.
Trump carried Roxbury by 18.5 points in 2024, and Republican Jack Ciattarelli defeated Democrat Mikie Sherrill by nearly 11 points in last year’s gubernatorial election.
Democratic U.S. Sen. Cory Booker carried Roxbury by 226 votes, defeating Republican Justin Murphy, 4,745 to 4,519, or 49.7% to 47.3%.
The results don’t prove how many voters have changed their minds because of the detention center controversy, particularly in an election that produced substantial Democratic gains across New Jersey.
And for Bennett, who defeated Kean districtwide by 16 percentage points, Roxbury was one of the clearest examples of how far Democrats penetrated traditionally Republican territory in 2026.
text:
Roxbury, a Morris County Republican stronghold where Donald Trump won by nearly 19 points two years ago, voted Democratic in Tuesday’s congressional election after a bitter controversy over the Trump administration’s decision to locate an immigration detention center in the township.

Rep.-elect Rebecca Bennett (D-Bridgewater) defeated Rep. Tom Kean Jr. (R-Westfield) by 338 votes, 4,898 to 4,560, a remarkable turnaround in a municipality where Kean had posted landslide victories in his previous two congressional campaigns.

Bennett received 51.1% of the vote to Kean’s 47.5%, a 3.5-point victory that represents a swing of more than 21 percentage points since 2024.

In 2022, Kean carried Roxbury by more than 19 percentage points against then-Rep. Tom Malinowski (D-Ringoes); he won Roxbury by 5,611 votes – more than half of his 9,309-vote margin. He took a thousand-vote haircut in four years. (His margin against Sue Altman in 2024 was more than 18 points).

The township’s Republican credentials were hardly in doubt. Trump carried Roxbury by 18.5 points in 2024, and Republican Jack Ciattarelli defeated Democrat Mikie Sherrill by nearly 11 points in last year’s gubernatorial election.

But the Trump administration’s decision to purchase a warehouse on Route 46 for an Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention facility scrambled local politics, putting Republican elected officials at odds with a Republican president and, for a time, their own Republican congressman.

Roxbury’s all-Republican Township Council unanimously opposed the facility and joined the Sherrill administration in a federal lawsuit seeking to block the project.

Mayor Shawn Potillo and the council publicly criticized Kean, saying he had not provided the level of advocacy they expected on behalf of township residents.

Kean defended his involvement, saying he had contacted senior Department of Homeland Security officials and was working toward a solution. In February, he introduced legislation that would reimburse municipalities for costs associated with federal immigration detention facilities, including lost property tax revenue and infrastructure improvements.

But Kean stopped short of formally opposing the detention center until September 27, when he announced his opposition during his only debate with Bennett, sponsored by the New Jersey Globe and Rider University.

Bennett had opposed the project for months, siding with local Republican officials who maintained that the township lacked the infrastructure to accommodate a facility that could house as many as 1,500 detainees.

Instead of debating federal immigration policy, the issue was entirely local. Township officials raised concerns about water and sewer capacity, traffic, environmental damage, and the loss of local property tax revenue.

In May, federal officials agreed not to proceed with converting the warehouse into a detention facility until an environmental assessment was completed, following the lawsuit filed by Roxbury and the Sherrill administration.

Roxbury didn’t just vote against Kean.

Democratic U.S. Sen. Cory Booker carried Roxbury by 226 votes, defeating Republican Justin Murphy, 4,745 to 4,519, or 49.7% to 47.3%. Independent candidates received another 210 votes.

In the Morris County commissioner race, Democrat Christopher Russo defeated Republican incumbent Tayfun Selen by 141 votes, 4,712 to 4,571, or 50.7% to 49.2% of the votes cast for commissioner candidates.

The results were striking in a municipality that has traditionally given Republicans substantial margins in countywide, statewide, and congressional elections.

Bennett ran 153 votes ahead of Booker, while Kean received 41 more votes than Murphy. Russo received 33 fewer votes than Booker, while Selen received 11 more votes than Kean.

Bennett’s margin of victory was also larger than Booker’s or Russo’s, suggesting the Democratic nominee attracted support beyond voters who backed the rest of the Democratic ticket.

The election drew 9,738 voters from Roxbury’s 18,682 registered voters, a turnout of 52.12%. Of those ballots, 6,487 were cast on Election Day, 1,896 during early in-person voting and 1,355 by mail.

The results don’t prove how many voters have changed their minds because of the detention center controversy, particularly in an election that produced substantial Democratic gains across New Jersey.

But the magnitude of Kean’s drop in Roxbury, where he had previously enjoyed margins exceeding 18 points, shows how suddenly the township’s political landscape changed in a one election cycle.

For Republicans, the loss of Roxbury was particularly significant because the township had been a reliable source of votes in Kean’s two successful congressional campaigns.

And for Bennett, who defeated Kean districtwide by 16 percentage points, Roxbury was one of the clearest examples of how far Democrats penetrated traditionally Republican territory in 2026.

title: ACLU of Texas Border Poll Highlights Voter Rejection of ICE, Anti-Immigrant Policies
description:
The ACLU of Texas commissioned the survey to better understand how border residents across the political spectrum feel about the surge in immigration enforcement.
Key findings include: 53% of border residents think state and local immigration enforcement presence makes life harder without making their communities safer.
63% of border residents, including people who have a family member employed by a federal immigration enforcement agency, believe ICE tactics have gone too far.
64% of border residents want local and state law enforcement to prioritize preventing and solving crime rather than immigration enforcement.
The ACLU of Texas recommends several policies to prioritize public safety, improve conditions for residents, and represent the interests and prevailing views of border residents.
text:
AUSTIN, Texas – The American Civil Liberties Union of Texas conducted polling prior to the midterm election that revealed widespread concern among border residents about federal, state, and local immigration enforcement. Those findings bore out on Election Day as voters — especially Latino/e voters — overwhelmingly swept pro-ICE, anti-immigration candidates out of office.

“Voters along the border and throughout the state sent a resounding message to Texas leaders: We have had enough, get ICE out of our communities,” said Osvaldo Grimaldo (he/him), policy strategist on border and immigrants’ rights at the ACLU of Texas. “We’re not surprised by these election night results after our poll of El Paso and Rio Grande Valley showed residents felt that anti-immigration policies had gone too far. Latino voters have been impacted by this state’s harmful immigration policies and hope for the day that Texas creates a welcoming environment for our immigrant communities — now more than ever, that day is near.”

The report, entitled “Gone Too Far: Border Residents in Texas Are Concerned About Immigration Enforcement” and released in early October, shared results from a poll conducted by Change Research of 1,031 adults in El Paso County and four Rio Grande Valley counties (Cameron, Hidalgo, Starr, and Willacy) between August 25 and September 2.

The ACLU of Texas commissioned the survey to better understand how border residents across the political spectrum feel about the surge in immigration enforcement. Key findings include:

53% of border residents think state and local immigration enforcement presence makes life harder without making their communities safer. Only 34% say it makes their communities safer.

63% of border residents, including people who have a family member employed by a federal immigration enforcement agency, believe ICE tactics have gone too far.

64% of border residents want local and state law enforcement to prioritize preventing and solving crime rather than immigration enforcement.

“ICE isn’t helping by deporting our hardworking immigrants regardless of their status. This whole region and country has been built on the backs of immigrants,” said one respondent who lives in the RGV and voted for Donald Trump in the 2024 presidential election.

Across the surveyed regions, Trump had an approval rating of 34% and disapproval rating of 60% — with 57% disapproval in the RGV and 65% disapproval in El Paso. The president won the four surveyed Rio Grande Valley counties during the 2024 election but lost El Paso County.

The federal government continues to expand immigration enforcement presence along the Texas-Mexico border despite the disruption it causes for residents of all political backgrounds who live there. Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, who lost his re-election bid on Tuesday night, and the state legislature have also mandated local cooperation between law enforcement and ICE.

The ACLU of Texas recommends several policies to prioritize public safety, improve conditions for residents, and represent the interests and prevailing views of border residents. Those recommendations — which are explained in greater detail in the full report — are:

Halt 287(g) agreements and end existing local law enforcement collaboration with ICE.

End state police involvement in federal immigration enforcement.

Support victims of crime.

Tailor local law enforcement priorities to avoid targeting sensitive locations such as schools, places of worship, and hospitals.

A copy of the report with crosstabs is available here: https://www.aclutx.org/publications/gone-too-far-border-residents-in-texas-are-concerned-about-immigration-enforcement/

title: Federal courts in New Mexico, New York temporarily block ICE deportations of Afghans
authors: Julia Gentin, Gabriela Campos, New Mexican file photo
description: A federal court in New Mexico on Monday blocked the deportation of an Afghan national who had been held at the Torrance County Detention Facility.
text:
The winner of the sheriff race will replace retiring Sheriff…

Twenty new cases have been identified in the state since Wed…



A view of the Torrance County Detention Facility in September 2025

A federal court in New York on Tuesday blocked the Trump administration’s plans to deport Afghans to their Taliban-controlled country of origin through Pakistan in a temporary order that expires Saturday.

The decision came the day after a federal judge in New Mexico prohibited the removal of Sardar Akbari, 31, an Afghan national who had been held at the Torrance County Detention Facility in Estancia. That order also was temporary, pausing the deportation for 14 days, “until the Court is satisfied that the government has put in place adequate safeguards to protect Akbari against the risk of suicide,” according to a statement from the American Civil Liberties Union of New Mexico.

After learning of the federal government’s plans to send him to Pakistan, Akbari suffered an “acute mental health crisis,” the ACLU of New Mexico said in the statement.

Deportation flights for Afghans were set to go through Pakistan because the U.S. has no diplomatic relations with the Taliban government to arrange flights to Afghanistan. The State Department also places Afghanistan under a “Level 4 — Do not travel” advisor y “due to civil unrest, crime, terrorism, risk of wrongful detention, kidnapping, natural disasters, and limited health facilities.”

New York Judge Valerie Caproni’s order on Tuesday does not put an end to deportations through Pakistan. But it prevents the flights from taking off until Sunday.

Akbari is represented by the Clinical Law Program of the University of New Mexico Law School and the ACLU in his habeas proceedings, in which he is challenging the legality of his detention.

He has been in the custody of the federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement since late 2024 and was transported from the Torrance County facility to El Paso’s Camp East Montana — the nation’s largest immigrant detention center — Oct. 27. The move was to prepare him for deportation, according to court documents.

“Mr. Akbari’s case is a window into the abject horrors of our immigration system, and the government’s ‘third country removals’ in particular,” said Shaw Drake, assistant professor of Law at the UNM School of Law, in a statement. “If ICE is able to deport vulnerable immigrants like Mr. Akbari to a country other than his own without any notice or opportunity to claim fear, the fundamental due process safeguards to which we are all entitled are rendered virtually meaningless.”

Camp East Montana is plagued with controversies, including allegations of life-threatening medical neglect, coercive removals, inhumane confinement, three detainee deaths and an alleged riot, according to a July report from the ACLU.

The El Paso City Council voted unanimously Oct. 27 to draft a resolution calling for the detention center’s closure, though the decision ultimately falls to the federal government.

Julia Gentin is a reporter for The Las Cruces New Mexican, The Santa Fe New Mexican and Searchlight New Mexico through a partnership with Report for America, a national service program that places journalists into local newsrooms. She covers the Southern New Mexico region. Learn more about Report for America at reportforamerica.org .

name: Policy
title: What a Democratic Congress Means for Latin America
description:
Presidents facing opposition on Capitol Hill often turn toward foreign policy, where they retain considerable authority.
New Congressional leadership on Latin America Representative Gregory Meeks (D-NY), expected to chair the House Foreign Affairs Committee, has already delivered that message.
We anticipate even greater turbulence in U.S. policy toward Latin America over the next two years than in the last two.
Latin America watchers also should remain alert to issues that may appear to have receded.
Tags: Trump and Latin America, U.S. midterms, U.S. Policy
text:
Reading Time: 4 minutes

In a historic vote, Democrats pulled off a blue wave in the U.S. midterms that was stronger than many, including us, had anticipated in the months and weeks leading up to the elections. The party won both chambers handily, paving the way to restoring a congressional check on President Donald Trump’s approach to a broad range of issues, with Latin America high on the list.

Just as important as the new Congress will be the impact of opposition control on a president staring down his last two years in office. Presidents facing opposition on Capitol Hill often turn toward foreign policy, where they retain considerable authority.

Latin American governments and business leaders should now prepare for two main developments: a U.S. Congress ready to reclaim its authority and a president likely to respond to domestic constraints by becoming more aggressive abroad, particularly in the Western Hemisphere.

Some in the region will need to recalibrate their relationships with Washington. A case in point: Endorsements of Representative Maria Elvira Salazar (R-FL) by Colombia’s Abelardo De La Espriella, Argentina’s Javier Milei and Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado reflected a shortsighted approach. Although Salazar appears most likely to win narrowly, those endorsements were unwise: They tied foreign leaders and national causes to one side of an American election, inserted themselves into our democratic elections, and complicated relationships with Democrats.

Effective diplomacy requires playing the long game, and those who neglected Democrats should now seek to repair relationships.

New Congressional leadership on Latin America

Representative Gregory Meeks (D-NY), expected to chair the House Foreign Affairs Committee, has already delivered that message. In October, he warned that De La Espriella’s electoral intervention jeopardized bipartisan U.S. support for Colombia: “Congress will be watching,” he said. Looking ahead, Meeks’ longstanding commitment to Colombia across administrations makes his leadership especially important for that country and the wider Americas region.

Representative Joaquin Castro (D-TX), expected to lead the House Western Hemisphere Subcommittee, has previewed his agenda through actions while in the House minority. In September, he sought subpoenas for records concerning the administration’s oil agreement in Venezuela involving the controversial Barbados-based company North American Blue Energy Partners. Republicans blocked the motion. But now, with a majority, Castro can pursue that investigation.

In the Senate, Tim Kaine (D-VA), likely to lead the Western Hemisphere Subcommittee, brings a deep knowledge of the Americas to his position. Meanwhile, Senator Chris Coons (D-DE), the likely next Chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, has already challenged the administration’s Venezuela policy in hearings and through war powers votes. Earlier this year, Coons publicly pressed Secretary of State Marco Rubio over the failure to consult Congress before Maduro’s removal and backed efforts to restrict further military operations.

With new congressional leadership on Latin America in both chambers, those involved in deals in Venezuela (and elsewhere in the Americas) should expect scrutiny of beneficiaries and possible corruption. Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY), likely the next Speaker of the House, has identified countering corruption as the Democrats’ guiding principle for oversight next year.

Meanwhile, confirmations in the Senate will likely slow dramatically, particularly for controversial non-career nominees. Career diplomats with bipartisan credibility should expect to fare much better. Regional governments should anticipate vacancies and a reliance on acting officials.

Congressional Democrats’ agenda

As we previewed in May, immigration enforcement will also be central to oversight. Democrats will investigate ICE’s conduct, detention practices, and spending. But scrutiny does not mean ending funding: Republican reconciliation laws provided substantial enforcement resources to ICE through 2029.

The Trump administration’s use of El Salvador’s CECOT prison under its arrangement with Nayib Bukele will also face renewed scrutiny, including of the legal authorities for transferring detainees, their treatment, and Washington’s financing commitments. Other arrangements to send migrants to unsafe third countries—or those where integration will prove difficult—will raise similar questions.

Congress’s greatest leverage is its power of the purse, placing the House and Senate Appropriations Committees at the center of the coming policy debates. Democrats will seek to reclaim spending authority as they confront the administration’s dismantling of foreign assistance and withholding of approved funds. Expect debates over conditions, disclosure, and compliance with spending laws. Funding agreements will require negotiations with Republicans and the White House, and further shutdowns remain possible.

Democrats in Congress will be wise to look beyond oversight and put forward an affirmative regional agenda, showing the American public that they can deliver results, while—through the oversight agenda—restoring a congressional check on the executive. Investigating illegal and ineffective lethal boat strikes in the Caribbean and Pacific will be essential.

At the same time, Americans devastated by overdose deaths and Latin Americans confronting organized crime also deserve effective policy responses. Democrats should put forth credible legislative alternatives, particularly on the security front. In the economic realm, Democrats plan to quickly consider legislation to end Trump’s global tariffs and restore congressional control over trade policy.

Trump may take an even harder line

The midterms may begin the end of the Trump political era. But they do not end the president’s desire to seek to transform the Americas. We anticipate even greater turbulence in U.S. policy toward Latin America over the next two years than in the last two.

Cuba is the clearest place to watch. Constrained domestically, Trump will find a confrontation with the Caribbean island especially attractive. Confrontation could take the form of an even more aggressive drive toward negotiations that attempts to force economic and political change in the nation, or it could take the form of military force. The latter seems less likely in the short term than it did several months ago, principally due to resumed hostilities in Iran, but Trump’s willingness to use force and ambitions toward Cuba—especially if Havana refuses to negotiate—must be taken seriously.

Assuming Trump will inevitably retreat—or that a Democratic Congress would serve as a check on his power vis-à-vis Cuba—is dangerous.

Latin America watchers also should remain alert to issues that may appear to have receded. U.S. strikes against criminal groups in Mexico remain a possibility, with potentially profound consequences for bilateral cooperation and ongoing USMCA negotiations. The Panama Canal could also return to Trump’s agenda, even though it has slipped from the headlines. Governments and businesses should resist the temptation to treat a quieter period as evidence that these risks have passed. With Trump, an issue can quickly return to the center of the relationship without warning.

The Democratic wave gives Congress a renewed mandate to constrain presidential overreach and offer an alternate vision for the Americas. Governments and businesses should engage Congress early and substantively, while also preparing for a U.S. president determined to assert his power abroad as his options narrow at home.

Tags: Trump and Latin America, U.S. midterms, U.S. Policy

text:
Chuck Jenkins, the notoriously anti-immigrant Maryland sheriff who boasts of having helped deport 2,000 people, was wiped out in Tuesday’s blue wave.

Voters in Frederick County, a fast-growing and increasingly liberal area north of Washington, D.C., denied his bid for a sixth term. They opted for his opponent, Democrat Karl Bickel, by a margin of 56 to 44 percent.

César Díaz, president of the city council in Frederick, which is the county’s largest city, called Jenkins’s defeat “a repudiation of evil.”

“He is the face here of cruel, inhumane federal policy,” Díaz told Bolts late Tuesday. “Everybody knows somebody, or knows somebody who knows somebody, who’s been directly affected (by ICE). He’s proud of being the face of that, and people have had enough.”

Jenkins, 70, gained national fame for his staunch support of ICE, often appearing on Fox News and visiting with Donald Trump at both the White House and Mar-a-Lago. He joined ICE’s 287(g) program, which deputizes local officials to act on the agency’s behalf, in 2008, long before the program exploded in popularity among conservative sheriffs. He was an early backer of President Donald Trump, and vowed, during Trump’s first run for office, “As long as I am sheriff of Frederick County, we are going to work with ICE.”

Bickel, who is 76 and worked in the sheriff’s office in the 1990s, and who had run and lost against Jenkins in each of the previous three cycles, has vowed not to collaborate with ICE and says he plans to dispatch his deputies to monitor ICE activity in the county. “A lot of what ICE is doing, if a deputy did it they’d be fired or arrested,” Bickel told Bolts in August. “The use of force, the utilization of chemical agents, things like that. It’s just not right.”

In a brief text exchange Wednesday morning, Bickel said, “Now the real work begins.” Jenkins did not respond to a request for comment.

Ahead of the election, Bolts spoke with many immigrants in the county who said Jenkins has, since his first election in 2006, created a culture of fear in Frederick County, which is home to a large Latino population.

Some immigrants told Bolts they’ve been living in hiding lately, frequently unable to work and sometimes unable to obtain food and other basic needs as a result. Many have kept their children out of school and seen family members deported.

“We’re excited. We’re really excited,” one immigrant from El Salvador said of the election result. His stepfather was deported under Jenkins’ 287(g) program, and Bolts is not identifying him by name because he, too, is vulnerable to deportation.

“With him out of his position, Frederick will change for the better,” the man added. “What happened with my stepdad—it was because of policies like his. With him out of office, I hope it will change.”

Jenkins’ defeat speaks both to Frederick County’s changing demographics and to a huge amount of organizing in recent years by immigrant rights activists in the county and throughout Maryland. This coalition successfully lobbied the state legislature to ban 287(g) partnerships earlier this year and to install other immigrant protections—changes Jenkins and 16 other Maryland sheriffs vigorously opposed and sued to prevent.

Of these 17 sheriffs, most were running for reelection unopposed on Tuesday. That lack of competition is quite common across the country, as sheriffs frequently face no challengers, even in some places that are otherwise quite politically competitive.

This year’s blue wave did take out at least one other sheriff famous for harsh policing of immigrants: Republican Terry Johnson, of Alamance County, North Carolina, who faced a federal investigation for his profiling of Latinos, was denied a seventh term in office, losing narrowly to Democratic pastor Shannon Long.

Díaz, the Frederick council president, cautioned that defeating people like Jenkins and Johnson does not alone assuage the fears of immigrants who are still living under the threat of ICE.

“The community is under attack from more than just Chuck Jenkins,” he said. “But that fear did go down a tick after 287(g) was banned. Now Jenkins is gone, and the fear goes down another tick.”

title: Democrats Win Control Of Both Chambers Of Congress - Honolulu Civil Beat
description:
Democrats routed their rivals across the map, from Texas to Iowa to New Hampshire, including states Trump won by double digits just two years ago.
Even Republican Sen. Susan Collins of Maine, a battle-tested survivor of difficult elections, lost to Democrat Troy Jackson.
He sharply criticized North Carolina Republican Sen. Thom Tillis, who opted not to seek reelection.
Less of a surprise was Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff winning reelection in Georgia, defeating Rep. Mike Collins.
Democrats who won included Jamie Ager over Jennifer Capps Balkcom in North Carolina and Lindsay James over Joe Mitchell in Iowa.
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Democrats have won control of the U.S. House in addition to the U.S. Senate, delivering a shockingly decisive rebuke of Republican governance in Washington and ushering in a new era of congressional resistance to President Donald Trump.

The midterm elections that came to a close Tuesday channeled voters’ deep frustrations over high prices, the Iran war and concerns over government corruption. Democrats routed their rivals across the map, from Texas to Iowa to New Hampshire, including states Trump won by double digits just two years ago.

Even Republican Sen. Susan Collins of Maine, a battle-tested survivor of difficult elections, lost to Democrat Troy Jackson.

The results from across the country were a major blow to Trump, who spent nearly every day of the last month holding rallies to energize his supporters but was unable to stop a wipeout.

Democratic control will profoundly reshape Trump’s final two years in office and likely hamstring his agenda.

Party leaders have signaled they’ll use a foothold in Congress to ensure Trump’s final two years in office feature a series of investigations against top members of his administration and deeper scrutiny of how he’s enriched his family. Impeachment of Trump and his Cabinet officials is not off the table.

In celebratory events Tuesday night, Democratic Senate Leader Chuck Schumer called it a “generational remake of the Senate map.” Democratic House Leader Hakeem Jeffries said “the American people are crying out for transformational change.”

Trump immediately sought to shift blame for his party’s losses, posting on his social media site before polls even closed on the West Coast that he wasn’t on the ballot — even though he spent weeks asking voters to pretend like he was. He vowed to veto Democrat-controlled legislation, sharing a picture of a red baseball cap with “veto” stenciled in the style of his trademark “Make America Great Again” campaign swag.

In a late-night phone interview with Fox News, Trump said he didn’t consider the elections to be a personal defeat. Voters, he said, “didn’t like the candidates.”

Democrats had braced for Trump to again try to undermine the results if they won after he warned that noncitizens would cast ballots en masse and filed lawsuits in Alaska and California. Instead, he said on Fox that he would accept them.

Still, the Republican-controlled Congress had acted as a rubber stamp to much of Trump’s agenda. While the president has proven adept at steamrolling efforts to rein him in, Democrats will seek to reshape the remainder of his term. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and tech titan Elon Musk, a former top Trump adviser, are among possible targets for investigations.

Despite the results, Senate Majority Leader John Thune wrote on X that “Senate Republicans will not stand idly by as the far-left, socialist wing of the Democrat Party attempts to unwind everything we’ve done.” He said they will work with Trump “to stop the worst impulses of Democrat extremism.”

Democrats Charted An Extraordinary Path To Senate Victory

Midterm elections are typically difficult for the president’s party, but Republicans had originally expected that their Senate majority was safe. Instead, Democrats marched through some of the most conservative states in the nation.

Josh Turek defeated Rep. Ashley Hinson in Iowa, while Adam Hamilton ousted Sen. Roger Marshall in Kansas to become the state’s first Democratic senator since 1932. A cascade of surprising Democratic victories included James Talarico defeating Ken Paxton in Texas, Annie Andrews upsetting Darline Graham in South Carolina, Sherrod Brown topping Sen. Jon Husted in Ohio and Roy Cooper taking an open North Carolina seat.

Trump played an outsized role in the Texas, North Carolina and South Carolina races. He endorsed Paxton and helped him defeat incumbent Sen. John Cornyn in the Texas primary. He sharply criticized North Carolina Republican Sen. Thom Tillis, who opted not to seek reelection. He also supported Graham, despite concerns about her candidacy.

Less of a surprise was Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff winning reelection in Georgia, defeating Rep. Mike Collins. Rep. Chris Pappas also won a Senate race in New Hampshire, defeating former Sen. John Sununu to replace retiring Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen.

In the House, defeated Republicans included Rep. Tom Kean of New Jersey, who missed four months of votes in Washington this year as he underwent treatment for depression — a diagnosis he did not disclose until his return. Democrats who won included Jamie Ager over Jennifer Capps Balkcom in North Carolina and Lindsay James over Joe Mitchell in Iowa.

Bracing for a tough night, Republicans had spent the campaign’s final stretch pumping tens of millions of dollars into states and districts that Trump won handily two years ago, as Trump campaigned in heavily red areas. But even Republicans’ money advantage didn’t stem the Democratic tide.

“I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!” Trump wrote on his social media site.

The Electorate Is Frustrated And Unhappy

Voters were sour heading into Tuesday, with the midterm electorate deeply unhappy with the country’s direction and pessimistic about the future, according to The AP Voter Poll.

Most said they feel frustrated, with about three-quarters saying they feel “angry” or “dissatisfied” with the country’s current trajectory. Dissatisfaction was particularly high in blue states, but even in red states, a majority of voters were at least “dissatisfied.”

The economy was key to Trump’s White House comeback two years ago. But the poll found that three-quarters of voters say the economy is “not so good” or “poor.” About 8 in 10 say inflation has caused a “severe” or “moderate” financial hardship for their households.

Government corruption was also a big issue with voters. Roughly half cited it and the cost of living as “crucial” to their vote for Congress — higher than immigration enforcement policies, the war in Iran and artificial intelligence data centers. About 6 in 10 voters said Trump prioritizes his own personal interests more than the country’s interests.

Despite their relative advantage on issues, the Democratic Party is not much more popular with voters than the Republicans. Just under half of voters have a “somewhat” or “strongly” favorable view of the Democratic Party, while about 4 in 10 view Republicans positively.

Republicans tried to buck historical midterm precedent with an aggressive redistricting effort aimed at creating a more favorable congressional map. But in Florida and Texas, where Republicans hoped to pick up as many as nine seats, the plan looked to be falling short, with Democrats picking up targeted districts.

GOP Could Still Notch Some Key Senate Wins

Outstanding Senate battlegrounds include Alaska, where the Trump administration filed a lawsuit to block certification of Senate results if Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan loses the race, citing the presence of a second candidate named Dan Sullivan on the ballot.

Republicans also hoped to pick up Michigan, where Mike Rogers faces progressive Abdul El-Sayed — one of a crop of left-wing candidates who prevailed in Democratic primaries. El-Sayed’s former primary opponent, Haley Stevens, upended the race by endorsing Rogers, renewing focus on tensions over Israel and the party’s direction.

Beyond Washington, 36 states elected governors. Democrats Josh Shapiro in Pennsylvania, JB Pritzker in Illinois, Wes Moore in Maryland, Maura Healey in Massachusetts and Kathy Hochul in New York all won reelection. In a stunning upset in Texas, Gina Hinojosa defeated Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, who was seeking a fourth term.

In Ohio, Republican Vivek Ramaswamy lost to Democrat Amy Acton after his campaign faced backlash for an ad featuring Acton’s estranged mother, who lost custody of Acton decades ago after her husband, Acton’s stepfather, was indicted for raping Acton as a child.

Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms of Georgia will be the first Black female governor of any state. In neighboring Florida, Byron Donalds became the nation’s first Black Republican to be elected governor.

House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, in line to make history as the nation’s first Black speaker of the House if his party sweeps to power, has outlined a 100-day agenda focused on lowering the cost of living and aggressively overseeing the Trump administration.

The especially strong showing for Democrats could boost the party’s large crop of potential presidential candidates. It may also complicate the paths of Vice President JD Vance and other Republicans who may have been looking to turn their loyalty to Trump into momentum.

Associated Press journalists Joey Cappelletti, Lisa Mascaro, Linley Sanders, Aaron Kessler and Ali Swenson in Washington; Cody Jackson in Palm Beach Gardens, Fla.; and Allen Breed in Raleigh, N.C., contributed.

name: Policy
title: Democrats capture full control of Congress, NBC News projects, fueled by victories in deeply ...
authors: Sahil Kapur, Scott Wong, Peter Nicholas
description:
President Donald Trump told voters to pretend he was on the ballot in this year’s midterm elections.
With full control of the Senate, Democrats are positioned to block nominees Trump puts forward.
As the minority party, Democrats lacked the power to issue subpoenas and schedule oversight hearings.
The political future of Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., is unknown.
He would need a majority of the Senate GOP caucus in a closed-ballot election to carry on as minority leader.
text:
President Donald Trump told voters to pretend he was on the ballot in this year’s midterm elections.

They did. And they resoundingly rejected both his policies and his Republican Party.

Democrats have captured full control of Congress, NBC News projects, with voters delivering a forceful repudiation of Trump’s agenda, coupled with a clear-cut message that Congress has not done enough to provide checks on his administration and needs to do more to address affordability and corruption.

Follow live updates on the midterm elections

Democrats’ victory in the Senate comes after a swift and decisive win in the House, where Democrats are set to have what could be their largest majority in nearly two decades.

Democrats flipped seven Republican-held seats in Michigan, Maine, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, North Carolina, South Carolina and Texas. Some of those states Democrats had long dreamed of turning blue, and others were barely even on their radar a year ago as possibilities.

In a number of those states, Trump handpicked the nominees, sometimes over the objections of members of his own party who were concerned that they would be weak in the general election.

An early warning sign that it would be a tough night for Republicans came when South Carolina — a state even many Democrats thought was out of reach — fell early. Democrats made incursions deep into the heart of MAGA country, with gains far beyond what they were able to achieve in the 2018 midterm elections during Trump’s first term.

Forty-three percent of midterm voters surveyed in the NBC News Exit Poll said one of the reasons they voted the way they did was to express opposition to Trump, whose job approval rating is lower than that of any president on Election Day in nearly two decades.

Seventy-one percent of voters — including 41% of Republicans — also said there is not enough congressional oversight of Trump. Corruption, affordability, immigration and the Iran war were all key issues, as well.

The results were so bleak that Trump quickly ran away from them Tuesday evening. Trump said on social media that, in fact, he was not on the ballot, and that’s why Republicans lost: “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!”

The Democratic Party’s takeover will reverberate widely. With Democratic majorities in both chambers, the Trump administration will now have to contend with checks and investigations it avoided with a compliant Congress in Republican hands. The election results could influence the makeup of the Supreme Court, the arc of the 2028 presidential race and the fate of Trump’s legislative plans in the back half of his term.

But it also sets up an epic showdown with Trump that will test the constitutional power-sharing arrangement that has weathered war and civil strife over the past two centuries — but survived intact. With their newly minted majority, Democratic lawmakers will acquire an arsenal of oversight powers they’ll use to investigate a Trump administration they contend has escaped accountability.

Trump, in turn, has built a presidency rooted in a vision of unrivaled executive power. Neither side seems in a mood to compromise, meaning the next two years could bring legislative and executive branch clashes unlike anything since the Watergate era.

“What we’re going to do is lower costs, end all this rampant corruption and end the chaos. Plain and simple,” Chuck Schumer of New York, the Senate’s Democratic leader, said before the election in response to a question from NBC News about his priorities if his party won.

Democrats’ sweeping victory looked inconceivable when the midterm campaign season kicked off. The party prevailed despite an unfavorable map in which the major battlegrounds ran through red states that Trump won in all three of his presidential bids. Not since 2006 has the minority party flipped control of both chambers on a single night. Then-President George W. Bush, facing a voter backlash over the Iraq War, memorably lamented that the outcome was “a thumping.”

Trump sought to mobilize his core voters and preserve the GOP’s narrow majority in the House and the Senate by putting himself front and center. He kept up a packed campaign schedule in the final month of the campaign, but he and his party were dogged by his low job approval ratings, along with pronounced voter frustration with the economy.

Trump sought to blame his predecessor, Joe Biden, for rising prices, but voters didn’t seem to buy the argument. Gas prices spiked after Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu launched the Iran war in late February, and Americans disliked Trump’s handling of the conflict, creating another drag on Republican candidacies.

The election results are apt to make history, with House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., on the cusp of becoming the country’s first Black House speaker. Democrats are expected to hold their internal leadership elections the week of Nov. 16, when Jeffries will become his party’s nominee for speaker. Then, on Jan. 3, he must win 218 votes — a simple majority of all House members — to formally win the speaker’s gavel and become second in the line of presidential succession.

Schumer, who previously served four years as Senate majority leader, is expected to return to the top job once again after he exceeded expectations and led his party back from exile.

Democrats had been favored to win the House all season; they needed to flip a net of just three GOP-held seats to do so, and historically, the president’s party loses dozens of seats on average during midterm elections.

But as the campaign unfolded, Democrats grew more bullish about winning the Senate, as well. One reason was the minority vote. Latino voters helped propel Trump’s political comeback in 2024, but they turned away from him this cycle, citing high prices and his immigration crackdown. An NBC News poll released Sunday showed that Democrats enjoyed a 27-point lead among Latino voters, a marked contrast from the election in 2024, when Trump lost by only 7 points in the demographic.

The outcome could also leave an imprint on the Supreme Court. Before the election, multiple Senate Democrats cast doubt on whether they would confirm any Trump nominee to a vacancy on the Supreme Court if one were to arise in his final two years.

With full control of the Senate, Democrats are positioned to block nominees Trump puts forward.

“Well, given the history of Trump nominees, I think it is slim to none that we would support a nominee from this administration,” Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., a member of the Judiciary Committee, told NBC News in an interview before the elections. “Because we’ve seen this movie, we know how it ends, which is a politician in robes who is following Trump’s orders on most major questions.”

Looking ahead, the election results could recast the fight for the Republican presidential nomination in 2028. The presumed GOP front-runner is Vice President JD Vance. But if the outcome amounts to a rejection of Trump and his brand of politics, Vance may find that he has no glide path to the nomination.

As the minority party, Democrats lacked the power to issue subpoenas and schedule oversight hearings. That all changes come January, when the new Congress convenes. Democratic lawmakers are already signaling that they will look to rein in the spending and war-making powers Trump has wielded with little pushback from a compliant Republican-led Congress.

House Democrats have vowed to carry out aggressive oversight of Trump’s family, business dealings and administration, including the ICE and Homeland Security immigration crackdown and Trump’s pet renovation projects at the White House and other Washington-area landmarks.

At the tip of the spear of the investigations are Reps. Robert Garcia of California, the top Democrat on the Oversight Committee, and Jamie Raskin of Maryland, the top Democrat on the Judiciary Committee. Garcia has outlined his investigation strategy, focusing on what he calls “Trump family corruption,” including how Trump’s fortune has grown by billions of dollars since his 2024 campaign, as well as Jeffrey Epstein’s crimes and Trump’s immigration crackdown.

Judiciary Committee Democrats said they also have a long list of investigative targets that includes pardons for “wealthy criminals and MAGA loyalists,” and foreign governments’ “buying influence” through gifts and payments to the Trump family’s crypto empire.

Jeffries has said that Democrats aren’t focused on impeaching Trump but that they also haven’t ruled it out. Trump was impeached twice during his first term but acquitted both times by the Senate.

“The cost of living is way too high, and Donald Trump — along with his Republican sycophantic members of Congress — have actually decided not to do anything about it because so many of them are so focused on enriching themselves, their family members, their friends and their donors. There is a cost to corruption,” Jeffries told reporters before the election.

“These are all things that are going to need to be thoroughly investigated as part of our pledge to hold the crooks accountable, beginning on day one,” he said.

Given the election results, Republicans may be motivated to usher in pieces of their legislative agenda during the lame-duck session before they officially relinquish control of the House on Jan. 3. They could include another party-line “reconciliation” bill to advance Trump’s spending and tax priorities, along with a debt ceiling increase before a 2027 deadline.

The political future of Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., is unknown. He would need a majority of the Senate GOP caucus in a closed-ballot election to carry on as minority leader. But he has had an up-and-down relationship with Trump, who has vented frustration with him for failing to eliminate the filibuster to pass the SAVE America Act, which would overhaul the country’s election laws.

Another mystery is the fate of Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., who has run the House for the past three years. He could stay on as minority leader, but in the face of the defeat across the board, some rank-and-file Republicans are likely to demand new leadership.

name: Policy
title: Criminal Justice, Civil Liberties, and the New Congress - Cato Institute
description:
Criminal law and civil liberties are likely to be at the top of the legislative agenda once they take office in January.
Federal agents should not be able to access a person’s historical location data without a judicial warrant.
Demilitarizing law enforcement: Congress can immediately end funding for National Guard and Customs and Border Protection deployments for law enforcement within the interior of the country.
The federal government routinely uses state and local law enforcement to carry out law enforcement and immigration operations, but this creates a liability loophole.
The federal criminal legal system—and state systems subsidized by federal grants—are sprawling, intrusive, and unaccountable.
text:
Democrats won control of both houses of Congress in last night’s midterm elections. Criminal law and civil liberties are likely to be at the top of the legislative agenda once they take office in January. Here are issues they should prioritize—some in response to abuses committed by the Trump Administration, others as efforts to extend an olive branch to the executive branch and their Republican colleagues.

Flock surveillance reform: To begin with common ground, Congress should move swiftly to act on the public’s bipartisan and intense demand for thorough regulation of surveillance using automated license plate readers (ALPRs). Federal agents should not be able to access a person’s historical location data without a judicial warrant. Data transfer across agencies and to third parties should be strictly limited. Auditable documentation should record who accesses data and for what purposes. The law should require human beings to approve any actions that affect personal liberty—this role cannot be delegated to devices and AI systems. While Congress cannot directly dictate state laws on ALPRs, it should use its control over federal law enforcement grants to impose its own requirements on surveillance transparency, security, accountability, and privacy.

Demilitarizing law enforcement: Congress can immediately end funding for National Guard and Customs and Border Protection deployments for law enforcement within the interior of the country. It should ban the use of ethnic profiling in immigration enforcement. Neither of these measures is likely to attract Republican support, but restrictions on the transfer of surplus military equipment to law enforcement agencies might, especially if the GOP still recalls the Clinton Administration’s use of armored vehicles, explosives, and SWAT gear at Waco and in the Elian Gonzalez case.

Overcriminalization and federalism: Returning to the possibility of consensus, the Trump Administration is reclassifying marijuana out of Schedule I. Many Republicans believe marijuana is a federalism issue best left to the states. Congress could act swiftly to remove federal criminal prohibitions on marijuana and finally give cannabis-related businesses equal opportunities to access banking and credit cards, an effort that has stalled for years.

Civil forfeiture reform is another area where bipartisanship remains strong. Most Americans would be aghast to learn that Alaska is attempting to keep an octogenarian veteran’s $95,000 plane because one of his passengers carried a couple of cases of beer on board in violation of a dry-village law. Friends of federalism might be surprised to learn that after Nevada enacted state laws prohibiting law enforcement from retaining forfeited money and property, officers simply sent cases to federal prosecutors and received kickbacks. Congress can directly put an end to such “equitable sharing” and require criminal convictions for forfeiture cases brought directly by the federal government. It can use grant conditions to push states to end abusive civil forfeiture, too.

Should the Democrats be willing to change some of their own past positions, they could also revisit the scope of federal gun control. There is no justification for a lifetime ban on anyone convicted of any felony ever possessing a firearm or ammo again. Congress can limit the law to violent felonies. While this would advance the Second Amendment in ways Democrats may not otherwise endorse, it would also significantly reduce federal overcriminalization, together with burdens on the criminal legal system as a whole.

Remedies for abuse: Democrats won last night in part on Americans’ outrage over law enforcement abuses committed by the Trump Administration, from deadly shootings by immigration agents to all-out attacks on dissidents, including spying by military-grade drones. Yet many victims of government abuse stand no chance of receiving relief from the courts due to a slew of judge-invented immunity doctrines and other procedural barriers. Congress should start by codifying the Supreme Court’s Bivens decision (which the Court itself may otherwise abolish soon), guaranteeing that people whose rights are violated by federal agents can bring suit and receive damages. The broader the law doing so, the likelier it is to win bipartisan support: while Republicans are unlikely to back a measure targeting only, say, immigration operations, much of the public can sympathize with people like Curtrina Martin, whose house was ransacked by federal agents who went to the wrong address. The notion that where there’s a right, there’s a remedy is a better framing for reform than one reaching only to the most high-profile abuses of the moment.

Congress should also specify that officers serving on joint federal-state task forces are subject to suit for rights violations. The federal government routinely uses state and local law enforcement to carry out law enforcement and immigration operations, but this creates a liability loophole. In the recent case Mohamud v. Weyker, for example, a Minnesota police officer working on a joint human-trafficking task force concocted a non-existent criminal conspiracy and had innocent people jailed. But when one of the victims sought relief, the courts held that the officer could not be sued as a state officer because she was working on a federal task force—nor as a federal officer because she was employed by a state agency. Congress should close this gap.

Finally, Congress should think big and end noxious immunity doctrines. Qualified immunity shields state law enforcement from liability for violating people’s rights unless there is a previous case with extremely similar facts arising within the same jurisdiction. Absolute prosecutorial immunity insulates prosecutors from liability, even when they lie and hide evidence in death-penalty cases. Judicial immunity has made it hard to hold judges accountable, even for egregious behavior such as personally leading a search party through a party’s home during a hearing. Each of these doctrines can be abolished today through congressional action—and the possibility of government abuses arising from different corners should inspire bipartisan support for doing so.

The federal criminal legal system—and state systems subsidized by federal grants—are sprawling, intrusive, and unaccountable. The new Congress can do much to ensure it actually protects and serves Americans.

text:
Print, fold, and keep this ’zine on hand so you know how and where to report an ICE sighting. You can submit photos and video, and search for ICE license plate information, anytime at ICEout.org. The Washington Immigration Solidarity Network announced staff layoffs in October, and its Deportation Defense Hotline is only monitored Monday–Friday, 7 a.m. to 2 p.m.

ICE Is in Your Neighborhood: Now What?

FILM IT

Use your phone to record everything. If you are in public, or on your own property, you have a right to film. Note the time, location, the number of agents, what they’re wearing, their equipment and/or weapons, and license plate numbers.

OFFER TO HELP

If ICE is detaining someone, ask the person(s) being detained for their name, and if they have an emergency contact you can reach out to.

ASK QUESTIONS

Telling the agents, “I’m just observing, I will not interfere,” can de-escalate the situation. Ask the officers what agency they’re with, why they’re detaining the person, and where they’re taking them.

GATHER WITNESSES

Exchange contact information with anyone else at the scene. They may have more videos, prior contact with the detainee, or know how to contact their friends or family.

KNOW YOUR AGENCIES

Avoid spreading misinformation. Was it really ICE? Virtually all sectors of federal law enforcement have participated in ICE raids, but it’s important to confirm that what you witnessed was, in fact, an ICE arrest or raid. By state law, Seattle police cannot collaborate with ICE.

If your rights have been violated, file a complaint with the Washington State Office of the Attorney General at atg.wa.gov. For immigration help, contact the Northwest Immigrant Rights Project at NWIRP.org or Legal Immigration Services of Olympia at lisowa.org.

ICE ACTIVITY SURGED THIS SUMMER

According to the Deportation Data Project, ICE arrested about 1,400 people in Washington across June and July (up from about 230 in February). While witnesses and bystanders have been invaluable in documenting ICE’s tactics and potential rights violations, it isn’t for everyone. People have been injured and killed when interacting with ICE agents. Recording and reporting ICE activity is just one way to help.

title: How ICE Quietly Escaped the Midterms Heat - Newsweek
description:
For much of Trump’s second term, immigration enforcement was one of the defining features of his presidency.
Immigration may not have been the issue voters most wanted politicians to address, but it still weighed heavily on their decisions.
Asked how important immigration enforcement policies were to their congressional vote, 36 percent called them crucial, and another 36 percent said they were a major factor.
Fifty-five percent of Latino voters also said they viewed their congressional vote as a vote against Trump in the same study.
Unpopular, But Not Necessarily Electorally Decisive The midterms leave ICE facing widespread public disapproval but little evidence that immigration enforcement was the decisive issue for most voters.
text:
President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown faced widespread public opposition at the ballot box, but that anger did not translate into immigration becoming the defining issue of the election.

More than half of voters said the administration’s enforcement actions had gone too far, and six in 10 disapproved of ICE’s performance. Yet just 14 percent named immigration as the country’s most important issue, far behind the economy and concerns about democracy, according to exit polls. The economy came first, at 39 percent, followed by the state of democracy at 32 percent. Healthcare, foreign policy, and crime ranked further behind.

The exit poll found 57 percent believed the administration’s immigration enforcement had gone too far, while 20 percent said it had not gone far enough and 22 percent considered it about right. Sixty percent disapproved of the way ICE was handling its job, compared with 40 percent who approved.

Read More on News

The results leave ICE facing a new Democratic-controlled Congress, and questions about whether public anger will translate into political consequences.

"The change in power in Congress gives Democrats the ability to conduct oversight on immigration enforcement. It seems likely that Democrats will focus hearings and investigations on ICE's activities and tactics, and on the management of DHS overall," Julia Gelatt, associate director of the U.S. immigration policy program at the Migration Policy Institute, told Newsweek.

For much of Trump’s second term, immigration enforcement was one of the defining features of his presidency. Footage of masked federal agents carrying out raids, arrests and deportations became a regular part of the national conversation. The deaths of people during immigration enforcement operations, protests against ICE and a growing backlash over the administration’s mass deportation plans put the agency under intense scrutiny.

Views on enforcement also tracked closely with voting behavior. Among those who said the administration had gone too far, 89 percent backed Democratic candidates. Among voters who wanted tougher enforcement, 91 percent voted Republican.

Immigration may not have been the issue voters most wanted politicians to address, but it still weighed heavily on their decisions. Asked how important immigration enforcement policies were to their congressional vote, 36 percent called them crucial, and another 36 percent said they were a major factor.

Immigration enforcement mattered to many voters, but it was not the issue that dominated the wider electorate.

The Issues That Crowded Out Immigration

At least nine people have been killed in shootings involving immigration agents during Trump’s second term, as of November 3, 2026, according to The Trace. Its investigation identified 32 incidents in which agents shot at people, leaving a further 15 injured, and warned that the figures are likely an undercount because shootings are not always publicly reported.

The election was dominated by the economy and concerns about democracy. Nearly four in 10 voters named the economy as the country’s most important issue, compared with nearly a third who chose democracy. Three-quarters said the economy was in poor or not very good condition.

"It seems like voters were primarily focused on cost-of-living issues in their votes in this election. Immigration was surely an issue for some voters, particularly those who live in immigrant families or communities, or in places heavily affected by immigration enforcement. But it did not seem to be the top issue driving most voters' decisions," Gelatt said.

Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress, flipping at least seven Senate seats and more than two dozen House districts in a major rebuke to Trump and the Republicans.

Immigration enforcement also divided voters along party lines. Among those who said it was crucial to their vote, 58 percent backed the Republican congressional candidate and 41 percent the Democrat. Among those who said it was a minor factor or not a factor, Democrats led by a wide margin.

Despite widespread disapproval of ICE, Republicans retained a narrow advantage on immigration overall. Asked which party was better able to handle the issue, 44 percent chose the Republicans and 41 percent the Democrats, while 15 percent said neither. The figures suggest that opposition to the administration’s enforcement tactics did not necessarily translate into greater confidence in Democrats on immigration.

Immigration was also competing with other concerns that mattered to even more voters. Some 73 percent said immigration enforcement was a crucial or major factor in their congressional vote, compared with 89 percent who said the same of the cost of living and 90 percent for government corruption.

A Warning From Latino Voters

The results among Latino voters offer another measure of the political risks facing Republicans as the administration continues its immigration crackdown.

Republicans had made gains with Hispanic voters in the 2024 presidential election, securing 46 percent of the vote share, helping Trump build a broader coalition.

The Associated Press Voter Poll, a survey of about 80,000 voters, found that roughly six in 10 Hispanic voters backed Democratic candidates in their local House races. Around a third supported Republicans, compared with roughly four in 10 who voted for Trump two years ago.

The shift was particularly significant in Texas, where Democrats won the governor’s race and a Senate seat, ending decades of Republican dominance in statewide elections.

Economic concerns also shaped Latino voters’ choices.

Seventy percent of Hispanic registered voters believed the administration’s policies had been harmful to Hispanic people, according to a study by the nonpartisan think tank Pew Research Center. Fifty-five percent of Latino voters also said they viewed their congressional vote as a vote against Trump in the same study.

"Polling of Latino voters before the election suggested that affordability was a bigger issue for most Latino voters than immigration, but that immigration was also an issue of high concern. So I think it's fair to say that immigration policies played a role, but it's not clear that immigration is the main driver of Latino voters' decision making," Gelatt said.

The results suggest Republicans cannot take their recent gains among Hispanic voters for granted, particularly as the administration continues to pursue its enforcement agenda.

New Congress Means New Scrutiny

The more immediate consequence for ICE may come from the change in control of Congress.

Democrats will take control of the House and Senate in January, giving them greater power to investigate the administration, hold hearings, and scrutinize agencies including ICE and Customs and Border Protection, two arms that fall under the umbrella of the Department of Homeland Security.

Congress cannot directly control ICE’s day-to-day operations, and the president retains broad authority over immigration enforcement. But lawmakers can use oversight and the budget process to demand information, investigate agency practices, and pressure the administration to impose additional guardrails.

"Democrats also have a better chance for meaningfully shaping the budgets available to ICE and other immigration agencies, but President Trump's veto power will mean that any legislation, including funding bills, will have to be bipartisan to become law. It remains to be seen to what extent Republicans will break with the Trump administration on immigration and immigration enforcement issues," Gelatt said.

The election could also have consequences at the state level. In Texas, Democrat Gina Hinojosa’s major upset victory over Republican Greg Abbott ends more than three decades of GOP control of the governor’s office. Abbott had been a prominent ally of the administration’s hard-line crackdown and deployed state resources to support enforcement efforts.

Three other Republican-held governorships flipped to Democrats, although the incoming governors have taken differing positions on cooperation with federal immigration authorities.

Unpopular, But Not Necessarily Electorally Decisive

The midterms leave ICE facing widespread public disapproval but little evidence that immigration enforcement was the decisive issue for most voters. The agency may have avoided becoming the defining issue of the election, but Democratic control of Congress could now turn that opposition into sustained investigations and scrutiny.

Update, 11/04/26, 11:59 a.m. ET: this article was updated with comment from Gelatt.

title: As blue wave sweeps country, Illinois Democrats want to unwind Trump policies 'as quickly ...
description:
Voters across America — and Illinois — sent a loud and clear message to President Donald Trump on Election Night as Democrats flipped seats across the country in a referendum on the president’s aggressive immigration policies, the war in Iran and the economy.

text:
Voters across America — and Illinois — sent a loud and clear message to President Donald Trump on Election Night as Democrats flipped seats across the country in a referendum on the president’s aggressive immigration policies, the war in Iran and the economy.

A strong blue wave means Democrats will provide a check on Trump’s final two years in office and will enact an aggressive legislative agenda to roll back some of the Trump administration’s most unpopular policies. Democrats were able to capitalize on messages about affordability and gas prices, while Republicans sought to paint their Democratic opponents as socialists who would focus on a far-left agenda instead of the economy or a plethora of other issues.

In Illinois, Democratic members of Congress are hopeful they can begin to pass legislation to unwind Trump policies. To U.S. Rep. Delia Ramirez, the plan is to “do every damn thing we can to protect them [constituents] as quickly as possible.”

“I think Democrats need to be able to demonstrate that we’re going to do everything in our power to be able to pass the kind of legislation that’s going to make their lives better,” Ramirez said on Election Day.

“Strategically, what I’d like to see is us win the House and Senate, pass everything we possibly can that really brings relief from both chambers,” she added. “Leave it to Donald Trump to decide if he wants to be able to take his party in the next election, and then let’s make sure that a Democrat wins the White House, so that in fact, when we are there in 2029, we are immediately getting these things signed into law because we’ve already passed it before.”

Ramirez, one of the state delegation’s most progressive members, said she has her own wish list, including immigration reform, a plan to abolish the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, raising the minimum wage and advancing care through Medicare for All. She also wants to see Democrats take on economic issues like housing and affordability.

Democratic majorities mean votes will be forced that will require Republicans to take difficult stances and force Trump to either sign or veto legislation. There’s also a sense that Republicans will begin realistic conversations about what a post-Trump world will look like — and that Democrats should take advantage of that discussion.

Democrats are also expected to use the House Oversight Committee to conduct investigations and hearings into the Trump administration, with some in Illinois wanting a focus on White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

Sen. Tammy Duckworth, who will become the state’s senior senator when Sen. Dick Durbin retires in January, has been a vocal critic of Hegseth, with fiery back-and-forth exchanges going viral during his confirmation hearings and other congressional hearings.

Duckworth says she voted to impeach Trump three times and would do it again, but she’s more concerned about unwinding damage from cuts stemming from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, including saving the state’s nine safety net hospitals and 93 nursing homes from closing. It’s on the heavy-handed list she wants to focus on should Democrats win big.

“And I want to make sure that we restore SNAP benefits, and I want to stop the war in Iran so that we stop sacrificing our brave men and women in uniform to Trump’s personal attempts to distract the American people,” Duckworth said. “And yeah, if it’s appropriate, then we’ll do the investigations for impeachment. But it’s more than just Trump. It’s his Cabinet. It is the people around him, and just their failure to serve the American people as they were charged to do when they were confirmed.”

As for whether Trump might enact further retribution on blue states after Tuesday’s losses, Duckworth said Illinois has seen plenty, but Democrats aren’t backing down.

“The more he tries to bully us, the more we’re going to stand up to him,” Duckworth said. “Because that’s what you do to bullies. You stand up to them and they shrink away.”
